cards.core: Assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity, and every transaction keeps both sides equal.
cards.detail: Assets are what the business owns, liabilities are what it owes outsiders, and owner's equity is the owner's claim (assets minus liabilities). The equation is the base of double entry accounting and of the balance sheet. Expanded, equity = capital + revenue minus expenses minus drawings, which shows how income and withdrawals change equity. If the equation does not balance, there is an error.
cards.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity
cards.example: Hodges and Sons balance sheet: assets $769,001 = liabilities $17,020 + owner's equity $751,981.
cards.say_it: Every transaction we record changes at least two items, but the equation always stays in balance, which is our first check that the books are right.
cards.mistakes: Thinking a transaction can change only one side; it changes both sides equally or two items on the same side in opposite directions.

cards.core: Owners usually forget equity, receivables, payables, depreciation and tax accounts, so suggest them.
cards.detail: When a judge gives a partial list, a strong answer points out gaps. Common missing accounts: Owner's Capital and Drawings (or Retained Earnings), Accounts Receivable for billed customers, Accounts Payable for unpaid bills, Accumulated Depreciation and Depreciation Expense for buildings and equipment, Interest Expense on loans, Insurance, Utilities, and Payroll Taxes Payable. Asking the owner follow up questions shows professionalism.
cards.example: Edgewood Equestrian listed a mortgage and a line of credit but no Interest Expense, and buildings but no Accumulated Depreciation; both should be added.
cards.say_it: Since you have a mortgage, I added Interest Expense, and since your barn and stables wear out, I added Depreciation Expense and Accumulated Depreciation.

cards.core: Record a cost as an asset if it gives benefit beyond this period, and as an expense if it is used up now.
cards.detail: Long-lived, costly items such as equipment, vehicles and buildings are capitalized (recorded as assets) and depreciated over their useful lives. Small items used up quickly, like cleaning supplies or small tools, are expensed. Supplies on hand at period end are an asset; the used part is an expense. Getting this wrong misstates both the balance sheet and net income, and it is one of the most common errors judges plant in role plays.
cards.example: Monaco Company recorded $1,200 of office equipment as office supplies; the correction is debit Office Equipment $1,200, credit Office Supplies $1,200, and then depreciation is recorded on it.
cards.say_it: Because the equipment will be used for three years, it belongs on the balance sheet as an asset and is expensed gradually through depreciation.
cards.mistakes: Expensing a refrigerator or treadmill, or capitalizing pitchforks and cleaning supplies.

cards.core: Build the chart from the business facts: list what it owns, owes, earns and spends, then group, classify and number each account.
cards.detail: Steps: (1) read the scenario for every asset, debt, revenue stream and cost, (2) classify each, (3) add standard accounts the owner may have missed (Owner's Capital, Drawings, Accounts Receivable, Accounts Payable, Accumulated Depreciation, payroll taxes payable), (4) number them with gaps so new accounts fit later, and (5) keep it short; add accounts only as needed. Use sub accounts for separate revenue streams so the owner can see which one earns the most.
cards.example: Gator Guides: Tour Income with sub accounts for small airboat, large airboat and pontoon tours; Gift Shop Income for snacks, apparel and souvenirs; Notes Payable $4,000 for the pontoons; no Land account because the land is leased.
cards.say_it: I added separate revenue sub accounts for each tour type, so every month you can see exactly which tour is making you the most money.
cards.mistakes: Adding a Land account when the land is leased, or forgetting equity entirely.

cards.core: A business transaction is any event that changes the business's financial position and can be measured in money.
cards.detail: Transactions change at least two accounts and are recorded at cost (the money measurement and cost concepts). Events that cannot be measured in money, such as hiring an employee or signing a deal that has not started, are not recorded until money changes or is owed. The business entity concept means only the business's transactions are recorded, not the owner's personal ones, which is why owner investments and withdrawals get their own accounts.
cards.example: Paying $23,500 of wages is a transaction; interviewing a new barista is not, until wages are earned.
cards.say_it: We record this event because it changed what the business owns or owes in dollars, and every transaction touches at least two accounts so the equation stays in balance.
cards.mistakes: Recording the owner's personal purchases in the business books, which breaks the business entity concept.

cards.core: Buying an asset on credit raises assets and liabilities by the same amount and does not change equity.
cards.detail: When equipment is bought on account or with a loan, the asset account and Accounts Payable or Notes Payable both increase. Owner's equity is not affected by the purchase itself; it changes later through the revenue the asset helps earn and the depreciation expense recorded on it. If the asset is bought for cash instead, it is an asset exchange: Cash down, Equipment up, liabilities unchanged.
cards.formula: Assets up = Liabilities up
cards.example: Timber Valley Landscaping buys $50,000 of equipment on credit: Equipment +$50,000, Accounts Payable +$50,000. With $50,000 more sales and $10,000 depreciation a year, net income and equity rise $40,000 a year.
cards.say_it: If you paid cash instead of using credit, assets would stay the same in total because cash goes down as equipment goes up, and you would have no new liability.
cards.mistakes: Saying the equipment purchase reduces net income; only the yearly depreciation does.

cards.core: A cash transaction is paid immediately; a credit (on account) transaction is paid later and creates a receivable or payable.
cards.detail: The difference decides which account is used. A cash sale debits Cash; a credit sale debits Accounts Receivable. A cash purchase credits Cash; a credit purchase credits Accounts Payable. Credit terms such as n/30 (full amount due in 30 days) or 2/10, n/30 (2% discount if paid in 10 days) tell you when the cash will move. Under accrual accounting both are recorded when they happen, not when cash moves.
cards.example: Gator Guides bills corporate tour groups (credit sale: Accounts Receivable) but walk up customers pay at the dock (cash sale: Cash); it buys supplies on n/30 terms (Accounts Payable).
cards.say_it: Because the customer will pay in 30 days, this is a credit sale, so I debit Accounts Receivable and still record the revenue today.

cards.core: A chart of accounts is a numbered list of every account a business uses, grouped by type.
cards.detail: It is one of the first things set up in an accounting system and is used every time a transaction is recorded. Accounts are usually grouped and numbered in financial statement order: 100s assets, 200s liabilities, 300s equity, 400s revenue, 500s and up expenses. The numbers let software sort accounts into the ledger, trial balance and statements. Building it requires understanding the business: what it sells, what it owns, what it owes and how it is organized (an environmental scan).
cards.formula: 100s Assets, 200s Liabilities, 300s Equity, 400s Revenue, 500s Expenses
cards.example: New gym: 110 Cash, 120 Accounts Receivable, 150 Equipment, 210 Accounts Payable, 310 Owner's Capital, 410 Membership Revenue, 510 Salaries Expense.
cards.say_it: I organized your chart of accounts by number so the 100s are what you own, the 200s what you owe, and so on, which lets the software build your statements automatically.
cards.mistakes: Listing accounts randomly or mixing balance sheet and income statement accounts.

cards.core: Assets, liabilities and equity go on the balance sheet; revenue and expenses go on the income statement.
cards.detail: Assets are things owned with future benefit (cash, receivables, equipment, horses, land). Liabilities are obligations (accounts payable, mortgage, line of credit). Equity is the owner's interest (capital, retained earnings), shown on the balance sheet and the statement of owner's equity. Revenue is earned from selling goods or services; expenses are the costs of earning it. Owner's withdrawals reduce equity but are not expenses. Correct classification decides which statement an amount lands on and whether it affects net income.
cards.example: New gym: Equipment, Cash and Accounts Receivable are assets; Accounts Payable is a liability; Owner's Capital is equity (all balance sheet); Salaries Expense is on the income statement. Edgewood Equestrian: boarding income is revenue, hay is an expense, the mortgage is a liability.
cards.say_it: Your trainers' salaries go on the income statement as an expense, but the treadmills are an asset on the balance sheet because they'll serve you for years.
cards.mistakes: Treating owner's withdrawals as an expense, or forgetting to include any equity account.

cards.core: Owner's equity grows with capital and revenue and shrinks with expenses and drawings.
cards.detail: The expanded equation breaks equity into its parts so you can see how income statement activity reaches the balance sheet. Revenue increases equity, expenses decrease it, and their difference (net income) flows into capital at closing. Owner investments increase capital directly; withdrawals (drawings) reduce it directly and are never expenses.
cards.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Capital + Revenue minus Expenses minus Drawings
cards.example: Best Coffee: equity rises $100,000 + $50,000 of revenue and falls $23,500 of wage expense, for $126,500; assets $162,500 = liabilities $36,000 + equity $126,500.
cards.say_it: Revenue and expenses are really just temporary pieces of owner's equity, which is why net income ends up increasing your capital at year end.
cards.mistakes: Treating drawings as an expense; drawings reduce equity but do not affect net income.

cards.core: Every account is an asset, liability, owner's equity, revenue or expense account.
cards.detail: Assets are resources owned that give future benefit (Cash, Accounts Receivable, Supplies, Equipment, Land). Liabilities are debts owed (Accounts Payable, Notes Payable, Mortgage, Unearned Revenue). Equity is the owner's claim (Capital, Drawings, Retained Earnings). Revenue is income from selling goods or services (Sales, Service Revenue, Rent Income). Expenses are costs used up to earn revenue (Wages, Rent, Utilities, Depreciation). Assets, liabilities and equity go on the balance sheet; revenue and expenses go on the income statement.
cards.example: Edgewood Equestrian: boarding and lesson income are revenue; hay, grain and wages are expenses; horses, stables and land are assets; the mortgage and line of credit are liabilities; the owner listed no equity account.
cards.say_it: Horses are assets here because the ranch will use them for years to earn boarding and lesson revenue, while hay is an expense because it is used up quickly.
cards.mistakes: Classifying a long-lived item as an expense or a monthly bill as an asset.

cards.core: Most transactions are one of four types: a sale, a purchase, a cash receipt or a cash payment.
cards.detail: A sale earns revenue (on account it creates Accounts Receivable; for cash it increases Cash). A purchase acquires goods or services (on account it creates Accounts Payable). A cash receipt brings money in (cash sale, customer paying an invoice, owner investment). A cash payment sends money out (paying an expense, paying a vendor, owner withdrawal). Naming the type first makes the journal entry and the effect on the accounting equation easy to work out, and each type maps to a special journal.
cards.example: Best Coffee: $100,000 beans sold on account (sale), $36,000 beans bought on account (purchase), $50,000 cash from a customer for 5,000 bags (receipt, a cash sale), $23,500 wages paid (payment).
cards.say_it: The first transaction is a credit sale, so revenue is earned now even though the cash comes later, which is why we record Accounts Receivable instead of Cash.
cards.mistakes: Calling a sale on account a receipt; no cash has been received yet.

cards.core: For each transaction, name the accounts, decide if each is an asset, liability or equity, and show the increase or decrease on each side.
cards.detail: Steps: (1) identify the two or more accounts affected, (2) classify each, (3) decide up or down, (4) write the change in a table under Assets, Liabilities and Equity, (5) check that both sides changed by the same net amount, and (6) total the columns at the end. Revenue and expense changes go in the equity column. A mathematical depiction (a running table) is what judges want to see when asked to show the impact.
cards.formula: Change in Assets = Change in Liabilities + Change in Equity
cards.example: Best Coffee: A/R +100,000 | Equity +100,000; Inventory +36,000 | A/P +36,000; Cash +50,000 | Equity +50,000; Cash minus 23,500 | Equity minus 23,500. Totals: assets 162,500 = liabilities 36,000 + equity 126,500.
cards.say_it: Let me show you each transaction on the equation in a table so you can see that after every single one, the left side still equals the right side.
cards.mistakes: Putting revenue in the assets column instead of showing its effect on equity.

cards.core: A source document is the paper or electronic proof that a transaction happened and is the starting point for every entry.
cards.detail: Source documents give the date, amount, parties and purpose of a transaction, which is why they are step one of the accounting cycle and the evidence auditors check. Common ones: sales invoice (sale on account), sales receipt or cash register tape (cash sale), vendor invoice (purchase on account), check stub or payment record (cash payment), receipt (cash received), memorandum (internal transaction such as a correction), bank statement, time cards and payroll records. Keeping them organized supports the books, the tax return and any audit.
cards.example: Photos YourWay used the bank statement, deposit slips, the check register and the returned NSF notice as the source documents for its bank reconciliation.
cards.say_it: Before I record anything I want the source document, because it proves the amount and the date and it is what an auditor or the IRS will ask to see.
cards.mistakes: Recording an entry from memory or a phone call with no document to support it.

cards.term: Where insurance fits in the accounts
cards.core: Insurance paid in advance is Prepaid Insurance (an asset); the part used up each month becomes Insurance Expense.
cards.detail: Insurance is usually paid for several months at once, so the payment buys a future benefit and is recorded as the current asset Prepaid Insurance. Each month an adjusting entry moves the expired part to Insurance Expense on the income statement. Businesses that rent assets or host customers often need liability insurance; employers need workers' compensation; property owners need property coverage. Judges like to ask what insurance a business needs and where it goes in the accounts.
cards.example: Locally Picked pays $3,000 on June 30 for six months: debit Prepaid Insurance $3,000, credit Cash $3,000; then each month July through December debit Insurance Expense $500, credit Prepaid Insurance $500.
cards.say_it: The $3,000 buys six months of protection, so it starts as an asset and we expense $500 each month as the coverage is used.
cards.mistakes: Expensing the whole six month premium in the month it is paid.

cards.core: If the accounting equation does not balance, an error has been made somewhere in the books.
cards.detail: Double entry accounting records equal debits and credits for every transaction, which keeps assets equal to liabilities plus equity. An imbalance signals a one sided entry, a math error or a posting mistake. A balanced equation does not prove everything is right (an error can affect both sides), but it is the first quick test. Errors left in the books distort net income, equity and decisions such as borrowing or expanding.
cards.example: Dance Frenzy: after correcting the intern's errors, assets $180,187 = liabilities $1,511 + owner's equity $178,676.
cards.say_it: The equation staying in balance is our proof that every transaction was recorded with both sides, which gives you confidence in the balance sheet you show the bank.
cards.mistakes: Believing that a balanced equation means there are no errors at all.

cards.core: An asset exchange swaps one asset for another, so total assets and the equation totals do not change.
cards.detail: Buying supplies or equipment for cash, or collecting a receivable, is an exchange of one asset for another. Cash goes down and another asset goes up by the same amount. Liabilities and equity are not affected and no revenue or expense is recorded. Recognizing this helps students explain why a cash purchase of supplies is not an expense yet.
cards.formula: Asset up = Asset down
cards.example: Backyard pool rental buys $300 of flotation devices and barbecue supplies: debit Supplies $300, credit Cash $300; total assets stay the same.
cards.say_it: Buying supplies for cash is just an exchange of one asset for another, so it does not lower profit until the supplies are used.
cards.mistakes: Recording a supplies purchase as an expense right away when the supplies will last a while.

cards.core: External transactions involve outside parties; internal transactions happen inside the business, such as using up supplies or depreciation.
cards.detail: External transactions (with customers, vendors, lenders, employees, the owner) usually have an outside source document. Internal transactions have no outside party and are usually recorded as adjusting entries supported by a memorandum: supplies used, insurance expired, depreciation, accrued wages. Both change the accounts and both must be recorded for the statements to be accurate.
cards.example: JKL Furniture: buying wood from a supplier is external; recording a month of depreciation on its saws is internal.
cards.say_it: Depreciation is an internal transaction, so no one sends us a bill for it, and that is exactly why we must remember to record it as an adjusting entry.

cards.core: Each type of transaction has its own document: invoice for credit sales and purchases, receipt for cash, check for payments, memo for internal items.
cards.detail: Knowing which document goes with which transaction helps you classify it correctly. Sales on account use a sales invoice; cash sales use a sales receipt or register tape; purchases use a purchase requisition, purchase order, receiving report and vendor invoice; payments use a check or electronic payment record; cash received uses a receipt or remittance slip; bank activity uses deposit slips and the bank statement; returns use debit or credit memos; internal entries use a memorandum. Electronic versions count as long as they are kept and backed up.
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop: a debit memo documents the damaged surfboards sent back, the vendor invoice shows terms 2/10, n/30, and a sales receipt documents the cash sale.
cards.say_it: A debit memo tells the vendor we are reducing what we owe them because we returned goods, so we record it as a decrease to Accounts Payable.
cards.mistakes: Mixing up debit memos (buyer reduces payable) and credit memos (seller reduces receivable).

cards.core: The accounting cycle is the set of steps repeated every period to turn transactions into financial statements.
cards.detail: The usual eight steps are: identify and analyze transactions from source documents, journalize, post to the general ledger, prepare an unadjusted trial balance, prepare a worksheet, record adjusting entries, prepare the financial statements, and record closing entries (then a post-closing trial balance). The cycle repeats every month, quarter or year so owners get timely information. Every transaction eventually ends up in the financial statements through this path.
cards.formula: Analyze, Journalize, Post, Trial balance, Worksheet, Adjust, Statements, Close (then post-closing trial balance)
cards.example: Best Coffee sells $100,000 of beans on account: the invoice is the source document, the sale is journalized (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales), posted to both ledger accounts, shows up on the trial balance, flows to the income statement, and Sales is closed to capital at year end.
cards.say_it: Every transaction you make travels the same path: source document, journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments, statements and finally closing, so the cycle is how your raw receipts become reports you can trust.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting that adjusting entries come before the statements and closing entries come after them.

cards.core: Adjusting entries are made at the end of a period so revenue and expenses land in the right period and balances are up to date.
cards.detail: They are needed because some changes happen without a new source document: time passes, assets are used up, and revenue or expenses build up. The four main kinds are prepaid (deferred) expenses used up, unearned (deferred) revenue earned, accrued expenses (owed but not yet paid or recorded) and accrued revenue (earned but not yet billed), plus estimates such as depreciation, bad debts, warranties and inventory write-downs. Each adjusting entry affects one income statement account and one balance sheet account, and never Cash. They are journalized in the general journal and posted before statements are prepared.
cards.example: Monaco Company: one year of straight-line depreciation on $1,200 of office equipment over 3 years, debit Depreciation Expense $400, credit Accumulated Depreciation $400.
cards.say_it: An adjusting entry never touches cash; it just moves amounts between the balance sheet and the income statement so this period shows the right profit.
cards.mistakes: Including Cash in an adjusting entry, or forgetting adjustments before preparing statements.

cards.core: Closing entries reset revenue, expense and drawings accounts to zero and move their balances into Owner's Capital.
cards.detail: At year end the temporary accounts are closed so the next period starts fresh. With an Income Summary account the four steps are: (1) debit each revenue, credit Income Summary; (2) debit Income Summary, credit each expense; (3) close Income Summary (the net income) to Owner's Capital; (4) debit Owner's Capital, credit Drawings. Some companies close revenue and expenses directly to Capital. Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) are never closed.
cards.formula: Revenue, Expenses, Income Summary, Drawings (REID)
cards.example: Dance Frenzy closes revenue straight to capital: debit Revenue $1,112,432, credit Owner's Capital $1,112,432.
cards.say_it: Closing entries reset the scoreboard: revenue and expenses start next year at zero, and this year's profit becomes part of your capital.
cards.mistakes: Closing Cash or another permanent account.

cards.core: To fix an error, write the wrong entry, write the correct entry, then journalize only the difference.
cards.detail: A correcting entry fixes a mistake already posted; erasing or deleting posted entries destroys the audit trail. Compare the two entries account by account: debit what was under-debited or over-credited, credit what was over-debited or under-credited. Explain the effect each error had on assets, liabilities, equity and net income. Correcting entries can be made any time an error is found, while adjusting entries are made at period end for items that were never recorded.
cards.formula: Correction = Correct entry minus Wrong entry (account by account)
cards.example: Monaco: $500 of supplies on account was recorded as Equipment $50 and Accounts Payable $50. Correction: debit Supplies $500, credit Equipment $50, credit Accounts Payable $450.
cards.say_it: Instead of erasing the mistake, I wrote one correcting entry for the difference so the records still show what happened and how it was fixed.
cards.mistakes: Reversing the whole wrong entry and rewriting it when a single difference entry would do, or deleting the original.

cards.core: Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) carry balances forward; temporary accounts (revenue, expenses, drawings) are closed each year.
cards.detail: Permanent or real accounts are balance sheet accounts whose balances continue into the next period. Temporary or nominal accounts measure activity for one period only and are reset to zero by closing entries. Income Summary is also temporary. Knowing the difference is the key to spotting closing errors and to building a post-closing trial balance.
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's intern credited Cash for $145,000 as if closing it; Cash is permanent, so the correction is debit Cash $145,000, credit Owner's Capital $145,000.
cards.say_it: Cash is a permanent account, so its balance must carry into next year; only revenue, expenses and drawings get closed.

cards.core: At period end, move the used-up part of a prepaid asset to expense: debit the expense, credit the prepaid account.
cards.detail: Prepaid rent, prepaid insurance and supplies are assets when bought. The adjusting entry records only the portion used this period. For supplies, count what is left: supplies used = beginning supplies + purchases minus supplies on hand. For time-based prepaids, divide the total by the months covered and multiply by months used.
cards.formula: Amount used = Total prepaid / months covered x months used
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop has $1,625 of supplies on the books; if a count shows $400 left, debit Supplies Expense $1,225, credit Supplies $1,225.
cards.say_it: We only expense the part of the insurance that has actually expired, and the rest stays on the balance sheet as an asset for next month.
cards.mistakes: Recording the amount left on hand as the expense instead of the amount used.

cards.core: A transposition swaps digits and a slide moves the decimal; both create differences evenly divisible by 9.
cards.detail: If the trial balance or a reconciliation is off, find the difference. If it is divisible by 9, look for a transposition (830 written as 380) or a slide (450 written as 45). If the difference is twice an item, the item was probably placed on the wrong side. If it equals an item, an entry may be missing on one side. These quick tests are a great way to impress a judge.
cards.formula: Difference / 9 = whole number suggests transposition or slide
cards.example: Monaco recorded an $830 payment as $380; difference $450, and 450 / 9 = 50, a sign of a transposition. Correction: debit Accounts Payable $450, credit Cash $450.
cards.say_it: The difference of $450 divides evenly by 9, which told me right away to look for two digits that were swapped.

cards.core: A trial balance lists every ledger account balance on one date to prove total debits equal total credits.
cards.detail: It is prepared after posting and before adjustments (unadjusted), again after adjustments (adjusted), and after closing (post-closing). It is the starting point for the worksheet and the financial statements. It will not balance if an entry had unequal debits and credits, a balance was miscalculated, or a posting went to the wrong column. A balanced trial balance is necessary but does not prove the books are correct.
cards.formula: Total debit balances = Total credit balances
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop: debit balances (assets, drawings, expenses) total $53,450 and credit balances (Accounts Payable $4,900, Owner's Capital $21,450, Service Revenue $27,100) total $53,450.
cards.say_it: The trial balance proves our debits equal our credits, and it is the base we use to adjust the accounts and build your financial statements.
cards.mistakes: Calling a balanced trial balance proof of no errors.

cards.core: Record expenses that were incurred but not yet paid or billed: debit the expense, credit a payable.
cards.detail: Common accruals are wages earned by employees after the last payday, interest owed on a loan, utilities used and taxes owed. Accruing them follows the matching principle and shows the true liability. When paid next period, debit the payable and credit Cash, so the expense is not counted twice.
cards.formula: Dr Expense, Cr Wages (or Interest, Utilities) Payable
cards.example: Employees earn $600 of wages on December 29 to 31 that will be paid January 4: debit Wages Expense $600, credit Wages Payable $600.
cards.say_it: Your employees already earned those wages this year, so the cost belongs to this year even though the paycheck goes out in January.

cards.core: Correcting entries fix mistakes; adjusting entries update correct records for the passage of time or estimates at period end.
cards.detail: An adjusting entry is required even when no one made a mistake, because some revenue and expenses build up without a transaction (depreciation, expired insurance, accrued wages). A correcting entry exists only because something was recorded wrongly. Correcting entries can involve Cash; adjusting entries never do. Judges ask this often.
cards.example: Monaco: moving the $1,200 of equipment out of Office Supplies is a correcting entry; recording $400 of depreciation on it is an adjusting entry.
cards.say_it: The correcting entry fixes the bookkeeper's mistake, while the depreciation entry would be needed even if every entry had been perfect.

cards.term: Effects of errors on the statements
cards.core: For each error, explain which accounts were wrong and whether assets, liabilities, equity or net income were over or understated.
cards.detail: Judges ask which errors would have changed income if undetected. Errors between two balance sheet accounts (Supplies vs. Equipment) do not change net income now but may change later depreciation. Errors involving an expense or revenue account change net income and equity. Recording a withdrawal as an expense understates net income but leaves total equity correct. Capitalizing vs. expensing errors affect both the balance sheet and income.
cards.example: Monaco: recording $1,200 of equipment as supplies, if expensed, understated assets and net income now, and $400 of yearly depreciation would never have been recorded.
cards.say_it: Only the errors that touched an expense account changed net income; the others just put the right amount in the wrong balance sheet account.

cards.term: Errors a trial balance cannot find
cards.core: A trial balance cannot catch errors that keep debits equal to credits, such as wrong accounts, wrong equal amounts or missing entries.
cards.detail: Errors it misses: an entry posted to the wrong account but the right column, a wrong amount entered on both sides of a balanced entry, a transaction never recorded, a transaction recorded twice, debit and credit reversed, and compensating errors that offset. That is why source documents, account reviews, bank reconciliations and schedules of receivables and payables are still needed.
cards.example: A $200 haircut supply purchase debited to Equipment instead of Supplies still leaves Sam's trial balance equal at $53,450, but both accounts are wrong.
cards.say_it: A balanced trial balance tells us the math is right, but not that every number is in the right account, so we still review the source documents.

cards.core: Income Summary is a temporary account used only during closing to collect revenue and expenses before net income goes to capital.
cards.detail: Revenues are credited into Income Summary and expenses are debited into it, so its balance equals net income (credit balance) or net loss (debit balance). That balance is then closed to Owner's Capital. Using it gives a clear audit trail of net income. A business may skip it and close revenue and expenses directly to Capital; the result is the same.
cards.example: If revenue is $27,100 and expenses are $19,990, Income Summary ends with a $7,110 credit, closed with debit Income Summary $7,110, credit Owner's Capital $7,110.
cards.say_it: The balance left in Income Summary after closing revenue and expenses is exactly this year's net income, which we then move to your capital.
cards.mistakes: Leaving Income Summary with a balance after closing.

cards.core: A post-closing trial balance lists only permanent accounts after closing to prove the ledger is balanced for the new period.
cards.detail: It is the last step of the accounting cycle. It should contain assets, contra assets, liabilities and Owner's Capital, and no revenue, expense, drawings or Income Summary accounts. If a temporary account appears, closing was incomplete. Owner's Capital should now equal beginning capital plus net income minus drawings.
cards.formula: Ending capital = Beginning capital + Net income minus Drawings
cards.example: Dance Frenzy corrected post-closing trial balance: Cash 145,000, Prepaid Insurance 4,332, Supplies 2,213, Furniture 4,321, Equipment 24,321 = 180,187 debits; Accounts Payable 1,511 + Owner's Capital 178,676 = 180,187 credits.
cards.say_it: A revenue account still showing on the post-closing trial balance was the sign that the intern never closed it.
cards.mistakes: Including revenue or expense accounts on the post-closing trial balance.

pis.text: Prepare a post-closing trial balance

examples.title: Dance Frenzy dance studio: correcting an intern's closing entries and the post-closing trial balance

cards.core: List accounts in ledger order, put each balance in its normal column, total both columns and compare.
cards.detail: Steps: (1) write the heading (business name, Trial Balance, date), (2) list accounts in chart of accounts order: assets, liabilities, capital, drawings, revenue, expenses, (3) place each balance in the debit or credit column by its normal balance, (4) total both columns and double rule them if equal, (5) if they differ, find the difference and search for errors. Contra accounts go in the column opposite their partner.
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop: Cash 19,175, Supplies 1,625, Prepaid Insurance 2,100, Prepaid Rent 2,300, Accounts Receivable 1,050, Equipment 3,100, Drawings 4,110, Rent Expense 8,470, Supplies Expense 680, Advertising 970, Insurance 5,570, Utilities 4,300 = 53,450 debits; credits 4,900 + 21,450 + 27,100 = 53,450.
cards.say_it: I placed each account in its normal balance column, assets, drawings and expenses on the debit side and liabilities, capital and revenue on the credit side, and both columns total $53,450.
cards.mistakes: Putting Drawings in the credit column because it is part of equity.

cards.core: A worksheet is an internal working paper that organizes the trial balance, adjustments and statement columns before the formal statements.
cards.detail: The ten-column worksheet has debit and credit columns for the trial balance, adjustments, adjusted trial balance, income statement and balance sheet. Each adjusted balance is extended to either the income statement columns (revenue, expenses) or the balance sheet columns (assets, liabilities, capital, drawings). The difference between the income statement columns is net income (or loss), which is added to the balance sheet credit column so those columns balance. It is never given to outsiders.
cards.formula: Net income = Income statement credit total minus Income statement debit total
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop: Cash, Accounts Receivable, Merchandise Inventory and Accounts Payable go to the balance sheet columns; Sales and Cost of Goods Sold go to the income statement columns.
cards.say_it: The worksheet is my scratch pad that lets me see the effect of every adjustment and the net income before I prepare the formal statements.
cards.mistakes: Extending Drawings to the income statement columns; it goes to the balance sheet debit column.

cards.core: The cycle uses an unadjusted trial balance, an adjusted trial balance and a post-closing trial balance.
cards.detail: The unadjusted trial balance is prepared right after posting regular entries. The adjusted trial balance includes adjusting entries and is the source for the financial statements. The post-closing trial balance is prepared after closing entries and lists only permanent accounts (assets, contra assets, liabilities and owner's capital), proving the ledger is ready for the new period.
cards.example: Sam's $53,450 trial balance is unadjusted because prepaid rent and insurance have not yet been adjusted for the months used.
cards.say_it: This is the unadjusted trial balance, so before we prepare statements we still need to record the rent and insurance you used up this year.

cards.core: Record revenue earned but not yet billed or collected: debit a receivable, credit revenue.
cards.detail: Examples include services finished but not yet invoiced, and interest earned on a note receivable. The entry follows revenue recognition: the work is done, so the revenue belongs to this period. When the customer pays, debit Cash and credit the receivable.
cards.formula: Dr Accounts (or Interest) Receivable, Cr Revenue
cards.example: A landscaper finishes a $1,500 job on December 30 but sends the invoice on January 3: debit Accounts Receivable $1,500, credit Service Revenue $1,500 on December 31.
cards.say_it: The job was finished in December, so the revenue is December revenue, even though the invoice goes out in January.

cards.core: Enter the trial balance, add adjustments, combine them into the adjusted trial balance, extend each line, then find net income.
cards.detail: Steps: (1) copy the unadjusted trial balance, (2) enter each adjusting entry in the adjustments columns with a matching letter for its debit and credit, (3) add or subtract to get each adjusted balance, (4) extend revenue and expenses to the income statement columns and all other accounts to the balance sheet columns, (5) total the income statement columns; if credits exceed debits the difference is net income, (6) add net income to the balance sheet credit column and to the income statement debit column, and confirm both pairs balance.
cards.example: If income statement credits are $4,200 (Sales) and debits are $2,500 (Cost of Goods Sold), net income is $1,700, written in the income statement debit column and the balance sheet credit column.
cards.say_it: If the balance sheet columns balance after I add net income, I know the adjustments and extensions were done correctly.
cards.mistakes: Adding net income to the balance sheet debit column instead of the credit column.

cards.core: Accounting software automates journalizing, posting, reconciling and reporting, so staff spend more time on analysis.
cards.detail: Accounting applications record transactions and post them to the general ledger automatically, produce trial balances, statements and aging reports on demand, and include modules for sales, purchases, payables, inventory, payroll and bank reconciliation. They sort accounts into statements using the chart of accounts numbering. Bank feeds, point of sale integration and receipt capture bring data in without retyping. Benefits: speed, fewer math errors, real-time information and audit trails. Data still needs review, and access must be controlled.
cards.example: EcoQuest numbers its accounts by group (100s assets, 200s liabilities, 300s equity, 400s revenue, 500s expenses) so the software sorts them into the right statements.
cards.say_it: Software does the posting and math, which frees us to analyze the results and make decisions instead of adding columns.

cards.core: Give each user a personal login with only the access their job needs, protected by multifactor authentication.
cards.detail: Role-based access means a cashier can record sales but not change prices or delete entries, and a bookkeeper can enter bills but not approve payments. Individual logins create an audit trail showing who did what. Multifactor authentication blocks most account takeovers. Access should be removed immediately when employees leave. These are internal controls that also support segregation of duties and protect against identity theft and fraud.
cards.example: Riverside Hardware sets user access levels so each person sees and changes only what their job requires, and adds multifactor authentication before connecting the bank.
cards.say_it: Separate logins and access levels mean no single person can both create and approve a payment, which protects the business and the employees.

cards.core: Dashboards, data analytics and compliance technology turn accounting data into faster decisions and better control.
cards.detail: Business intelligence dashboards show key numbers (sales, margins, cash, ratios) in real time. Analytics tools run trend and regression forecasts, scenario analysis and fraud detection on full data sets rather than samples. Automation and artificial intelligence match transactions, flag unusual entries and read invoices. RegTech automates compliance tasks such as anti-money-laundering monitoring, sanctions screening and audit trails. Technology changes accounting jobs toward analysis and advising, but needs strong data controls.
cards.example: Harborview Community Bank uses risk dashboards for the board and automated AML monitoring; Peak Performance Gym uses a trend model and a BI dashboard to forecast for its bank.
cards.say_it: A dashboard gives the board one view of all our key numbers and risks, so they can act in days instead of waiting for a quarterly report.

cards.core: Cloud software runs online for a subscription with anywhere access; desktop software is installed locally and bought or licensed.
cards.detail: Cloud advantages: access from any location and device, several users at once, automatic updates and backups, bank feeds and app integrations, and lower upfront cost. Disadvantages: needs reliable internet, monthly fees never end, data sits with a provider and conversion takes time. Desktop advantages: works offline, one-time or periodic license, data stays on your computer. Disadvantages: one location, manual backups and updates, harder to share. Compare total yearly cost, security, ease of training and growth needs.
cards.example: Riverside Hardware: desktop $1,200 + $3,600 + ($6,000 / 3) = $6,800 a year vs. cloud $450 x 12 = $5,400, saving $1,400 a year plus remote access for both stores.
cards.say_it: The cloud system saves $1,400 a year and lets both stores work in the same books, and the staff training is simpler because the screens are the same everywhere.

cards.core: Keep 3 copies of important data, on 2 types of media, with 1 copy off site.
cards.detail: Accounting data can be lost to hardware failure, theft, ransomware or a fire. The 3-2-1 rule protects it: the original plus two backups, stored on two different kinds of storage (for example a cloud service and an external drive), with at least one copy in another location. Cloud accounting providers back up automatically, but a business should still export its data regularly in case the provider fails or the account is locked.
cards.example: Riverside Hardware follows the 3-2-1 rule and exports its full ledger every month, which answers the judge's question about what happens if the cloud company goes out of business.
cards.say_it: Even with a cloud system, we export a full copy of our books every month, so our records survive even if the provider does not.

cards.core: Bank feeds, point of sale links, receipt apps and e-invoices bring transactions into the books automatically.
cards.detail: Bank and credit card feeds import every transaction daily for matching and reconciliation. Point of sale (POS) integration posts each day's sales by product and payment type. Receipt capture apps turn photos into expense entries with the image attached. Vendors can send electronic invoices straight into accounts payable. Automation cuts data entry and errors, but accounts must be mapped correctly during setup and imported data still needs review.
cards.example: Riverside Hardware connects its two stores' cash registers and its bank to the cloud system so sales and payments flow in without retyping.
cards.say_it: Automating data entry gives us daily numbers instead of monthly ones, but someone still reviews the imports every week.

cards.core: Auditors must be independent in fact and in appearance, free of financial or family ties that could bias them.
cards.detail: Independence in fact means the auditor's judgment is actually unbiased; independence in appearance means a reasonable outsider would see it that way. Threats include owning stock in the client, loans, close family members in key client roles, providing certain consulting services, or long relationships. When a threat appears, the firm removes the person from the engagement, applies safeguards and documents the action, or declines the engagement. Without independence, the audit opinion has no value to users.
cards.example: A member of Keystone's audit team is the CFO's nephew. The firm removes him from the engagement right away and documents the action in the audit file.
cards.say_it: Even if he would be completely fair, the bank has to see us as independent, so he comes off the engagement today.

cards.term: Cutoff testing and search for unrecorded liabilities
cards.core: Cutoff tests check that transactions near year end are recorded in the right period; the search for unrecorded liabilities finds missing expenses.
cards.detail: Cutoff testing compares shipping and receiving documents dated just before and after year end with the dates sales and purchases were recorded. Sales shipped in January but recorded in December overstate revenue. The search for unrecorded liabilities reviews payments and invoices received after year end to find costs that belonged to the old year but were not recorded. Errors found become proposed adjusting entries.
cards.example: Keystone: an unrecorded December utility invoice found in January payments leads to a proposed adjustment: Dr Utilities Expense, Cr Accounts Payable for the December amount. Its cutoff errors suggest expanding cutoff testing.
cards.say_it: We look at January payments because a December bill paid in January is still a December expense, and it's easy to miss.

cards.core: Internal auditors are employees who test controls and improve operations; external auditors are independent CPAs who give an opinion to outsiders.
cards.detail: Internal audit works for the company, reports to management and the audit committee, reviews controls and operations year round, and helps catch errors and fraud. External audit is performed by an independent CPA firm for outside users (banks, investors, regulators), focuses on whether the financial statements are fairly presented under GAAP, and ends in a published opinion. External auditors may use some of the internal auditors' work but remain responsible for their own opinion.
cards.example: Tasty Dairy Delight: the internal auditor is an employee who tests internal controls; the external auditor is independent and gives the bank an opinion on the financial statements.
cards.say_it: Your internal auditor helps you run a tighter business; the external auditor is the independent outsider the bank trusts.
cards.mistakes: Calling the external auditor an internal user because the auditor works with company records.

Tasty Dairy Delight frozen yogurt shop: GAAP, internal vs. external users, and auditing

cards.core: Auditors send confirmations directly to customers asking them to verify the balance they owe; evidence from outsiders is the most reliable.
cards.detail: The auditor controls the sending and receiving so management cannot alter replies. Positive confirmations ask the customer to reply either way; negative ones ask for a reply only if the balance is wrong. When customers do not reply, the auditor uses alternative procedures: checking cash received after year end, invoices and shipping documents. If management refuses to let the auditor confirm, it is a scope limitation that must be reported to the audit committee and can change the opinion.
cards.example: Keystone's CFO refuses confirmations for three customers owing $480,000, 16 times materiality, saying they always pay. The auditor tries alternative procedures and reports the restriction to the audit committee.
cards.say_it: Even if your customers always pay, we need evidence from outside the company, so either we confirm the balances or we check the cash received after year end.

cards.core: Audit risk equals inherent risk times control risk times detection risk; higher risk means more testing.
cards.detail: Audit risk is the chance the auditor gives a clean opinion on statements that are materially misstated. Inherent risk is how likely an account is to be misstated before controls (complex estimates, cash). Control risk is the chance the company's controls fail to catch it. Detection risk is the chance the auditor's own tests miss it, and it is the only part the auditor controls. When inherent and control risks are high, the auditor lowers detection risk by doing more and stronger substantive testing.
cards.formula: Audit risk = Inherent risk x Control risk x Detection risk
cards.example: Illustration: acceptable audit risk 5%, inherent risk 100%, control risk 50%: detection risk = 0.05 / (1.00 x 0.50) = 10%. Keystone's cutoff errors raise risk, so the auditor expands cutoff testing.
cards.say_it: Because the cutoff errors show your controls aren't catching timing problems, we'll do more testing around year end.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: Auditors test a sample of items instead of every transaction and project the results to the whole population.
cards.detail: Testing everything would cost too much, so auditors select samples, statistically or by judgment, and test them. Large or unusual items are usually tested in full, with a sample of the rest. Errors found in the sample are projected to the population and compared with materiality. Sampling is one reason an audit gives reasonable rather than absolute assurance. Data analytics software now lets auditors scan entire populations for unusual entries.
cards.example: Illustration: an auditor tests all receivables over $50,000 and a random sample of 40 smaller ones; if the sample shows a 1% overstatement, it is projected across the remaining balance.
cards.say_it: We test a sample and the largest items, which gives strong evidence without checking every invoice, and that's why our assurance is reasonable rather than absolute.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: Auditors gather evidence through inspection, observation, confirmation, inquiry, recalculation, analytical procedures, vouching and tracing.
cards.detail: Inspection: examining documents or assets. Observation: watching a process, such as the inventory count. Confirmation: written replies directly from third parties (customers, banks). Inquiry: asking management and staff, never enough on its own. Recalculation and reperformance: redoing computations or controls. Analytical procedures: comparing ratios and trends to spot unusual changes. Vouching (from the records back to documents) tests that recorded items really happened; tracing (from documents forward to the records) tests that everything was recorded. Tests of controls check that controls work; substantive tests check the balances.
cards.example: Keystone: confirm receivables, observe the inventory count, run analytical procedures on margins, vouch large sales to shipping documents, and trace January invoices back to December to find unrecorded liabilities.
cards.say_it: We can't just take management's word; inquiry has to be backed up with documents, confirmations and our own recalculations.

pis.text: Describe auditing techniques/procedures
Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: Materiality is the size of misstatement that could change a user's decision; performance materiality is a lower amount used to plan testing.
cards.detail: Auditors set overall materiality using a benchmark, such as 5 percent of pre-tax income (or a percentage of revenue or assets). Performance materiality, often 50 to 75 percent of overall materiality, is used so that many small undetected errors do not add up to a material amount. Misstatements found are totaled and compared with these levels; immaterial ones should still be corrected or listed on the summary of uncorrected misstatements. Materiality also depends on nature: a small fraud can be material.
cards.formula: Materiality = Benchmark x Percentage (for example 5% x Pre-tax income); Performance materiality = Materiality x 75%
cards.example: Keystone: materiality 5% x 600,000 = $30,000; performance materiality 75% x 30,000 = $22,500. Misstatements found 12,000 + 3,000 = $15,000, below both, so not material, but management should still correct them.
cards.say_it: The $15,000 of errors is below our $30,000 materiality, so it won't change our opinion, but we still ask you to correct them.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements
Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: An audit moves through acceptance, planning and risk assessment, testing controls and balances, completion and the report.
cards.detail: 1. Client acceptance: check independence and integrity, sign an engagement letter that sets scope, timing and fees. 2. Planning: understand the business and its controls, set materiality, assess risks. 3. Fieldwork: test controls and perform substantive procedures (confirmations, observation, cutoff, analytics). 4. Completion: evaluate misstatements, review subsequent events, obtain a management representation letter, and communicate with the audit committee. 5. Reporting: issue the opinion. Documentation in workpapers supports every step.
cards.example: Keystone's first-year audit: confirm independence (the CFO's nephew is removed from the team), set $30,000 materiality, test cutoff and confirm receivables, propose the utility adjustment, then meet the audit committee before issuing the opinion.
cards.say_it: We're in fieldwork now; before we sign the opinion we'll summarize the misstatements and meet with your audit committee.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements
Describe auditing techniques/procedures

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: Errors found in an audit become proposed adjusting entries; any management does not record are listed on the summary of uncorrected misstatements.
cards.detail: The auditor writes the correcting entry for each misstatement found and asks management to record it, since the statements are management's responsibility. Uncorrected items are totaled on a summary and compared with materiality, alone and together. If the total uncorrected amount is material, the auditor cannot give a clean opinion. The management representation letter confirms that management believes uncorrected items are immaterial.
cards.example: Keystone: the unrecorded December utility invoice becomes Dr Utilities Expense, Cr Accounts Payable; together with other errors the total is $15,000, below $30,000 materiality, but management is still asked to book them.
cards.say_it: These adjustments are small, but recording them now makes your statements cleaner and keeps them off our list of uncorrected misstatements.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: A scope limitation is a restriction that stops the auditor from getting enough evidence, which can lead to a qualified opinion or a disclaimer.
cards.detail: Limitations can come from circumstances (records destroyed in a fire) or from management (refusing access to customers, records or staff). A management-imposed limitation is serious because it suggests something may be hidden. The auditor first tries alternative procedures, then communicates the issue to those charged with governance, usually the audit committee. If evidence still cannot be obtained, the auditor modifies the opinion or may withdraw from the engagement.
cards.example: Keystone's CFO blocks confirmations on $480,000 of receivables. The auditor documents it, tries subsequent cash receipts and shipping documents, and takes it to the audit committee.
cards.say_it: When management blocks evidence, it's a scope limitation, and we're required to take it to the audit committee before deciding on our opinion.

pis.text: Conduct audit engagements
Explain the nature of audits and assurance engagements

examples.title: Keystone Components: first-year audit, materiality and a scope limitation

cards.core: The four audit opinions are unmodified (clean), qualified, adverse and disclaimer.
cards.detail: Unmodified: the statements are fairly presented in all material respects. Qualified: fairly presented except for one material but not pervasive issue (a misstatement or a scope limitation). Adverse: the statements are materially and pervasively misstated, so they are not fairly presented. Disclaimer: the auditor could not get enough evidence to form any opinion, because a scope limitation is material and pervasive. Lenders usually require a clean opinion.
cards.example: If Keystone's auditor still cannot verify the $480,000 of receivables, the result is a qualified opinion if the issue is material but not pervasive, or a disclaimer if it is pervasive, but not a clean opinion.
cards.say_it: If we can't verify those receivables, the best we can give is a qualified opinion, and your bank will notice that.

cards.core: A budget is a written plan of expected revenue, costs and resources for a future period, used to plan and control.
cards.detail: Budgets turn goals into numbers. They help a business plan (how much to buy, produce and hire), coordinate departments (sales, purchasing, production, finance work from the same forecast), communicate targets, control spending by comparing actual results with the plan, and evaluate managers. A budget is a forecast, so it is revised as actual sales and costs come in. Small businesses often start with a simple monthly revenue and expense budget and a cash budget.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum Piping builds a first-quarter purchases budget from the sales manager's forecast; the Society for Marketers compares budget with actual each quarter for its board.
cards.say_it: A budget is our plan in dollars: it tells purchasing what to order, tells finance how much cash we need, and lets us spot problems early by comparing actual results each month.

Society for Marketers (non-profit): changing the fiscal year to the calendar year, accounting cycle, reporting timeline and annual report
Rocking Ribs restaurant: low-season staffing, fixed vs. variable costs and cost-volume-profit

cards.core: Each month compare actual results with the budget, explain big differences and take action.
cards.detail: Line up budget and actual for each revenue and expense, compute the difference in dollars and percent, and label it favorable (helps income) or unfavorable (hurts income). Focus on large or controllable differences, find the cause (volume, price, waste, timing), assign follow-up to the responsible manager and revise the forecast if conditions changed. When volume differs a lot from plan, compare with a flexible budget instead of the original static one.
cards.example: If advertising was budgeted at $1,000 and actual was $1,400, that is a $400 (40%) unfavorable variance that needs an explanation, such as an unplanned campaign.
cards.say_it: Every month I compare actual results with the budget and explain any difference over 10%, so problems are caught while they are still small.

cards.core: Budgets can be built top-down, bottom-up (participative), incrementally from last year, or zero-based from scratch.
cards.detail: Top-down: senior management sets targets and passes them down; fast but may be unrealistic. Bottom-up (participative): managers closest to the work build the estimates; more accurate and builds buy-in, but slower and may include padding. Incremental: start from last year and adjust by a percentage; simple but carries old waste forward. Zero-based: every cost must be justified from zero each period; finds waste but takes time. Rolling budgets add a new month or quarter as each one ends.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum uses bottom-up input from its sales manager for the unit forecast.
cards.say_it: I recommend a bottom-up budget, because the sales manager knows our customers best and people commit to numbers they helped create.

pis.text: Describe the nature of budgets

examples.title: Matrix Aluminum Piping: first-quarter purchases budget with 15% safety stock, plus safety stock and sales budget considerations

cards.term: Budgeting backward from a profit target
cards.core: Start with expected sales, subtract the profit target and known costs, and what remains is the most you can spend.
cards.detail: When a business has a profit goal, it can find the spending limit for a cost such as payroll: budgeted sales minus target profit minus fixed costs minus other variable costs = amount available. Then compare each staffing or spending option with that limit. This ties scheduling and purchasing decisions directly to the profit plan.
cards.formula: Available for the cost = Sales minus Target profit minus Fixed costs minus Other costs
cards.example: Rocking Ribs low season: meat $40,000 x 1.5 = $60,000 sales; target profit 10% = $6,000; $60,000 minus $6,000 minus fixed $4,300 minus meat $40,000 = $9,700 for salaries.
cards.say_it: We can spend at most $9,700 on salaries this month and still earn our 10% profit, so I would schedule three servers and one cook for $8,400.

cards.core: A capital budget plans major long-term purchases, such as equipment or a new location, and how to pay for them.
cards.detail: Capital spending is large and hard to reverse, so it is planned separately from the operating budget. Each project is evaluated with tools such as payback period, net present value (present value of future cash inflows minus cost) and return on investment, then ranked against available funds. The capital budget also decides financing: cash, loan, lease or new owner investment. Its loan and depreciation figures feed the cash budget and budgeted statements.
cards.example: Harbor Fresh's truck decision is a capital budgeting choice: buying costs $85,054 in present value versus $96,885 to lease.
cards.say_it: Because the truck is a five-year commitment, I evaluated it with present value instead of comparing this year's cash only.

examples.title: Harbor Fresh Seafood: borrow or lease a truck, time value of money and the balance sheet

cards.core: A cash budget shows beginning cash plus expected receipts minus expected payments, and any borrowing needed to keep a minimum balance.
cards.detail: The cash budget turns the sales, purchases and expense budgets into the timing of cash. Receipts come from cash sales and collections of receivables (based on collection patterns); disbursements include payments for purchases, wages, rent, taxes and loan payments. Noncash expenses such as depreciation are left out. If ending cash falls below the minimum, the budget shows the borrowing needed; a surplus can repay loans or be invested.
cards.formula: Ending cash = Beginning cash + Cash receipts minus Cash disbursements (+ Borrowing minus Repayments)
cards.example: Illustration: beginning cash $20,000 + collections $60,000 minus payments $75,000 = $5,000. With a $10,000 minimum balance, the company plans to borrow $5,000.
cards.say_it: The cash budget shows we'll dip below our minimum in March, so we should arrange the line of credit now rather than scramble later.
cards.mistakes: Including depreciation as a cash payment.

cards.core: Incremental budgets adjust last period's numbers; zero-based budgets require every item to be justified from zero.
cards.detail: Incremental budgeting is quick and stable but carries forward past waste. Zero-based budgeting makes managers justify each cost every period, which can uncover savings but takes much more time. Other systems: activity-based budgeting (budget the activities that drive costs), rolling or continuous budgets (always plan a set number of months ahead, adding a new month as one ends), and flexible budgets (adjusted to actual volume). The best choice depends on the company's size, stability and goals.
cards.example: Illustration: a department with last year's $50,000 supply budget gets $51,500 under a 3% incremental approach; under zero-based budgeting it must justify each supply purchase from $0.
cards.say_it: For a company that has never reviewed its overhead, a zero-based budget once every few years can uncover costs that incremental budgeting keeps rolling forward.

cards.core: The sales budget comes first; it drives the purchases or production budget, expense budgets, the cash budget and budgeted statements.
cards.detail: A master budget is a set of linked budgets. The sales budget (units x price) is the starting point because nearly every cost depends on volume. A merchandiser then prepares a purchases budget; a manufacturer prepares production, materials, labor and overhead budgets. Selling and administrative expense budgets follow. The cash budget pulls together expected receipts and payments. Finally come the budgeted income statement and balance sheet. A capital budget covers long-term asset purchases.
cards.example: At Matrix Aluminum, the sales forecast of 400,000 pipes in January sets the safety stock and the 417,500-unit purchase quantity, which in turn sets the cash needed to pay suppliers.
cards.say_it: Everything starts with the sales budget, so if that forecast is wrong, every other budget is wrong too, which is why we build it with the sales team.

cards.core: A preliminary budget is a first draft built from detailed estimates, then reviewed, tested and revised before approval.
cards.detail: Steps: gather detail from each department (unit sales, prices, lead times, staffing); compute the schedules; check the math and links between schedules; compare with past results and goals; discuss differences with department managers; revise and submit for approval. After approval, compare budget with actual results regularly (monthly or quarterly) and update the forecast when conditions change. Clear documentation of each assumption makes later variance analysis easier.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum's first-quarter purchases budget is preliminary: it will be revised as actual January sales and supplier lead times come in. Society for Marketers' board gets quarterly budget versus actual reports.
cards.say_it: This is a preliminary budget based on today's forecast; we'll compare it with actual sales each month and adjust purchases before they become a problem.

pis.text: Process preliminary budget detail
Explain types of budgeting systems (e.g., top-down, bottom-up, incremental, etc.)

examples.title: Matrix Aluminum Piping: first-quarter purchases budget with 15% safety stock, plus safety stock and sales budget considerations
Society for Marketers (non-profit): changing the fiscal year to the calendar year, accounting cycle, reporting timeline and annual report

cards.core: Budgeted purchases equal budgeted sales plus desired ending inventory minus beginning inventory.
cards.detail: The purchases budget tells a merchandiser how many units to buy each period. Desired ending inventory is usually a percentage of next period's sales (the safety stock). Each period's ending inventory becomes the next period's beginning inventory, so the months chain together, and the last month needs the following month's sales forecast. Multiply units by the expected unit cost to get dollar purchases for the cash budget.
cards.formula: Units to purchase = Budgeted sales + Desired ending inventory minus Beginning inventory
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum: January ending inventory 15% x 450,000 = 67,500; units needed 400,000 + 67,500 = 467,500; minus 50,000 beginning = 417,500. February 532,500 minus 67,500 = 465,000. March 625,000 minus 82,500 = 542,500. Quarter 1,425,000 units x $15 = $21,375,000.
cards.say_it: We only buy the gap: what we'll sell plus the cushion we want at month end, minus what's already on the shelf.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting that each month's beginning inventory equals the prior month's ending inventory.

cards.core: Safety stock is extra inventory kept to protect against supplier delays or unexpected demand.
cards.detail: The right level balances the cost of running out (lost sales, rush shipping, unhappy customers) against the cost of carrying extra inventory (cash tied up, storage, insurance, obsolescence). Factors: past demand swings and stock-outs, supplier reliability and ratings, lead time, supplier location and weather, material shortages, and how critical the product is to customers. Safety stock is often set as a percentage of next period's sales.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum keeps 15% of next month's sales because its supplier is in northeast Canada, where winter storms can delay shipments; each extra pipe ties up about $15 of cash.
cards.say_it: Our first quarter needs more safety stock than summer because winter storms near the supplier make deliveries less reliable.

cards.core: The sales budget forecasts units and dollars to be sold and is the starting point for every other budget.
cards.detail: Sales budget = forecast units x expected price, by month and product. Drivers to consider: historical sales trends and seasonality, the overall economy, the health of the customers' industries, competitors, planned price changes and raw material prices, marketing plans, and known customer contracts. Input from the sales team makes it a bottom-up estimate. Because it drives purchases, production and cash, it should be updated as actual results arrive.
cards.formula: Budgeted sales = Forecast units x Expected selling price
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum's forecast reflects the March peak of 550,000 units, the health of aerospace, automobile and railroad customers, and aluminum price forecasts.
cards.say_it: Our sales forecast reflects the March peak and the outlook for our aerospace and auto customers, and we'll update it monthly as orders come in.

cards.core: Top-down budgets are set by senior management; bottom-up budgets are built from estimates by the people closest to the work.
cards.detail: Top-down (imposed) budgeting is fast and aligned with company goals, but managers may see targets as unrealistic and feel little ownership. Bottom-up (participative) budgeting uses frontline knowledge, such as the sales manager's unit forecast, and builds commitment, but takes longer and can include padding (budgetary slack). Many companies combine them: leaders set overall targets and departments build the details, then the two are negotiated.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum's purchases budget starts from the sales manager's unit forecast (bottom-up), while the CFO may still set an overall company spending limit (top-down).
cards.say_it: Using the sales manager's forecast makes this a bottom-up budget, so the people who must hit the numbers helped set them.

pis.text: Explain types of budgeting systems (e.g., top-down, bottom-up, incremental, etc.)

examples.title: Matrix Aluminum Piping: first-quarter purchases budget with 15% safety stock, plus safety stock and sales budget considerations

cards.core: A flexible budget restates revenue and costs for the actual level of activity, using standard prices and costs.
cards.detail: A flexible budget keeps the budgeted selling price, standard variable cost per unit and total fixed costs, but uses the actual volume. It answers: what should revenue and costs have been for the output we actually achieved? Comparing actual results with it isolates how well prices and costs were managed. It can be prepared for several volumes before the period (for planning) or for the actual volume after (for control).
cards.formula: Flexible budget cost = Actual units x Standard variable cost per unit + Budgeted fixed costs
cards.example: Crumb & Co. at 12,000 loaves: revenue 12,000 x $6.00 = $72,000; flour $12,000; labor $18,000; variable overhead $6,000; fixed overhead $6,000; flexible budget operating income $30,000.
cards.say_it: The flexible budget shows what 12,000 loaves should have cost, so now we can fairly judge how well we controlled our costs.
