examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: Future revenue and expenses are projected with trend analysis, regression, percentage growth and scenario analysis.
cards.detail: Trend (time series) analysis uses past patterns over time. Regression fits the best straight line through past data. Percentage of sales or growth rate methods apply an expected growth rate to current figures. Scenario or sensitivity analysis tests expected, pessimistic and optimistic cases, and simulation runs many outcomes. Good forecasts separate variable costs (which grow with volume) from fixed costs (which may rise with inflation), use accurate data from the accounting system, and state their assumptions.
cards.example: Peak Performance Gym used a regression trend of members by year, then built revenue, variable costs and fixed costs from it, plus a pessimistic case.
cards.say_it: Our forecast starts from a clear trend in your membership, and we test it with a weaker scenario so the bank sees we can repay even in a bad year.

pis.text: Project future revenues and expenses

examples.title: Peak Performance Gym: forecasting next year's results with a trend model for a bank loan

cards.core: Attainable standards are tight but reachable with efficient work; ideal standards assume perfection and usually discourage workers.
cards.detail: Ideal standards allow no waste, breakdowns or downtime, so they are almost never met and can demotivate staff. Practical (attainable) standards allow for normal waste and breaks, so they motivate and make variances meaningful. Standards should be reviewed regularly and changed when methods, prices or products really change, but they should not simply be raised or lowered to match whatever happened, or the variances lose their meaning.
cards.example: Crumb & Co.'s owner asks whether to raise the labor standard to 0.108 hours per loaf because that is what happened. Better: find out why 100 extra hours were used; change the standard only if the process has truly changed.
cards.say_it: If we just reset the standards to match what happened, we'll never see the problems, so let's change a standard only when the process itself changes.

pis.text: Discuss the role of standard costing in the preparation and analysis of budgets

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: A regression trend line, y = intercept + slope x X, projects a value by plugging in a future period.
cards.detail: The slope is how much the predicted value changes per period; the intercept is the starting value. Spreadsheet functions such as TREND, FORECAST and LINEST compute them. R squared (0 to 1) shows how well the line fits past data; near 1 means a close fit, but it does not guarantee the future, since competition, capacity limits or the economy can change the trend.
cards.formula: Forecast = Intercept + Slope x Period number
cards.example: Peak Performance Gym: Members = 346 + 58 x Year. Year 6: 346 + 58 x 6 = 694 members. R squared 0.99 means a very close fit to the last five years.
cards.say_it: The trend adds about 58 members a year, which points to 694 next year, but a 0.99 fit to the past is not a promise about the future.

pis.text: Project future revenues and expenses

examples.title: Peak Performance Gym: forecasting next year's results with a trend model for a bank loan

cards.core: Units to produce equal budgeted sales plus desired ending finished goods minus beginning finished goods.
cards.detail: A manufacturer uses the production budget in place of a purchases budget for its products. It then feeds the direct materials purchases budget (materials needed for production plus desired ending materials minus beginning materials), the direct labor budget (units x standard hours x rate) and the overhead budget. The same chain logic applies: ending inventory of one period is the next period's beginning inventory.
cards.formula: Units to produce = Budgeted sales + Desired ending finished goods minus Beginning finished goods
cards.example: Illustration: a candle maker expects to sell 8,000 candles, wants 1,000 on hand at the end and has 1,500 now: 8,000 + 1,000 minus 1,500 = 7,500 candles to produce.
cards.say_it: We only need to make 7,500 candles, because 500 of the units we'll sell are already sitting in finished goods.

pis.text: Process preliminary budget detail

cards.core: Project revenue from forecast volume times price, variable costs from volume times unit cost, and fixed costs from this year adjusted for inflation.
cards.detail: Step 1: forecast volume (customers, members, units). Step 2: revenue = volume x expected price. Step 3: variable costs = volume x variable cost per unit. Step 4: fixed costs = current fixed costs adjusted for expected increases (inflation, new hires, rent changes). Step 5: operating income = revenue minus variable costs minus fixed costs. Step 6: check capacity limits and build pessimistic and optimistic cases. Present a range with assumptions to the user, such as a lender.
cards.formula: Projected operating income = (Volume x Price) minus (Volume x Variable cost) minus Fixed costs x (1 + Inflation rate)
cards.example: Peak Performance: revenue 694 x $600 = $416,400; variable 694 x $120 = $83,280; fixed $180,000 x 1.03 = $185,400; operating income $147,720. Pessimistic (625 members): revenue $375,000, variable $75,000, operating income $114,600.
cards.say_it: Even if membership comes in 10% below the trend, the gym still earns about $114,600, which shows the bank the loan can be repaid.

pis.text: Project future revenues and expenses

examples.title: Peak Performance Gym: forecasting next year's results with a trend model for a bank loan

cards.core: Present expected, pessimistic and optimistic forecasts, and cap any forecast at the business's real capacity.
cards.detail: A single number hides risk; a range builds credibility with lenders and owners. Pessimistic cases cut volume or price; optimistic cases raise them. Every forecast must also respect physical limits: a gym can only hold so many members, a factory can only run so many hours. Using only the optimistic number for a lender is misleading and may break trust. State the assumptions behind each scenario.
cards.example: Peak Performance: if the gym can hold only 650 members, maximum revenue is 650 x $600 = $390,000, so the 694-member forecast must be capped; operating income would be 390,000 minus 78,000 minus 185,400 = $126,600.
cards.say_it: I wouldn't show the bank only the optimistic case; a range with a realistic capacity cap shows we've thought about the risks.

examples.title: Peak Performance Gym: forecasting next year's results with a trend model for a bank loan

cards.core: Budgets are built by multiplying the planned number of units by the standard cost of each input per unit.
cards.detail: Standard costs make budgeting faster and consistent. Step 1: forecast units from the sales budget. Step 2: multiply by the standard quantity of each input to find materials and labor hours needed. Step 3: multiply by standard prices and rates to get budgeted costs. Step 4: add budgeted fixed costs. After the period, the same standards are used to build the flexible budget and compute variances, so planning and control use one set of numbers.
cards.formula: Budgeted cost of an input = Budgeted units x Standard quantity per unit x Standard price
cards.example: Crumb & Co. static budget for 10,000 loaves: flour 10,000 x 2 lbs x $0.50 = $10,000; labor 10,000 x 0.1 hours x $15 = $15,000; variable overhead $5,000; fixed overhead $6,000.
cards.say_it: Our budget comes straight from the standard cost card, so when we compare actual results we know exactly which standard was missed.

pis.text: Discuss the role of standard costing in the preparation and analysis of budgets
Describe the nature of flexible budgets

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: A static budget is prepared for one planned level of activity and is not adjusted when actual volume changes.
cards.detail: The master budget is a static budget: it is built on one sales forecast. It is useful for planning, but comparing it directly with actual results is misleading when volume differs, because variable costs should rise or fall with volume. A higher actual cost may simply reflect more sales, and real cost problems can hide behind extra revenue. That is why performance is evaluated with a flexible budget.
cards.example: Crumb & Co. Bakery planned 10,000 loaves (static operating income $24,000) but sold 12,000. Actual income of $23,400 looks only $600 short, yet at 12,000 loaves the bakery should have earned $30,000.
cards.say_it: Being only $600 under the static budget sounds fine, but that budget was for 10,000 loaves; at the 12,000 we actually sold, we should have made $30,000.
cards.mistakes: Judging cost control by comparing actual costs to a budget for a different volume.

pis.text: Describe the nature of flexible budgets
Discuss the role of standard costing in the preparation and analysis of budgets

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: A static budget is set for one activity level; a flexible budget is adjusted to the actual level of activity.
cards.detail: Comparing actual results at a higher volume with a static budget mixes two effects: selling more (which raises variable costs) and how well costs were controlled. A flexible budget recalculates revenue and variable costs at the actual volume while fixed costs stay the same, so performance is judged fairly. The difference between static and flexible is the sales volume variance; the difference between flexible and actual is the flexible budget variance.
cards.example: Crumb and Co. planned 10,000 loaves (static profit $24,000) but sold 12,000 and earned $23,400. Only $600 short looks fine, but the flexible budget at 12,000 loaves says it should have earned $30,000.
cards.say_it: Compared with the static budget we look only $600 short, but at the volume we actually sold we should have earned $30,000, so $6,600 of poor performance is hiding behind the extra sales.

cards.core: Expand only if accurate statements show the current business is profitable and the new location can cover its own costs.
cards.detail: Step 1: make sure the books are correct (closing and statements accurate). Step 2: check the current locations' profit, cash flow and debt. Step 3: estimate the new location's overhead (rent, utilities, insurance, administration) and operating costs (wages, supplies), its expected revenue and its break-even. Step 4: plan the funding (cash, loan, investor) and its effect on ratios. Step 5: consider market demand, management time and risk, then recommend with a timeline and checkpoints.
cards.example: Judge question at Dance Frenzy: "Should the owner open another studio location?" First fix the closing errors, then use the corrected $1,112,432 of revenue and the existing studios' costs to estimate the fourth studio's break-even.
cards.say_it: I would open the new studio only after we fix the records and confirm that its expected enrollment covers the new rent and instructor costs within the first year.

cards.core: Stay sustainable by tracking results monthly, controlling costs, keeping a cash reserve and diversifying revenue.
cards.detail: Practical measures a judge expects: keep accurate books from day one, prepare monthly statements and compare them with a budget, separate fixed and recurring costs from one-time costs, build a cash reserve of several months of fixed costs, avoid taking on debt the cash flow cannot carry, price to cover full cost and a profit, diversify revenue sources, watch key ratios such as profit margin and current ratio, and plan for taxes. This is a recurring judge question for start-ups.
cards.example: Judge question at EcoQuest: "What measures can I take to ensure my business remains financially sustainable?" Answer: monthly budget vs. actual, a reserve for server costs, recording in-app purchases properly and reinvesting part of the profit in marketing.
cards.say_it: To stay sustainable, I would set a monthly budget, keep three months of hosting and fixed costs in reserve, and only scale marketing as revenue grows.

cards.core: Define the goal, gather the numbers, compare options on cost, risk and timing, decide, then review the result.
cards.detail: A responsible financial decision follows a process: 1. Define the problem and the goal. 2. Gather accurate information (statements, budgets, quotes, rates). 3. List alternatives, including doing nothing. 4. Compare them on cost (in today's dollars), benefits, risk, liquidity and effect on ratios and covenants, plus qualitative factors like ethics, customers and employees. 5. Choose and act. 6. Monitor results and adjust. It avoids impulse decisions and decisions based on one number alone.
cards.example: Swift Route compares factoring ($8,000, no new debt) with a loan ($3,000, adds $200,000 of debt) and chooses factoring to protect its debt covenant.
cards.say_it: I compared every option on cost, risk and its effect on our loan agreements, and the cheapest option is not the responsible one here because it could put us in default.

cards.core: Finance manages a company's money: raising funds, deciding how to use and invest them, and keeping enough cash to operate.
cards.detail: Finance answers three questions: where will the money come from (owner investment, loans, investors), how should it be used (equipment, inventory, marketing, expansion), and how do we manage daily cash so bills are paid (working capital). Accounting supplies the information finance needs: accounting looks back and records what happened, finance looks ahead and plans. Together they let the owner track cash, measure profitability, plan budgets and give lenders and investors reliable information.
cards.example: EcoQuest's owner invests $5,000, earns $2,000 of in-app purchases and pays $1,000 for servers; finance decides whether to reinvest the $1,000 profit in marketing or keep a cash reserve for hosting costs.
cards.say_it: Accounting tells us what happened, and finance uses that to decide what to do next with our money, such as how much to spend on marketing and how much to keep in reserve.

cards.core: Manage the timing of cash in and out so the business can always pay its bills and keep a reserve.
cards.detail: A profitable business can still fail if cash runs out. Cash flow management means speeding up cash in (prompt invoicing, deposits, early payment discounts offered, collection follow-up), timing cash out (pay on the due date, take discounts that are worth it, negotiate terms), controlling inventory, keeping a reserve and a line of credit, and forecasting with a cash budget. Separate one-time costs from recurring ones when judging a period's cash flow.
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us: receipts $703 minus payments $510 = $193 net cash increase for the week; the $150 for display racks is a one-time cost, so future weeks should look even better.
cards.say_it: The week was cash positive at $193, and since the display racks will not repeat, our normal weekly cash flow is closer to $343.

cards.core: Debt must be repaid with interest but keeps ownership; equity brings cash with no repayment but shares ownership.
cards.detail: Debt financing includes bank loans, lines of credit, notes, bonds and leases; interest is tax deductible, but required payments add risk and can trigger covenants. Equity financing includes the owner's own investment, partners, angel investors, venture capital and selling stock (an IPO); there is no required repayment, but owners give up part of control and profit. Other sources: trade credit, factoring receivables, grants and crowdfunding. Start-ups usually rely on owner equity first because lenders want a track record.
cards.example: EcoQuest starts with $5,000 of owner equity (debit Cash, credit Owner's Capital); Harbor Fresh uses debt (a $100,000 note); Lakeshore Brewing plans to raise equity through an IPO.
cards.say_it: A loan keeps you as the only owner but adds a fixed payment; an investor adds no payment but takes a share of every future profit.

cards.term: Deciding whether to spend on growth
cards.core: Spend on advertising or growth only if current assets cover upcoming bills and the expected return beats the cost.
cards.detail: Before spending cash on advertising, equipment or expansion, check: current assets compared with current liabilities (can we still pay our bills?), the cash reserve needed for slow periods, and the expected payback: how many extra sales are needed to cover the cost, using contribution margin. Start with small, measurable campaigns and track results. If current assets are thin, improve cash first or use low-cost promotion.
cards.example: Judge question at Canine Condos: "Based on your review of our current assets, should we put money towards advertising?" A good answer checks that cash covers accounts payable, then ties the ad budget to the extra boarding days needed to pay for it.
cards.say_it: If an ad campaign costs $1,000 and each extra boarding night contributes $25, we need 40 extra nights to break even on it, so I would test a small campaign first.

cards.core: Accounting records and reports what happened; finance uses that information to plan, raise and invest money.
cards.detail: Accountants journalize transactions, prepare statements, file taxes and ensure records follow GAAP. Finance professionals budget, forecast, analyze investments, manage cash, arrange loans or investors, and manage financial risk. In a small business the owner or one bookkeeper does both; in a large company the controller leads accounting and the treasurer leads finance, both reporting to the chief financial officer (CFO).
cards.example: The controller at Northwind Outdoor measures each division's ROI; the finance team uses that to decide which projects to fund.
cards.say_it: Good accounting is the foundation for good finance, because you cannot plan the future with numbers you do not trust.

cards.core: Opportunity cost is the benefit you give up by choosing one option instead of the next best one.
cards.detail: Every use of money, space or time means not using it for something else. Opportunity costs do not appear in the accounting records, but they matter in decisions: cash kept idle gives up interest, factory space used for one product gives up rent, and capacity used for a special order may give up regular sales. Include opportunity cost as a relevant cost when comparing alternatives.
cards.example: CoreTech: if buying the component frees factory space that could be rented for $15,000 a year, buying saves $10,000 + $15,000 = $25,000 a year instead of $10,000.
cards.say_it: The $15,000 of rent we could earn is an opportunity cost of making the part ourselves, so it makes buying even more attractive.

cards.core: Base the decision on the numbers, then check non-financial factors such as quality, customers, employees and risk.
cards.detail: Quantitative factors are measurable: revenue, costs, cash flows, present value, ratios. Qualitative factors are harder to measure but can change the decision: supplier reliability, quality control, customer reaction, employee morale, brand image, legal and ethical issues, and flexibility. A strong role play answer gives the number first, then two or three qualitative risks, and says whether they change the recommendation. When the numerical advantage is small, qualitative factors matter more.
cards.example: CoreTech saves only $1 a unit by buying overseas, so supply delays, quality control and the risk to its designs could outweigh the $10,000 saving.
cards.say_it: The numbers favor buying by $10,000 a year, but with only a $1 margin, a supplier delay could wipe that out, so I would add backup supply terms to the contract.

cards.core: Finance makes investing decisions (what to buy), financing decisions (how to pay) and working capital decisions (daily cash).
cards.detail: Investing (capital budgeting) decisions choose long-term assets, such as buying a truck or opening a studio, using tools like present value. Financing decisions choose the mix of debt (loans, bonds, leases) and equity (owner investment, stock), balancing cost against risk and covenants. Working capital decisions manage cash, receivables, inventory and payables so the business can pay its bills, for example taking discounts, factoring receivables or setting safety stock. Every recommendation in a finance role play fits one of these three.
cards.example: Harbor Fresh: investing (does it need the truck?), financing (loan or lease?); Swift Route: working capital (factor receivables or borrow short term?).
cards.say_it: This is a financing decision, so I compare the cost of each option and its effect on our debt ratio, not just which one gives cash fastest.

cards.core: Future value is what money grows to when interest is earned on both the principal and past interest.
cards.detail: Simple interest is earned only on the original principal. Compound interest is earned on principal plus interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time. The more often interest compounds and the longer the money is invested, the larger the future value. This is why saving early matters so much for goals like retirement or replacing equipment.
cards.formula: FV = PV x (1 + r)^n, where r is the rate per period and n is the number of periods
cards.example: $10,000 invested at 6% for 5 years: 10,000 x 1.06^5 = 10,000 x 1.3382 = $13,382. With simple interest it would be only $13,000.
cards.say_it: Because interest compounds, starting to save for the equipment replacement now costs us far less each year than waiting.

cards.term: Present value of a single amount
cards.core: Present value is today's worth of a future amount, found by discounting at an interest rate.
cards.detail: Discounting is the reverse of compounding. The present value factor for $1 is 1 / (1 + r)^n; tables list these factors. A higher interest rate or a longer wait makes the present value smaller. Present value is used to value future cash such as an asset's salvage value, a bond's face value, or a lump sum payment in a settlement.
cards.formula: PV = Future amount x 1 / (1 + r)^n = Future amount x PV factor
cards.example: Harbor Fresh's truck should be worth $20,000 in 5 years. At 6%, PV = 20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946.
cards.say_it: The truck's $20,000 resale value is worth only about $14,946 in today's dollars, and that is the number I subtract from the cost of buying.

cards.core: An annuity is a series of equal payments; its present value is payment x the PV annuity factor.
cards.detail: An ordinary annuity pays at the end of each period, like most loan and lease payments. Instead of discounting each payment one by one, multiply the payment by the present value of an annuity factor for the rate and number of periods. This tells you how much a stream of payments is worth today, which is how lenders set payments and how a lessee measures a lease liability.
cards.formula: PV of ordinary annuity = Payment x [1 minus (1 + r)^(minus n)] / r = Payment x PV annuity factor
cards.example: Harbor Fresh lease: 5 payments of $23,000 at 6%: 23,000 x 4.2124 = $96,885, even though total cash paid is $115,000.
cards.say_it: Five lease payments of $23,000 total $115,000 in cash, but their present value is $96,885, which is also the lease liability on the balance sheet.

cards.core: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because today's dollar can earn interest.
cards.detail: Money received today can be invested to grow, and money promised later carries risk and loses buying power to inflation. So amounts at different dates cannot be compared directly: they must be moved to the same point in time. Compounding moves money forward (future value); discounting moves future amounts back to today (present value). Time value of money is the basis for loans, leases, savings, retirement planning and investment decisions.
cards.example: Harbor Fresh Seafood compares a $118,000 loan plan with a $115,000 lease plan; because the payments happen at different times, it compares present values ($85,054 net to buy vs. $96,885 to lease) instead of total cash.
cards.say_it: The lease looks cheaper in total dollars, but once we put every payment into today's dollars, buying is about $11,831 cheaper.
cards.mistakes: Adding up payments made in different years as if they were worth the same.

cards.core: A bank reconciliation adjusts both the bank balance and the book balance until they match, which proves cash.
cards.detail: Bank side: start with the bank statement balance, add deposits in transit, subtract outstanding checks, and fix bank errors. Book side: start with the checkbook or ledger balance, add interest earned and collections made by the bank, subtract service charges, NSF checks and EFT payments not yet recorded, and fix book errors. Both adjusted balances must be equal. Only book side items need journal entries. Reconcile every month.
cards.formula: Bank balance + deposits in transit minus outstanding checks = Book balance + interest minus service charges minus NSF checks
cards.example: ABC Manufacturing: bank $12,250 + $4,000 deposits in transit minus $2,000 outstanding checks = $14,250; books $14,300 minus $50 service charge = $14,250. Cash is proved.
cards.say_it: Both sides now show $14,250, which proves our cash, and I will record only the $50 service charge because that is the only item not yet in our books.
cards.mistakes: Adding outstanding checks or placing a book item on the bank side.

cards.term: Journal entries from a bank reconciliation
cards.core: After reconciling, journalize every book side item so the Cash account equals the adjusted balance.
cards.detail: Service charge: debit Bank Service Charge (or Miscellaneous) Expense, credit Cash. Interest earned: debit Cash, credit Interest Revenue. NSF check: debit Accounts Receivable (the customer still owes), credit Cash; a bank fee for the NSF may be added to what the customer owes. Bank collection of a note: debit Cash, credit Notes Receivable and Interest Revenue. Book errors are corrected for the difference.
cards.example: Photos YourWay: debit Service Charge Expense $10, credit Cash $10; debit Cash $5, credit Interest Revenue $5; debit Accounts Receivable (Linda Walker) $125, credit Cash $125. Net change to Cash: minus $130. ABC: debit Miscellaneous Expense $50, credit Cash $50.
cards.say_it: The NSF check goes back to Accounts Receivable because Linda Walker still owes us the $125; we just do not have the cash yet.
cards.mistakes: Recording an NSF check as an expense or bad debt immediately.

cards.core: Every cash payment credits Cash; the debit is an expense, an asset, a liability being paid or drawings.
cards.detail: Debits for cash payments: an expense account for costs used now (advertising, repairs), an asset for items with future benefit (inventory, equipment, prepaid insurance), Accounts Payable when paying a vendor bill, and Drawings when the owner withdraws cash. A charitable donation is debited to Charitable Contributions Expense (or Donation Expense). The cash payments journal summarizes these by column.
cards.formula: Dr Expense / Asset / A/P / Drawings, Cr Cash
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us: Advertising Expense $100, Supplies Expense $150 (display racks; could be Store Equipment), Inventory $200 (food restock), Repair and Maintenance Expense $60; total payments $510.
cards.say_it: The $200 pet food restock is recorded as inventory, not an expense, because it is still on the shelf until it is sold.
cards.mistakes: Expensing inventory purchases in a perpetual system.

cards.core: Every cash receipt debits Cash; the credit depends on why the money came in.
cards.detail: Credits for cash receipts: a revenue account for cash sales, Accounts Receivable when a customer pays an invoice, Owner's Capital for an owner investment, Notes Payable for a loan, Unearned Revenue for payment before delivery. Use separate revenue accounts for product lines so the owner can see the sales mix. In a cash receipts journal these are summarized by column.
cards.formula: Dr Cash, Cr Revenue / A/R / Capital / Unearned Revenue
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us week: food $183, toys $420, collars and leashes $75, loyalty program $25; each is debit Cash and credit Sales Revenue for that line; total receipts $703.
cards.say_it: I credited separate revenue accounts for food, toys and supplies so you can see that toys brought in about 60% of this week's cash.

cards.core: Control cash by depositing receipts daily, matching deposits to sales records, paying by approved check or transfer, and reconciling the bank monthly.
cards.detail: Cash is the asset most easily stolen. Receipts: count with two people, deposit intact each day, and match deposits to the POS Z-report or cash register tape. Payments: pay only approved, supported invoices (purchase order, receiving report and invoice agree, a three-way match), use prenumbered checks, and have the owner sign. Use a petty cash fund with receipts for small payments. Reconcile the bank statement monthly by someone who does not handle cash, and investigate differences.
cards.example: Bella Vista's deposits were short $900 a month for three months ($2,700). A daily deposit matched to the POS Z-report and a reconciliation by someone other than Dana would have caught it in the first week.
cards.say_it: If someone other than the cashier matches each day's deposit to the POS report, a $900 shortage shows up in days instead of months.

cards.core: A check is outstanding from the time it is written until the bank pays it; then it has cleared.
cards.detail: Cash clearing is the process of a check moving from the payee's bank back to the writer's bank for payment. Until it clears, the check reduces the company's books but not the bank balance. To find outstanding checks, compare the checks in the check register with the paid checks on the bank statement; any not listed are outstanding. Last month's outstanding checks that still have not cleared stay on the list.
cards.example: ABC Manufacturing wrote checks totaling $2,000 that do not appear on the bank statement, so they are subtracted from the bank balance on the reconciliation.
cards.say_it: A check is outstanding if it is in our check register but has not appeared as paid on the bank statement yet.

cards.core: Endorse each check For Deposit Only as soon as it arrives, list it on a deposit slip and deposit promptly.
cards.detail: A restrictive endorsement means the check can only be deposited into the company account, so a stolen check is useless. The deposit slip lists currency, coins and each check and becomes a source document matched to the bank statement. Depositing all receipts intact each day means every dollar received shows on the bank statement, which makes the reconciliation a strong check on cash.
cards.example: A pet store's $183 food sales and $420 toy sales for the week should be deposited and each deposit slip kept to match the bank statement.
cards.say_it: Stamping every check For Deposit Only the moment it arrives means that even if it is lost, no one else can cash it.

cards.term: Deposits in transit and outstanding checks
cards.core: Deposits in transit are added to the bank balance and outstanding checks are subtracted; they need no journal entry.
cards.detail: These are timing differences: the company has already recorded them, but the bank has not processed them yet. A deposit in transit was made late in the month and appears on next month's statement. Outstanding checks have been written and recorded but not cashed. Because the books are already correct for these items, no journal entry is made.
cards.example: Photos YourWay: bank $35,421 + $734 deposits in transit minus $4,940 outstanding checks = $31,215.
cards.say_it: Deposits in transit and outstanding checks are already in our books, the bank just has not caught up, so they do not need journal entries.
cards.mistakes: Journalizing deposits in transit or outstanding checks.

cards.core: To set up petty cash, debit Petty Cash and credit Cash for the fund amount.
cards.detail: A check is written to the custodian and cashed. Petty Cash is a current asset. This is the only time the Petty Cash account is debited unless the fund size is changed; spending from the fund is not journalized until it is replenished.
cards.formula: Dr Petty Cash, Cr Cash

cards.say_it: Setting up the fund just moves $200 from the bank into a cash box, so it is an asset exchange and no expense yet.

cards.core: Internal controls are rules inside the business; external controls come from outsiders such as the bank and auditors.
cards.detail: Internal controls include segregation of duties, prenumbered documents, locked cash drawers, approval of payments, petty cash rules and manager approval for voids. External controls include the bank statement, signature cards, positive pay services, independent audits and fidelity bonds (insurance against employee theft). Using both gives a stronger system than either alone.
cards.example: ABC Manufacturing: the monthly bank statement is an external control, and the rule that checks need approval before signing is an internal control.
cards.say_it: The bank statement is an outside record we do not control, so comparing it with our books each month is one of the best checks we have.

cards.core: Net cash for a period equals total cash receipts minus total cash payments.
cards.detail: This simple reconciliation shows whether cash grew or shrank. Compare it with the actual change in the register and bank balance to confirm nothing is missing. Then interpret it: separate one-time costs from recurring ones, compare inventory restocks with sales of that product, and look at the sales mix, because positive cash flow in one week does not guarantee profit.
cards.formula: Net cash = Cash receipts minus Cash payments
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us: $703 receipts minus $510 payments = $193 increase; the $150 display racks are one-time, so future weeks should be stronger, but no toy inventory was bought even though toys sold best.
cards.say_it: Cash grew $193 this week, and since the display racks were a one-time cost, a normal week should be even better, but we should restock toys soon.

cards.core: Petty cash is a small fund of currency kept on hand to pay small expenses without writing checks.
cards.detail: It is an imprest fund: a fixed amount set by management, held by one custodian, and used only with signed petty cash vouchers (receipts). At any time cash plus vouchers should equal the fund amount. It saves time and check fees on immaterial purchases such as postage or office snacks, while still controlling cash.
cards.formula: Cash on hand + vouchers = Fund amount
cards.example: ABC Manufacturing sets up a $200 petty cash fund for small purchases.
cards.say_it: Petty cash lets us buy a $6 roll of tape without writing a check, and the vouchers prove where every dollar went.

cards.core: Businesses charge an NSF fee and use controls such as verification, electronic payments and check limits to avoid bounced checks.
cards.detail: When a customer's check bounces, the bank charges the business a fee and the cash is gone, so many businesses pass a returned check fee to the customer to cover costs and discourage it. Protections include check verification services, accepting cards or electronic payments, requiring ID, limiting check amounts, and requiring payment in certified funds from customers who bounced a check before.
cards.example: Photos YourWay could charge Linda Walker a returned check fee on top of the $125 and ask for card payment going forward.
cards.say_it: Charging a returned check fee covers what the bank charges us, and offering card or electronic payment removes most of the risk.

cards.core: To refill petty cash, debit each expense from the vouchers, record any cash short or over, and credit Cash.
cards.detail: At month end or when the fund is low, total the vouchers by expense, count the cash, and write a check to bring the fund back to its set amount. Petty Cash itself is not debited when replenishing. If cash plus vouchers is less than the fund, debit Cash Short and Over (an expense); if more, credit it.
cards.formula: Replenishment = Fund amount minus cash on hand
cards.example: A $200 fund has $38 left and vouchers for postage $52, supplies $65 and delivery $40 ($157). Replenish $162: debit Postage $52, Supplies $65, Delivery $40 and Cash Short and Over $5; credit Cash $162.
cards.say_it: The replenishment check brings the fund back to exactly $200, and the $5 shortage is recorded so we notice if it keeps happening.
cards.mistakes: Debiting Petty Cash instead of the expenses when refilling.

cards.term: Service charges, interest and NSF checks
cards.core: Service charges and NSF checks reduce the book balance, interest increases it, and each needs a journal entry.
cards.detail: These are items the bank already processed that the company learns about only from the bank statement. A service charge is a fee the bank took out. Interest earned was added by the bank. An NSF (non-sufficient funds) check is a customer check that bounced, so the deposit was reversed and the customer still owes the money. If a book item is placed on the wrong side, the reconciliation will be off by twice that amount.
cards.example: Photos YourWay: books $31,345 + $5 interest minus $10 service charge minus $125 NSF = $31,215. The intern had added the $10 and subtracted the $5, giving $31,225, off by $10 = 2 x $5.
cards.say_it: The bank already took the $10 fee, so it lowers our book balance, and the $5 interest was already added, so it raises it.
cards.mistakes: Adding the service charge to the book balance.

cards.core: A signature card is filed with the bank and lists the people allowed to sign checks for the business account.
cards.detail: The bank compares signatures on checks with the card, so only authorized people can spend the company's money. Limiting signers, requiring two signatures above a set amount, and updating the card when an employee leaves are strong external controls. A signature stamp that others can use defeats this control.
cards.example: At Bella Vista Bistro an employee used the owner's signature stamp to send checks the owner never saw; the owner should sign checks personally or require dual approval.
cards.say_it: I recommend removing anyone who has left the company from the signature card today and requiring two signatures on checks over a set amount.

cards.core: Even a few cents of difference must be found, because it may hide a larger error or theft.
cards.detail: A small net difference can be the result of two larger errors that partly offset each other, or the first sign of someone skimming. Monthly reconciliation catches errors and fraud early and confirms the true cash available. Judges commonly ask whether being off a few cents matters; the professional answer is yes, investigate it.
cards.example: A reconciliation off by $0.27 could be a $500 missing deposit offset by a $499.73 recording error; only investigating reveals it.
cards.say_it: Yes, even a few cents matters, because a tiny difference can be two big mistakes canceling each other out, and it is our only proof that cash is right.

cards.core: Cost allocation assigns shared (indirect) costs to products, services or departments using an allocation base.
cards.detail: Allocation is needed to find the full cost of a product for inventory, pricing and reporting. Choose a base that reflects what causes the cost: direct labor hours, machine hours, square feet, number of setups, sales dollars or hours open. Good allocation gives realistic product costs; poor allocation distorts them. Remember that allocating a cost never changes the total cost the company pays, so allocated common costs are ignored in keep or drop decisions.
cards.example: Rocking Ribs spreads $4,300 of fixed overhead over 336 open hours: about $12.80 per hour open.
cards.say_it: Allocation helps us see the full cost of each hour we are open, but it does not make the rent go away if we close an hour early.

cards.term: Direct materials, direct labor and overhead
cards.core: Product cost has three parts: direct materials, direct labor and manufacturing overhead.
cards.detail: Direct materials can be traced to a unit (aluminum, paper, wax). Direct labor is the wages of workers who make the product. Manufacturing overhead is every other factory cost that cannot be traced to one unit: indirect materials, supervisors, factory rent, utilities, depreciation, setups and inspections. Prime cost = direct materials + direct labor. Conversion cost = direct labor + overhead. Selling and administrative costs are period costs, not product costs.
cards.formula: Prime cost = DM + DL; Conversion cost = DL + MOH; Product cost = DM + DL + MOH
cards.example: Precision Machining: direct materials $25 + direct labor $20 = $45 prime cost per valve; overhead is then assigned on top ($10 plantwide, giving $55).
cards.say_it: Materials and labor are easy to trace, so the real question is how we assign the overhead, and that's where our current system goes wrong.

cards.core: Absorption costing puts all manufacturing costs, including fixed overhead, into the cost of each unit; GAAP and the IRS require it.
cards.detail: Under absorption (full) costing, unit product cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead + fixed manufacturing overhead per unit. Fixed overhead per unit = total fixed overhead divided by units produced, so it falls as production rises. Fixed overhead attached to unsold units stays in ending inventory on the balance sheet until they are sold. The income statement shows sales, cost of goods sold and gross profit, then selling and administrative expenses. It is required for external financial statements and the tax return.
cards.formula: Absorption unit cost = DM + DL + Variable MOH + (Fixed MOH / Units produced)
cards.example: Lumen Candle: fixed overhead $40,000 / 10,000 candles = $4; unit cost $6 + $4 = $10. COGS 8,000 x $10 = $80,000; ending inventory 2,000 x $10 = $20,000; operating income $22,000.
cards.say_it: For the bank and our tax return we must use absorption costing, which puts $4 of fixed overhead into every candle we make.

cards.core: Use job costing for custom work, process costing for identical mass products, standards for control, and ABC when overhead is driven by complexity.
cards.detail: Match the system to how the business operates. Job costing: unique orders where each customer's job differs (custom notebooks, repairs, consulting). Process costing: continuous production of identical units (candles, piping, beverages). Standard costing: layered on either system to set budgets and measure variances. Activity-based costing: when overhead is large and products differ in setups, inspections or customer service. Weigh the extra accuracy against the cost of collecting the data, and explain the choice in plain language.
cards.example: Precision Machining makes both high-volume Standard Valves and complex Custom Valves with big setup and inspection costs, so ABC is worth the effort there; Crumb & Co. Bakery benefits most from standard costs to control flour and labor.
cards.say_it: Because your overhead comes from setups and inspections rather than labor hours, activity-based costing will give you much more accurate prices.

cards.core: Cost accounting measures and reports what it costs to make each product or deliver each service so managers can decide.
cards.detail: Cost accounting gathers material, labor and overhead costs, assigns them to products, jobs or services, and reports unit costs and profitability. Managers use it to set prices, choose which products to offer, decide how much to produce, control spending and value inventory. The main systems are job order costing, process costing, standard costing and activity-based costing, and they can be combined (for example a job order system using standard costs).
cards.example: Rocking Ribs' owner uses total and unit costs to decide staffing and food orders; Precision Machining learns from ABC that each Custom Valve really costs $111, not $55.
cards.say_it: Good cost data tells you which products actually make money, which is the starting point for every pricing decision.

cards.core: A job cost sheet adds the direct materials, direct labor and applied overhead of one job to find its total and unit cost.
cards.detail: Maintaining the sheet: Step 1, record direct materials from each materials requisition. Step 2, record direct labor from time tickets (hours x rate). Step 3, apply overhead using the predetermined rate times the job's actual activity (such as labor or machine hours). Step 4, total the three columns when the job is done, and divide by units for unit cost. The open sheets support the Work in Process balance; completed sheets support Finished Goods and then Cost of Goods Sold. Compare the job's cost with its price to measure job profit.
cards.formula: Job cost = Direct materials + Direct labor + (Predetermined overhead rate x Actual activity); Unit cost = Job cost / Units
cards.example: Illustration: Job 42 of 100 notebooks uses $1,200 of materials and 30 labor hours at $18 ($540); overhead at $20 per labor hour = $600. Job cost $2,340; unit cost $23.40. If sold for $3,000, job profit is $660.
cards.say_it: This job cost sheet shows the order really cost $2,340, so we can see the exact profit on it and price the next order better.
cards.mistakes: Applying actual overhead (unknown until year end) instead of the predetermined rate.

cards.core: Job order costing tracks costs separately for each unique job or batch, using a job cost sheet.
cards.detail: Job costing fits businesses whose products or services differ by customer: custom furniture, print runs, construction, repairs, law and accounting work. Each job gets a job cost sheet that collects direct materials (from requisitions), direct labor (from time tickets) and applied overhead (predetermined rate x actual activity). The total divided by units in the job gives the unit cost. Costs flow from Work in Process to Finished Goods to Cost of Goods Sold.
cards.example: Jotter's foil-imprint notebook order can be tracked on one job cost sheet; a custom aerospace valve order at Precision Machining is another job.
cards.say_it: Because every order you take is different, a job cost sheet for each one will show exactly what that order cost and whether the price covered it.

cards.core: JIT buys materials and makes products only as they are needed, cutting inventory and carrying costs but raising stockout risk.
cards.detail: JIT relies on reliable, nearby suppliers delivering small, frequent shipments. For managerial accounting it means smaller inventory balances, fewer inventory transactions and variances, and simpler costing such as backflush or value stream costing. Savings come from lower carrying costs and cash freed from inventory. Risks are stockouts, supplier delays and lost sales; they are reduced with strong supplier contracts and a small safety stock of key materials.
cards.example: EverGreen Packaging: JIT cuts average inventory 60% from $2,000,000 to $800,000, carrying cost falls from $400,000 to $160,000 ($240,000 saved), or $190,000 net of a $50,000 supplier charge, and frees $1,200,000 of cash.
cards.say_it: JIT saves us $190,000 a year and frees $1.2 million of cash, but we need reliable suppliers and a small safety stock to avoid missing a big order.
cards.formula: Carrying cost = Average inventory x Carrying cost rate

cards.term: Predetermined overhead rate and applied overhead
cards.core: Overhead is applied to products using a rate set before the year: estimated overhead divided by an estimated activity base.
cards.detail: Actual overhead is not known until the year ends, so companies estimate it and pick an allocation base such as direct labor hours, machine hours or open hours. Applied overhead = rate x actual activity used. At year end, if actual overhead is higher than applied, overhead was underapplied (costs were too low) and Cost of Goods Sold is usually increased; if lower, it was overapplied and Cost of Goods Sold is decreased. A single rate for the whole factory is a plantwide rate.
cards.formula: Predetermined overhead rate = Estimated overhead / Estimated activity base; Applied overhead = Rate x Actual activity
cards.example: Precision Machining: 100,000 / 10,000 direct labor hours = $10 per DLH. Rocking Ribs: $4,300 of fixed overhead over 336 open hours is about $12.80 per hour. Illustration: actual overhead $205,000, applied $198,000, so $7,000 underapplied is added to Cost of Goods Sold.
cards.say_it: We charge overhead at $10 per labor hour as we go, then true it up at year end against what we actually spent.

cards.core: Product costs attach to inventory and are expensed when goods are sold; period costs are expensed in the period they occur.
cards.detail: Product costs (direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead) sit in inventory as an asset until the item is sold, then become cost of goods sold. Period costs, such as selling, advertising and administrative expenses, are expensed right away under both costing methods. The only cost that changes category between methods is fixed manufacturing overhead: a product cost under absorption costing, a period cost under variable costing. This timing difference explains why the two methods give different income.
cards.example: Lumen: the $18,000 of selling and administrative cost is a period cost under both methods. The $40,000 of fixed factory overhead is a product cost under absorption ($8,000 of it waits in ending inventory) and a period cost under variable costing.
cards.say_it: Office and selling costs are expensed right away either way; the only difference is whether factory fixed overhead waits in inventory.

cards.core: An activity rate is the cost pool total divided by the total quantity of its cost driver.
cards.detail: A cost driver is the factor that causes an activity's cost: number of setups, inspections, orders, deliveries or machine hours. Each pool's activity rate is its total cost divided by total driver quantity. A product's overhead equals the sum of (activity rate x driver quantity it uses) across all pools, and its unit overhead is that total divided by units produced. Checking that all pools add back to total overhead proves the allocation.
cards.formula: Activity rate = Cost pool / Total driver quantity; Product overhead = Sum of (Rate x Driver use)
cards.say_it: Each setup costs us $600, and the Custom Valve uses 70 of the 100 setups, so most of that overhead belongs to it.

cards.core: ABC assigns overhead to products based on how much of each activity, such as setups or inspections, they actually use.
cards.detail: Traditional systems spread overhead with one volume-based rate, usually labor or machine hours. ABC groups overhead into activity cost pools (setups, inspections, material handling), finds the cost driver for each pool, computes an activity rate, and charges products for the drivers they use. It gives more accurate costs when products differ in complexity or batch size. ABC is mainly an internal decision tool; GAAP inventory must still follow absorption costing (manufacturing costs only), so ABC results that include selling or administrative costs cannot go directly into external statements.
cards.example: Precision Machining: $60,000 / 100 setups = $600 per setup; $40,000 / 200 inspections = $200 each. Custom valves: (70 x $600) + (120 x $200) = $66,000 / 1,000 units = $66 overhead, $111 total cost.
cards.say_it: ABC charges the Custom Valve for the setups and inspections it really causes, which is why its true cost is $111, not $55.
cards.mistakes: Saying ABC changes total overhead; it only changes how the same total is divided among products.
cards.formula: Activity rate = Cost pool total / Total driver quantity

cards.core: A cost driver is the factor that causes an activity's cost to rise or fall, such as the number of setups.
cards.detail: Volume-based drivers (direct labor hours, machine hours, units) work well when overhead rises with production volume. Many overhead costs are driven by batches, complexity or customer demands instead: setups, inspections, purchase orders, engineering changes. Choosing the right driver is what makes cost allocation accurate.
cards.example: Precision Machining's setup costs are driven by the number of setups, not labor hours: custom valves are 10% of labor hours but 70% of setups.
cards.say_it: Setups cost money each time we change over a machine, so the number of setups, not labor hours, is the fair way to assign that cost.

cards.core: Cost of quality = prevention + appraisal + internal failure + external failure costs.
cards.detail: Prevention costs stop defects before they happen (training, maintenance, better design). Appraisal costs find defects (inspection, testing). Internal failure costs come from defects caught before shipping (scrap, rework). External failure costs come from defects customers find (returns, replacements, warranty, lost sales and goodwill). Spending more on prevention usually cuts failure costs by more, which is the logic of total quality management (TQM).
cards.formula: Cost of quality = Prevention + Appraisal + Internal failure + External failure
cards.example: EverGreen: $50,000 + $80,000 + $300,000 + $170,000 = $600,000, with 78% in failure costs. Adding $150,000 of prevention to cut failures 50% ($235,000) saves $85,000 a year.
cards.say_it: We spend 78% of our quality budget fixing mistakes, so moving money into prevention saves $85,000 a year before even counting customer goodwill.

cards.core: Equivalent units turn partly finished units into the number of whole units the work would have completed.
cards.detail: In process costing, some units are still in process at the end of the period. Under the weighted average method, equivalent units = units completed + (ending work in process units x percent complete). Materials and conversion costs (labor and overhead) are often computed separately because materials may be added at the start while conversion happens evenly. Cost per equivalent unit is then used to value both completed units and ending work in process.
cards.formula: Equivalent units (weighted average) = Units completed + (Ending WIP units x % complete)
cards.example: Illustration: 1,000 candles finished and 400 in process, 50% complete for conversion. Conversion equivalent units = 1,000 + 200 = 1,200. If wax is added at the start, materials equivalent units = 1,400. Conversion costs of $6,000 give $5 per equivalent unit.
cards.say_it: Four hundred half-finished candles count as two hundred whole candles of labor and overhead, so we spread the cost over 1,200 equivalent units.

cards.core: Lean production removes waste, such as extra inventory, waiting, defects and unneeded steps, from every process.
cards.detail: Lean organizes work around the flow of value to the customer. For accounting it changes what is measured: costs are often gathered by value stream (an entire product flow) rather than by job or department, overhead allocations shrink because more costs are directly traceable to a value stream, and reports emphasize non-financial measures. It also reduces inventory, so absorption costing income becomes closer to variable costing income.
cards.example: EverGreen Packaging's plant going lean would track cost per value stream for its box line and report cycle time and on-time delivery to managers alongside costs.
cards.say_it: Going lean means our reports should follow the whole product flow and show cycle time and defects, not just cost variances by department.

cards.core: Process costing averages costs over large numbers of identical units moving through departments.
cards.detail: Process costing fits continuous mass production of the same product: candles, paint, cereal, soft drinks, chemicals, aluminum pipe. Costs are collected by department (mixing, molding, packaging) for a period, then divided by the equivalent units produced to get a cost per unit. Partly finished units at period end are converted into equivalent whole units. Unlike job costing, there is no need to track each order separately.
cards.formula: Cost per equivalent unit = Total department costs / Equivalent units
cards.example: Lumen Candle Company makes thousands of identical candles, so a process cost system that averages department costs over all candles made fits better than a job cost sheet for each candle.
cards.say_it: Since every candle is the same, we don't need a cost sheet per order; we average each department's costs over the candles it produced.

cards.core: A single volume-based overhead rate overcosts simple high-volume products and undercosts complex low-volume ones.
cards.detail: When overhead is caused by batches and complexity but is spread by labor hours, the high-volume product carries costs it does not cause, and the low-volume custom product looks cheaper than it is. Managers may then overprice the profitable product (losing bids) and underprice the costly one (selling it at a loss). Measuring the distortion means comparing traditional and ABC unit costs and multiplying the difference by units. Fixes include repricing, charging setup fees, larger batches and fewer setups.
cards.example: Precision: Standard Valve overcosted by 55 minus 48.78 = $6.22 per unit ($56,000 total); Custom undercosted by $56 per unit ($56,000). At a $70 price each Custom Valve loses $41, a $41,000 loss a year.
cards.say_it: Your Standard Valve has been paying $56,000 a year of the Custom Valve's costs, which is why you lose bids on one and lose money on the other.

cards.term: Reconciling absorption and variable costing income
cards.core: The income difference equals fixed overhead per unit times the change in inventory units (produced minus sold).
cards.detail: When production is greater than sales, absorption costing defers some fixed overhead in ending inventory, so absorption income is higher. When sales are greater than production, inventory falls and previously deferred fixed overhead is released, so variable costing income is higher. When production equals sales, both give the same income. Total spending is identical; only the timing of the fixed overhead expense differs.
cards.formula: Absorption income minus Variable income = Fixed MOH per unit x (Units produced minus Units sold)
cards.example: Lumen: 22,000 minus 14,000 = $8,000 = $4 x (10,000 minus 8,000). If only 8,000 candles were made, fixed overhead would be $5 each, COGS 8,000 x $11 = $88,000, and absorption income would be $14,000, the same as variable costing.
cards.say_it: The extra $8,000 of absorption profit isn't new money; it's $4 of fixed overhead sitting in each of the 2,000 unsold candles.

cards.core: Segment margin = Contribution margin minus Traceable fixed costs; it is the best measure of a segment's long-run profit.
cards.detail: A segment is a part of the business (a division, product line, store or region) with its own cost and profit report. The segment margin shows what the segment adds toward the company's common costs and profit. Managers should be evaluated on segment margin (or contribution margin for short-run decisions), not on net income after arbitrary allocations they cannot control.
cards.formula: Segment margin = Sales minus Variable costs minus Traceable fixed costs
cards.example: FitTech Smart Shoes: $100,000 minus $60,000 = $40,000.
cards.say_it: I would evaluate the shoe division manager on the $40,000 segment margin, because the $65,000 of headquarters cost is outside her control.

cards.core: Standard costing sets the expected quantity and price of each input per unit, then compares actual costs with those standards.
cards.detail: A standard cost card lists, for one unit, the standard quantity and standard price of materials, the standard hours and rate of labor, and the overhead rate. Standards are the building blocks of budgets: budgeted cost = budgeted units x standard cost per unit. After the period, actual costs are compared with standard costs allowed for the actual output, and the variances are investigated. Standard costing works with job or process systems and supports pricing and cost control.
cards.formula: Standard cost per unit = Sum of (Standard quantity x Standard price) for each input
cards.example: Crumb & Co. Bakery standard per loaf: flour 2 lbs x $0.50 = $1.00; labor 0.1 hour x $15 = $1.50; variable overhead $0.50; standard variable cost $3.00 per loaf.
cards.say_it: Our standard says a loaf should cost $3.00 in variable costs, so any difference from that tells us exactly where to look.
cards.mistakes: Changing standards to make unfavorable variances disappear.

cards.core: TQM is a company-wide effort to improve quality continuously so defects are prevented rather than found and fixed later.
cards.detail: TQM shifts spending toward prevention (training, maintenance, better design, supplier quality) to reduce failures. Managerial accounting supports it with a cost of quality report that shows how much poor quality really costs and tracks the shift over time. Cutting inspections alone does not reduce quality only if prevention has improved first; otherwise defects reach customers and external failure costs rise.
cards.example: EverGreen: TQM adds $150,000 of prevention and cuts failure costs 50% ($235,000), a net saving of $85,000 a year; the new cost of quality is $515,000.
cards.say_it: Spending $150,000 to prevent defects saves $235,000 of fixing them, so TQM pays for itself and protects our customers too.

cards.core: Traceable fixed costs exist only because of a segment; common fixed costs support the whole company and remain if a segment is dropped.
cards.detail: Traceable examples: a division's own supervisors, its advertising, equipment used only by it. Common examples: headquarters rent, the CEO's salary, company-wide software. Common costs are often allocated to segments using sales or floor space, but the allocation does not change the total the company pays, so allocations can make a profitable segment look unprofitable.
cards.example: FitTech: shoe supervisors and shoe advertising ($60,000) are traceable; headquarters rent and the CEO salary allocated to shoes ($65,000) are common.
cards.say_it: The headquarters costs do not disappear if we close Smart Shoes; they just move to the other two divisions.

cards.core: Lean companies simplify costing by assigning costs to whole value streams and recording costs at the end of production (backflush).
cards.detail: Value stream costing collects all the costs of a product flow, including labor, machines, materials and support, and divides by units shipped, avoiding detailed job tracking and overhead allocations. Backflush costing, used with JIT, skips recording each step through work in process and assigns standard costs when goods are finished or sold, because inventory is so small. Both reduce bookkeeping and reflect how a lean plant actually runs.
cards.example: EverGreen's corrugated box line could be one value stream: total weekly costs of the line divided by boxes shipped gives the cost per box without tracking each order.
cards.say_it: With almost no inventory, we don't need to track every job through work in process; costing the whole value stream is simpler and just as useful.

cards.core: Variable costing includes only variable manufacturing costs in each unit and expenses all fixed overhead in the period.
cards.detail: Under variable (direct) costing, unit product cost = direct materials + direct labor + variable overhead. Fixed manufacturing overhead is treated like a period cost and expensed in full each period, no matter how many units are sold. The income statement uses the contribution format: sales minus all variable costs = contribution margin, minus all fixed costs = operating income. It is used internally for CVP, pricing and performance evaluation because income moves with sales, not production. It is not allowed for GAAP external reports.
cards.formula: Variable unit cost = DM + DL + Variable MOH
cards.example: Lumen Candle: unit cost $6. Sales $120,000 minus variable costs $56,000 = contribution margin $64,000; minus fixed costs $50,000 = operating income $14,000.
cards.say_it: Variable costing shows profit only when candles are sold, which makes it the better tool for judging the manager and making decisions.

cards.core: Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit; at that volume profit is zero.
cards.detail: At break-even, total revenue equals total costs (variable plus fixed). Dividing fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit tells how many units must be sold before any profit is earned. Round up to the next whole unit, since a fraction of a unit cannot be sold. Break-even is a starting point: managers compare it with expected sales to judge risk and then plan for a target profit.
cards.formula: Break-even units = Fixed costs / (Price minus Variable cost per unit)
cards.example: Jotter at $4.75: 19,000 / 3.25 = 5,846.2, so about 5,847 notebooks are needed to cover all costs, far below the planned 30,000.
cards.say_it: We cover all our fixed costs after about 5,850 notebooks, so a 30,000 run carries very little risk of a loss.
cards.mistakes: Dividing fixed costs by the selling price instead of the contribution margin.

cards.core: Contribution margin is sales minus variable costs: what is left to cover fixed costs and then profit.
cards.detail: Contribution margin per unit is price minus variable cost per unit. The contribution margin ratio is contribution margin divided by sales, showing the share of each sales dollar available for fixed costs and profit. Once fixed costs are covered, every additional unit's contribution margin is pure profit. It is the key number for break-even, target profit, special orders and variable costing income statements.
cards.formula: CM per unit = Price minus Variable cost per unit; CM ratio = CM / Sales
cards.example: Jotter at a $4.75 price: 4.75 minus 1.50 = $3.25 per notebook; CM ratio 3.25 / 4.75 = about 68.4%. Crumb & Co.: $6.00 minus $3.00 variable = $3.00 per loaf.
cards.say_it: Each notebook contributes $3.25 toward our $19,000 of fixed costs, and once those are covered, every $3.25 is profit.
cards.mistakes: Subtracting fixed cost per unit when computing contribution margin.

cards.core: CVP analysis shows how changes in price, volume and costs affect profit.
cards.detail: CVP uses the relationship Profit = (Price x Units) minus (Variable cost per unit x Units) minus Fixed costs. It answers what-if questions: what happens to profit if we cut the price, add an employee, sell 10% more, or lease a new machine? It is used for profit planning, pricing, choosing production volume and finding break-even. Assumptions: costs can be split into fixed and variable, prices and unit costs stay constant within the relevant range.
cards.formula: Profit = (Price minus Variable cost per unit) x Units minus Fixed costs
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 units and $4.75: (4.75 minus 1.50) x 30,000 minus 19,000 = $78,500 profit; at 10,000 units only $13,500.
cards.say_it: CVP shows that producing 30,000 notebooks earns $78,500 versus $13,500 at 10,000, because the fixed costs are spread over more units.

cards.core: Variable costs change in total with volume but stay the same per unit; fixed costs stay the same in total but fall per unit as volume rises.
cards.detail: Cost behavior is the base of CVP, budgets and pricing. Variable costs: materials, direct labor paid per unit, sales commissions, packaging, food ingredients. Fixed costs: rent, insurance, salaried supervisors, equipment rental, depreciation. Because fixed cost per unit falls as volume grows, total cost per unit drops at higher volumes. These patterns hold only within the relevant range, the normal operating range where the cost structure stays the same.
cards.example: Jotter Manufacturers: variable cost $1.50 per notebook at every volume; fixed costs $19,000 total, so fixed cost per unit is $1.90 at 10,000, $0.95 at 20,000 and $0.63 at 30,000. Rocking Ribs: rent, insurance and utilities of $4,300 are fixed; meat and payroll are variable.
cards.say_it: Your $19,000 of fixed costs don't change with volume, so every extra notebook spreads them thinner and lowers the cost of each unit.
cards.mistakes: Saying fixed cost per unit is constant, or treating a per-unit fixed cost as if it would change total cost.

cards.core: Profit improves by raising price, increasing volume, lowering variable cost per unit or cutting fixed costs.
cards.detail: Every recommendation to improve a profit margin fits one of these CVP levers, and the best answers test each against the numbers. Raising price increases contribution margin but may lose customers. Increasing volume (marketing, new services) spreads fixed costs. Lowering variable costs (better suppliers, less waste) raises margin on every unit. Cutting fixed costs (renegotiating rent, sharing equipment) lowers break-even. Recommend a break-even and target profit analysis first, then judge results against trends and industry averages.
cards.example: Canine Condos' 7.5% margin ($2,858 / $38,000): raise boarding prices, advertise to fill more kennels, and cut supplies ($8,166) and cleaning ($4,440) costs. Rocking Ribs: schedule fewer staff and order meat to match forecast demand in the low season.
cards.say_it: There are only four ways to raise your margin: price, volume, variable cost and fixed cost, so let's test each one against your break-even point.

cards.core: Cost-based pricing adds a markup to cost to set the price, then checks it against competitors and customer value.
cards.detail: A markup on cost turns cost into a selling price, for example cost x 1.5. Cost-based pricing needs a full picture of every cost so the price covers costs and earns the desired margin. The price must still make sense in the market: if competitors sell a similar product for less, customers may switch. Profit margin and markup are different: a 50 percent markup on cost is a 33 percent margin on the selling price.
cards.formula: Price = Cost x (1 + Markup %); Margin on price = (Price minus Cost) / Price
cards.example: Rocking Ribs marks meat up 1.5 times: $40,000 of meat produces $60,000 of sales. Jotter: at a $2.13 cost per unit, pricing at $4.49 to $4.75 earns about $2.36 to $2.62 per notebook and stays at or below the competitor's $4.75.
cards.say_it: Our cost is $2.13, so we can price at or just under the competitor's $4.75 and still earn more than $2 per notebook.
cards.mistakes: Confusing markup on cost with margin on sales.

cards.core: Units needed for a target profit equal fixed costs plus target profit, divided by contribution margin per unit.
cards.detail: Target profit analysis extends break-even: treat the desired profit like an extra fixed cost that must be covered. It tells managers the sales volume needed to reach a profit goal, which can then be compared with capacity and the market. A target can also be set as a percentage of sales, as Rocking Ribs does with its 10 percent profit goal, by working backward from expected sales.
cards.formula: Target units = (Fixed costs + Target profit) / CM per unit; Target sales dollars = (Fixed costs + Target profit) / CM ratio
cards.example: Illustration with Jotter's numbers: to earn $30,000, (19,000 + 30,000) / 3.25 = 15,077 notebooks. Rocking Ribs: 10% of $60,000 low-season sales = $6,000 target profit.
cards.say_it: To earn $30,000 we need about 15,100 notebooks, which is well inside our normal production range.

cards.core: Break-even sales dollars equal fixed costs divided by the contribution margin ratio.
cards.detail: Service businesses and multi-product businesses often think in dollars rather than units. Divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio to get the sales revenue needed to break even. Put another way, at break-even, sales equal variable costs plus fixed costs, which is how Rocking Ribs' role play states it. The answer should match break-even units times price.
cards.formula: Break-even sales = Fixed costs / CM ratio; Sales = Variable costs + Fixed costs at break-even
cards.example: Jotter: CM ratio 3.25 / 4.75 = 0.684; 19,000 / 0.684 = about $27,769, which equals 5,846.2 units x $4.75.
cards.say_it: We need about $27,800 of notebook sales just to break even, and everything above that adds about 68 cents of profit per dollar.

cards.term: Building a cost schedule at different volumes
cards.core: Hold variable cost per unit and total fixed cost constant, then compute total cost and cost per unit at each volume.
cards.detail: Step 1: find variable cost per unit (total variable cost divided by units). Step 2: total variable cost at each volume = units x variable cost per unit. Step 3: total fixed cost stays the same at every volume; fixed cost per unit = fixed cost divided by units. Step 4: total cost = variable + fixed. Step 5: total cost per unit = total cost divided by units. The schedule shows how unit cost falls with volume and supports pricing and quantity decisions.
cards.formula: Total cost = (Units x Variable cost per unit) + Fixed costs; Cost per unit = Total cost / Units
cards.say_it: At 30,000 notebooks our full cost is only $2.13 each, compared with $3.40 at 10,000, which gives us room to price against the competitor's $4.75.

cards.term: Fixed cost per unit falls with volume
cards.core: Fixed cost per unit = total fixed cost / units, so making more units spreads the same fixed cost thinner.
cards.detail: Because total fixed cost does not change, each extra unit lowers the fixed cost carried by every unit, which lowers total cost per unit. This is why higher volume can raise profit per unit and why economies of scale exist. But per-unit fixed costs are misleading for short-term decisions: the total does not go away if one unit is not made.
cards.formula: Fixed cost per unit = Total fixed cost / Units; Total cost per unit = Variable cost per unit + Fixed cost per unit
cards.say_it: At 30,000 notebooks our fixed cost per unit drops to 63 cents, so making more lowers our cost per notebook to $2.13.

cards.core: Margin of safety is how far sales can fall below expected sales before the business reaches break-even.
cards.detail: Margin of safety measures risk. It can be shown in units, in dollars, or as a percentage of expected sales. A large margin means sales could drop a lot before a loss; a small margin means even a mild slowdown is dangerous. It is a strong point to make when recommending a production quantity or presenting a forecast to a lender.
cards.formula: Margin of safety = Expected sales minus Break-even sales; Margin of safety % = Margin of safety / Expected sales
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 notebooks x $4.75 = $142,500 of sales; break-even about $27,769; margin of safety about $114,731, or about 80% of sales.
cards.say_it: Even if sales fell by 80%, we would still break even, so this plan has a very comfortable margin of safety.

pis.text: Discuss the use of cost-volume-profit analysis

cards.core: Operating leverage shows how sharply profit changes when sales change; businesses with high fixed costs have more of it.
cards.detail: The degree of operating leverage is contribution margin divided by operating income. If it is 2, a 10 percent rise in sales raises operating income by about 20 percent, and a 10 percent drop cuts it by about 20 percent. Businesses with mostly fixed costs (gyms, factories) gain a lot when sales rise but are risky when sales fall. Businesses with mostly variable costs are safer but grow profit more slowly. It connects CVP to business risk.
cards.formula: Degree of operating leverage = Contribution margin / Operating income
cards.example: Jotter at 30,000 notebooks: CM 30,000 x 3.25 = $97,500; operating income 97,500 minus 19,000 = $78,500; leverage 97,500 / 78,500 = about 1.24, so a 10% sales increase raises income about 12.4%.
cards.say_it: Because most of our costs are fixed, a slow season hits profit harder than sales, which is why the low-season staffing plan matters so much.

pis.text: Discuss the use of cost-volume-profit analysis

cards.term: Relevant costs for a special order
cards.core: Accept a special order if its price is above the costs that change because of it, as long as regular sales are not lost.
cards.detail: Relevant costs are future costs that differ between the choices. For a special order with idle capacity, the relevant costs are usually the variable production costs plus any extra costs for the order; fixed overhead that will be paid anyway and costs that will not occur (such as commissions not paid on this order) are irrelevant. Compare the price with the relevant cost per unit and multiply by the units. If the plant is at full capacity, add the contribution margin lost on displaced regular sales as an opportunity cost. Then weigh qualitative risks.
cards.formula: Change in operating income = (Special price minus Relevant cost per unit) x Units minus Opportunity cost
cards.example: Velocity Athletic Gear: relevant cost = materials $15 + labor $10 + variable overhead $5 + printing $2 = $32. At $35: $3 x 5,000 = $15,000 more operating income. The lowest acceptable price is $32. At full capacity the order would displace regular sales and lower income.
cards.say_it: The $38 product cost includes $8 of fixed overhead we pay anyway, so any price above our $32 relevant cost adds profit, $15,000 on this order.
cards.mistakes: Rejecting the order because the price is below full (absorption) cost per unit.

cards.core: CVP results are reliable only within the relevant range, where fixed costs and per-unit variable costs stay the same.
cards.detail: Beyond normal capacity, a business may need another machine, a bigger building or overtime, so fixed costs step up and variable costs per unit can rise. Prices may also have to fall to sell more. CVP also assumes everything produced is sold and the sales mix stays constant. When a judge asks about a volume outside the analyzed range, the answer is to recheck the cost structure (capacity, overtime, discounts, storage) before assuming unit cost keeps falling.
cards.example: Jotter judge question about 40,000 or more notebooks: the $19,000 of fixed cost and $1.50 variable cost apply only to the normal 10,000 to 30,000 range, so we must check machine capacity, overtime pay and whether the market can absorb that many.
cards.say_it: Before we go to 40,000, I'd want to confirm we don't need a second foil machine or overtime, because that would change the fixed and variable costs our analysis is built on.
