cards.core: A sunk cost is already spent and never relevant; an opportunity cost is the benefit given up and is always relevant.
cards.detail: Sunk costs, like money already paid for equipment, cannot be changed by any decision, so they should be ignored. Opportunity costs are not recorded in the accounts, but they matter: when capacity is full, using it for one purpose means giving up the contribution margin from another. Idle capacity has no opportunity cost. These two ideas explain most special order, make or buy and transfer pricing answers.
cards.example: Velocity has 10,000 jerseys of idle capacity, so the 5,000-jersey order has no opportunity cost. If the plant were full, the lost margin on regular jerseys would be an opportunity cost; Northwind's minimum transfer price at full capacity rises from $8 to $13 for the same reason.
cards.say_it: What we paid for the machines is sunk and doesn't matter; what matters is whether this order pushes out regular sales, and with idle capacity it doesn't.

cards.core: 2/10, n/30 means take 2% off if you pay within 10 days; otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days.
cards.detail: Credit terms tell the buyer when payment is due and whether there is a discount for paying early. Skipping the discount is a hidden cost of credit: you pay 2% more for using the money 20 extra days, which works out to about 37% a year. That is why a business should almost always take the discount, even if it must borrow at a normal bank rate. n/30 alone means the full amount is due in 30 days with no discount.
cards.formula: Annual cost of skipping the discount = discount % / (100% minus discount %) x 365 / (full days minus discount days)
cards.example: Locally Picked sells $1,000 on June 10 with terms 2/10, n/30: the grocery store pays $980 by June 20 or $1,000 by July 10. Skipping the discount costs 2/98 x 365/20 = about 37% a year.
cards.say_it: Taking the 2% discount is like earning 37% a year on our money, so it is worth paying early even if we use our line of credit to do it.
cards.mistakes: Thinking 2% is too small to matter; on an annual basis it is far more expensive than a bank loan.

cards.core: Lenders judge borrowers on character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions.
cards.detail: Character is the borrower's honesty and payment history (credit reports, references). Capacity is the ability to repay from income or cash flow (profit margin, debt to income). Capital is the owner's own money in the business, a cushion if things go wrong (equity, debt ratio). Collateral is property the lender can claim if the loan is not repaid, or a personal guarantee. Conditions are the purpose of the loan, the economy and the industry. Strong Cs earn approval and better rates.
cards.example: Bayside: weak character (pays 15 days late), weak capacity (2% net margin vs. 4% industry), thin capital (80% debt ratio), so Coastal offers a smaller line with a personal guarantee.
cards.say_it: Using the five Cs, Bayside's character and capacity are the weak spots, so I would ask for a personal guarantee to strengthen the collateral side.
cards.formula: Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral, Conditions

cards.core: Credit lets a buyer get goods or money now and pay later, based on trust that payment will be made.
cards.detail: For buyers, credit smooths cash flow (buy supplies now, pay after selling), finances big purchases like equipment or a home, and handles emergencies. For sellers, offering credit wins customers and increases sales. For the economy, credit moves savings to people and businesses who can use them productively. The costs are interest or lost discounts, and the risk that the borrower cannot repay. A good payment record builds a credit reputation that earns larger limits and lower rates later.
cards.example: Coastal Wholesale offers Bayside trade credit to win its business, but every credit sale is a risk: if Bayside does not pay, Coastal loses both the cost of the goods and its profit, and its cash is tied up while it waits.
cards.say_it: Credit helps both sides: you can buy now and pay after you earn the revenue, and we gain a loyal customer, as long as the payment terms are kept.

cards.term: Trade credit (line of credit with a supplier)
cards.core: Trade credit is a supplier letting a business buy on account up to a limit, with set terms such as net 30.
cards.detail: Trade credit is the most common form of business credit. The supplier sets a credit limit (the most the customer can owe at one time) and terms (n/30, 2/10 n/30). For the seller it creates Accounts Receivable, a current asset; for the buyer it creates Accounts Payable, a current liability. Sellers manage the risk by checking credit before approving, monitoring how many days customers take to pay, and holding orders that would go over the limit.
cards.example: Bayside asks Coastal Wholesale for a $50,000 line on net 30 terms, but CRM data shows it pays in about 45 days, roughly 15 days late on average.
cards.say_it: Accounts receivable is really a loan we give our customers, so we should approve it with the same care a bank uses.

cards.core: Convert a short-term fee into a yearly rate so different financing options can be compared fairly.
cards.detail: A fee that looks small for a short period can be very expensive per year. Divide the cost by the cash actually received to get the rate for the period, then multiply by the number of such periods in a year. This puts factoring fees, skipped discounts and short-term loans on the same yearly basis as a bank's annual rate.
cards.formula: Annual rate = (Cost / Cash received) x (360 / Days)
cards.example: Swift Route factoring: $8,000 fee / $192,000 received = 4.2% for 60 days; x 360/60 = 6 periods, about 25% a year, versus 9% for the bank loan.
cards.say_it: Factoring costs about 25% a year compared with 9% for the loan, so we would only choose it to protect our debt covenant.

cards.core: Show the lender your purpose, financial statements, forecasts and how you will repay.
cards.detail: Lenders want to know how much you need and why, how you will repay, and what happens if things go wrong. A business loan application usually includes a business plan, recent income statements and balance sheets, tax returns, cash flow forecasts, a list of debts, collateral offered and the owner's personal financial statement and credit history. Consumer loans need proof of income, employment and identity. Compare offers by APR, term, fees and fixed or variable rate before signing.
cards.example: Peak Performance Gym builds a trend forecast of next year's results for its bank: expected operating income $147,720 and a pessimistic case of $114,600 with 10% fewer members.
cards.say_it: I would give the bank both the expected case and the pessimistic case, because showing that we can repay even in a bad year builds more trust than an optimistic number.
cards.mistakes: Giving the lender only the most optimistic forecast.

cards.core: Collateral is property a lender can take if a loan is not repaid; a personal guarantee makes the owner personally liable.
cards.detail: Secured loans are backed by collateral such as a truck, equipment, inventory or real estate, so they carry lower rates. Unsecured loans and credit lines rely on creditworthiness alone. For small businesses, especially LLCs and corporations where the owner's personal assets are normally protected, lenders often require a personal guarantee, so the owner promises to pay personally if the business cannot. Deposits and letters of credit are other ways to reduce a seller's risk.
cards.example: Coastal Wholesale offers Bayside a $20,000 line if its owner signs a personal guarantee, which reduces Coastal's risk without refusing the sale.
cards.say_it: A personal guarantee lets us extend credit to a riskier customer because the owner's own assets stand behind the business's promise to pay.

cards.core: Keep debt payments affordable, pay high-rate debt first and stop adding new debt.
cards.detail: Measure debt with the debt-to-income ratio (monthly debt payments / gross monthly income); lenders prefer under about 36%. To reduce debt: list every debt with its balance and rate, pay minimums on all, then put extra money on the highest-rate debt first (avalanche method, saves the most interest) or the smallest balance first (snowball method, builds motivation). Avoid new borrowing, consider consolidating at a lower rate, and contact lenders early if you cannot pay. Businesses watch the debt ratio, debt-to-equity and loan covenants.
cards.formula: Debt-to-income = Monthly debt payments / Gross monthly income
cards.example: Monthly debts $900 / gross income $3,000 = 30% debt-to-income, an acceptable level.
cards.say_it: Bayside already finances 80% of its assets with debt, so adding a large line of credit would make its debt harder to control, not easier.

cards.core: Interest = Principal x Rate x Time; the cost of credit is the total interest and fees paid.
cards.detail: The cost of credit is everything paid beyond the amount borrowed: interest, plus fees such as origination, late or annual fees. Simple interest uses the principal, the annual rate and the time in years; for short business loans banks often use a 360-day year, so time = days / 360. Comparing loans means comparing the total cost and the annual rate, not just the monthly payment.
cards.formula: Interest = Principal x Annual rate x Time (in years, or days / 360)
cards.example: Swift Route Logistics: $200,000 x 9% x 60/360 = $3,000 of interest on a 60-day bank loan, versus an $8,000 factoring fee.
cards.say_it: The bank loan costs $3,000 for 60 days, which is $5,000 less than factoring, so cost alone favors the loan; the question is whether the extra debt breaks our covenant.
cards.mistakes: Using the full annual rate for a 60-day loan instead of multiplying by 60/360.

cards.term: Credit risk of selling on account
cards.core: Selling on credit raises sales but risks late payment, bad debts and cash tied up in receivables.
cards.detail: When a business sells on account, it has earned revenue but not collected cash. Some customers pay late, which strains cash flow, and some never pay, which creates bad debt expense. Businesses manage this risk with credit checks, credit limits, clear terms, early payment discounts, prompt invoicing, aging reports and collection follow-up. When cash is needed sooner, receivables can be factored (sold) for a fee.
cards.example: Cascade Medical Supplies has $50,000 of receivables more than 60 days past due, and Swift Route Logistics considers factoring $200,000 of receivables for a 4% fee to get cash now.
cards.say_it: Our profit means little if customers do not pay, so I would track days to collect and tighten terms for any account more than 30 days late.

cards.core: A fixed rate stays the same for the life of the loan; a variable rate moves with market rates.
cards.detail: Variable (adjustable) rates are tied to a benchmark, so payments rise when the Federal Reserve raises rates and fall when it cuts. They usually start lower than fixed rates. Fixed rates give certainty for budgeting. Borrowers choose fixed when they expect rates to rise or need predictable payments; lenders and banks face interest rate risk when their loans are fixed but their deposit costs move.
cards.example: Harbor Fresh's fixed 6% loan does not change if the Fed raises rates next year; only new or variable-rate borrowing would cost more.
cards.say_it: Locking in a fixed 6% now protects us if rates rise, and our payment schedule stays exactly as planned.

cards.core: Guard personal data, use strong security, watch accounts and freeze credit to prevent identity theft.
cards.detail: Identity theft is using someone's personal information (Social Security number, account numbers, logins) to open accounts or make purchases. Prevention: shred documents, never share data in response to unexpected calls, texts or emails (phishing), use multifactor authentication, check statements and credit reports, and freeze your credit with all three bureaus. If it happens: report it at IdentityTheft.gov, place a fraud alert or freeze, contact the affected companies and change passwords. Businesses must protect customer and employee data such as payroll records and W-2s.
cards.example: A payroll clerk receives an email "from the owner" asking for every employee's W-2; it is a common scam, so the clerk verifies by phone before sending anything.
cards.say_it: Our payroll and customer files hold Social Security and bank numbers, so access should be limited by role and protected with multifactor authentication.

cards.core: Check the ratios, the payment history and references, then approve, limit or deny with clear conditions.
cards.detail: Step 1: compute liquidity, leverage and profitability ratios from the applicant's statements and compare them with industry averages. Step 2: review payment history with your own company (CRM or receivables aging) and outside sources: credit bureau reports, trade references and bank references. Step 3: weigh the five Cs. Step 4: decide: full approval, a smaller limit, shorter terms, a deposit or guarantee, or cash on delivery. Step 5: set a review date so the customer can earn a larger limit. Communicate the decision respectfully to keep the relationship.
cards.example: Bayside: current ratio 1.2 (industry 1.5), quick ratio 0.53 (0.8), debt ratio 80% (60%), net margin 2% (4%), pays 45 days on 30-day terms. Recommendation: a $20,000 line with a personal guarantee, reviewed after 6 months of on-time payments.
cards.say_it: Some sales are better than none only if they are collected, so I would offer a smaller line now and a clear path to the full $50,000 after six months of on-time payments.
cards.mistakes: Approving the full request because the customer is large, or denying it outright without offering a safer alternative.

cards.core: APR is the yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain fees, shown as a percentage.
cards.detail: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR and the finance charge so borrowers can compare offers on the same basis. APR includes interest and some required fees, so it is usually higher than the stated interest rate. Credit cards often have APRs above 20%, while secured loans like mortgages and auto loans are lower because collateral reduces the lender's risk. Always compare APRs and total finance charges, not monthly payments alone.
cards.example: Two $10,000 loans both at 7% interest: one charges a $500 fee, so its APR is higher and it costs more in total.
cards.say_it: I compare financing offers by APR and total finance charge, because a lower monthly payment can hide a longer term and more interest.

cards.core: A credit score (300 to 850) summarizes credit risk; payment history and amounts owed matter most.
cards.detail: FICO scores weigh payment history (about 35%), amounts owed and credit utilization (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%) and credit mix (10%). Higher scores get approvals, lower interest rates and better insurance and rental terms. Businesses also have credit ratings from agencies such as Dun and Bradstreet, based on how they pay suppliers. Late payments can stay on a report for up to seven years.
cards.example: A borrower with a 780 score might get a 6.5% car loan, while a 600 score might pay 12% or more on the same loan.
cards.say_it: Paying our suppliers on time is not just polite; it builds the business credit rating we will need for a future bank loan.

cards.core: A covenant is a condition in a loan agreement, such as a maximum debt-to-equity ratio, that the borrower must meet.
cards.detail: Lenders protect themselves with covenants: limits on debt ratios, minimum current ratios, limits on dividends or owner withdrawals, and requirements to send financial statements on time. Breaking a covenant can let the lender demand immediate repayment or raise the rate. That is why a business must check how a financing choice affects its ratios, not only its interest cost.
cards.example: Swift Route Logistics chooses factoring (about 25% a year) over a 9% bank loan, because the loan would add $200,000 of liabilities and could push debt-to-equity past its lenders' limit.
cards.say_it: The loan is cheaper, but breaking our covenant could cost far more than the extra $5,000, so factoring is the safer choice right now.

cards.core: Each payment covers interest on the unpaid balance first, then reduces principal, so interest falls over time.
cards.detail: A loan schedule lists, for each period, the beginning balance, interest (balance x rate), principal repaid, total payment and ending balance. With equal principal payments, total payments shrink as interest falls. With level payments (like most car loans and mortgages), early payments are mostly interest and later payments mostly principal. On the balance sheet, the principal due within the next year is a current liability and the rest is long-term.
cards.formula: Interest for the period = Unpaid principal x Rate
cards.example: Harbor Fresh $100,000 loan, 6%, $20,000 principal a year: interest $6,000, $4,800, $3,600, $2,400, $1,200 = $18,000; payments fall from $26,000 to $21,200. After Year 1: note $80,000, current portion $20,000, long-term $60,000.
cards.say_it: Our payments are highest in Year 1 at $26,000, so the cash budget has to plan for that, but interest drops every year as we pay down the note.

cards.core: Explain the decision with facts, offer a workable alternative and show the customer a path to more credit.
cards.detail: A credit decision is also a relationship decision. Start by thanking the customer for their business, share the main facts behind the decision without lecturing, and propose options that protect both sides: a smaller limit, shorter terms, a deposit, a personal guarantee, or cash on delivery with an early payment discount. State exactly what would change the decision (for example, six months of on-time payments or improved ratios). Listen to objections and look for a win for both sides.
cards.example: Judge question at Coastal Wholesale: "What would change your mind in six months?" Answer: six months of payments within 30 days, plus updated statements showing the current ratio moving toward 1.5.
cards.say_it: We value your business, so instead of saying no we would like to start with a $20,000 line and raise it as soon as your payments show you are on track.

cards.core: Check your credit reports from all three bureaus each year and dispute any errors.
cards.detail: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion each keep a credit report. Free reports are available at AnnualCreditReport.com. Check personal information, every account and balance, late payments, and inquiries. Unknown accounts can be a sign of identity theft. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, you can dispute inaccurate information with the bureau and the company that reported it, and they must investigate, usually within 30 days. A business checks a customer's history through a credit bureau report, trade references and bank references.
cards.example: Before approving Bayside, Coastal Wholesale checks a credit bureau report, trade references and bank references, and compares them with its own CRM payment history.
cards.say_it: Past payment behavior is one of the best predictors of future behavior, so I verified Bayside's history with both our own records and outside references.

cards.core: Use credit for planned needs you can repay on time, keep balances low and pay in full when possible.
cards.detail: Wise credit use means borrowing only for things that are worth more than they cost (education, equipment that earns income, a home), never for routine spending you cannot afford. Pay every bill on time, pay credit cards in full to avoid interest, keep credit card balances under about 30% of the limit, read the terms before signing, and avoid opening many accounts at once. For a business, match the loan length to the asset's life and keep debt at a level the cash flow can carry.
cards.example: Financing a $100,000 delivery truck that will earn revenue for 5 years with a 5-year loan is wise; using a credit card for payroll is not.
cards.say_it: I would finance the equipment with a term loan that matches its useful life, and keep the credit card only for small purchases paid in full.

cards.core: Accurate bills, on-time payments and honest reports build the company's reputation with customers, suppliers and lenders.
cards.detail: The accounting department touches outsiders constantly: customers receive its invoices and statements, suppliers receive its payments, banks and investors receive its reports, and the government receives its tax filings. Errors (wrong invoices, late payments, misstated reports) make the whole company look careless, while accuracy and transparency make it look reliable. Ethical, professional accounting therefore supports the brand.
cards.example: Judge question at JKL Furniture: "How does the accounting department help reinforce the company's image?" Answer: correct invoices, paying suppliers on time and trustworthy reports for the bank.
cards.say_it: Every invoice and every on-time payment is a message about our company, so accurate accounting is part of our brand.

cards.core: Earnings management is manipulating the timing or amount of revenue and expenses to hit a target; it is unethical and can be fraud.
cards.detail: Common forms: recording sales before goods ship, delaying expense recording to next period, overproducing to defer fixed overhead into inventory, changing estimates (warranty, bad debts, useful lives) without real reason, or leaving out liabilities. Some choices are legal but misleading; others violate GAAP. The pressure usually comes from bonuses, loan covenants or investor expectations. Controls include consistent policies, management review, audit and bonus plans based on measures that are hard to manipulate.
cards.example: Office Supplies Company: a manager could ship cartridges before a real order exists to boost October net income and his bonus. Lumen Candle: overproducing 2,000 candles raises absorption income by $8,000 without one extra sale.
cards.say_it: Pulling November's sale into October would make this month look better, but it breaks the revenue recognition rule and just borrows profit from next month.

cards.core: Accounting ethics means honest, accurate, objective and confidential records so users can trust the numbers.
cards.detail: Owners, lenders, investors, employees and the government all make decisions based on financial statements they cannot check themselves, so the information is only valuable if it is trustworthy. Ethical accountants follow GAAP even under pressure, record transactions in the right period, disclose estimates and risks, avoid conflicts of interest, keep client and employee information confidential, and speak up about errors or fraud. Professional codes (such as the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct) require integrity, objectivity and due care. Unethical accounting can lead to fines, lawsuits, prison and business failure.
cards.example: Judge questions "Why are ethics important in accounting?" (JKL Furniture) and "How does ethics apply to accounting?" (Edgewood Equestrian): because users rely on the numbers to lend, invest, pay taxes and run the business.
cards.say_it: Our financial statements are only worth something if people can trust them, so I will record every item by the rules even when the result is not the number we hoped for.

cards.core: Ethical finance means honesty with investors and lenders, avoiding conflicts of interest, and putting clients' interests first.
cards.detail: Finance professionals manage other people's money and influence markets, so trust is essential. Key duties: give honest forecasts and disclosures to lenders and investors, avoid and disclose conflicts of interest, never trade on inside (nonpublic) information, follow fiduciary duty when managing others' money, treat customers fairly in lending and sales, and keep information confidential. Unethical finance, such as misleading loan applications or hiding risks, destroys trust and can bring legal penalties.
cards.example: Judge question at Peak Performance Gym: "Can I just use the optimistic number for the bank?" No: give the expected and pessimistic cases ($147,720 and $114,600) and the assumptions behind them.
cards.say_it: Giving the bank only the optimistic number might get the loan faster, but if results fall short we lose their trust, so I would show all the scenarios honestly.

cards.core: Accountants and finance staff keep pay, client and company financial data private unless law or consent allows sharing.
cards.detail: Accountants see sensitive information: salaries, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, client tax returns, plans for layoffs or mergers. Professional codes and laws require keeping it confidential, sharing it only with people who need it for their job, with consent, or when legally required. Limit access in systems by role, lock paper records and never discuss one employee's pay with another. Breaches can bring lawsuits and identity theft.
cards.example: Judge question at Summit Climbing Gym: "Brooke asked what Alex makes. Can I tell her?" The owner should not share Alex's pay; payroll records are confidential.
cards.say_it: I would keep Alex's pay confidential, because payroll records are private and sharing them would break employees' trust.

cards.term: Ethics of bonus and incentive plans
cards.core: Bonuses motivate, but they must be tied to measures that cannot be easily manipulated and reward what is best for the company.
cards.detail: Bonuses based on revenue encourage sales but ignore costs; bonuses based on net income encourage cost control but tempt managers to shift revenue and expenses between periods; ROI-based bonuses can cause managers to reject good projects (goal incongruence). Better designs combine several measures (contribution margin, residual income, customer and quality measures), use company-wide profit for part of the bonus, set a clear written policy and include review controls. Incentives matter because they motivate the team and link pay to results.
cards.example: Lumen Candle's 10% bonus is $2,200 under absorption costing vs. $1,400 under variable costing: an $800 gain from overproducing. Basing it on variable costing income removes that incentive.
cards.say_it: Incentives are worth offering because they focus the team on results, but I would base them on collected sales and contribution margin, so nobody gains by gaming the timing.

cards.core: A fiduciary must act in the best interest of the people whose money or organization they manage.
cards.detail: Board members, trustees, financial advisers who manage client accounts and company officers owe fiduciary duties: the duty of care (make informed, careful decisions, such as reviewing financial reports and the audit) and the duty of loyalty (put the organization's or client's interest ahead of their own and avoid conflicts of interest). Nonprofit boards also must make sure funds are used for the mission. Good governance practices, like regular financial reporting, an annual audit and independent directors, help meet these duties.
cards.example: The Society for Marketers' board needs quarterly financial reports, an annual audit and on-time Form 990 filing to carry out its fiduciary duty.
cards.say_it: Regular financial reports and an independent audit are how the board proves it is watching the members' money carefully.

cards.core: Intentionally misstating or leaving out amounts or disclosures to mislead users is fraud.
cards.detail: Examples: hiding liabilities such as warranty or refund obligations, inventing sales, overstating inventory, or omitting required notes. It differs from an honest error because it is intentional. Consequences include restated statements, SEC or IRS penalties, lawsuits from investors and lenders, loss of professional licenses and criminal charges. The fraud triangle explains why it happens: pressure, opportunity and rationalization. An accountant's duty is to present the statements fairly, even when a boss wants a better number.
cards.example: Voltra's founder wants to expense only the $2,500 of repairs paid; GAAP requires a $6,000 warranty expense and a $4,500 refund liability. Knowingly leaving them out to inflate profit would be fraudulent financial reporting.
cards.say_it: Even sophisticated investors cannot see a liability we leave out of the notes, so omitting it to look more profitable would be misleading and could be fraud.

cards.term: Leaving out provisions to boost profit
cards.core: Knowingly leaving out warranty, refund or lawsuit liabilities to make profit look better is fraudulent financial reporting.
cards.detail: Managers sometimes want to expense only what has been paid so this year's income and their bonus look higher. GAAP requires provisions because the obligations already exist. Intentionally omitting them misstates the statements, misleads lenders and investors, breaks the accountant's duty to present fairly, and can bring legal penalties and loss of credibility. The ethical accountant explains the rule, shows the correct numbers and, if pressured, escalates to the owner, board or audit committee.
cards.example: Voltra's founder wanted to expense only $2,500 of repairs. GAAP income is $5,300 lower and liabilities $8,000 higher. Nexus: GAAP expenses are $50,000 instead of $12,000, so income is $38,000 lower than the vice president's plan.
cards.say_it: I understand the bonus pressure, but leaving out an $8,000 obligation we already know about would mislead our investors, and my job is to present the numbers fairly.

cards.core: Sustainability and other non-financial claims must be measurable and supported, or they mislead users.
cards.detail: Companies increasingly report environmental and social data such as energy use and emissions. Greenwashing means making environmental claims that are false, exaggerated or unsupported; it can cost customers and bring legal or regulatory trouble. Ethical reporting uses clear definitions, the same method every year, documented estimates and, as the data becomes important, outside assurance. The same honesty standard applies to financial forecasts and marketing claims.
cards.example: Judge question at EverGreen Packaging: "Our competitor claims to be carbon neutral. Should we just say the same?" No: report only what can be measured and supported.
cards.say_it: We should report only the environmental results we can measure and prove, because one exaggerated claim can undo the trust we are trying to build.

cards.core: Under absorption costing, building extra inventory raises reported profit without selling anything, which can be abused to boost bonuses.
cards.detail: Because fixed overhead is spread over more units and part of it is deferred in inventory, producing more than can be sold makes absorption income look higher. It is legal, but it uses cash, adds storage and handling costs, risks obsolescence, and puts the manager's bonus ahead of the owners' interests, making reported profit misleading. Fixes: base bonuses on variable costing income, contribution margin or sales; cap inventory growth; and track inventory turnover and cash flow.
cards.example: Lumen's bonus is 10% of income: $2,200 under absorption ($22,000) vs $1,400 under variable costing ($14,000), an $800 gain for producing 2,000 candles nobody bought.
cards.say_it: It's legal to make more candles, but doing it just to raise the bonus shows profit we haven't earned, so I'd tie the bonus to variable costing income instead.

cards.core: Accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred; cash basis records only when cash moves.
cards.detail: Under the accrual basis, a sale delivered on credit is revenue now, and an October bill paid in November is an October expense. This matches expenses to the revenue they helped earn, so each period's profit is measured correctly. GAAP requires accrual accounting, and lenders and larger customers expect it. The cash basis is simpler and is allowed for taxes for many small businesses, but it can show profit in the wrong period. The cash flow statement fills in the cash picture that accrual statements do not show directly.
cards.example: Locally Picked delivers $1,000 of produce on June 10 on credit: accrual records June revenue (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales); cash basis would wait until payment arrives in June or July.
cards.say_it: Accrual accounting shows your true profit for each month, because it counts the produce you delivered in June as June revenue even if the store pays in July.
cards.mistakes: Saying cash basis is GAAP for small businesses; it is not GAAP, although it may be allowed for tax.

cards.core: Accounting identifies, records, summarizes and communicates a business's financial information to users.
cards.detail: Accounting is the information system of a business, often called the language of business. It records transactions (journalizing), sorts and stores them (posting to ledgers), summarizes them (trial balance and financial statements) and communicates them to users who make decisions. Financial accounting reports to outside users under GAAP; managerial accounting serves inside users; tax accounting follows tax law. Every transaction affects at least two accounts and keeps the accounting equation in balance.
cards.example: For JKL Furniture, accounting means recording every sale, purchase, receipt and payment, then summarizing them into reports that keep the growing company financially healthy.
cards.say_it: Accounting is how we turn hundreds of daily transactions into a few clear reports that tell you whether the business is healthy.

cards.core: A price must cover every cost of making and selling the product and still leave the desired profit.
cards.detail: Pricing needs a full picture of costs: variable costs per unit, fixed costs spread over expected volume, and overhead. Cost data shows the lowest price that avoids a loss (break-even), the price needed for a target margin, and how the company's cost compares with a competitor's price. Then demand and competition decide where in that range to set the price. Without cost information a company can sell a lot and still lose money.
cards.example: Jotter's notebook costs $2.13 per unit at 30,000 units; pricing at or slightly below the competitor's $4.75 (for example $4.49 to $4.75) leaves about $2.36 to $2.62 of margin per notebook.
cards.say_it: Our cost data shows we can match the competitor's $4.75 price and still earn about $2.62 a notebook at 30,000 units, so price is a weapon we can use.

cards.core: Financial accounting reports past results to outsiders under GAAP; managerial accounting helps insiders plan and decide.
cards.detail: Financial accounting produces general purpose statements (income statement, balance sheet, cash flows, equity) for investors, lenders and regulators; it must follow GAAP, covers the whole company and looks at the past. Managerial accounting produces whatever reports managers need (budgets, cost analyses, segment reports, variance reports); it does not have to follow GAAP, can focus on a product or department, is often future focused and is prepared as often as needed. Tax accounting follows the tax code.
cards.example: Precision Machining can use activity-based costs to price custom valves internally, but its audited external statements must use GAAP absorption costing.
cards.say_it: The activity-based numbers are for our internal pricing decisions; the bank still gets GAAP statements.

cards.term: How often to review the finances
cards.core: Review key numbers weekly, prepare statements monthly and do a deeper review quarterly and yearly.
cards.detail: A common rhythm for a small business: weekly cash and sales summaries; monthly income statement, balance sheet and budget vs. actual comparison; quarterly review of trends, ratios and tax estimates (and board reports for nonprofits); yearly closing, tax filing, audit if required and next year's budget. Reviewing often lets the owner catch problems, such as rising costs or slow collections, while they are still small. This is a recurring judge question.
cards.example: Judge questions: "How often should we analyze our profitability?" (Canine Condos) and "How often should we meet to discuss finances?" (Edgewood Equestrian). Answer: at least monthly, with a deeper quarterly review.
cards.say_it: I recommend a short monthly meeting to review the income statement against the budget, plus a quarterly deep dive on trends, ratios and taxes.

cards.core: Keep organized source documents and records so every transaction can be proved, reported and taxed correctly.
cards.detail: Good records start with source documents: invoices, receipts, bank statements, pay records, contracts and 1099s. Use a separate business bank account and card, record transactions promptly, file or scan documents so each can be matched to its entry, and back up digital files. Records support the financial statements, tax returns, loan applications and audits, and they show the owner what is really happening. For vehicles and meals, write down the business purpose at the time (a mileage log, who attended).
cards.example: Maya Chen keeps a mileage log, separate business accounts and scanned receipts with the business purpose written on each meal receipt, so her $19,000 of Schedule C deductions can be supported.
cards.say_it: If a deduction or transaction is not supported by a source document, we cannot prove it to a lender or the IRS, so the record keeping system matters as much as the numbers.
cards.mistakes: Mixing personal and business spending in one account, which breaks the business entity concept and makes deductions hard to prove.

cards.core: Owners, managers, lenders, investors and government all need accurate financial information to make decisions.
cards.detail: Financial information shows whether a business is profitable (income statement), what it owns and owes (balance sheet) and whether it has enough cash (cash flow). Managers use it to set prices, control costs, plan staffing, restock inventory and decide on expansion. Owners and investors use it to judge performance. Banks and suppliers use it to decide whether to lend or extend credit. Government uses it for taxes, and nonprofit boards use it to meet their fiduciary duty. Without it, decisions are guesses.
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's owner is deciding whether to open a fourth studio; Sam's Barbershop wants to hire; Dogs-R-Us uses its weekly cash summary to see that toys ($420) outsold food ($183) and that toy stock needs checking.
cards.say_it: Accurate financial information is what turns your decision about the new location from a guess into a plan, because it shows exactly what each studio earns and costs.

cards.core: Managers plan and control; owners and investors judge performance; creditors judge repayment; government collects taxes.
cards.detail: Each user asks a different question. Managers: what should we price, cut, buy or expand? Owners and investors: is the business earning a good return and growing? Banks and suppliers (creditors): can it pay us back on time? Government: how much tax is owed and are laws being followed? Employees and unions: is the company stable? Donors and members of a nonprofit: is our money used for the mission? Knowing the user tells you which report and level of detail to give.

cards.say_it: The bank wants to know if we can repay, while you as owner want to know which products make money, so I will prepare the right report for each.

cards.core: Turn the numbers into a decision: state the question, find the relevant figures, compare options and recommend.
cards.detail: Judges want a recommendation backed by numbers. Start with the decision (hire, expand, price, restock, borrow). Identify the figures that matter: revenue trends, costs (fixed and variable), margins, cash available and debt. Compare alternatives or compare with a benchmark (last year, the budget, the industry). Explain the result in plain words, add non-financial factors, and end with a clear recommendation and what to monitor next.
cards.example: Rocking Ribs: low-season sales $60,000 minus fixed costs $4,300, meat $40,000 and a $6,000 profit target leaves $9,700 for salaries, so 3 servers and 2 cooks ($11,760) cannot be scheduled but 3 servers and 1 cook ($8,400) can.
cards.say_it: Based on these numbers I recommend three servers and one cook, because that keeps payroll under the $9,700 we can afford and protects our 10% profit target.

cards.core: Errors in the records lead to wrong decisions, wrong taxes, lost money and lost trust.
cards.detail: In a growing business, small errors multiply: wrong bills get paid, customers are not billed or collected from, inventory runs short, taxes are misstated and reports mislead the owner and the bank. Accurate records are also required by law (tax and payroll) and by lenders. Controls such as source documents, trial balances, bank reconciliations and reviews catch errors early. Accuracy protects the company's reputation with customers and suppliers.
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's intern closed Cash instead of Revenue, leaving Owner's Capital with an impossible $1,078,756 debit balance; after correction it is a $178,676 credit. Decisions about a fourth studio based on the wrong numbers would be badly misled.
cards.say_it: Before we decide on expansion we have to fix these closing errors, because a decision is only as good as the numbers behind it.

cards.core: A fiscal year is the 12-month accounting and tax year a business chooses; it need not match the calendar year.
cards.detail: Many businesses end their fiscal year when activity is lowest, so closing and counting inventory is easier, or match the calendar year for simplicity. Changing the year-end creates a short year (transition period) with its own accounting cycle, closing entries, audit and tax return. The change needs IRS notice or approval (most entities file Form 1128; a tax-exempt organization generally files a short-period Form 990). Budgets must be rebuilt for the short year.
cards.example: The Society for Marketers moves from a July to June year to a calendar year so its October conference, nearly 60% of transactions, closes within one fiscal year; July 1 to December 31 becomes a six-month short year.
cards.say_it: Ending our year on December 31 puts the whole conference in one year and matches our corporate partners' reporting, which makes comparisons easier.
cards.mistakes: Assuming a fiscal year must run January to December.

cards.core: Expansions usually lift stock prices and loan demand; recessions raise defaults and push investors toward safety.
cards.detail: The business cycle moves through expansion, peak, contraction (recession) and trough. In expansions, profits rise, stock prices tend to climb, lending grows and rates often rise. In recessions, profits fall, unemployment rises, more borrowers default, investors move money to safe assets like Treasury bonds, and the Fed cuts rates. Markets often move ahead of the economy because prices reflect expectations. Businesses use economic forecasts to plan sales budgets, credit policies and borrowing.
cards.example: Matrix Aluminum's sales budget considers the health of the aerospace, auto and railroad industries, because a slowdown there would cut pipe orders.
cards.say_it: Before setting next year's sales budget, I would check economic forecasts for our customers' industries, because their slowdown becomes our slowdown.

cards.core: The capital market trades long-term securities such as stocks and bonds, with higher return and risk.
cards.detail: Companies raise long-term money in the capital market by issuing stock (equity) and bonds (debt); governments issue long-term bonds. The primary market is where new securities are first sold, such as an IPO handled by investment banks. The secondary market, such as the New York Stock Exchange or Nasdaq, is where investors trade existing securities with each other. The SEC regulates the capital market to protect investors through required disclosure.
cards.example: Lakeshore Brewing prepares for an IPO in the capital market, which brings new public company costs of about $840,000 in the first year for audits, governance and compliance.
cards.say_it: The capital market is for long-term money: a company raises funds there for growth, and investors accept more risk for higher expected returns.

cards.core: Economies of scale mean cost per customer falls as a firm grows because fixed costs are spread over more customers.
cards.detail: A bank pays roughly the same for core software, cybersecurity and compliance staff whether it has 20,000 or 60,000 customers. Doubling the customer base after a merger cuts the cost per customer, which allows lower fees or higher profit. Economies of scale are the same idea as fixed cost per unit falling as volume rises in managerial accounting. Past a point, very large firms can face diseconomies of scale, such as slow decisions.
cards.example: If compliance costs $3 million a year, it is $150 per customer for 20,000 customers but $50 per customer for 60,000.
cards.say_it: Merging spreads our fixed compliance and technology costs over three times as many customers, which is the main financial reason banks consolidate.

cards.core: The Federal Reserve raises rates to slow inflation and cuts them to boost a weak economy, moving all financial markets.
cards.detail: When the economy grows quickly and inflation rises, the Federal Reserve raises its target rate; borrowing gets more expensive, bond prices fall, and stock prices often weaken. In a recession the Fed cuts rates to encourage borrowing and spending. Rates affect businesses directly: the cost of new loans, the value of future cash flows (higher rates mean lower present values), what banks pay on deposits, and customer demand. Other conditions such as unemployment, GDP growth and consumer confidence also move markets.
cards.example: If deposit rates at Harborview rise from 2% to 3.5% while its fixed loans stay at 5%, net interest income falls from $6.4 million to $3.7 million.
cards.say_it: Rising rates do not change our fixed 6% loan, but they raise the cost of any new borrowing, so locking in today's rate has real value.

cards.core: A stock is part ownership of a company; a bond is a loan to a company or government.
cards.detail: Stockholders own part of the company, may receive dividends, can vote, and gain or lose as the share price changes; they are paid last if the company fails. Bondholders are creditors who receive fixed interest payments and their principal back at maturity; they are paid before stockholders. Bond prices fall when market interest rates rise. For the issuing company, bonds are a liability with required interest, while stock is equity with no required payment.
cards.example: A $1,000 bond paying 5% gives $50 a year and $1,000 back at maturity; a share bought at $40 paying a $1.20 dividend gives 3% but its price can rise or fall.
cards.say_it: Issuing bonds keeps ownership with the current owners but adds required interest; issuing stock brings in cash with no repayment but gives up some ownership.

cards.core: Stress testing models how earnings and capital would hold up under a bad scenario, such as a sharp rate rise.
cards.detail: A stress test changes key assumptions, such as interest rates, loan defaults or sales volume, to a difficult level and recalculates results. If the business still meets its obligations, it is resilient; if not, it needs a plan (more capital, hedges, lower costs). Banks are required to stress test, but any business can do a simple version with a pessimistic budget scenario. It is the same idea as a downside case in a forecast.
cards.example: Harborview tests a rise in deposit costs to 3.5%: net interest income falls 42%. Peak Performance Gym tests 10% fewer members: operating income falls from $147,720 to $114,600.
cards.say_it: I ran a pessimistic case, and even with 10% fewer members we still earn $114,600, which shows the bank we can repay in a bad year.

cards.core: Consolidation is financial firms merging into fewer, larger firms to gain scale and services.
cards.detail: Banks, insurers and brokerages merge or acquire one another to gain economies of scale (spreading large technology and compliance costs over more customers), a wider branch network, more deposits to lend, new products and geographic reach. Convergence means the lines between banking, insurance and investing blur, so one firm offers all three. Risks include integration problems, culture clashes, cyber risk during system conversions, and less competition, which regulators review before approving mergers.
cards.example: Harborview Community Bank's merger with Lakeside brings scale, but the conversion raises cyberattack risk (scored 20) and integration risk (scored 12).
cards.say_it: Banks consolidate mainly to spread fixed technology and compliance costs over more customers, but the merger only pays off if the integration is managed well.

cards.core: An option protects against bad currency moves for a fee; a natural hedge offsets risk through the business itself.
cards.detail: A currency option gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy currency at a set rate, so the company is protected if the rate rises and can still benefit if it falls; the cost is an upfront premium. A natural hedge offsets currency risk with the business, such as earning revenue in euros to pay euro costs. Other tools: asking the supplier to bill in dollars (shifts the risk to the supplier, who may raise the price), paying early, and price adjustment clauses.
cards.example: Judge question: "Could we just ask the supplier to bill us in dollars?" Yes, but the supplier then carries the risk and will likely build it into a higher price.
cards.say_it: Billing in dollars moves the risk to the supplier, but nothing is free, so I would compare that higher price with the cost of a forward contract.

cards.core: Spreading money across many investments lowers the chance that one loss hurts the whole portfolio.
cards.detail: Diversification means owning different types of assets (stocks, bonds, cash), different companies, industries and countries, so poor results in one area are offset by others. Mutual funds and ETFs make diversification easy for small investors. It reduces company-specific risk but cannot remove market-wide risk such as a recession. Asset allocation, how money is split among asset types, should shift toward safer investments as the goal gets closer.
cards.example: Putting $10,000 in one stock that falls 50% loses $5,000; spreading it across a 500-stock index fund means one company's collapse barely matters.
cards.say_it: Rather than buying one company's stock, a diversified fund gives us growth with much less risk from any single business failing.

cards.core: Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the current share price.
cards.detail: Yield shows the cash income return from owning a stock, like an interest rate. It goes up when the price falls and down when the price rises, even if the dividend does not change. Total return is the yield plus any change in the share price, so a high yield can still lose money if the price drops. Dividends are not guaranteed; the board can cut them.
cards.formula: Dividend yield = Annual dividend per share / Price per share
cards.example: OUTD pays $1.20 a year and trades at $40.00: 1.20 / 40.00 = 3.0%.
cards.say_it: A 3% yield beats a savings account only if the price holds; a 10% price drop would turn the year into a loss.

cards.term: Effect of a merger on customers
cards.core: After a financial merger customers may see new systems, account numbers, fees or branches, so clear communication is vital.
cards.detail: Customers of a merged bank may benefit from more ATMs, branches and products, and from larger lending limits. They may also face new account numbers, online banking logins, changed fees, closed branches and a period of service problems during the system conversion. Deposit insurance limits apply per bank, so customers with large balances at both merging banks should check their coverage. A merger plan should include a customer communication timeline, staff training and extra support during conversion.
cards.example: Harborview plans conversion messages to every Lakeside customer, extra call center staff during conversion weekend and retention bonuses for key loan officers.
cards.say_it: Customers judge a merger by how smooth the change feels, so we should tell them early what changes, what stays the same and who to call.

cards.core: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another; dollar cost = foreign amount x rate.
cards.detail: Rates are quoted like EUR 1 = $1.10. If the euro strengthens (more dollars per euro), U.S. buyers of European goods pay more and U.S. exporters to Europe earn more dollars. If the euro weakens, the reverse happens. Rates move with interest rates, inflation, trade balances and investor confidence. U.S. GAAP requires an unpaid foreign currency payable to be updated to the year-end rate, with the change reported as a foreign exchange gain or loss.
cards.formula: Dollar amount = Foreign currency amount x Exchange rate (dollars per unit of foreign currency)
cards.example: A EUR 50,000 invoice: at $1.08 it costs $54,000 (Nov 15); at $1.12, $56,000 (Dec 31); at $1.10, $55,000 when paid (Jan 14), $1,000 more than expected.
cards.say_it: The invoice is fixed in euros, so every cent the euro rises costs us $500 on this order and about $6,000 a year on all our European purchases.

cards.core: Transaction risk is the chance that the exchange rate moves between the purchase date and the payment date.
cards.detail: When a company buys or sells on credit in a foreign currency, the amount in that currency is fixed but its value in dollars is not. The risk starts on the transaction date and ends when cash is paid. The foreign supplier bears no risk because it is paid in its own currency. Ways to manage it include forward contracts, currency options, paying early, invoicing in dollars, natural hedges and price adjustment clauses.
cards.example: Global Imports expected to pay $54,000 but paid $55,000 because the euro rose from $1.08 to $1.10 during its 60-day credit period.
cards.say_it: Our risk lasts from the day we order on credit until the day we pay, and the supplier carries none of it because it is paid in euros.

pis.text: Explain the nature and scope of financial globalization

examples.title: Global Imports LLC: exchange rate risk and hedging a euro purchase

cards.core: Financial globalization links banking, currency and capital markets across countries, so money and risk move worldwide.
cards.detail: Because of technology and open markets, businesses can borrow, invest and trade across borders, and investors can buy foreign stocks and bonds. Benefits: access to more suppliers, customers and capital, often at lower cost. Risks: exchange rate changes, events in one country spreading quickly to others (contagion), different laws and accounting rules (IFRS vs. U.S. GAAP), and political risk. Every importer or exporter that deals in a foreign currency faces exchange rate risk.
cards.example: Global Imports buys textiles from Europe priced in euros; because currency markets move daily, its dollar cost changes between the order date and the payment date.
cards.say_it: Globalization lets us buy the best fabric anywhere in the world, but the exchange rate becomes part of our cost of goods, so we need a policy to manage it.

pis.text: Explain the nature and scope of financial globalization

examples.title: Global Imports LLC: exchange rate risk and hedging a euro purchase

cards.term: Foreign exchange, commodities and insurance markets
cards.core: Currencies trade in the foreign exchange market, raw materials in commodities markets, and risk in insurance markets.
cards.detail: The foreign exchange market is where currencies are bought and sold for immediate delivery or future dates (forward contracts); it is the largest market in the world. Commodities markets trade raw goods like oil, wheat and aluminum, often through futures contracts that let businesses lock in prices. The insurance market is where people and businesses transfer risk to insurers by paying premiums. Derivatives markets trade contracts whose value comes from other assets. All of them help businesses manage price risk.
cards.example: A pipe maker worried about aluminum prices could buy futures in the commodities market to lock in metal costs; Global Imports uses the foreign exchange market to lock in a euro rate.
cards.say_it: Financial markets do more than raise money: they let us lock in prices for currency and raw materials so our costs are predictable.

pis.text: Explain types of financial markets (e.g., money market, capital market, insurance market, commodities markets, etc.)

examples.title: Global Imports LLC: exchange rate risk and hedging a euro purchase

cards.core: A forward contract locks in an exchange rate for a future date: it buys certainty, not profit.
cards.detail: Hedging is taking an offsetting position to reduce risk. A forward contract with a bank fixes the rate today for currency delivered on a set future date. If the currency rises, the hedge saves money; if it falls, the hedge costs more than not hedging. Either way, the company knows its cost on the day it orders, which protects margins and budgets. Hedging is risk control, not speculation, and the company should hedge according to a written policy.
cards.example: Forward rate $1.09: 50,000 x 1.09 = $54,500. It saves $500 compared with the $55,000 paid at $1.10, but if the euro had fallen to $1.05 the unhedged cost would have been $52,500, so the hedge would have cost $2,000 more.
cards.say_it: Sometimes the hedge will cost us money, but we pay that price for knowing our exact cost when we set our selling prices.
cards.mistakes: Judging a hedge only by whether it "won" after the fact.

cards.core: Interest rate risk is the chance that changing market rates reduce earnings or the value of assets.
cards.detail: Interest rate risk comes from mismatches: a bank with fixed-rate loans and variable deposit costs loses when rates rise; a bondholder loses value when rates rise because new bonds pay more; a borrower with a variable-rate loan pays more. Falling rates bring their own risk: borrowers refinance high-rate loans, and banks earn less on new loans. The risk is managed by matching rates, using variable-rate products, hedging and stress testing.
cards.example: Judge question at Harborview: "If rates fall instead, is our risk gone?" No: loans may refinance at lower rates and earnings can still drop, so the bank must watch both directions.
cards.say_it: Our risk is not just rising rates; it is the mismatch between what we earn and what we pay, so the fix is to balance fixed and variable rates.

cards.core: A stock table shows the 52-week high and low, dividend, yield, P/E ratio, last price and net change.
cards.detail: Read each column: 52-week high and low show the price range over the past year (a measure of volatility). Dividend is the annual amount paid per share. Yield is dividend divided by price. P/E is price divided by earnings per share. Last (close) is the latest price, and net change is the difference from the previous close (so previous close = last minus net change). Volume shows shares traded. Use the table to judge income, valuation and risk, then compare with other companies.
cards.example: OUTD: 52-week $31.50 to $48.20, dividend $1.20, last $40.00, net change +$0.75, P/E 15. Yield = 1.20 / 40 = 3.0%; EPS = 40 / 15 = about $2.67; previous close = $39.25.
cards.say_it: The table shows a 3% yield and a P/E of 15, but the 52-week range tells me the price swung about 35%, which is the risk I care about for short-term cash.

cards.core: Match the investment to when the cash is needed: short-term cash goes to safe, liquid investments.
cards.detail: Step 1: find out when and how much cash the business will need (cash budget). Step 2: rank goals: safety of principal first, liquidity second, return third for short-term money. Step 3: choose from money market instruments: Treasury bills, money market funds, CDs that mature by the needed date, or high-yield business savings. Step 4: avoid stocks and long-term bonds for money needed within a year, since their prices can fall. Step 5: review rates and FDIC limits, and spread large balances if needed.
cards.example: Oakridge Outfitters needs its $500,000 in 6 months for expansion, so the recommendation is Treasury bills, a money market fund or a 6-month CD, not its own stock.
cards.say_it: Because we need this money in six months, safety and liquidity come first, so I recommend six-month Treasury bills over stock.

cards.core: The money market trades short-term (one year or less), low-risk, highly liquid debt.
cards.detail: Money market instruments include Treasury bills, commercial paper (short-term company IOUs), certificates of deposit, and money market funds. Businesses use the money market to earn interest on cash they will need soon, and to borrow for short periods. Returns are lower than the capital market, but prices barely move, so the money is safe and available.
cards.example: Oakridge Outfitters parks $500,000 needed in 6 months in Treasury bills or a money market fund.
cards.say_it: The money market is where we keep cash we will need within a year: it earns interest without the price swings of stocks.

cards.core: Funds pool many investors' money to buy a diversified mix of stocks, bonds or other assets.
cards.detail: A mutual fund is priced once a day at its net asset value; an exchange-traded fund (ETF) trades on an exchange all day like a stock. Index funds track a market index and have very low fees; actively managed funds try to beat the market and charge more. The expense ratio is the yearly fee as a percentage of the investment. Money market funds invest in very short-term, safe securities and are a common place for business cash.
cards.example: An expense ratio of 0.05% costs $5 a year on $10,000; a 1.00% ratio costs $100 a year on the same amount.
cards.say_it: For idle business cash, a money market fund is a liquid option; for long-term savings, a low-cost index fund gives broad diversification.

examples.title: Oakridge Outfitters: idle cash, securities and changes in equity

cards.core: P/E is the share price divided by earnings per share: what investors pay for each dollar of earnings.
cards.detail: A high P/E means investors expect strong growth or see low risk; a low P/E may mean the stock is cheap or that investors expect problems. P/E is most useful when comparing companies in the same industry or a company with its own history. Earnings per share (EPS) is net income available to common shareholders divided by shares outstanding, so EPS can be backed out as price / P/E.
cards.formula: P/E = Price per share / Earnings per share; EPS = Price / P/E
cards.example: OUTD at $40.00 with a P/E of 15: EPS = 40 / 15 = about $2.67.
cards.say_it: A P/E of 15 means investors pay $15 for every $1 of yearly earnings, which I would compare with other outdoor retailers before calling it cheap or expensive.

cards.core: New securities are sold to investors in the primary market and then traded among investors in the secondary market.
cards.detail: In the primary market, the issuing company receives the money, usually with an investment bank underwriting the sale (an initial public offering is the first sale of stock to the public). In the secondary market, investors buy and sell from each other on exchanges; the company receives nothing from these trades, but an active secondary market makes its securities liquid and gives a market price. This liquidity is why investors are willing to buy new issues.
cards.example: When Lakeshore Brewing sells new shares in its IPO, it gets the cash; when an investor later sells those shares on an exchange, the cash goes to the selling investor.
cards.say_it: Our company only receives money when shares are first issued; after that, stock price changes affect our owners' wealth, not our cash.

examples.title: Lakeshore Brewing: governance and compliance before an IPO

cards.core: Higher expected returns come with higher risk of losing money; safety and liquidity cost return.
cards.detail: Investors demand extra return for taking extra risk. Treasury bills pay little because they are nearly risk free; stocks have higher long-run returns but can drop sharply in a single year. Liquidity, how fast an investment becomes cash without losing value, also matters: money needed soon should not be in investments whose price swings. Inflation risk works the other way: keeping long-term money only in cash loses buying power.
cards.example: Oakridge's stock (OUTD) pays a 3% dividend but swung between $31.50 and $48.20 in a year, about 35% from high to low; a T-bill pays less but cannot lose that much in 6 months.
cards.say_it: A 3% dividend is attractive, but a 35% price drop could wipe out years of dividends right when we need the cash, so the risk does not fit a six-month need.
cards.mistakes: Comparing a stock's dividend yield to a savings rate while ignoring that the stock's price can fall.

cards.core: Investors research securities through SEC EDGAR filings, company investor sites, brokerages and financial news.
cards.detail: SEC EDGAR is a free online database of public company filings: the 10-K (audited annual report), 10-Q (quarterly report), 8-K (major events) and proxy statements. Company investor relations websites post earnings releases and presentations. Brokerage platforms offer research reports, ratings and screening tools. Financial news and market data services (newspapers, websites, apps) publish prices and stock tables. Good investors rely on official filings first and treat social media tips with caution.
cards.example: Before buying a stock, Oakridge's controller reads the company's latest 10-K on EDGAR for audited results and the 10-Q for the most recent quarter.
cards.say_it: I start with the company's 10-K on EDGAR because it contains audited financial statements, then check the latest 10-Q and news.

cards.core: Treasury bills (one year or less), notes (2 to 10 years) and bonds (20 to 30 years) are U.S. government debt.
cards.detail: Treasury securities are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, so they are considered the safest investments in dollars. Treasury bills are sold at a discount and pay face value at maturity (the difference is the interest). Notes and bonds pay interest every six months. Their rates are benchmarks for the whole economy. Because T-bills mature quickly and trade easily, a company can count them as cash equivalents when they mature within three months of purchase.
cards.example: A $10,000 26-week T-bill bought for $9,800 pays $10,000 at maturity: $200 of interest, about 2% for half a year.
cards.say_it: Treasury bills give us near-zero credit risk and can be sold any day, which fits money we need back in six months.

cards.core: Common investments are savings and CDs, bonds, stocks, mutual funds and ETFs, and real estate.
cards.detail: Savings accounts, money market accounts and certificates of deposit (CDs) are low risk and low return. Bonds are loans to governments or companies that pay interest and repay the face value at maturity. Stocks are ownership shares that can pay dividends and rise or fall in price. Mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) pool many investors' money into a diversified portfolio. Real estate earns rent and appreciation but is hard to sell quickly. Commodities and alternatives are riskier. The right choice depends on the goal, time horizon and risk tolerance.
cards.example: Money needed in 6 months belongs in a CD or Treasury bills; money for retirement in 40 years can go into a stock index fund.
cards.say_it: I match the investment to when we need the money: short-term cash in safe, liquid investments and only long-term money in stocks.

cards.core: A ratio means little alone; compare it with past results, the budget, the industry average or competitors.
cards.detail: Trend analysis compares the same ratio over several periods to show improvement or decline. Industry comparison shows how the company stacks up against similar businesses (from trade associations or financial data services). Budget comparison shows whether results met the plan. Competitor comparison shows relative strength. Look for ratios that all point the same way before drawing a conclusion.
cards.example: Bayside vs. industry: current ratio 1.2 vs. 1.5, quick ratio 0.53 vs. 0.8, debt ratio 80% vs. 60%, net margin 2% vs. 4%: every ratio is weaker, so the credit risk is clearly higher than normal.
cards.say_it: Every one of Bayside's ratios is worse than the industry average, and its payment history agrees, so this is a consistent warning, not one bad number.

cards.term: Judging how a business is doing
cards.core: Judge performance by looking at profit, margins, cash, debt and trends, then compare with a benchmark.
cards.detail: Questions to answer: Is there net income, and is it growing? What is the profit margin and gross margin? Does the business have enough cash and current assets to pay current liabilities? How much is financed by debt? Is cash from operations positive? Then compare with the company's own past, its budget, the industry average or a competitor. Close with the strengths, the concerns and one or two actions. This is a frequent judge question.
cards.example: Hodges and Sons in 2015: net income $502,126 on $540,253 of revenue (a 93% margin), $502,126 of cash and only $17,020 of liabilities: very profitable and very liquid.
cards.say_it: The client had an excellent year: it kept about 93 cents of every revenue dollar and has almost no debt, so my only suggestion is to put some of that idle cash to work.

cards.core: Profit margin = Net income / Total revenue: the cents of profit kept from each sales dollar.
cards.detail: Profit (net profit) margin measures profitability relative to sales. A higher margin is more favorable, but what counts as good depends on the industry: grocery stores earn a few percent, software companies much more. To improve it, raise prices, increase volume to spread fixed costs, or cut variable and fixed costs. Always benchmark it against the company's past results, the industry average or a competitor.
cards.formula: Profit margin = Net income / Total revenue x 100
cards.example: Canine Condos: $2,858 / $38,000 = 7.5%, about 8 cents of profit per dollar of boarding revenue. Bayside: $18,000 / $900,000 = 2%, half the 4% industry average.
cards.say_it: Canine Condos keeps about 8 cents of profit from every dollar of boarding revenue, and I would compare that with other boarding businesses before calling it good or weak.

cards.core: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities: the ability to pay short-term debts.
cards.detail: A current ratio above 1 means current assets exceed current liabilities. Many lenders like 1.5 to 2, but it varies by industry. Too low signals possible trouble paying bills; very high may mean idle cash or too much inventory. Working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) is the same idea in dollars. It is a key ratio for creditors and suppliers deciding whether to extend credit.
cards.formula: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities; Working capital = Current assets minus Current liabilities
cards.example: Bayside: $180,000 / $150,000 = 1.2 (industry 1.5); working capital $30,000.
cards.say_it: Bayside has only $1.20 of current assets for every dollar it owes in the next year, below the industry's $1.50, so paying us on time will be tight.

cards.core: Debt ratio = Total liabilities / Total assets; debt-to-equity = Total liabilities / Total equity.
cards.detail: These leverage (solvency) ratios show how much of the business is financed with borrowed money. Higher leverage means more required payments and less cushion if sales fall, so lenders charge more or say no, and covenants often cap the ratio. Some debt is healthy because it lets a business grow, but the cash flow must be able to carry it.
cards.formula: Debt ratio = Total liabilities / Total assets; Debt-to-equity = Total liabilities / Total equity
cards.example: Bayside: $400,000 / $500,000 = 80% debt ratio (industry 60%); debt-to-equity = $400,000 / $100,000 = 4.0. Swift Route avoids a loan because $200,000 more debt would raise debt-to-equity past its covenant.
cards.say_it: Eighty percent of Bayside's assets are financed by creditors, so we would be one more lender standing in line if its sales slow down.

cards.core: Quick ratio = (Cash + short-term investments + receivables) / Current liabilities, leaving out inventory.
cards.detail: The quick ratio is a stricter liquidity test because inventory and prepaid items may not turn into cash quickly. A quick ratio near 1 means the business could pay current debts without selling inventory. A company with a decent current ratio but a low quick ratio has much of its current assets tied up in inventory.
cards.formula: Quick ratio = (Cash + Short-term investments + Accounts receivable) / Current liabilities
cards.example: Bayside: ($30,000 cash + $50,000 receivables) / $150,000 = 0.53 (industry 0.8), because most of its current assets are inventory.
cards.say_it: Without selling inventory, Bayside could cover only 53 cents of each dollar it owes soon, which is why I would not approve the full line.

cards.core: An annual report presents a year's audited financial statements, notes and management's discussion to owners, members and other outside users.
cards.detail: A typical annual report includes a letter from the leader (CEO or board chair), highlights of the year, management's discussion and analysis (MD&A) of results and risks, the independent auditor's report, the financial statements (balance sheet, income statement, statement of cash flows, statement of equity), and notes explaining policies and estimates. Public companies also file a more detailed Form 10-K with the SEC. Nonprofits include their statement of financial position, statement of activities and often charts of income sources and expense categories. Users include investors, lenders, donors, members and regulators.
cards.example: Society for Marketers' annual report: the completed audit, the Statement of Financial Position, the Statement of Activities, and pie charts of major income sources and expense categories for members, donors and funders.
cards.say_it: The annual report is how we show members and donors, in one place, that our finances are audited, healthy and tied to our mission.

cards.core: The balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and owner's equity at one point in time and proves the accounting equation.
cards.detail: Also called the statement of financial position, it is a snapshot dated a single day (for example, December 31). Assets are resources with future value the company owns or controls; liabilities are debts owed to others; owner's equity is the owner's claim. Items are grouped as current (within one year) and long-term so readers can judge liquidity and solvency. Ending capital from the statement of owner's equity appears in the equity section. Lenders use it to judge whether the business can repay.
cards.example: Hodges and Sons at December 31, 2015: assets $769,001 (cash $502,126, receivables $1,875, equipment $265,000) = liabilities $17,020 + owner's equity $751,981.
cards.say_it: The balance sheet shows that on December 31 the business owned $769,001 and owed only $17,020, so it is in a very strong position.

cards.core: The income statement reports revenue, expenses and net income or loss over a period of time.
cards.detail: Also called the profit and loss (P&L) statement, it answers "Did we make money this period?" It lists only revenue and expense accounts: assets, liabilities, owner's capital and withdrawals are left out. The heading names the period (for the month ended, for the year ended). Net income flows into the statement of owner's equity (or retained earnings). It should be prepared at least monthly so managers can act on prices, volume and costs.
cards.example: Canine Condos: boarding revenue $38,000 minus expenses $35,142 = net income $2,858 for four months.
cards.say_it: The income statement shows performance over a period, so it tells us whether the four months were profitable, while the balance sheet shows where we stand on one day.

cards.core: Net income = total revenue minus total expenses; a negative result is a net loss.
cards.detail: Net income is the bottom line: the profit earned in a period after all expenses. It increases owner's equity; a net loss decreases it. Owner withdrawals, loan principal payments and asset purchases are not expenses, so they do not reduce net income. Under accrual accounting, net income is not the same as the change in cash.
cards.formula: Net income = Revenue minus Expenses
cards.example: Sam's Barbershop: service revenue $27,100 minus expenses $19,990 (rent $8,470, supplies $680, advertising $970, insurance $5,570, utilities $4,300) = $7,110 before adjustments.
cards.say_it: Net income is $7,110 for the year, but that is before adjusting entries, so the final figure will be lower once we record used-up prepaid rent and insurance.
cards.mistakes: Subtracting owner's drawings as an expense.

cards.core: Owner's equity is the owner's claim on the assets: investment plus net income minus withdrawals and losses.
cards.detail: For a sole proprietorship, equity is shown as Owner's Capital; for a corporation it is stockholders' equity, made up of contributed capital (common stock) and retained earnings. Equity increases with owner investments and net income and decreases with withdrawals (dividends for a corporation) and net losses. It is also simply total assets minus total liabilities. A debit balance in capital is a warning sign that losses or withdrawals exceed investment, or that there is an error.
cards.example: Timber Valley Landscaping: an extra $40,000 of net income raises owner's equity by $40,000. Dance Frenzy's capital showed an impossible $1,078,756 debit until the closing errors were fixed.
cards.say_it: Every dollar of profit you leave in the business increases your equity, which is your ownership stake in what the business has.

cards.core: Net income and cash flow differ because of credit sales, unpaid bills, inventory, depreciation and loan payments.
cards.detail: Under accrual accounting, a sale on account raises net income before any cash arrives; an unpaid bill lowers net income before cash leaves; buying inventory uses cash before it becomes an expense; depreciation lowers income with no cash paid; loan principal payments and owner withdrawals use cash without being expenses. A profitable company can run out of cash, and a company with lots of cash can be unprofitable. That is why owners need both the income statement and a cash summary.
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us spent $200 restocking food inventory: it is a cash payment but not yet an expense, because cost of goods sold is recorded only when the food is sold.
cards.say_it: We can be profitable and still short of cash if customers pay slowly, so I watch receivables and the cash budget as closely as net income.
