cards.core: Bonds are long-term debt sold to investors that pay interest at a stated rate and repay face value at maturity.
cards.detail: If the market rate is higher than the stated rate, bonds sell at a discount (below face); if lower, at a premium (above face). The discount or premium is amortized over the bond's life, adjusting interest expense. Entry at issue below face: debit Cash, debit Discount on Bonds Payable, credit Bonds Payable at face. Bonds Payable is reported net of the discount (carrying value).
cards.formula: Cash interest = Face value x Stated rate x Time | Interest expense = Cash interest + Discount amortized
cards.example: $100,000 of 10-year 6% bonds sold at 98: debit Cash $98,000, debit Discount on Bonds Payable $2,000, credit Bonds Payable $100,000. Semiannual cash interest $3,000; straight-line discount amortization $2,000 / 20 = $100; interest expense $3,100.
cards.say_it: Investors paid only $98,000 because our 6% rate is below the market rate, so the $2,000 discount becomes extra interest expense over the bond's life.

pis.text: Account for long-term liabilities (e.g., bonds payable, notes payable, leases, etc.)

cards.core: Under current U.S. GAAP, most leases over 12 months put a right-of-use asset and a lease liability on the balance sheet.
cards.detail: Since ASC 842, lessees record the present value of lease payments as a lease liability and a matching right-of-use asset, so leasing no longer keeps debt off the books. Short-term leases of 12 months or less can be kept off the balance sheet. Like loans, the lease liability is split into current and long-term portions.
cards.formula: Lease liability = Present value of lease payments
cards.example: Harbor Fresh lease: 5 payments of $23,000 at 6%, PV = $23,000 x 4.2124 = $96,885, recorded as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
cards.say_it: Leasing would not hide the debt from the bank, because the lease also goes on the balance sheet at about $96,885.
cards.mistakes: Claiming a lease keeps the obligation off the balance sheet under current GAAP.

cards.term: Loss contingencies: probable, reasonably possible, remote
cards.core: Accrue a loss that is probable and can be estimated, disclose one that is reasonably possible, and ignore one that is remote.
cards.detail: A loss contingency is a possible loss that depends on a future event, such as the outcome of a lawsuit, from something that already happened. U.S. GAAP (ASC 450) asks two questions: how likely is the loss, and can it be reasonably estimated? Probable and estimable: record a journal entry (debit Loss, credit Estimated Liability) and describe it in the notes. Reasonably possible (or probable but not estimable): no entry, but disclose the nature and possible amount in the notes. Remote: no entry and usually no disclosure. Gain contingencies are not recorded until realized.
cards.example: Nexus Appliances: the probable class action is accrued; the reasonably possible $100,000 patent claim is disclosed only; the remote distributor claim is ignored.
cards.say_it: Recording the class action is not admitting guilt; it tells lenders and investors about a probable cash outflow so they are not misled.
cards.mistakes: Accruing a reasonably possible loss, or leaving a probable loss off the books to protect a bonus.

cards.term: Present value in borrow or lease decisions
cards.core: Compare financing options by present value, not total cash paid, because money paid later is worth less today.
cards.detail: The present value of a single future amount uses a present value of $1 factor; a series of equal payments uses an annuity factor. Discounting all cash flows at the same rate puts options on equal terms. Include any residual value you keep when buying. Higher interest rates lower present values and make new borrowing and leasing more expensive.
cards.formula: PV = Future amount x PV factor | PV of annuity = Payment x Annuity factor
cards.example: Harbor Fresh: lease PV $96,885; buying costs $100,000 minus PV of $20,000 residual ($20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946) = $85,054, so buying is about $11,831 cheaper.
cards.say_it: Even though the loan pays out $118,000 versus $115,000 for the lease, buying is cheaper in present value terms because we keep a truck worth $20,000.
cards.mistakes: Comparing total payments and ignoring timing and residual value.

cards.core: Restructuring costs such as severance and lease exit costs are recorded as liabilities when the obligation is actually incurred.
cards.detail: A restructuring is a planned change such as closing a plant, exiting a product line or cutting staff. Under U.S. GAAP (ASC 420), a liability for exit costs is recorded when it is incurred, for example when one-time termination benefits have been communicated to the affected employees, not merely when management approves a plan. IFRS (IAS 37) records a provision once there is a detailed formal plan and the company has created a valid expectation by announcing it. Costs of continuing operations, such as retraining kept staff or new marketing, are not part of the provision.
cards.example: A company tells 20 employees in November that their jobs end in January with $3,000 severance each and no further service required. It records Dr Restructuring Expense 60,000, Cr Severance Liability 60,000 in November.
cards.say_it: We record the severance when we have actually communicated it to the employees, because that is when the obligation exists under U.S. GAAP.
cards.mistakes: Recording a big restructuring reserve before any obligation exists, which can be used to manage future earnings.

cards.core: Accumulated depreciation is a contra asset holding all depreciation to date; cost minus accumulated depreciation is book value.
cards.detail: Depreciation is credited to Accumulated Depreciation instead of the asset so the original cost stays visible. It has a normal credit balance and is shown under the asset on the balance sheet. Book value (carrying value) is the undepreciated cost, not market value. When book value reaches salvage value, depreciation stops.
cards.formula: Book value = Cost minus Accumulated depreciation
cards.example: Monaco: $1,200 minus $400 = $800 after Year 1. Titan DDB: $120,000 minus $76,800 = $43,200 after Year 2.
cards.say_it: We keep the $1,200 cost on the books and show the $400 of depreciation separately, so you can see both what you paid and how much has been used up.
cards.mistakes: Crediting the Equipment account directly for depreciation.

cards.core: Depreciation spreads the cost of a long-term asset over the years it helps earn revenue.
cards.detail: It applies the matching principle: part of the cost is expensed each year of the useful life. It is an allocation of cost, not a measure of market value. It needs three inputs: cost, estimated useful life and salvage (residual) value. Land is never depreciated. Depreciation is a non-cash expense: it lowers net income but uses no cash.
cards.formula: Depreciable cost = Cost minus Salvage value
cards.example: Timber Valley: $50,000 equipment, 5 years, no salvage = $10,000 a year; with $50,000 of added sales, net income rises $40,000 a year.
cards.say_it: Depreciation does not use cash each year; it just spreads the cost of the equipment over the years it helps you earn money.
cards.mistakes: Depreciating land, or thinking book value equals what the asset could be sold for.

cards.core: Straight-line gives equal depreciation each year; double-declining-balance takes twice the straight-line rate on the remaining book value.
cards.detail: Straight-line: (cost minus salvage value) / useful life. Double-declining-balance (DDB): rate = 2 / useful life, applied to beginning book value; salvage is ignored in the formula, but depreciation stops when book value reaches salvage. Entry each year: debit Depreciation Expense, credit Accumulated Depreciation. Book value = cost minus accumulated depreciation. Total depreciation over the life is the same; DDB just moves expense earlier. Choose the method that matches how the asset is used up, not to manage earnings; tax returns use MACRS regardless.
cards.formula: Straight-line = (Cost minus Salvage) / Life; DDB = (2 / Life) x Beginning book value
cards.example: Titan Hauling tractor, $120,000 cost, $20,000 salvage, 5 years: straight-line $20,000 a year. DDB 40%: Year 1 $48,000, Year 2 40% x 72,000 = $28,800, book value $43,200.
cards.say_it: Double-declining-balance doesn't lower total depreciation; it just records more of it in the early years when the tractor works hardest.
cards.mistakes: Subtracting salvage value before applying the DDB rate, or depreciating below salvage value.

cards.core: To record a sale, update depreciation, remove the asset and its accumulated depreciation, record the cash, and book a gain or loss.
cards.detail: Gain or loss = cash received minus book value. The entry debits Cash and Accumulated Depreciation, credits the asset at original cost, and credits Gain on Sale (or debits Loss on Sale) for the difference. Gains and losses on disposal appear in the other revenues and gains (or other expenses and losses) section of a multi-step income statement, below operating income. Scrapping an asset with no proceeds is a loss equal to its book value.
cards.formula: Gain (loss) = Proceeds minus Book value
cards.example: Titan sells the tractor for $45,000; book value $43,200; gain $1,800: debit Cash $45,000, debit Accumulated Depreciation $76,800, credit Tractor $120,000, credit Gain on Sale $1,800.
cards.say_it: We sold the tractor for $1,800 more than its book value, so we record a gain, and it appears below operating income because selling tractors is not our main business.
cards.mistakes: Comparing the sale price with original cost instead of book value.

cards.core: If an asset's carrying value cannot be recovered from its future cash flows, write it down to fair value and record an impairment loss.
cards.detail: Under U.S. GAAP (ASC 360) a triggering event (new regulations, damage, falling demand) starts a two-step test. Step 1 (recoverability): compare carrying value with undiscounted future cash flows; if cash flows are lower, the asset is impaired. Step 2 (measurement): loss = carrying value minus fair value. The loss is a non-cash charge in operating income, the written-down value becomes the new basis for depreciation, and U.S. GAAP does not allow reversal (IFRS does).
cards.formula: Impaired if Carrying value > Undiscounted cash flows | Loss = Carrying value minus Fair value
cards.example: Horizon drones: carrying value $150,000 > cash flows $140,000, so impaired; loss $150,000 minus $110,000 = $40,000: debit Impairment Loss $40,000, credit Accumulated Depreciation $40,000. Next year depreciation $110,000 / 4 = $27,500 instead of $37,500.
cards.say_it: If the cash flows had been $160,000, the drones would pass Step 1 and we would record no impairment at all, even though fair value is lower.
cards.mistakes: Using fair value in Step 1 instead of undiscounted cash flows.

cards.core: If an asset is owned for only part of the year, multiply the annual depreciation by months owned divided by 12.
cards.detail: Assets bought or sold during the year are depreciated only for the months they were in use. Companies often round to the nearest month (bought by the 15th counts as a full month). Depreciation must be brought up to date on the date of disposal before figuring a gain or loss.
cards.formula: Depreciation = Annual depreciation x Months owned / 12
cards.example: Monaco office equipment bought April 1: $400 x 9 / 12 = $300 for the first year.
cards.say_it: Since the equipment was only used for nine months this year, we record nine months of depreciation, $300, not the full $400.

cards.term: Recording the cost of a long-term asset
cards.core: Record a long-term asset at its full cost, including every amount needed to get it ready for use.
cards.detail: Cost includes the purchase price, sales tax, freight, installation, setup and testing. Land cost includes the price, closing costs and costs to clear or prepare the land. Interest on a loan and later repairs are expenses, not part of the cost. The entry debits the asset and credits Cash, Accounts Payable or Notes Payable.
cards.formula: Cost = Price + Tax + Freight + Installation + Testing
cards.example: Equipment priced $48,000 with $1,200 freight and $800 installation is recorded at $50,000: debit Equipment $50,000, credit Accounts Payable $50,000.
cards.say_it: The freight and installation were needed to get the machine working, so they are part of its cost and will be depreciated with it.
cards.mistakes: Expensing freight and installation on a new machine.

cards.core: Straight-line depreciation charges the same amount every year: cost minus salvage, divided by useful life.
cards.detail: It is the simplest and most common method and fits assets that are used evenly over time. The adjusting entry is debit Depreciation Expense, credit Accumulated Depreciation. A longer useful life lowers yearly expense and raises net income in each year.
cards.formula: Annual depreciation = (Cost minus Salvage value) / Useful life
cards.example: Monaco: $1,200 / 3 = $400 a year. Titan: ($120,000 minus $20,000) / 5 = $20,000. Timber Valley with a 10 year life: $50,000 / 10 = $5,000, so yearly net income would be $45,000 instead of $40,000.
cards.say_it: With a 10 year life the yearly depreciation drops to $5,000, so each year shows more profit, but the total cost is the same.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting to subtract salvage value.

cards.core: Long-term assets are tangible (property, plant and equipment), intangible (patents, trademarks, goodwill) or natural resources (timber, oil, minerals).
cards.detail: They are used in the business for more than one year and are not held for sale. Tangible assets are depreciated (except land), intangible assets with limited lives are amortized, and natural resources are depleted as they are extracted. All are recorded at cost and reported on the balance sheet at book value. They must be tested for impairment when events suggest their value has dropped.
cards.formula: Tangible: depreciation | Intangible: amortization | Natural resources: depletion
cards.example: Titan Hauling's tractor and Horizon Delivery's drones are tangible; a patent for a battery design is intangible; a gravel pit is a natural resource.
cards.say_it: The drones are tangible long-term assets, so we spread their cost over their useful life with depreciation instead of expensing them all at once.

cards.core: Units-of-activity depreciation charges cost per unit of use, such as per mile or machine hour.
cards.detail: It fits assets whose wear depends on use rather than time, like delivery trucks or production machines. First find the rate per unit, then multiply by the units used this year. Expense rises in busy years and falls in slow years.
cards.formula: Rate = (Cost minus Salvage) / Total estimated units | Depreciation = Rate x Units used
cards.example: A truck costs $50,000 with $5,000 salvage and 150,000 expected miles: $45,000 / 150,000 = $0.30 a mile; driven 30,000 miles, depreciation is $9,000.
cards.say_it: Because your truck wears out with miles, not years, charging depreciation per mile matches the cost to how hard you used it.

cards.core: Amortization spreads the cost of an intangible asset with a limited life over that life, usually straight-line.
cards.detail: Intangible assets have no physical form: patents (legal life 20 years), copyrights, trademarks, franchises, software and customer lists. Purchased intangibles are recorded at cost; most internally developed ones (research costs) are expensed under U.S. GAAP. Intangibles with indefinite lives, such as goodwill and some trademarks, are not amortized but tested for impairment (private companies may elect to amortize goodwill).
cards.formula: Annual amortization = Cost / Useful life
cards.example: A company buys a patent for $60,000 with a 10 year useful life: debit Amortization Expense $6,000, credit Patent (or Accumulated Amortization) $6,000 each year.
cards.say_it: The patent will protect our product for 10 years, so we expense $6,000 of its cost each year it helps us earn revenue.
cards.mistakes: Amortizing goodwill as a public company, or using the legal life when the useful life is shorter.

cards.core: Companies use GAAP methods for their books but MACRS for U.S. tax returns, so the book method does not change cash taxes.
cards.detail: MACRS (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System) is the IRS depreciation system, with set recovery periods and no salvage value; bonus depreciation and Section 179 can speed deductions further. The book method should reflect how the asset is used up. Differences between book and tax depreciation are temporary and create deferred tax amounts on the balance sheet. Choosing a book method to manage earnings is unethical.
cards.example: Titan believes DDB will cut its tax bill, but its tax return uses MACRS either way; DDB only lowers reported pre-tax book income by $28,000 in Year 1.
cards.say_it: Your tax return uses MACRS no matter which method we use on the books, so we should choose the book method that best matches how the tractor wears out.
cards.mistakes: Believing the book depreciation method sets the tax deduction.

cards.core: Depletion spreads the cost of a natural resource over the units extracted, like units-of-activity depreciation.
cards.detail: Natural resources such as timber, oil, gas and minerals are used up as they are removed. Find a rate per unit (cost minus salvage, divided by total estimated units), then multiply by units extracted. The cost of units extracted but not yet sold stays in inventory.
cards.formula: Depletion rate = (Cost minus Salvage) / Total estimated units | Depletion = Rate x Units extracted
cards.example: A gravel pit costs $500,000 with $50,000 salvage and 900,000 tons: rate $0.50 a ton; 90,000 tons extracted = $45,000 depletion.
cards.say_it: We charge depletion for each ton we dig out, because the pit is literally being used up as we sell the gravel.

cards.core: Double-declining-balance multiplies beginning book value by twice the straight-line rate, so depreciation is highest in early years.
cards.detail: It is an accelerated method for assets that lose usefulness quickly. Rate = 2 / useful life. Salvage is ignored in the formula, but book value may never go below salvage, so the last years' depreciation is limited to the amount that brings book value down to salvage. It lowers reported income early and raises it later; total depreciation over the life is the same as straight-line.
cards.formula: DDB depreciation = Beginning book value x (2 / Useful life)
cards.say_it: Double-declining puts more cost in the early years, when the tractor is newest and most productive, but it can never take book value below the $20,000 salvage value.
cards.mistakes: Subtracting salvage before applying the DDB rate.

cards.core: Analyze past sales and customer data for patterns, then forecast demand to plan staffing, purchases and budgets.
cards.detail: Data mining looks at stored data from many angles (by day, hour, season, product, customer type) to find useful patterns. Trend analysis and regression project future results from past data. Good forecasts reduce costly mistakes in both directions: too much staff or inventory wastes money, too little loses sales. Present forecasts with expected, pessimistic and optimistic cases, and never give a lender only the optimistic one.
cards.example: Rocking Ribs mines past sales to match low-season staff and meat orders to actual traffic, because meat cooked 14 hours ahead and not sold is wasted. Peak Performance Gym projects 694 members for its bank forecast.
cards.say_it: Our sales history shows when customers actually come and what they order, so we can schedule and order to match instead of guessing.

cards.core: Managerial accounting gives internal managers cost and performance information to plan, control and decide.
cards.detail: It measures, analyzes and reports the cost, profitability and performance of products, departments and decisions. Typical reports: budgets, cost of each product or service, cost-volume-profit analysis, variance reports, segment margins, special order and make or buy analyses. Unlike financial accounting, it is not bound by GAAP, is future focused, can be as detailed or as frequent as needed, and can include non-financial measures like defect rates or cycle time.
cards.example: Rocking Ribs uses cost data to decide low-season staffing; FitTech uses segment margins to decide whether to keep its shoe division.
cards.say_it: Managerial accounting is about decisions, so I will show only the costs that change with your choice and leave out the ones that stay the same either way.

cards.core: Absorption costing puts fixed factory overhead in product cost; variable costing expenses it in the period.
cards.detail: Absorption (full) costing, required for external reports and taxes, includes direct materials, direct labor, variable overhead and fixed manufacturing overhead in each unit. Variable (direct) costing includes only variable manufacturing costs and expenses all fixed overhead as a period cost; it is used internally because it shows contribution margin. When production exceeds sales, absorption income is higher because some fixed overhead is deferred in ending inventory.
cards.formula: Absorption income minus Variable income = Fixed overhead per unit x (Units produced minus Units sold)
cards.example: Lumen Candle: absorption income $22,000 vs. variable $14,000; difference $8,000 = 2,000 unsold candles x $4 fixed overhead each.
cards.say_it: Absorption costing made profit $8,000 higher only because we built 2,000 extra candles, not because we sold more, so I would base the bonus on variable costing income.

cards.core: Avoidable fixed costs disappear if an activity stops; unavoidable (common) fixed costs continue whatever is decided.
cards.detail: Avoidable fixed costs exist only because of a product or segment, such as a supervisor or equipment lease used only for that product, or traceable advertising. Unavoidable costs, such as allocated factory rent or headquarters salaries, are paid either way; stopping the product just reassigns them to other products. Only avoidable costs are relevant in make or buy and keep or drop decisions.
cards.example: CoreTech: the $30,000 of Component X supervisor and lease costs are avoidable, but allocated rent and depreciation ($50,000) stay, so the real saving from buying is $10,000, not $60,000.
cards.say_it: The VP's $60,000 saving counts $50,000 of rent and depreciation that will not go away; they just move to other products, so the true saving is $10,000.

cards.core: Costs to make or package a product for sale, like jars and labels, are product costs that become cost of goods sold.
cards.detail: Materials, packaging and labor used to get goods ready for sale belong to the cost of the product. They are held in inventory until the goods are sold, then become cost of goods sold, which lowers gross profit. Costs of selling (delivery to customers, advertising, market booth fees) and running the office are operating (period) expenses. Correct classification makes gross profit and pricing decisions accurate.
cards.example: Judge question at Locally Picked: "How should expenses for bottling honey be classified?" The jars, lids, labels and bottling labor are part of the cost of the honey (inventory, then cost of goods sold), not office expenses.
cards.say_it: Bottling costs are part of what it costs to make each jar of honey, so they belong in cost of goods sold, and they tell us the minimum price per jar.

cards.core: Direct costs can be traced to one product or department; indirect costs are shared and must be allocated.
cards.detail: Direct materials and direct labor are traced to each unit. Indirect costs, such as factory rent, supervisor salaries, utilities, setups and inspections (manufacturing overhead), support many products and are assigned using an allocation base. Whether a cost is direct depends on the cost object: a store manager's salary is direct to that store but indirect to each product sold there. Prime cost is direct materials plus direct labor.
cards.formula: Prime cost = Direct materials + Direct labor
cards.example: Precision Machining: direct materials $25 and direct labor $20 per valve (prime cost $45); setups and inspections are indirect overhead allocated to each valve.
cards.say_it: Materials and labor can be traced to each valve, but setups are shared, so how we allocate them changes the reported cost of each product.

cards.core: Marginal analysis compares only the extra revenue and extra cost caused by a decision.
cards.detail: If the incremental revenue from a decision exceeds its incremental cost, the decision raises profit. It is the logic behind special orders, make or buy, keep or drop, adding a product line, scheduling one more employee, transfer pricing and production levels. In economics terms, keep producing while marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost. Fixed costs that do not change are ignored.
cards.example: Northwind: buying fabric outside costs $13 a yard; making it inside with idle capacity costs $8, so transferring 20,000 yards internally saves the company 20,000 x $5 = $100,000.
cards.say_it: The only question is what changes: this order adds $35 of revenue and $32 of cost per jersey, so each one adds $3 of profit.

cards.core: Overhead covers the ongoing costs of running the business; operating costs are the materials, labor and machinery used to deliver the product.
cards.detail: Overhead costs are fairly static and tied to general business functions: rent, utilities, insurance, accounting and administrative salaries, and facility costs. Operating costs are the direct costs of making the product or delivering the service, such as materials, production labor or instructor wages, and machinery use. Both must be covered by the selling price. When opening a new location, overhead is mostly new fixed cost, while operating costs grow with the number of customers.
cards.example: Dance Frenzy's fourth studio would add overhead (rent, utilities, insurance, front desk) and operating costs (instructor wages, supplies); Jotter's overhead includes accounting staff and facility costs.
cards.say_it: Before opening another studio, we need to know the new overhead, since rent and utilities start on day one whether or not students sign up.

cards.core: Relevant costs are future costs that differ between the alternatives; only they affect the decision.
cards.detail: Differential analysis compares only the revenues and costs that change between two choices. Relevant: variable costs that will be incurred or avoided, avoidable fixed costs, and opportunity costs. Not relevant: sunk costs, allocated common costs and future costs that are the same under every option. Full absorption cost per unit is not used for these short-term decisions because it includes fixed costs that will not change.
cards.example: Velocity Athletic Gear special order: relevant costs are materials $15, labor $10, variable overhead $5 and printing $2 = $32; the $8 of fixed overhead and the $3 commission (not paid on this order) are not relevant.
cards.say_it: The $38 product cost includes $8 of fixed overhead we pay anyway, so the real cost of this order is $32 per jersey.

cards.core: A sunk cost was spent in the past and cannot be recovered, so it is never relevant to a decision.
cards.detail: Past equipment purchases (shown as depreciation), money spent on research already done, or nonrefundable deposits do not change whatever is decided now. Including them leads to bad choices, such as continuing a failing project to "not waste" past spending. Only future costs and revenues that differ between options matter.
cards.example: CoreTech's depreciation on existing equipment is a sunk cost: it continues whether CoreTech makes or buys Component X, so it is left out of the decision.
cards.say_it: We already paid for that equipment, and nothing we decide today gets that money back, so it should not affect the choice.
cards.mistakes: Refusing to change course because of money already spent.

cards.core: Keep a segment if its segment margin is positive, because dropping it loses that margin while common costs remain.
cards.detail: Step 1: compute contribution margin (sales minus variable costs). Step 2: subtract traceable fixed costs to get the segment margin. Step 3: ignore allocated common costs: they stay if the segment is dropped and are shifted to other segments. Step 4: if the segment margin is positive, dropping it lowers company profit by that amount (plus any lost sales in other segments). Step 5: consider ways to improve it and qualitative factors like linked customer purchases and morale.
cards.example: FitTech Smart Shoes: $300,000 minus $200,000 = $100,000 contribution margin, minus $60,000 traceable = $40,000 segment margin. It shows a $25,000 net loss only after a $65,000 common cost allocation, so dropping it would lower company profit by $40,000.
cards.say_it: Smart Shoes looks like a loser only because of the $65,000 allocation; it actually adds $40,000 to company profit, so we should keep it and improve it.

cards.core: Compare the relevant cost to make (variable + avoidable fixed costs) with the price to buy, then weigh the risks.
cards.detail: Relevant cost to make = variable costs + avoidable fixed costs + any opportunity cost of the space or capacity. Unavoidable allocated costs and sunk costs are left out. If the purchase price is lower, buying increases operating income by the difference x units. Then consider supplier reliability, quality control, protecting designs, and how hard it would be to restart production later. A thin margin means small price changes can reverse the decision.
cards.example: CoreTech: make $15 + $12 + $5 + $3 = $35 relevant cost vs. buy $34: buying saves $1 x 10,000 = $10,000 a year. If the supplier later charges $36, making becomes $10,000 cheaper.
cards.say_it: Buying saves $10,000 a year, but if the supplier raises the price to $36, making is cheaper again, so I would negotiate a fixed price for several years.

cards.core: Businesses and people pay with cash, checks, debit cards, credit cards and electronic funds transfers.
cards.detail: A financial exchange is any way value moves from a buyer to a seller. Cash and debit cards move money right away from what you already have; checks are written orders telling a bank to pay; credit cards and trade credit let you pay later, which creates a debt; electronic funds transfers (EFT) such as ACH, direct deposit and wire transfers move money between bank accounts without paper. For a business, each form changes how fast cash arrives, what fees are paid, and whether a receivable or payable is created.
cards.example: Dogs-R-Us takes $703 of cash and card receipts in one week; a card sale settles in the bank in a day or two, while a sale on account would sit in Accounts Receivable until the customer pays.
cards.say_it: Whichever way the customer pays, we record the sale when it is earned, but the payment method decides when the cash actually reaches our bank account and what fees we pay.
cards.mistakes: Treating a credit card sale to a customer as "credit" on the books: to the store it is a cash sale (minus the processing fee), because the card company pays the store.

cards.core: Verify each bill, pay it on time (or early for a discount) and record the payment.
cards.detail: Before paying, match the invoice to the purchase order and receiving record (a three-way match) so you only pay for what was ordered and received. Schedule payments by due date to avoid late fees and protect your credit, and take early payment discounts when they are cheaper than borrowing. Pay by check, EFT or autopay, keep the paid invoice, and record the payment: debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash. Paying late hurts supplier relationships and credit ratings; paying too early gives up cash you could use.
cards.example: Office Supplies Company receives a $500 web hosting invoice in October (debit Expense, credit Accounts Payable) and pays it November 15 (debit Accounts Payable $500, credit Cash $500).
cards.say_it: Our accounts payable process pays only verified invoices, on their due dates, so we keep our cash as long as possible without hurting our credit.
cards.mistakes: Paying a bill from a statement or a phone call without checking it against the purchase order and receiving report.

cards.core: An EFT moves money electronically between bank accounts with no paper check.
cards.detail: Examples of EFT are direct deposit of paychecks, ACH payments to suppliers, wire transfers, online bill pay, debit card purchases and tax deposits through the government's EFTPS system. EFT saves time, cuts postage and check printing costs and reduces the lag between paying and the payment clearing. Because there is no paper trail, a business needs strong controls: approval before sending, user logins and a monthly bank reconciliation to catch errors or fraud.
cards.example: Summit Climbing Gym deposits its federal payroll taxes through EFTPS instead of mailing a check, and ABC Manufacturing uses EFT to pay suppliers without writing checks.
cards.say_it: Switching our supplier payments to EFT saves us check and postage costs and lets us time each payment to the due date, but we will still require approval before any transfer goes out.

cards.core: Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of measure (unit of account) and a store of value.
cards.detail: As a medium of exchange, money lets people trade without bartering. As a unit of measure, it gives every item a common price, which is why accounting records only transactions that can be measured in dollars (the money measurement concept). As a store of value, money can be saved and spent later, although inflation slowly reduces what it can buy. These functions explain why a business keeps its books in one currency and why idle cash should earn interest.
cards.example: Hodges and Sons records its DJ equipment at $265,000 because dollars are the common unit of measure; the owner's skill or the brand name is not recorded because it cannot be measured reliably in money.
cards.say_it: Because money is our unit of measure, the financial statements only show things we can put a dollar amount on, so I also look at non-financial facts like customer loyalty.

cards.core: Stamping "For deposit only" on the back of a check means it can only be deposited to the business account.
cards.detail: An endorsement is the signature on the back of a check that transfers it. A blank endorsement (just a signature) lets anyone cash it if it is lost. A restrictive endorsement such as "For deposit only to ABC Manufacturing" limits the check to deposit in the company account, which protects against theft. It is a basic cash control, along with depositing receipts promptly and separating the person who opens mail from the person who records payments.
cards.example: In ABC Manufacturing's cash control training, every check received is stamped "For deposit only" the moment the mail is opened.
cards.say_it: We should stamp every incoming check with a restrictive endorsement right away, because cash is our most liquid asset and the easiest to steal.

cards.core: Financial institutions move money from savers to borrowers, process payments and manage risk.
cards.detail: Financial institutions act as intermediaries: they collect deposits and premiums from savers and lend or invest them with businesses, governments and households who need funds. They also run the payment system (checks, cards, EFT), keep money safe, pool and spread risk, and give advice. Banks earn mainly the spread between the interest they earn on loans and the interest they pay on deposits. Because the system depends on trust, banks are regulated and deposits are insured by the FDIC (credit unions by the NCUA), generally up to $250,000 per depositor per bank.
cards.example: Harborview Community Bank earns 5% on $200 million of loans and pays 2% on $180 million of deposits, which is how it makes money as an intermediary.
cards.say_it: Banks connect people who have extra money with people who need it, and they earn the difference between the two interest rates.

cards.core: Compare providers on safety, services, fees, interest rates, convenience and customer service.
cards.detail: Start with what you need: checking, savings, loans, payroll services, merchant card processing, investment accounts or online access. Then compare: safety (FDIC or NCUA insurance, financial strength), fees (monthly, overdraft, ATM, wire), interest paid on deposits and charged on loans, minimum balances, branch and ATM locations, mobile and online tools, integration with accounting software, and the quality of service and advice. A business also values a banker who knows it when it needs a loan.
cards.example: A small store choosing between a bank charging $15 a month with free payroll deposits and a credit union with no fee but no bank feed to its accounting software should weigh the time saved by the feed.
cards.say_it: I would choose the bank that connects to our accounting software and offers a line of credit, even if the fee is slightly higher, because it saves time and gives us a relationship for future loans.

cards.core: Banks, credit unions, brokerages, insurers and investment banks each handle money for others in different ways.
cards.detail: Commercial banks take deposits, make loans and offer checking, savings, CDs and business services. Credit unions are member-owned nonprofits offering similar services, often with lower fees. Savings institutions focus on savings and home loans. Brokerage firms buy and sell stocks, bonds and funds for investors. Insurance companies protect against losses and invest the premiums they collect. Investment banks help companies raise money by issuing stocks and bonds (for example in an IPO). Finance companies and fintech apps lend or process payments, often to riskier borrowers or online.
cards.example: Oakridge Outfitters could hold its idle $500,000 in a 6-month CD at its commercial bank or buy Treasury bills through a brokerage firm.
cards.say_it: Each institution has a different role: our bank handles daily cash and loans, a brokerage handles investments, and an investment bank would only matter if we went public.

cards.core: A check shows the date, payee, amount in numbers and words, a memo and an authorized signature.
cards.detail: To write a check, fill in the date, the payee's exact name, the amount in figures and in words (the words control if they differ), a memo explaining the purpose, and sign it. Record it right away in the check register so the book balance stays accurate. Business controls for checks include prenumbered checks, signature cards on file at the bank, approval of the invoice before signing, two signatures above a set amount, and never signing blank checks.
cards.example: ABC Manufacturing keeps signature cards on file and requires check approval before signing; a $2,000 check written on the 28th that has not cleared appears on the bank reconciliation as an outstanding check.
cards.say_it: Every check we write should match an approved invoice and be recorded immediately, so our checkbook balance is always reliable.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting to record a check in the register, which makes the book balance too high.

cards.core: Banks are for-profit and owned by shareholders; credit unions are nonprofit cooperatives owned by their members.
cards.detail: Both offer checking, savings, loans and cards. Banks serve anyone, often have larger branch and ATM networks, more business services and more technology. Credit unions require membership (based on employer, location or group), return profits to members through lower loan rates, higher savings rates and lower fees, but may have fewer business services. Bank deposits are insured by the FDIC and credit union deposits by the NCUA, generally up to $250,000 per depositor per institution per ownership category. Online banks offer higher rates but no branches.
cards.example: A student might choose a credit union for a low-rate car loan, while a growing retailer might choose a commercial bank for merchant services, payroll and a line of credit.
cards.say_it: For our business, a commercial bank makes sense because we need merchant services, payroll and a credit line in one place.

cards.core: A debit card spends money you already have; a credit card borrows money you must repay.
cards.detail: A debit card pulls money straight from a checking account, so there is no bill and no interest, but fraud on it takes money out of your account until the bank fixes it. A credit card is a revolving loan: you get a monthly bill, and if you do not pay the full balance by the due date you pay interest, often 20% a year or more. Used wisely, a credit card builds credit history and has stronger fraud protection; used carelessly, it creates expensive debt.
cards.example: Spending $500 on a debit card lowers your checking balance by $500 today. Spending $500 on a credit card at 24% APR and paying only interest costs about $10 a month ($500 x 24% / 12) while the $500 still remains owed.
cards.say_it: I recommend a business credit card for small purchases only if the balance is paid in full each month, so we get the record keeping and fraud protection without paying interest.
cards.mistakes: Thinking a credit card payment is "spending your own money"; it is borrowing until the bill is paid.

cards.core: FDIC and NCUA insurance protect bank and credit union deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per institution, per ownership category.
cards.detail: If an insured bank fails, the FDIC repays insured deposits (checking, savings, money market deposit accounts and CDs). It does not cover stocks, bonds, mutual funds or other investments, even if bought through a bank. Businesses with large balances spread money across institutions, use different ownership categories, or buy Treasury bills, which are backed directly by the U.S. government. Checking insurance is a key step when choosing a financial institution.
cards.example: Oakridge's $500,000 in one bank's CD would be only partly insured; splitting it between two banks or buying Treasury bills keeps all of it protected.
cards.say_it: Because $500,000 is above the $250,000 FDIC limit, I would split it across banks or use Treasury bills so every dollar is protected.

cards.core: Inflation is a general rise in prices, so each dollar buys less over time and weakens money as a store of value.
cards.detail: Inflation is usually measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI). When inflation is 3% a year, something that costs $100 today costs about $103 next year. Money kept in cash loses purchasing power, which is why savings should earn interest at least equal to inflation. The real interest rate is roughly the stated rate minus inflation. For businesses, inflation raises costs of materials and wages, so budgets and prices must be updated, and it pushes the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates.
cards.formula: Real interest rate is about Nominal rate minus Inflation rate
cards.example: A savings account paying 2% during 3% inflation has a real return of about minus 1%: the balance grows but buys less.
cards.say_it: Our cash reserve should earn at least the inflation rate, otherwise it quietly loses value even though the balance never goes down.

cards.core: Protect online financial accounts with strong unique passwords, multifactor authentication, alerts and regular review.
cards.detail: Online banking, payment apps and cloud accounting software are convenient but are targets for fraud. Good practice: use a different strong password for each account and a password manager, turn on multifactor authentication, give each user their own login with only the access their job needs, set balance and transaction alerts, review activity at least weekly, use secure networks (not public Wi-Fi) and log out on shared devices. Bank feeds connect accounting software to the bank in read-only mode, so the software can see transactions but cannot move money.
cards.example: Riverside Hardware's move to the cloud includes individual user logins, access levels and multifactor authentication before the bank feed is connected.
cards.say_it: Connecting the bank to our software is safe if we use multifactor authentication and separate logins, and the feed only reads transactions; it cannot send money.
cards.mistakes: Sharing one login among several employees, which makes it impossible to tell who changed what.

cards.core: Net interest income is interest earned on loans and investments minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings.
cards.detail: Net interest income is a bank's main source of earnings. It shrinks when deposit rates rise faster than loan rates, which happens when loans are at fixed rates and deposits reprice with the market. That mismatch is interest rate risk. Banks manage it by matching fixed and variable rates, adjusting deposit pricing, offering variable-rate loans and stress testing earnings under different rate paths.
cards.formula: Net interest income = Interest earned minus Interest paid
cards.example: Harborview: $200M x 5% = $10.0M earned minus $180M x 2% = $3.6M paid = $6.4M. If deposit costs rise to 3.5%, interest paid is $6.3M and net interest income falls to $3.7M, a 42% drop.
cards.say_it: Our loans are locked at fixed rates while our deposit costs move with the market, so a rate increase could cut net interest income by 42%.

cards.core: Currency includes coins, paper money (banknotes) and government IOUs such as Treasury bills, notes and bonds.
cards.detail: In the United States, coins are made by the U.S. Mint and paper banknotes (Federal Reserve notes) are issued by the Federal Reserve. Both are legal tender, meaning they must be accepted to pay debts. Government securities are promises by the U.S. Treasury to repay: Treasury bills mature in one year or less, Treasury notes in 2 to 10 years, and Treasury bonds in 20 or 30 years. Bills are so safe and easy to sell that businesses treat them as near cash (cash equivalents when they mature within three months).
cards.example: Oakridge Outfitters needs its $500,000 back in six months, so Treasury bills are a good place to park it: they are backed by the U.S. government and can be sold quickly.
cards.say_it: Treasury bills are almost as safe and liquid as cash, so they let idle money earn interest without putting it at risk.

cards.core: Accounts payable is money the business owes vendors for goods or services bought on credit; it is a current liability.
cards.detail: Accounts Payable increases with a credit when a purchase is made on account and decreases with a debit when the bill is paid. It is a short-term IOU, usually due in 30 to 60 days, so it appears under current liabilities. Paying on time protects the company's credit rating and lets it take purchase discounts. The accounts payable job is to pay only bills that are legitimate, accurate and approved.
cards.formula: Purchase: Dr Asset or Expense, Cr A/P | Payment: Dr A/P, Cr Cash
cards.example: Locally Picked buys a $2,000 refrigerator on account to pay in July: debit Equipment $2,000, credit Accounts Payable $2,000; in July debit Accounts Payable $2,000, credit Cash $2,000.
cards.say_it: Accounts payable is basically an IOU to our vendors, so it is a liability we must pay within the agreed terms to protect our credit.
cards.mistakes: Debiting Accounts Payable when buying on credit.

cards.term: Foreign currency payables and exchange gains or losses
cards.core: A payable owed in a foreign currency is updated to the year-end rate, and the change is a foreign exchange gain or loss.
cards.detail: At purchase, record inventory and the payable in dollars at that day's rate. At the balance sheet date, remeasure the unpaid balance at the current rate and record a foreign exchange gain or loss (U.S. GAAP). At payment, the difference between the updated payable and the dollars actually paid is another gain or loss. A forward contract locks in the rate, buying certainty rather than profit.
cards.formula: Dollar amount = Foreign currency amount x Exchange rate
cards.example: Global Imports owes 50,000 euros. Nov 15 at $1.08: Dr Inventory 54,000, Cr Accounts Payable 54,000. Dec 31 at $1.12: Dr Foreign Exchange Loss 2,000, Cr Accounts Payable 2,000. Jan 14 at $1.10: Dr Accounts Payable 56,000, Cr Cash 55,000, Cr Foreign Exchange Gain 1,000. Net cost $1,000 above plan.
cards.say_it: Because we owe euros, every move in the exchange rate changes our cost, so we update the payable at year end and report the gain or loss.

cards.core: Borrowing creates a note payable; interest is principal times annual rate times the fraction of the year.
cards.detail: When a business borrows: debit Cash, credit Notes Payable. Interest expense accrues over time and is recorded at period end even if not yet paid (debit Interest Expense, credit Interest Payable). At repayment: debit Notes Payable and Interest Payable or Interest Expense, credit Cash. Short-term notes use a 360-day banker's year in many problems. A loan raises liabilities and the debt-to-equity ratio, which can affect loan covenants.
cards.formula: Interest = Principal x Annual rate x Time (days / 360)
cards.example: Swift Route: $200,000 x 9% x 60/360 = $3,000. Borrow: Dr Cash 200,000, Cr Notes Payable 200,000. Repay: Dr Notes Payable 200,000, Dr Interest Expense 3,000, Cr Cash 203,000.
cards.say_it: The loan only costs $3,000 in interest, but it adds a $200,000 liability, which raises our debt-to-equity ratio.

cards.core: Paying a bill already recorded is debit Accounts Payable, credit Cash, with no new expense.
cards.detail: The expense or asset was recorded when the purchase was made. Payment only settles the liability. Before paying, confirm the invoice was approved and matched, check the due date and discount terms, and mark the invoice paid. Posting the payment to the vendor's account in the accounts payable subsidiary ledger keeps vendor balances current.
cards.formula: Dr A/P, Cr Cash
cards.example: Monaco Company pays $830 on account: debit Accounts Payable $830, credit Cash $830. (The bookkeeper recorded $380, so a $450 correcting entry was needed.)
cards.say_it: This payment does not create an expense, because the expense was already recorded when we received the bill; it just reduces what we owe.
cards.mistakes: Debiting an expense again when the bill is paid.

cards.core: A purchase moves through a requisition, a purchase order, a receiving report and a vendor invoice, and sometimes a voucher.
cards.detail: Purchase requisition: an internal request from a department for goods. Purchase order (PO): the official order sent to the vendor listing items, quantities and prices. Receiving report: prepared when goods arrive, listing what actually came. Vendor invoice: the bill showing amount owed and credit terms. Voucher: an internal form that gathers the documents and approves payment. Each document is a control that keeps the business from paying for goods it did not order or receive.
cards.formula: Requisition, Purchase order, Receiving report, Invoice, Voucher, Payment
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop orders surfboards with a PO, counts them on a receiving report, and gets a $4,000 invoice with terms 2/10, n/30.
cards.say_it: Each document is a checkpoint, so we only pay for what we ordered, at the price we agreed, and what actually arrived.

cards.core: Under a perpetual system, purchases, returns and early payment discounts all adjust Merchandise Inventory.
cards.detail: Purchase on account: debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Accounts Payable. Return to vendor: debit Accounts Payable, credit Merchandise Inventory. Terms 2/10, n/30 mean a 2 percent discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount in 30 days. Paying within the discount period: debit Accounts Payable for the full balance, credit Cash for the amount paid and credit Merchandise Inventory for the discount, because the discount lowers the cost of the goods, not income. Taking the discount is usually worth it, since skipping 2 percent to pay 20 days later is like paying about 37 percent interest a year.
cards.formula: Discount = Balance owed x Discount rate; Cash paid = Balance minus Discount
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop pays a $3,600 balance within 10 days: discount 3,600 x 2% = $72; Dr Accounts Payable 3,600, Cr Cash 3,528, Cr Merchandise Inventory 72.
cards.say_it: We record the $72 discount as a reduction of inventory because it lowers what the surfboards really cost us.

cards.core: In a perpetual system, a purchase on account is debit Merchandise Inventory, credit Accounts Payable.
cards.detail: In a perpetual system, the cost of goods bought for resale goes straight to the Merchandise Inventory asset. (In a periodic system it is debited to a Purchases account instead.) Freight paid by the buyer (FOB shipping point) is added to inventory cost. Supplies or equipment bought on account are debited to those asset accounts instead.
cards.formula: Perpetual: Dr Merchandise Inventory, Cr A/P | Periodic: Dr Purchases, Cr A/P
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop buys surfboards for $4,000 on account, terms 2/10, n/30: debit Merchandise Inventory $4,000, credit Accounts Payable $4,000.
cards.say_it: Because we use a perpetual system, the surfboards go right into inventory, and they become cost of goods sold only when we sell them.

cards.core: A schedule of accounts payable lists each vendor's balance and its total must equal Accounts Payable in the general ledger.
cards.detail: Steps: write the heading (business name, Schedule of Accounts Payable, date), list each vendor with a credit balance from the subsidiary ledger, total the list, and compare it with the controlling account. If they differ, a posting error exists. Even a business with only two or three vendors benefits, because it proves the records agree and shows exactly who must be paid.
cards.formula: Total of vendor balances = Accounts Payable controlling account
cards.example: Piper's Pets: Kitty Litters $1,245 + Lions, Tigers, and Bears Oh My $630 + Office Super Store $2,120 = $3,995.
cards.say_it: Your schedule shows you owe three vendors $3,995 in total, and that agrees with the Accounts Payable balance on your balance sheet.

cards.core: Pay a vendor only when the purchase order, receiving report and invoice agree on items, quantities and prices.
cards.detail: The three-way match is the key control in accounts payable. It stops payment for goods never ordered, never received or billed at the wrong price, and helps catch duplicate invoices and fictitious vendors. Any difference is investigated before payment. Automated systems can perform the match electronically, but someone must still review exceptions.
cards.formula: PO = Receiving report = Invoice, then pay
cards.example: If Coastal Surf Shop ordered 10 boards, received 9 and was billed for 10, the match fails and the shop pays for 9 or asks for a credit.
cards.say_it: Before any check goes out, I compare the purchase order, the receiving report and the invoice, so we never pay for something we did not order or receive.

cards.term: Vendor file and accounts payable ledger
cards.core: Keep a file and a subsidiary ledger account for every vendor, and post each invoice and payment to it.
cards.detail: The vendor file holds contact information, tax ID (Form W-9), payment terms and approval. The accounts payable subsidiary ledger shows what is owed to each vendor; each invoice is credited and each payment debited. Only approved, verified vendors should be added, which prevents fictitious vendor fraud. At month end prepare a schedule of accounts payable and agree it to the controlling account.
cards.example: Bella Vista Bistro paid $1,850 three times to DK Supply, a vendor with only a P.O. box and no purchase orders; requiring owner approval and a W-9 before adding vendors would have stopped it.
cards.say_it: Before any new vendor is added to the system, the owner approves it and we collect a W-9, which blocks fake vendor schemes.

cards.core: Returning goods to a vendor reduces what you owe: debit Accounts Payable, credit Merchandise Inventory.
cards.detail: The buyer documents the return with a debit memo (it debits the vendor's payable account). In a perpetual system inventory is reduced; in a periodic system the credit goes to Purchases Returns and Allowances. An allowance is a price reduction for damaged goods kept. Any purchase discount is figured on the amount owed after returns.
cards.formula: Dr A/P, Cr Merchandise Inventory
cards.example: Coastal Surf Shop returns $400 of damaged boards: debit Accounts Payable $400, credit Merchandise Inventory $400; it now owes $3,600.
cards.say_it: Because we sent back $400 of damaged boards, we owe the vendor only $3,600, and the discount is figured on that lower amount.
cards.mistakes: Taking the discount on the original $4,000 instead of the amount owed after the return.

cards.core: A voucher system requires an approved voucher, backed by matched documents, before any check is written.
cards.detail: A voucher is an internal document that collects the purchase order, receiving report and invoice, records the account to charge, and is approved by an authorized person. Approved vouchers are filed by due date so payments are made on time and discounts are not missed. After payment, the voucher is marked paid so the invoice cannot be paid twice.
cards.example: A company files each approved voucher by due date; a $3,600 invoice with terms 2/10 is filed under day 10 so the $72 discount is not missed.
cards.say_it: Filing approved vouchers by due date means we pay on time, capture every discount and never pay the same invoice twice.

cards.core: Keep time cards and an earnings record for each employee showing hours, gross pay, each deduction, net pay and year-to-date totals.
cards.detail: Time cards or time sheets prove the hours worked each day and support the pay calculation. The employee earnings record summarizes every pay period and the year-to-date totals needed for wage base limits, quarterly Form 941 and year-end W-2s. Also keep each employee's Form W-4 (withholding choices) and Form I-9 (work eligibility). Keep payroll tax records at least 4 years, stored securely with limited access, because pay is confidential.
cards.example: Green Thumb Landscaping must keep timecards and an earnings record for each worker, including summer workers Chloe and Dev, and store them safely, not in the truck.
cards.say_it: The earnings record tracks each person's year-to-date pay, which tells us when they pass the unemployment tax wage base and gives us the numbers for their W-2.

cards.core: Deductions withheld from gross pay include FICA, federal and state income tax, and voluntary items like health insurance or retirement.
cards.detail: Required: Social Security 6.2% (up to the annual wage base, $184,500 for 2026), Medicare 1.45% (no limit, plus an extra 0.9% employee only on wages over $200,000), federal income tax based on the employee's Form W-4 and IRS tables, and state and local income tax where they apply. Voluntary: health insurance premiums, 401(k) contributions, union dues, charitable gifts. These amounts belong to the government or other parties, so the employer records them as liabilities until paid.
cards.formula: FICA = Social Security 6.2% + Medicare 1.45% = 7.65%
cards.example: Summit gym: Social Security 6.2% x $2,000 = $124; Medicare 1.45% x $2,000 = $29; federal income tax $170; state income tax 3% = $60; total deductions $383.
cards.say_it: The amounts we withhold are not our money, we are holding them for the government, so we record them as liabilities until we deposit them.
cards.mistakes: Applying the Social Security rate to wages above the wage base.

cards.core: Whether a worker is an employee depends on how much control the business has, not on what the owner calls them.
cards.detail: If the business controls when, where and how the work is done, provides the tools and the worker is part of the regular operation, the worker is generally an employee, and the business must withhold taxes and pay employer payroll taxes. True contractors run their own business, set their own methods, and receive Form 1099-NEC; they pay their own self-employment tax. Misclassifying employees brings back taxes, penalties and interest.
cards.example: Summit Climbing Gym sets staff schedules and trains them on gym rules, so they are employees; calling them contractors to skip payroll taxes would be misclassification.
cards.say_it: You cannot just call them contractors, because you set their hours and tell them how to work, so the IRS would treat them as employees and charge back taxes and penalties.

cards.core: The employer matches employee FICA and also pays FUTA and SUTA, which are not withheld from workers.
cards.detail: Employer FICA equals the employee's 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare. FUTA is 6.0% on the first $7,000 per employee, but with full credit for state unemployment taxes the net rate is 0.6% ($42 maximum per employee). SUTA rates and wage bases vary by state and by the employer's claims history. These are recorded as Payroll Tax Expense.
cards.formula: Employer taxes = SS 6.2% + Medicare 1.45% + FUTA 0.6% (first $7,000) + SUTA (state rate and base)
cards.example: Summit gym: Social Security $124 + Medicare $29 + FUTA 0.6% x $2,000 = $12 + SUTA 3% x $2,000 = $60, total $225.
cards.say_it: On top of the $2,000 of wages, the gym owes $225 of its own payroll taxes, so this payroll really costs $2,225.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting the employer match or withholding FUTA from employees.

cards.core: Form 941 is the quarterly federal return for withholding and FICA; Form 940 is the annual FUTA return.
cards.detail: Form 941 reports wages paid, federal income tax withheld and both shares of Social Security and Medicare for the quarter; it is due the last day of the month after each quarter (April 30, July 31, October 31, January 31). Form 940 reports annual FUTA and is due January 31. Deposits must already have been made through EFTPS; the returns reconcile them.
cards.example: Green Thumb files its fourth-quarter Form 941 and its annual Form 940 by January 31.
cards.say_it: Form 941 is our quarterly report card to the IRS showing that what we withheld and deposited match.
cards.mistakes: Mixing up which form is quarterly and which is annual.

cards.core: Every employee gets a Form W-2 by January 31, and the employer sends all W-2s with a W-3 summary to the Social Security Administration.
cards.detail: The W-2 shows the employee's yearly wages, federal and state income tax withheld, and Social Security and Medicare wages and taxes. Anyone who was an employee during the year gets one, even part-time or seasonal workers. Form W-3 totals all W-2s and must agree with the year's Forms 941. Independent contractors get Form 1099-NEC instead.
cards.example: Chloe and Dev only worked during the summer but were employees, so Green Thumb must give each a W-2 by January 31.
cards.say_it: Yes, summer workers still get W-2s, because anyone who was on payroll during the year needs one to file their tax return.

cards.core: Deposit federal income tax withheld plus both halves of FICA electronically through EFTPS on the required schedule, then clear the liabilities.
cards.detail: Federal income tax withheld and employee and employer Social Security and Medicare are deposited together through EFTPS on a monthly or semiweekly schedule based on the employer's past liability. FUTA is deposited quarterly only when it exceeds $500. SUTA and state withholding go to the state. Benefit withholdings go to the insurer or plan. Entry: debit each payable, credit Cash.
cards.formula: Dr FIT Payable, SS Tax Payable, Medicare Tax Payable | Cr Cash
cards.example: Summit gym deposit: federal income tax $170 + Social Security $124 x 2 = $248 + Medicare $29 x 2 = $58, total $476: debit the three payables, credit Cash $476.
cards.say_it: We deposit both our share and the employees' share of FICA together with the income tax withheld, through EFTPS, on time to avoid penalties.
cards.mistakes: Paying only the employee share of FICA.

cards.core: An employer's payroll cost is gross wages plus its share of FICA, FUTA, SUTA and workers' compensation insurance.
cards.detail: Gross wages are the main expense. On top, the employer pays a matching 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare (employer FICA), federal unemployment tax (FUTA) and state unemployment tax (SUTA) up to their wage bases, and workers' compensation insurance for on-the-job injuries. Benefits such as an employer share of health insurance or retirement are also payroll costs. Amounts withheld from employees (income tax, employee FICA) are not employer expenses; the business only holds and remits them.
cards.formula: Total payroll cost = Gross wages + Employer payroll taxes + Workers' comp + Employer benefits
cards.example: Summit Climbing Gym: $2,000 of gross wages plus $225 of employer taxes = $2,225 true cost. Green Thumb: $10,749.50 of employer taxes and insurance on $83,000 of wages.
cards.say_it: Hiring someone at $20 an hour really costs more than $20, because you also pay your share of FICA, unemployment taxes and workers' comp.
cards.mistakes: Counting employee withholdings as an employer expense.

cards.core: Gross earnings are regular hours times the pay rate plus overtime hours at 1.5 times the rate.
cards.detail: Under federal law, hourly (nonexempt) employees earn overtime at one and a half times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Salaried employees earn their salary per period (annual salary / number of pay periods). Commissions and bonuses are added to gross pay. Gross pay is the starting point for every deduction and payroll tax.
cards.formula: Gross pay = (Regular hours x rate) + (Overtime hours x rate x 1.5)
cards.example: Alex: 40 x $20 = $800 + 5 x $30 = $150, total $950; Brooke 35 x $18 = $630; Carlos 30 x $14 = $420; total gross payroll $2,000.
cards.say_it: Alex worked 45 hours, so the 5 hours over 40 are paid at $30, which is time and a half of his $20 rate.
cards.mistakes: Paying overtime on hours over 8 in a day instead of over 40 in a week (federal rule), or paying 1.5 times on all hours.

cards.core: Record employer taxes with debit Payroll Tax Expense and credits to Social Security, Medicare, FUTA and SUTA payable.
cards.detail: This is a second entry made with each payroll. The employer's FICA match is credited to the same Social Security and Medicare payable accounts used for employee withholdings, so those liabilities double. Workers' compensation and employer benefits are recorded as their own expenses.
cards.formula: Dr Payroll Tax Expense | Cr SS Tax Payable, Medicare Tax Payable, FUTA Payable, SUTA Payable
cards.example: Summit gym: debit Payroll Tax Expense $225; credit Social Security Tax Payable $124, Medicare Tax Payable $29, FUTA Tax Payable $12, SUTA Tax Payable $60.
cards.say_it: The $225 is the gym's own tax cost, so it is an expense, unlike the withholdings, which are the employees' money.

cards.core: Record payroll with debit Wages Expense for gross pay, credits to a liability for each withholding, and credit Wages Payable or Cash for net pay.
cards.detail: The entry balances at gross pay. Each withholding gets its own payable (Social Security Tax Payable, Medicare Tax Payable, Employee Federal Income Tax Payable, State Income Tax Payable, Health Insurance Payable). When employees are paid: debit Wages Payable, credit Cash.

cards.example: Summit gym: debit Wages Expense $2,000; credit Social Security Tax Payable $124, Medicare Tax Payable $29, Federal Income Tax Payable $170, State Income Tax Payable $60, Wages Payable $1,617.
cards.say_it: Wages Expense is the full $2,000 the gym earned the right to pay, and each withholding becomes a liability until we deposit it.

cards.core: Pay information is confidential, so the employer should not share one employee's pay with another.
cards.detail: Payroll records include pay rates, Social Security numbers and deductions, so access should be limited to people who need it. An employer should not disclose a worker's pay to coworkers, although under U.S. labor law employees themselves are generally allowed to discuss their own pay. Secure storage, limited software access and shredding old records protect employees and the business.
cards.example: At Summit Climbing Gym, Brooke asks what Alex makes; the owner should politely decline to share Alex's pay, while not forbidding employees from discussing their own wages.
cards.say_it: I would keep Alex's pay private, because payroll records are confidential, but I would not tell employees they cannot talk about their own pay.

cards.core: Unemployment taxes and Social Security apply only up to each employee's wage base for the year; use year-to-date pay to check.
cards.detail: For each employee, taxable wages = the lesser of their pay and the wage base (or the part of this period's pay that is still below the base). FUTA uses $7,000 per employee. SUTA uses the state base (for example $10,000). Social Security uses the annual federal base; Medicare has no base. Earnings records with year-to-date totals make this easy.
cards.formula: Taxable wages = smaller of (YTD pay) and (wage base), per employee
cards.say_it: Our two full-time workers each passed the $7,000 FUTA base, so only their first $7,000 is taxed, which keeps FUTA at just $150.
cards.mistakes: Applying FUTA or SUTA to total wages instead of capping each employee.

cards.core: Employers register with the state, report new hires, pay SUTA and state withholding, and follow state wage rules.
cards.detail: State duties usually include registering for withholding and unemployment tax accounts, reporting every new hire (including seasonal workers) within a set number of days, filing quarterly unemployment wage reports, filing state withholding returns, carrying workers' compensation, and following state minimum wage and final paycheck rules. Some cities also have local income taxes.
cards.example: Green Thumb must report its seasonal hires to the state, file state unemployment reports with the $930 of SUTA, and keep workers' comp coverage.
cards.say_it: Besides the IRS, the state needs its own registrations and reports, including a new hire report for every seasonal worker.

cards.core: Workers' compensation is employer-paid insurance that covers medical costs and lost wages for job injuries.
cards.detail: It is required by state law for most employers, whether or not they have ever had an injury, and the premium is a payroll expense usually priced per $100 of wages by job risk class. It protects employees and also protects the employer from most injury lawsuits. Skipping it can bring fines and personal liability.
cards.formula: Premium = Wages / 100 x rate per $100
cards.example: Green Thumb Landscaping: $83,000 / 100 x $4 = $3,320.
cards.say_it: Even if you have never had an injury, state law requires workers' comp, and one accident without it could cost far more than the $3,320 premium.

cards.core: A manager should be evaluated only on the costs and revenues they can control or strongly influence.
cards.detail: The controllability principle makes performance reports fair and motivating. A store manager can control staffing hours and supplies but not the corporate headquarters cost allocated to the store. Responsibility reports often separate controllable items from allocated common costs, and segment margin (contribution margin minus traceable fixed costs) is used to judge a segment before common costs. Holding managers responsible for uncontrollable items leads to frustration and bad decisions such as dropping a profitable segment.
cards.example: FitTech's Smart Shoes division shows a net loss only after allocated common costs; its segment margin of $40,000 is positive, so dropping it would lower company income by $40,000.
cards.say_it: Let's judge the division manager on segment margin, which they control, rather than on a net loss created by headquarters costs they cannot change.

cards.core: Goal incongruence happens when a performance measure makes a manager's best choice different from the company's best choice.
cards.detail: Performance measures and bonuses drive behavior. If a manager is paid on division ROI, she may reject a project earning 20 percent, above the company's 12 percent hurdle, because it would lower her 25 percent ROI. If a plant manager is paid on absorption costing income, he may overproduce inventory. If a selling division wants the highest transfer price, it may refuse an internal deal that saves the company money. The fix is to design measures (residual income, company-wide profit sharing, balanced scorecard) that align managers with the whole company.
cards.example: Northwind's Apparel manager rejects the jacket line to protect her bonus; Lumen Candle's manager could raise his bonus by $800 just by building 2,000 extra candles.
cards.say_it: The problem isn't the manager, it's the measure: ROI rewards her for turning down a project that makes the company money.

cards.core: Lean and quality-focused companies track measures like cycle time, defect rate, on-time delivery and inventory turnover alongside costs.
cards.detail: Traditional cost variances can reward the wrong behavior in a lean plant (for example, producing extra units to absorb overhead). Non-financial measures give faster, clearer signals to workers and managers. Common ones: manufacturing cycle time, throughput, first pass yield or defect rate, on-time delivery, customer complaints and inventory turnover. They fit the internal process perspective of a balanced scorecard.
cards.formula: Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory
cards.example: EverGreen's board could see defect rate per 1,000 boxes, on-time delivery percentage and inventory turnover each month next to the $190,000 JIT and $85,000 TQM savings.
cards.say_it: Defect rate and on-time delivery tell the plant manager every week whether lean is working, long before the cost reports come out.

cards.core: A balanced scorecard measures performance from four perspectives: financial, customer, internal business process, and learning and growth.
cards.detail: Financial measures alone look backward and can be gamed in the short run. The balanced scorecard links strategy to a few measures in each perspective. Financial: ROI, residual income, profit growth. Customer: satisfaction, retention, market share. Internal business process: cycle time, defect rate, on-time delivery. Learning and growth: employee training hours, retention, new product ideas. The perspectives are connected: trained employees improve processes, which please customers, which drives financial results.
cards.example: Northwind could score each division on residual income (financial), repeat customer rate (customer), on-time internal deliveries of fabric (process) and training hours per employee (learning and growth).
cards.say_it: Adding a balanced scorecard keeps managers focused on the long run, not just on this quarter's ROI.

cards.term: Cost, revenue, profit and investment centers
cards.core: Cost centers control costs, revenue centers control sales, profit centers control both, and investment centers also control assets.
cards.detail: Cost center: the manager controls only costs (maintenance, human resources, a production department); judged on cost budgets and variances. Revenue center: judged mainly on revenue brought in (a sales department). Profit center: controls revenues and costs (a single store or product line); judged on profit or segment margin. Investment center: controls revenues, costs and the operating assets invested (a division); judged on return on investment (ROI) or residual income. The higher the center, the more of the business the manager is responsible for.
cards.example: Northwind: the HR department is a cost center, the sales team a revenue center, a single retail store a profit center, and the Fabric and Apparel Divisions investment centers (Fabric ROI 15%, Apparel ROI 25%).
cards.say_it: Because each division manager decides on sales, costs and the assets they use, they are investment centers, so ROI and residual income are the right measures.
cards.mistakes: Judging a cost center manager on profit, or a profit center manager on assets they cannot control.

cards.core: Customer profitability analysis subtracts the product costs and the service costs each customer causes from that customer's revenue.
cards.detail: Not every customer is equally profitable. Besides product cost, customers cause costs for orders processed, deliveries, rush shipments, returns, sales visits and support calls. Using activity-based costing, these costs are traced to each customer to find who really earns money. Managers can then reward profitable customers, charge fees for costly services, set minimum order sizes or change terms for customers who lose money.
cards.formula: Customer profit = Revenue minus Product costs minus Customer service costs
cards.example: Illustration: Customer A buys $100,000 with $60,000 product cost but causes $30,000 of rush orders and returns, so profit is $10,000. Customer B buys $80,000 with $48,000 product cost and $8,000 of service cost, so profit is $24,000, even though B buys less.
cards.say_it: Your biggest customer isn't your most profitable one once we count all the rush deliveries and returns, so let's look at a delivery fee or a minimum order.

pis.text: Describe common management accounting performance measures (e.g., balanced scorecard, return on investment [ROI], customer profitability analysis, etc.)

cards.core: Residual income is operating income left after charging the minimum required return on the assets used.
cards.detail: Residual income measures dollars earned above the company's hurdle rate. Any project with a positive residual income earns more than the minimum required return, so a manager judged on residual income will accept every project that is good for the company. This fixes the main weakness of ROI. Its drawback is that larger divisions naturally show larger dollar amounts, so it is less useful for comparing divisions of different sizes. Economic value added (EVA) is a similar measure.
cards.formula: Residual income = Operating income minus (Minimum required rate x Operating assets)
cards.example: Northwind jacket line: 80,000 minus (12% x 400,000) = 80,000 minus 48,000 = $32,000, positive, so accept. Its ROI of 20% would lower Apparel's ROI from 25% to 23.75% (380,000 / 1,600,000), which is why the manager wanted to reject it.
cards.say_it: The jacket line earns $32,000 more than our 12% minimum, so on residual income it is clearly a good project even though it pulls the division's ROI down.
