cards.core: A responsibility center is a part of a business whose manager is held accountable for specific results.
cards.detail: Responsibility accounting divides a company into units and reports each unit's results to the manager who controls them. The type of center depends on what the manager controls: costs only, revenues, both revenues and costs, or revenues, costs and the assets invested. Reports should hold managers accountable only for items they can control (the controllability principle). Choosing the right center type determines which performance measure is fair: cost variances, revenue targets, profit, or ROI and residual income.
cards.example: At Northwind Outdoor, the Fabric and Apparel Division managers control sales, costs and their operating assets, so each division is a responsibility center judged on its return on assets.
cards.say_it: We should measure each manager only on what they control, so first we decide what type of responsibility center each division really is.

pis.text: Differentiate among management accounting responsibility centers (i.e., cost, profit, investment, revenue)

cards.core: ROI is operating income as a percentage of the average operating assets used to earn it.
cards.detail: ROI lets managers compare divisions of different sizes. It can be split (DuPont) into margin (operating income divided by sales) times turnover (sales divided by average operating assets), so ROI rises by increasing sales, cutting costs or using fewer assets. ROI is popular because it is simple and comparable, but it can cause goal incongruence: a manager with a high ROI may reject a project that beats the company's required return because it would lower the division's average.
cards.formula: ROI = Operating income / Average operating assets = Margin x Turnover
cards.example: Northwind: Fabric 240,000 / 1,600,000 = 15%; Apparel 300,000 / 1,200,000 = 25%. Illustration of DuPont: if Fabric had $2,000,000 of sales, margin 12% x turnover 1.25 = 15%.
cards.say_it: Apparel earns 25 cents of operating income for every dollar of assets, compared with 15 cents for Fabric, and both beat our 12% minimum.
cards.mistakes: Using net income or total company assets instead of the division's operating income and operating assets.

cards.core: A transfer price is what one division charges another division of the same company for goods or services.
cards.detail: Transfer prices matter because they move profit between divisions, which changes each manager's ROI and bonus, but inside the company they cancel out: the seller's revenue is the buyer's cost. What changes company profit is whether the transfer happens at all and which costs are avoided. A good transfer price encourages both managers to make the choice that is best for the whole company, keeps divisions autonomous and is seen as fair. Across countries, transfer prices also shift taxable income, so tax rules require arm's length prices.
cards.example: Northwind's Fabric Division can supply 20,000 yards to the Apparel Division. Whatever price they agree on, the company saves $100,000 by making the fabric inside ($8 cost) instead of buying it outside ($13).
cards.say_it: The price itself just moves profit between divisions; what matters for the company is that the transfer happens, because it saves us $100,000.
cards.formula: Minimum transfer price = Variable cost per unit + Lost contribution margin per unit

cards.core: The selling division's minimum is variable cost plus lost contribution margin; the buying division's maximum is the outside price.
cards.detail: The selling division should not accept less than the variable cost of the transfer plus any contribution margin it gives up on outside sales (opportunity cost). With idle capacity, no outside sales are lost, so the minimum is just the variable cost (minus any costs avoided on internal sales, such as selling commissions). The buying division will not pay more than what an outside supplier charges. Any price in between makes both divisions better off. If the minimum is above the maximum, the company is better off buying outside.
cards.formula: Minimum = Variable cost per unit + Lost contribution margin per unit; Maximum = Outside market price
cards.example: Northwind with idle capacity: minimum $8 (the $1 selling cost is avoided internally), maximum $13. A negotiated $10.50 gives Fabric 20,000 x 2.50 = $50,000 more and saves Apparel $50,000. At full capacity: minimum = 8 + lost margin 5 = $13, so the company is indifferent.
cards.say_it: Since Fabric has idle capacity, any price from $8 to $13 works; $14 is outside the range and would push Apparel to buy outside, costing the company $100,000.
cards.mistakes: Including fixed costs in the minimum or ignoring whether the seller has idle capacity.

pis.text: Explain the role of transfer pricing in managerial accounting

examples.title: Northwind Outdoor: responsibility centers, ROI, residual income and transfer pricing

cards.core: Transfer prices are usually set at market price, at cost (or cost plus a markup), or by negotiation between division managers.
cards.detail: Market-based prices work well when an outside market exists and the seller is at capacity. Cost-based prices (variable cost, full cost, or cost plus a markup) are simple but can pass inefficiency to the buyer and give the seller no profit incentive. Negotiated prices respect division autonomy and usually land within the minimum to maximum range. Headquarters should set a written policy and step in only when a dispute would hurt the company. Ordering one price takes away autonomy and can demotivate managers.
cards.example: Instead of ordering Fabric to charge $8, Northwind's headquarters adopts a negotiated policy with a floor of variable cost and a ceiling of the outside price, reviewed every year.
cards.say_it: Forcing an $8 price would give Fabric zero profit on the deal; a written negotiated policy keeps both managers motivated and still captures the company's savings.

cards.core: A gift to a qualified charity can lower taxes and build goodwill, but it reduces cash and profit.
cards.detail: Charitable giving means donating money, goods or time to nonprofit organizations. Only gifts to qualified organizations (such as 501(c)(3) charities) are tax deductible, and individuals benefit only if they itemize. For a business, a donation is recorded as a Charitable Contributions (Donations) Expense; donated inventory is recorded at cost. A sole proprietor's cash donation is generally deducted on the owner's personal return rather than as a business expense, while corporations can deduct gifts up to a limit. Always get a written receipt from the charity.
cards.example: If Dogs-R-Us gives $100 to the animal shelter: debit Charitable Contributions Expense $100, credit Cash $100. Donating $100 of dog food it bought for $60: debit Charitable Contributions Expense $60, credit Inventory $60.
cards.say_it: A donation to the shelter is a cash payment recorded as charitable contributions expense; it lowers net income but can build community goodwill for the store.
cards.mistakes: Recording donated goods at their selling price instead of their cost.

cards.core: Keep three to six months of essential expenses in savings so a surprise does not force borrowing.
cards.detail: An emergency fund covers job loss, medical bills or repairs without using credit cards. Businesses need the same thing: a cash reserve for slow seasons, late customers or broken equipment. The reserve should be in a safe, liquid place such as a savings or money market account. A cash budget shows how big the reserve should be, especially for seasonal businesses.
cards.example: A business with $8,000 of essential monthly costs should aim for a reserve of $24,000 to $48,000; Rocking Ribs needs a cushion for its low season, when profit drops.
cards.say_it: To stay financially sustainable, I recommend building a cash reserve of at least three months of fixed costs before spending heavily on growth.

cards.core: Before donating, confirm the charity is qualified, check how it uses money, and keep a written receipt.
cards.detail: Check the organization's tax-exempt status with the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search, read its Form 990 (which shows revenue, program spending, executive pay and fundraising costs), and review charity rating sites. A good sign is that most spending goes to programs rather than fundraising and administration. Give directly rather than through unknown callers, never pay by gift card or wire, and get a written acknowledgment for any gift of $250 or more to claim a deduction.
cards.example: The Society for Marketers, a nonprofit, files Form 990 each year, so donors and members can see how much of its spending goes to its programs.
cards.say_it: Before the store donates, I would check the shelter's nonprofit status and get a receipt, so the gift is properly documented.

cards.core: Employees are paid by hourly wage, salary, commission, bonus or piece rate, plus benefits.
cards.detail: Hourly workers earn a rate per hour, and nonexempt employees get at least 1.5 times their rate for hours over 40 a week. Salaried employees earn a fixed amount per year. Commission pays a percentage of sales, and bonuses reward meeting goals such as a profit target. Piece rate pays per unit produced. Benefits such as health insurance, retirement matches and paid time off are also compensation, so the true cost of an employee is more than the paycheck.
cards.example: At Summit Climbing Gym, Alex works 45 hours at $20: 40 x $20 = $800 plus 5 x $30 overtime = $150, so $950 gross pay.
cards.say_it: Tying part of the sales team's pay to results motivates them, but the plan must reward real, collected sales so nobody is tempted to book revenue early.

cards.core: A pay stub shows pay period, hours and rate, gross pay, each deduction, net pay and year-to-date totals.
cards.detail: Read a pay stub from top to bottom: check the pay period and pay date, hours worked (regular and overtime) and pay rate, then confirm gross pay. Next check each deduction: federal income tax (based on the W-4), state tax, Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%), and voluntary items like health insurance or 401(k). Net pay is what was deposited. Year-to-date (YTD) columns add up the year so far and should match the W-2 in January. Errors in hours, rate or withholding should be reported right away.
cards.example: Alex's stub: 40 regular hours at $20 and 5 overtime hours at $30 = $950 gross; Social Security $58.90, Medicare $13.78, federal tax $95.00, state tax $28.50; net pay $753.82.
cards.say_it: I check that Social Security is 6.2% and Medicare is 1.45% of gross pay, which is a quick way to catch payroll errors on any stub.

cards.core: Net worth is what you own (assets) minus what you owe (liabilities).
cards.detail: Net worth is a personal balance sheet. Assets include cash, savings, investments, retirement accounts, a car and a home at current market value. Liabilities include credit card balances, student loans, car loans and a mortgage. Positive and growing net worth means you are building wealth; negative net worth is common for students with loans. It is the personal version of the accounting equation, where owner's equity = assets minus liabilities.
cards.formula: Net worth = Total assets minus Total liabilities
cards.example: Assets: $3,000 savings + $9,000 car = $12,000. Liabilities: $7,000 car loan + $1,000 credit card = $8,000. Net worth = $4,000.
cards.say_it: Net worth is to a person what owner's equity is to a business: what would be left if every debt were paid off.

cards.core: Income can be earned (wages, salary, commissions, tips, business profit) or unearned (interest, dividends, rent, gains).
cards.detail: Earned income comes from working: hourly wages, salaries, overtime, commissions, tips, bonuses and self-employment profit. Unearned (passive or investment) income comes from money or property working for you: interest, dividends, rental income and capital gains. Other sources include transfer payments such as Social Security and unemployment benefits, gifts and inheritances. The source matters because it changes how the income is taxed and how stable it is.
cards.example: Maya Chen's $90,000 of client fees is earned self-employment income (subject to income tax and self-employment tax); the 3% dividend on a stock is unearned investment income.
cards.say_it: A business owner's income is the profit, not the sales, so I would plan your personal budget around net profit after taxes.

cards.core: An employer match adds money to your retirement account when you contribute, so always contribute enough to get it.
cards.detail: A common match is 50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of pay. Not contributing enough to get the full match leaves part of your compensation unclaimed. Matches may vest over time, meaning you keep them only after a set number of years. On a pay stub, 401(k) contributions appear as deductions; traditional contributions lower taxable wages for income tax, but not for Social Security and Medicare.
cards.example: Salary $40,000, employer matches 50% up to 6%: you contribute $2,400 and the employer adds $1,200, an instant 50% return.
cards.say_it: The match is part of total compensation, so when comparing job offers I look at benefits, not just the hourly rate.

cards.core: List net income, subtract fixed and variable expenses and savings, and adjust until it balances.
cards.detail: Step 1: total monthly net (take-home) income. Step 2: list fixed expenses that stay the same (rent, insurance, loan payments). Step 3: estimate variable expenses that change (food, gas, entertainment) from past records. Step 4: pay yourself first by setting a savings amount. Step 5: if expenses exceed income, cut variable spending or raise income. Step 6: track actual spending against the budget each month. A popular guide is 50/30/20: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and debt payoff.
cards.example: Net pay $2,400: needs $1,200 (50%), wants $720 (30%), savings and extra debt payments $480 (20%).
cards.say_it: A budget works only if we compare it to actual spending every month and adjust, the same way a business does budget vs. actual.
cards.mistakes: Building the budget on gross pay instead of take-home pay.

cards.core: Estate planning decides who receives your assets and who makes decisions if you die or cannot act.
cards.detail: Key tools are a will (who gets what and who is guardian of children), beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance (these pass outside the will), trusts (hold and manage assets for others, can avoid probate), a durable power of attorney for finances and a health care directive. For a business owner, estate planning includes a succession plan or buy-sell agreement so the business can continue. Plans should be reviewed after major life events.
cards.example: The owner of Dance Frenzy could use a buy-sell agreement funded by life insurance so a partner can buy her share and the studios keep running.
cards.say_it: For a family business, the estate plan and the succession plan go together, so the company survives the owner and the going concern assumption still holds.

pis.text: Explain the nature of estate planning

cards.core: Net pay (take-home pay) is gross pay minus all deductions.
cards.detail: Gross pay is total earnings before anything is taken out. Deductions include required withholdings (federal and state income tax, Social Security 6.2% and Medicare 1.45%) and voluntary ones (health insurance, retirement contributions, union dues). The employer holds the withholdings in trust and must send them to the government. Net pay is what the employee actually receives. For budgeting, a person should plan with net pay, not gross pay.
cards.formula: Net pay = Gross pay minus taxes withheld minus voluntary deductions
cards.example: Summit Climbing Gym payroll: gross $2,000 minus $383 of deductions ($124 Social Security, $29 Medicare, $170 federal tax, $60 state tax) = $1,617 net pay. Alex: $950 minus $196.18 = $753.82.
cards.say_it: The withheld taxes are not our money; we only hold them until we deposit them, so they are recorded as liabilities.
cards.mistakes: Budgeting with gross pay, which overstates spendable income by 20% or more.

cards.core: Net worth grows by saving and investing more, paying down debt, and buying assets that hold or gain value.
cards.detail: Net worth rises when assets grow (saving, investment growth, home equity) or liabilities shrink (paying down loans). It falls when people borrow for things that lose value quickly, such as an expensive car or vacations on credit. Tracking net worth over time is a better measure of financial health than income alone, because a high earner who spends everything can have low or negative net worth. The same logic applies to owner's equity: retained profit increases it, withdrawals and losses decrease it.
cards.example: Paying $3,000 off a credit card raises net worth by $0 that day (cash and debt both fall), but it stops interest charges, so future net worth grows faster.
cards.say_it: Paying off high-interest debt is one of the surest ways to grow net worth, because it is a guaranteed return equal to the interest rate.

cards.core: Pay for college with savings, scholarships, grants, work-study and loans, using free money first.
cards.detail: Start with the FAFSA, which determines eligibility for federal grants (such as Pell Grants), work-study and federal student loans. Scholarships and grants do not have to be repaid. Federal loans have fixed rates and flexible repayment; subsidized loans (need based) do not charge interest while you are in school, unsubsidized loans do. Private loans usually need a cosigner and have fewer protections. 529 plans let families save with tax-free growth for education. Community college and dual credit lower total cost.
cards.example: A $20,000 unsubsidized loan at 6% builds about $1,200 of interest per year while in school; a subsidized loan would not.
cards.say_it: I would compare the total cost of each option, including interest, and borrow only after using every grant and scholarship, because those do not need to be paid back.
cards.mistakes: Taking private loans before using federal aid, which usually costs more and has fewer repayment options.

cards.core: A personal financial statement lists your assets at market value and your debts to show your net worth.
cards.detail: Step 1: list assets: cash, savings, investments and retirement accounts at current value, then vehicles, home and other property at what they could sell for. Step 2: list liabilities: credit cards, student loans, car loans, mortgage and any other debts at their current balance. Step 3: net worth = assets minus liabilities. Step 4: update it once or twice a year to track progress. Lenders ask small business owners for a personal financial statement because owners often guarantee business loans personally.
cards.example: A bank lending to a new gym asks the owner for a personal financial statement: $60,000 of assets minus $35,000 of debts = $25,000 net worth to back a personal guarantee.
cards.say_it: Because you will personally guarantee the loan, the bank will want your personal financial statement as well as the business's balance sheet.

cards.core: Retirement planning means saving early in tax-advantaged accounts so compound growth can fund life after work.
cards.detail: Social Security replaces only part of a worker's income, so people save in employer plans such as a 401(k) (or 403(b) at nonprofits) and individual retirement accounts (IRAs). Traditional accounts give a tax deduction now and are taxed at withdrawal; Roth accounts use after-tax money but qualified withdrawals are tax free. Many employers match part of contributions, which is free money. Starting early matters most because of compounding. Self-employed people can use a SEP IRA or solo 401(k).
cards.example: Saving $200 a month from age 22 at 7% (compounded monthly) grows to roughly $655,000 by age 65; starting at 32 grows to only about $309,000.
cards.say_it: A small business can offer a simple retirement plan with a match to attract and keep good employees, and the match is a deductible expense.

pis.text: Discuss the nature of retirement planning

cards.core: Divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double.
cards.detail: The Rule of 72 is a quick mental shortcut for compound growth. It also works in reverse for debt and inflation: it shows how fast a credit card balance doubles if unpaid, or how fast inflation cuts buying power in half. It is an estimate, most accurate for rates between about 6% and 10%.
cards.formula: Years to double = 72 / annual interest rate (in percent)
cards.example: At 8%, money doubles in about 72 / 8 = 9 years. An unpaid credit card balance at 24% doubles in about 3 years.
cards.say_it: At 8% our reserve fund would roughly double in nine years, which shows why we should start saving for replacement equipment now.

pis.text: Explain the time value of money
Explain the need to save and invest

cards.core: The government pays the interest on subsidized loans while you are in school; unsubsidized loans build interest from day one.
cards.detail: Federal Direct Subsidized Loans are based on financial need, and interest does not accrue during school, the grace period or approved deferment. Unsubsidized loans are available regardless of need, but interest accrues from disbursement and is added to the balance (capitalized) if unpaid. Both have fixed rates set each year and offer income-driven repayment options. Private loans are credit based, often need a cosigner and lack federal protections, so they should come last.
cards.example: $5,000 unsubsidized at 6% for 4 years of school builds about $1,200 of interest ($5,000 x 6% x 4) before repayment starts; a subsidized loan would still be $5,000.
cards.say_it: I would accept subsidized loans first, then unsubsidized, and use private loans only if needed, because they cost the most and offer the fewest protections.

pis.text: Discuss options for financing a college education

cards.core: Saving builds a cushion for emergencies and goals; investing grows money faster than inflation.
cards.detail: Savings are money set aside in safe, liquid places such as a savings account, money market account or CD, for emergencies and short-term goals. Investing puts money into assets like stocks, bonds and funds that can earn higher returns over long periods but can lose value. People and businesses need both: savings for safety and liquidity, investments for long-term growth such as retirement or expansion. Inflation means cash left idle loses buying power each year.
cards.example: With 3% inflation, $10,000 kept in cash buys only about $7,400 worth of goods after 10 years (10,000 / 1.03^10).
cards.say_it: Money we need within a year belongs in savings, and only money we will not need for several years should be invested for growth.

cards.core: A will directs assets through probate; a trust can pass assets privately; beneficiary designations override the will.
cards.detail: A will names who receives property and who will care for minor children; it goes through probate, a public court process. A living trust holds assets for named beneficiaries and can avoid probate. Retirement accounts and life insurance pass directly to the named beneficiaries, so those designations must be kept up to date. Without a will, state law decides who inherits (intestacy). Business owners should also plan who will run or buy the business.
cards.example: If a business owner named an ex-spouse as beneficiary on a life insurance policy and never updated it, the money goes to the ex-spouse even if the will says otherwise.
cards.say_it: Estate planning is not only for the wealthy: a simple will and up-to-date beneficiaries protect your family and your business partners.

pis.text: Explain the nature of estate planning

cards.core: Accounts receivable is money customers owe for goods or services sold on credit; it is a current asset.
cards.detail: Accounts Receivable increases with a debit when a sale is made on account and decreases with a credit when the customer pays. It is really credit the business extends to its customers, so it must be billed, tracked and collected promptly. It is reported at the amount expected to be collected (net of an allowance for doubtful accounts). More credit customers means more invoices to follow up.
cards.formula: Sale: Dr A/R, Cr Sales | Collection: Dr Cash, Cr A/R
cards.example: Locally Picked delivers $1,000 of produce to a grocery store on account: debit Accounts Receivable $1,000, credit Sales $1,000.
cards.say_it: Accounts receivable is money we have earned but not yet collected, so it is an asset, and the faster we collect it the better our cash flow.
cards.mistakes: Calling accounts receivable a liability because it is money not yet received.

cards.core: The aging method sorts receivables by how overdue they are, applies a higher loss rate to older groups, and adjusts the allowance to that target.
cards.detail: It is a balance sheet approach focused on reporting receivables at what will be collected. The total of each age group times its rate is the required ending allowance. The adjusting entry is the target minus the current credit balance in the allowance (or plus a debit balance). Aging also shows which customers need collection follow up.
cards.formula: Adjustment = Target allowance minus existing credit balance
cards.example: Cascade: age group estimates $3,000 + $6,000 + $10,000 = $19,000 target; existing credit balance $2,000; debit Bad Debt Expense $17,000, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $17,000.
cards.say_it: The aging tells us we need $19,000 in the allowance, and since $2,000 is already there, this year's expense is $17,000.
cards.mistakes: Recording the full $19,000 target as expense.

cards.core: The allowance method estimates uncollectible accounts each year so bad debt expense matches the sales that caused it.
cards.detail: At year end an adjusting entry debits Bad Debt Expense and credits Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, a contra asset. Receivables are then shown at net realizable value (what is expected to be collected). GAAP requires this method when bad debts are material. The estimate can be made with the percent of sales method or the aging of receivables method.
cards.formula: Net A/R = Accounts receivable minus Allowance for doubtful accounts
cards.example: Cascade Medical Supplies: Accounts Receivable $500,000 minus allowance $19,000 = net receivables $481,000.
cards.say_it: We estimate bad debts now, in the same year as the sales, so this year's profit is not overstated and the balance sheet shows what we will really collect.

cards.core: Estimate bad debts at year end with Bad Debt Expense and the Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, so expense matches the sales that caused it.
cards.detail: The percent of sales method (income statement approach) multiplies credit sales by a loss rate to get the expense, ignoring the existing allowance. The aging method (balance sheet approach) multiplies each age group of receivables by its loss rate to get the target ending allowance, then records the amount needed to reach it: target minus an existing credit balance (or plus an existing debit balance). Entry: debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. Net realizable value = Accounts Receivable minus Allowance.
cards.formula: Percent of sales: Expense = Credit sales x Rate. Aging: Expense = Target allowance minus Existing credit balance
cards.example: Cascade Medical: percent of sales 2,000,000 x 1.5% = $30,000 expense (allowance becomes $32,000). Aging target 3,000 + 6,000 + 10,000 = $19,000; adjustment 19,000 minus 2,000 = $17,000. Net receivables 500,000 minus 19,000 = $481,000.
cards.say_it: The aging says we should have $19,000 in the allowance; we already have $2,000, so the adjusting entry is $17,000.
cards.mistakes: Using the aging total as the expense without subtracting the existing allowance balance.

cards.core: Factoring sells receivables to a finance company for immediate cash minus a fee; without recourse, it adds no debt.
cards.detail: Without recourse, the factor takes the loss if customers do not pay, and the transaction is a sale of an asset: cash replaces receivables and the fee is a Loss on Sale of Receivables. With recourse, the seller must repay the factor for uncollected accounts, so it keeps the credit risk (and may have to record a recourse liability). Compare factoring with a loan by annualizing the fee and by considering the effect on debt ratios and loan covenants.
cards.formula: Fee = Receivables sold x Fee rate; Annualized cost = (Fee / Cash received) x (360 / Days)
cards.example: Swift Route: factor $200,000 without recourse at 4%: Dr Cash 192,000, Dr Loss on Sale of Receivables 8,000, Cr Accounts Receivable 200,000. Cost about 8,000 / 192,000 x 6 = 25% a year, versus a 9% loan costing $3,000.
cards.say_it: Factoring costs $5,000 more than the loan, but it adds no debt, which keeps our debt-to-equity ratio inside the lender's limit.

cards.core: When a customer pays an invoice, debit Cash and credit Accounts Receivable, and post it to that customer's account.
cards.detail: No revenue is recorded at collection, because it was recorded when the sale was made. The payment is posted to the customer's account in the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger so their balance is current. Matching each payment to a specific invoice helps aging and collection work.
cards.formula: Dr Cash, Cr A/R
cards.example: Freddie Perkins pays $710 to Piper's Pets: debit Cash $710, credit Accounts Receivable (Freddie Perkins) $710; his balance is now $0.
cards.say_it: The revenue was recorded when we sold the goods, so this payment just turns the receivable into cash.

cards.core: When a customer pays within the discount period, the seller records the discount in Sales Discounts, a contra revenue account.
cards.detail: Credit terms such as 2/10, n/30 encourage early payment and speed up cash. At the sale: debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales for the full amount. If the customer pays within 10 days: debit Cash for the amount received, debit Sales Discounts for the discount, credit Accounts Receivable for the full amount. Net sales = Sales minus Sales Returns and Allowances minus Sales Discounts.
cards.formula: Cash received = Invoice minus (Invoice x Discount rate)
cards.example: Locally Picked sells $1,000 of produce on June 10, terms 2/10, n/30. If the grocery store pays by June 20: Dr Cash 980, Dr Sales Discounts 20, Cr Accounts Receivable 1,000. Otherwise $1,000 is due by July 10.
cards.say_it: Offering 2/10, n/30 costs us $20 on this sale but gets our cash 20 days sooner.

cards.core: A schedule of accounts receivable lists each customer's balance and its total must equal Accounts Receivable in the general ledger.
cards.detail: Steps: heading, list every customer with a debit balance from the subsidiary ledger, total, and compare with the controlling account. The schedule proves the subsidiary ledger is correct and shows who to follow up with. Without subsidiary ledgers, the business cannot report receivables accurately or support the full disclosure of what is collectible.
cards.formula: Total of customer balances = Accounts Receivable controlling account

cards.term: Writing off an account and the direct write-off method
cards.core: Under the allowance method a write-off (debit Allowance, credit Receivable) changes neither net income nor net receivables.
cards.detail: Because the expense was already estimated, writing off a specific customer only removes the account from both Accounts Receivable and the Allowance. If the customer later pays, reverse the write-off (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Allowance), then record the collection. The direct write-off method instead debits Bad Debt Expense only when an account is written off, which breaks matching, so GAAP allows it only when bad debts are immaterial; it is the method required for tax returns.
cards.example: Cascade writes off a failed clinic's $1,500: Dr Allowance for Doubtful Accounts 1,500, Cr Accounts Receivable 1,500. Net receivables and net income are unchanged.
cards.say_it: Writing off the clinic's $1,500 doesn't hit income again, because we already expensed it when we built the allowance.

cards.core: The direct write-off method records bad debt expense only when a specific account is known to be uncollectible.
cards.detail: Entry: debit Bad Debt Expense, credit Accounts Receivable. It is simple and is the method used for income tax, but it violates matching because the expense often lands in a later year than the sale, and receivables are overstated until then. GAAP allows it only when bad debts are immaterial.
cards.formula: Dr Bad Debt Expense, Cr A/R
cards.example: A small shop with a $90 uncollectible account and few credit sales can write it off directly: debit Bad Debt Expense $90, credit Accounts Receivable $90.
cards.say_it: Direct write-off is fine for a tiny business, but with material credit sales GAAP requires the allowance method so expenses match revenue.

cards.core: The percent of sales method sets bad debt expense as a percentage of credit sales, ignoring the existing allowance balance.
cards.detail: It is an income statement approach, focused on matching expense to sales. Multiply credit sales by the expected loss rate to get the expense, then add it to the existing allowance to find the ending allowance.
cards.formula: Bad debt expense = Credit sales x loss rate | Ending allowance = Beginning allowance + expense
cards.say_it: Under percent of sales I take 1.5% of credit sales as the expense, and the allowance simply grows by that amount.
cards.mistakes: Subtracting the existing allowance balance as you would under aging.

cards.core: A sales invoice documents a sale on account; a sales receipt documents a cash sale.
cards.detail: The seller prepares the sales invoice with the customer, items, prices, total and terms, keeps a copy as the source document for the entry, and posts it to the customer's account. A sales receipt or cash register tape supports a cash sale. Invoices should be prenumbered so missing ones can be spotted.

cards.say_it: The prenumbered sales invoice is our proof of the sale and tells the customer exactly what they owe and when.

cards.core: Insurance transfers the risk of a large loss to an insurer in exchange for a regular premium.
cards.detail: Insurance works by pooling risk: many policyholders pay premiums, and the insurer uses the pool to pay the few who suffer losses. It covers pure risks (only a chance of loss, such as fire, injury or lawsuits), not speculative risks like business failure from low sales. Key terms: the premium is the price of coverage; the deductible is what the insured pays first; the policy limit is the most the insurer pays; a claim is a request for payment. Insurance is one of four risk responses, along with avoiding, reducing and retaining risk.
cards.example: A backyard pool rental business pays a few hundred dollars a year for liability insurance so a single injury lawsuit cannot wipe out the owner's savings.
cards.say_it: Insurance lets us trade a small, certain cost, the premium, for protection against a large, uncertain loss.

cards.core: List the risks, estimate how likely and how costly each is, then insure the losses you cannot afford to absorb.
cards.detail: Step 1: identify risks: property damage, injuries to customers or employees, lawsuits, theft, data breaches, loss of a key person, lost income. Step 2: rate each for likelihood and impact. Step 3: choose a response: avoid (do not do the activity), reduce (safety rules, waivers, controls), transfer (insurance or contracts) or retain (pay small losses yourself). Step 4: buy coverage with limits high enough for the worst realistic loss and deductibles you can afford. Step 5: review coverage every year and after any change in the business, and talk with a licensed insurance agent.
cards.example: The pool rental owner should call her homeowners' insurance agent, because a rental business is usually excluded, add liability coverage, and have renters sign a liability waiver.
cards.say_it: I would insure the risks that could close the business, like an injury lawsuit, and handle small, predictable losses from our own cash.

cards.core: Risks can be avoided, reduced, transferred (insured) or retained.
cards.detail: Avoiding risk means not doing the risky activity. Reducing (controlling) risk means lowering the chance or size of a loss: safety training, internal controls, backups, waivers, inspections. Transferring risk shifts it to someone else: insurance, hedging contracts, or contract clauses. Retaining (accepting) risk means paying small or unlikely losses from your own funds. Most businesses combine all four, guided by how much risk they are willing to accept (risk appetite).
cards.example: A pool rental host reduces risk with safety rules and a waiver, transfers it with liability insurance, and retains small costs such as a broken pool chair.
cards.say_it: Insurance is only one tool: I would combine safety rules and waivers to reduce the risk with a liability policy to transfer what is left.

cards.core: Most businesses need property, general liability, workers' compensation and often business interruption insurance.
cards.detail: Property insurance covers buildings, equipment and inventory. General liability covers injuries to customers and damage to others' property. Professional liability (errors and omissions) covers mistakes in services. Workers' compensation, required in almost every state for employers, covers employee injuries. Commercial auto covers business vehicles. Business interruption covers lost income after a covered disaster. Cyber insurance covers data breaches. A fidelity bond (crime insurance) covers employee theft. Product liability matters for businesses that sell goods.
cards.example: A new gym needs general liability (members can be hurt), property coverage for treadmills and dumbbells, and workers' compensation for its personal trainers.
cards.say_it: For a gym, general liability is the most important policy because member injuries are the biggest risk, and workers' comp is required once we have employees.
cards.mistakes: Assuming a homeowner's policy covers a home-based business; it usually excludes business activity.

cards.core: A higher deductible lowers the premium but means you pay more of each loss yourself.
cards.detail: The premium is what you pay for the policy, monthly or yearly. The deductible is the amount you pay on each claim before insurance pays. The coverage limit is the maximum the insurer pays. Coinsurance or copays split costs after the deductible in some policies. Choosing a higher deductible makes sense if you have an emergency fund to cover it; the coverage limit should be high enough to protect against the worst realistic loss.
cards.example: A $10,000 equipment loss with a $1,000 deductible: the business pays $1,000 and the insurer pays $9,000.
cards.say_it: I would choose a higher deductible to lower our premium, since our cash reserve can cover a $1,000 loss, but I would not cut the liability limit.

cards.core: People protect themselves with health, auto, property (homeowners or renters), life and disability insurance.
cards.detail: Health insurance pays medical costs; auto liability insurance is required in nearly every state; homeowners or renters insurance covers belongings and personal liability; life insurance replaces income for dependents (term life is low cost for a set period, whole life adds savings at higher cost); disability insurance replaces income if illness or injury stops you from working. Needs change with life stage: a single student needs health, auto and renters coverage, while a parent with a mortgage needs life and disability coverage too.
cards.example: A rule of thumb for term life insurance is coverage of about 10 times annual income for someone with dependents: $500,000 for a $50,000 earner.
cards.say_it: Insurance needs depend on who relies on your income, so I would start with health, auto and renters coverage and add life insurance when you have dependents.

cards.core: Book income follows GAAP for investors; taxable income follows tax law, so the two often differ.
cards.detail: GAAP aims to show economic performance fairly; tax law has its own goals, such as encouraging investment or disallowing certain expenses. Differences are permanent (they never reverse, such as fines, the nondeductible half of meals, and municipal bond interest) or temporary (they reverse over time, such as different book and tax depreciation). To compute tax, start with book pre-tax income, add back expenses that are not deductible, and subtract income that is not taxable.
cards.formula: Taxable income = Book income + Nondeductible expenses minus Nontaxable income (plus or minus temporary differences)
cards.example: Brightline: book income $500,000 + nondeductible half of meals $10,000 + fine $5,000 minus municipal bond interest $20,000 = taxable income $495,000.
cards.say_it: The books follow GAAP and the return follows tax law, so we start with our $500,000 book income and adjust for the fine, the meals and the municipal interest to reach $495,000.

cards.core: Business meals with clients are generally only 50% deductible, so half the cost is a nondeductible difference.
cards.detail: A meal is deductible only if it has a clear business purpose, the taxpayer or an employee is present, and it is not lavish. Even then, generally only 50 percent of the cost is deductible. Entertainment such as sports tickets is not deductible at all. For a corporation, the nondeductible half is a permanent difference between book income and taxable income, so it is added back when computing taxable income. Records should show who attended and the business discussed.
cards.formula: Deductible meals = Meal cost x 50%
cards.example: Maya spent $1,000 on client meals, so she deducts $500. Brightline Robotics expensed $20,000 of meals on its books, so it adds back the nondeductible $10,000 to reach taxable income.
cards.say_it: Only half of client meals is deductible, so of your $1,000 of meals, $500 goes on Schedule C, and we should note the client and purpose on each receipt.

cards.term: Extension to file is not an extension to pay
cards.core: An extension gives 6 more months to file the return, but the tax is still due by the original due date.
cards.detail: Corporations request an extension with Form 7004 and individuals with Form 4868; both give 6 more months to file. The extension does not delay payment, so the company should estimate the tax and pay it by the original deadline. Unpaid tax after the due date is charged interest and a failure-to-pay penalty, and a return filed late without an extension is charged a larger failure-to-file penalty (generally 5 percent of unpaid tax per month, up to 25 percent). This is a very common judge question.
cards.example: Brightline files Form 7004, so its Form 1120 is not due until October 15, but it must still pay the estimated $13,950 balance by April 15 to avoid interest and penalties.
cards.say_it: Yes, we still pay by April 15; Form 7004 only gives us until October to file the paperwork, not more time to pay.
cards.mistakes: Telling the client the extension also delays the payment.

cards.core: FICA is 6.2% Social Security plus 1.45% Medicare withheld from the employee and matched by the employer.
cards.detail: FICA funds Social Security and Medicare. The employee pays 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% up to a yearly wage base, plus Medicare 1.45% on all wages) and the employer pays the same amount again. Self-employed people pay both halves, 15.3%, as self-employment tax. The employer's share is a payroll tax expense, which is why an employee costs more than their gross pay.
cards.formula: Employee FICA = gross pay x 7.65% (6.2% + 1.45%); employer matches the same amount
cards.example: On a $2,000 payroll: Social Security $124 and Medicare $29 withheld, and the employer pays another $124 and $29, plus FUTA $12 and SUTA $60, so total employer taxes are $225.
cards.say_it: The real cost of this $2,000 payroll is $2,225, because we match FICA and pay unemployment taxes on top of wages.
cards.mistakes: Forgetting the employer's matching share when budgeting for a new hire.

cards.core: C corporations pay their own 21% tax; sole proprietorships, partnerships, S corporations and most LLCs pass income to the owners.
cards.detail: A sole proprietor files Schedule C, a partnership files Form 1065 and gives each partner a Schedule K-1, and an S corporation files Form 1120-S with K-1s; the owners pay the tax. A single-member LLC is ignored for tax by default and still files Schedule C, so forming an LLC alone does not remove self-employment tax. An LLC or S corporation election can reduce SE tax only on profit above a reasonable salary that is itself taxed. A C corporation pays 21 percent on its taxable income, and dividends are taxed again to shareholders (double taxation).
cards.example: Maya's friend says an LLC avoids self-employment tax. As a single-member LLC she would still file Schedule C and pay about $10,000 of SE tax; only an S corporation election with a reasonable salary could change that, with extra payroll costs.
cards.say_it: An LLC protects you legally, but by itself it does not change your taxes; you would still report on Schedule C and pay self-employment tax.
cards.mistakes: Saying an LLC is a tax classification that automatically lowers tax.

cards.core: A tax liability is the amount of tax owed to a government; unpaid amounts are recorded as liabilities.
cards.detail: Individuals and businesses owe income taxes (federal, state, sometimes local), payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare, unemployment), self-employment tax, sales taxes collected from customers, and property taxes. Some taxes are the business's own expense (employer payroll tax, income tax of a corporation, property tax); others are collected for the government and only held in trust (employee withholdings, sales tax). Both kinds are liabilities until paid. Missing deadlines brings penalties and interest.
cards.example: Brightline Robotics owes $103,950 of federal income tax, has prepaid $90,000 in estimates, and records the remaining $13,950 as Income Taxes Payable, due April 15.
cards.say_it: Withheld payroll taxes and sales tax are the government's money, not ours, so I keep them separate and pay them on schedule.

cards.core: W-4 sets withholding, W-2 and 1099 report income, and Form 1040 is the individual return.
cards.detail: An employee fills out Form W-4 so the employer knows how much federal tax to withhold. After the year, the employer sends Form W-2 (wages and taxes withheld) by January 31; clients and banks send 1099 forms for freelance pay, interest and dividends. The taxpayer files Form 1040 by April 15, adding schedules as needed: Schedule C for self-employment profit, Schedule SE for self-employment tax, Schedule A for itemized deductions. Form 1040-ES is used for quarterly estimated payments.

cards.say_it: Every employee who earned wages during the year gets a W-2, even if they only worked the summer.

cards.core: Self-employed people pay income and SE tax in four estimated payments due April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
cards.detail: No one withholds tax from a freelancer's income, and the tax system is pay as you go, so the person sends estimated payments with Form 1040-ES. Estimate the year's total income tax plus self-employment tax and divide by four. Corporations also make quarterly estimated payments and record them as Prepaid Income Taxes until the year's tax is known. A practical habit is moving a set percentage of every client payment into a separate tax savings account.
cards.formula: Quarterly payment = Expected annual tax / 4
cards.example: Maya expects $10,000 of SE tax plus $8,000 of income tax = $18,000, so she pays $4,500 each on April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
cards.say_it: If you set aside about 20% of every client payment, the $4,500 quarterly payments will already be sitting in your tax account when they are due.
cards.mistakes: Waiting to pay everything in April, which triggers an underpayment penalty.

cards.core: Tax avoidance is legally lowering tax through planning; tax evasion is illegally hiding income or claiming false deductions.
cards.detail: Avoidance uses the rules as intended: timing purchases, electing Section 179, contributing to retirement plans, choosing an entity type, or investing in tax-exempt bonds. Evasion breaks the law: unreported cash income, fake or personal expenses claimed as business, or leaving items off the books. Evasion is a crime that can bring fines, penalties and prison, and a preparer who knowingly helps can lose the right to practice. The accountant's job is to minimize tax within the law and refuse requests that cross the line.
cards.example: Legal: Brightline earns tax-exempt municipal bond interest. Illegal: deducting Maya's Hawaii vacation as a business trip, or hiding cash payments from clients.
cards.say_it: My job is to make sure you pay the least tax the law allows, which is avoidance; putting your vacation on the return would be evasion, and that is a line I can't cross.

cards.core: A deduction lowers taxable income; a credit lowers the tax itself dollar for dollar, so a credit is worth more.
cards.detail: A deduction saves tax equal to the deduction times the taxpayer's marginal rate. A credit is subtracted directly from the tax owed. Some credits are refundable (they can create a refund beyond the tax owed) and others are not. When identifying tax issues for a client, the accountant should check both missed deductions (business expenses, retirement contributions) and credits the client may qualify for.
cards.formula: Tax saved by a deduction = Deduction x Marginal rate; Tax saved by a credit = Credit amount
cards.example: For a client in the 22% bracket, a $1,000 deduction saves $220, while a $1,000 credit saves $1,000. For a C corporation at 21%, a $1,000 deduction saves $210.
cards.say_it: A $1,000 credit saves you the full $1,000, but a $1,000 deduction only saves the tax on that income, about $220 at your rate.

cards.core: Late filing, late payment and underpaid estimates each bring IRS penalties plus interest on the unpaid tax.
cards.detail: The failure-to-file penalty is generally 5 percent of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to 25 percent. The failure-to-pay penalty is generally 0.5 percent per month, up to 25 percent. Interest is charged on unpaid tax and penalties until paid. Accuracy-related penalties apply to substantial understatements, and fraud brings much larger penalties and possible criminal charges. Penalties and fines are not deductible.
cards.example: If a client owing $10,000 files and pays two months late with no extension, the failure-to-file penalty alone is about 2 x 5% = 10% (reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty for the same months), plus interest.
cards.say_it: Filing late costs far more than paying late, so even if you cannot pay everything, file on time and pay what you can.

cards.term: Tax planning strategies to lessen the tax burden
cards.core: Lower a client's tax legally by timing income and expenses, using allowed deductions and credits, and choosing the right entity.
cards.detail: Good planning starts with identifying the client's tax issues: missed deductions, poor records, underpaid estimates, the wrong entity type or misclassified items. Common legal strategies: claim every ordinary and necessary expense; elect Section 179 or bonus depreciation for equipment; contribute to retirement plans such as a SEP IRA; deduct a qualifying home office; consider an S corporation election once profits are high enough to justify a salary and payroll costs; invest in tax-exempt bonds; and time year-end purchases. Each recommendation should be explained with its trade-off.
cards.example: For Maya: keep the $12,000 camera under Section 179, add a qualifying home office, open a SEP IRA, set up quarterly estimates of $4,500, and revisit the entity choice if profit keeps growing.
cards.say_it: The three biggest opportunities I see are documenting your home office, a retirement contribution, and steady quarterly estimates so you avoid penalties.

cards.core: Keep every deduction supported with receipts, logs and a separate business account so the return can be proven in an audit.
cards.detail: The taxpayer must prove income and deductions, so good records are the base of tax accounting. Key procedures: use a separate business bank account and credit card; save invoices, receipts, 1099 forms and bank statements, scanned into an organized folder or app; keep a mileage log as you drive (date, destination, business purpose, miles); write who attended and the business purpose on each meal receipt; keep home office measurements and photos; keep asset purchase records for depreciation. Records feed directly into the return and protect the client if the IRS asks questions.
cards.example: Maya Chen, a freelance photographer, should open a business checking account, scan every receipt the day she gets it, log business miles in an app, and keep the camera invoice to support her Section 179 deduction.
cards.say_it: If the IRS asks about your vehicle deduction, a mileage log written as you drive is what proves it, so let's set that up today.
cards.mistakes: Mixing personal and business spending in one account and trying to rebuild records at tax time.

cards.core: Individuals file Form 1040 by April 15; C corporations file Form 1120 by the 15th day of the 4th month after year end.
cards.detail: Know the main federal forms: Form 1040 for individuals with Schedule C (sole proprietor profit), Schedule SE (self-employment tax) and Form 1040-ES (estimated payments); Form 1065 for partnerships and Form 1120-S for S corporations (both due the 15th day of the 3rd month, March 15 for calendar years, with K-1s to owners); Form 1120 for C corporations (April 15 for a calendar-year company); and Form 990 for tax-exempt nonprofits (15th day of the 5th month). Preparing a return means gathering the records, computing taxable income, applying rates and credits, subtracting payments, reviewing and filing on time.
cards.example: Brightline Robotics, a calendar-year C corporation, files Form 1120 by April 15 and pays its $13,950 balance by then. Maya Chen files Form 1040 with Schedules C and SE by April 15.
cards.say_it: As a calendar-year C corporation we file Form 1120, due April 15, and any balance due has to be paid by that same date.

cards.core: Bonuses are taxable wages: income tax and Social Security and Medicare taxes apply.
cards.detail: A bonus is supplemental wages. The employer withholds federal income tax (often at a flat 22% rate for supplemental pay, or by adding it to regular wages), plus 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare, and state tax where it applies. The employer also pays its own matching payroll taxes on the bonus, and the bonus is a deductible wage expense for the business. Recipients often feel the bonus is "taxed more", but the final tax is settled on the annual return like any other wage.
cards.example: A $1,000 sales bonus might have $220 federal income tax, $62 Social Security and $14.50 Medicare withheld, leaving about $703.50 before state tax.
cards.say_it: Yes, bonus money is taxed like wages, so when we design the incentive plan we should budget for the employer payroll taxes on top of the bonus itself.

cards.core: When book and tax timing differ but reverse later, the company records a deferred tax liability or asset.
cards.detail: A temporary difference arises when an item is recognized in different years for books and for tax, such as depreciation (MACRS or Section 179 for tax, straight-line for books) or warranty expense (accrued for books, deducted for tax when paid). If tax deductions come first, taxable income is lower now and higher later, creating a deferred tax liability. If book expenses come first (like accrued warranties), a deferred tax asset results. Total depreciation over the asset's life is the same; only the timing differs.
cards.formula: Deferred tax = Cumulative temporary difference x Tax rate
cards.example: Illustration: book straight-line depreciation $20,000 but tax depreciation $48,000 in Year 1. The $28,000 difference x 21% = $5,880 deferred tax liability, which reverses as later tax depreciation is smaller.
cards.say_it: Using faster depreciation on the tax return does not erase tax; it delays it, which is why we record a deferred tax liability for the tax we will pay later.

cards.core: Debit Income Tax Expense for the year's tax, credit Prepaid Income Taxes for estimates paid, and credit Income Taxes Payable for the rest.
cards.detail: During the year each estimated payment is recorded as a debit to Prepaid Income Taxes and a credit to Cash. At year end, once the tax for the year is computed, the company records the full Income Tax Expense, clears the prepaid account, and records the remaining amount owed as a current liability, Income Taxes Payable. When the balance is paid with the return, Income Taxes Payable is debited and Cash is credited. If the estimates were larger than the tax, the excess is a receivable instead of a payable.
cards.formula: Dr Income Tax Expense (total tax); Cr Prepaid Income Taxes (estimates paid); Cr Income Taxes Payable (balance due)
cards.example: Brightline: Dr Income Tax Expense 103,950; Cr Prepaid Income Taxes 90,000; Cr Income Taxes Payable 13,950. Debits equal credits at $103,950. On April 15: Dr Income Taxes Payable 13,950, Cr Cash 13,950.
cards.say_it: The full $103,950 is this year's expense; $90,000 was already prepaid, so only $13,950 shows as a liability on the balance sheet.
cards.mistakes: Recording only the balance due as expense, which understates the year's tax expense.

examples.title: Brightline Robotics: corporate income tax

cards.core: A C corporation pays a flat 21% federal tax on its taxable income, not on its book income.
cards.detail: Since 2018 the federal rate for C corporations is a flat 21 percent of taxable income, with no brackets. Taxable income is found by starting with book (GAAP) pre-tax income and adjusting for differences between accounting rules and tax law. State income taxes may also apply. Estimated payments made during the year are subtracted from the total tax to find the balance due with the return.
cards.formula: Federal income tax = Taxable income x 21%; Balance due = Tax minus Estimated payments
cards.example: Brightline Robotics: taxable income $495,000 x 21% = $103,950. Estimated payments of $90,000 leave a balance due of $13,950.
cards.say_it: Our tax is 21% of taxable income, $103,950, and since we already paid $90,000 in estimates, we owe $13,950 by April 15.
cards.mistakes: Multiplying 21% by book income instead of taxable income.

cards.core: A space used regularly and only for business can be deducted at $5 per square foot, up to 300 square feet.
cards.detail: To qualify, the area must be used regularly and exclusively for the business and be the principal place of business (or a place to meet clients). The simplified method multiplies the square footage by $5, with a maximum of 300 square feet ($1,500). The regular method instead deducts the business percentage of actual home costs such as rent, utilities and insurance, which needs more records. A kitchen table also used for meals does not qualify.
cards.formula: Deduction = Square feet x $5 (maximum 300 square feet, or $1,500)
cards.example: Maya uses a 200 square foot room only for editing photos: 200 x $5 = $1,000 deduction.
cards.say_it: Because the room is used only for your business, the simplified method gives you a $1,000 deduction without tracking every utility bill; just keep the measurements and a photo.

cards.core: Individual tax flows from gross income to adjusted gross income to taxable income, then tax brackets, minus credits.
cards.detail: Step 1: total all gross income (wages, Schedule C profit, interest). Step 2: subtract adjustments such as half of SE tax and self-employed health insurance to get adjusted gross income (AGI). Step 3: subtract the larger of the standard deduction or itemized deductions (and certain other deductions) to get taxable income. Step 4: apply the progressive tax brackets. Step 5: subtract tax credits, add other taxes such as SE tax, then subtract withholding and estimated payments to find the refund or balance due.
cards.formula: Taxable income = Gross income minus Adjustments minus Standard or itemized deduction; Tax owed = Tax from brackets minus Credits + Other taxes
cards.example: Simplified for illustration: AGI $60,000 minus a $15,000 standard deduction = $45,000 taxable income. Tax from the brackets, minus a $500 credit, plus SE tax, minus $9,000 of estimated payments gives the amount still due.
cards.say_it: First we get to your adjusted gross income, then subtract your deduction to find taxable income, and only then do the brackets and credits come in.
cards.mistakes: Applying a tax rate to gross income instead of taxable income.

cards.term: Managing tax risk in a business
cards.core: Reduce tax risk with a deadline calendar, reviewed returns, documented positions and on-time estimated payments.
cards.detail: Tax risk is the chance of penalties, interest, audits or legal trouble from errors or missed deadlines. Practical controls: a tax calendar of every filing and payment date; a second preparer review before filing; written support for each significant position; reconciliation of book income to taxable income; secure retention of records for the audit period; and timely estimated payments. These controls also help the business plan its cash for tax payments.
cards.example: Brightline adds a calendar with its four estimated payment dates and the April 15 Form 1120 date, has a second accountant review the return, and keeps the meal and fine documentation with the workpapers.
cards.say_it: A simple tax calendar and a second review before we file are cheap insurance against penalties and interest.

cards.core: The marginal rate applies to the next dollar earned; the effective rate is total tax divided by income.
cards.detail: U.S. individual income tax is progressive: each bracket's rate applies only to the income inside that bracket, so moving into a higher bracket never taxes all income at the higher rate. The marginal rate is useful for planning (how much tax a new deduction saves). The effective rate shows the real overall burden. For a corporation, the federal rate is a flat 21 percent, but the effective rate on book income can differ because of permanent differences.
cards.formula: Effective tax rate = Total income tax / Income (book pre-tax income for a corporation)
cards.example: Brightline: tax $103,950 / book income $500,000 = about 20.8% effective, below the 21% statutory rate because tax-exempt interest outweighs the nondeductible items. Simplified individual illustration: 10% on the first $12,000 and 12% on the next $28,000 = $1,200 + $3,360 = $4,560 on $40,000, an 11.4% effective rate with a 12% marginal rate.
cards.say_it: Moving into a higher bracket only taxes the extra dollars at the higher rate, so earning more never lowers your take-home pay from income tax alone.
cards.mistakes: Believing a raise into a higher bracket makes all income taxed at the higher rate.

cards.core: A business expense is deductible only if it is ordinary (common in the industry) and necessary (helpful for earning income).
cards.detail: This is the main IRS test for business deductions. Ordinary means the expense is common and accepted in that kind of business; necessary means it is helpful and appropriate, not that it is required. Personal, living or family costs are never deductible as business expenses. Some items are always disallowed even if business related, such as fines and penalties paid to a government. Mixed-use items, such as a car used for both business and personal trips, are deducted only for the business portion.
cards.example: Deductible for a photographer: editing software, a camera, the business share of car costs. Not deductible: a Hawaii vacation, everyday clothing that can be worn outside work, and a traffic ticket (fines are never deductible).
cards.say_it: Your software is ordinary and necessary for a photographer, but the vacation is personal, so I can't put it on your return even if you took a few photos there.
cards.mistakes: Assuming anything paid with the business card is deductible.

cards.core: A permanent difference is an item counted for book or for tax but never both, such as fines, half of meals or municipal bond interest.
cards.detail: Permanent differences never reverse in later years, so they change the effective tax rate but create no deferred taxes. Common examples: government fines and penalties (expensed on the books, never deductible), the nondeductible 50 percent of business meals, and interest on municipal bonds (book income, but tax exempt). Leaving a fine off the books to avoid explaining it is not allowed, because GAAP requires every real expense to be recorded; it is simply added back on the tax return.
cards.example: Brightline's $5,000 fine stays on the income statement as an expense, then is added back for tax. Its $20,000 of municipal bond interest is income on the books but subtracted for tax.
cards.say_it: We can't leave the fine off the books; GAAP requires us to record it, and on the tax return we simply add it back because fines are never deductible.
cards.mistakes: Recording deferred taxes on a permanent difference.

cards.term: Preparing a personal income tax return
cards.core: Gather income forms and records, total income, subtract deductions, figure tax, subtract credits and payments.
cards.detail: Step 1: gather W-2s, 1099s, receipts and last year's return. Step 2: total gross income. Step 3: subtract adjustments (such as half of self-employment tax or student loan interest) to get adjusted gross income. Step 4: subtract the standard or itemized deduction to get taxable income. Step 5: calculate tax using the brackets, then subtract credits. Step 6: compare with tax already withheld or paid in estimates: the difference is a refund or balance due. File by April 15 (or extend the filing date, but still pay on time) and keep copies.
cards.example: If tax is $6,000 and $6,500 was withheld, the refund is $500; if only $5,200 was withheld, $800 is due by April 15.
cards.say_it: A refund is not a bonus; it means too much was withheld during the year, so I would adjust the W-4 and keep that cash working.

cards.core: Sales tax collected from customers is a liability owed to the state, never revenue for the business.
cards.detail: A retailer collects sales tax on taxable sales as an agent of the state or city. The tax is recorded as a credit to Sales Tax Payable at the time of the sale and is removed when it is sent to the government, usually monthly or quarterly. Including it in sales would overstate revenue. Good records include the taxable and exempt sales for each period and copies of the returns filed, and failing to remit collected tax brings penalties.
cards.formula: Sales tax = Taxable sales x Tax rate
cards.example: A $500 cash sale with 8% sales tax: Dr Cash 540, Cr Sales 500, Cr Sales Tax Payable 40. When remitted: Dr Sales Tax Payable 40, Cr Cash 40.
cards.say_it: The $40 of sales tax belongs to the state, so we record it as a liability, not as part of our $500 of sales.
cards.mistakes: Recording the sales tax as revenue or as an expense.

cards.core: A sole proprietor reports business income on Schedule C: net profit equals gross receipts minus deductible business expenses.
cards.detail: Sole proprietors and single-member LLCs report business results on Schedule C, attached to Form 1040. Net profit is subject to both income tax and self-employment tax. Only ordinary and necessary business expenses go on Schedule C; personal costs, fines and some special items (such as the self-employed health insurance deduction) do not. Getting net profit right is the starting point for every other calculation in a freelancer case.
cards.formula: Net profit = Gross receipts minus Deductible business expenses
cards.example: Maya Chen Studio: deductible expenses are camera $12,000 + software $2,500 + vehicle business portion $3,000 + meals $500 (50% of $1,000) + home office $1,000 = $19,000. Net profit = 90,000 minus 19,000 = $71,000.
cards.say_it: After we take out only the true business expenses, your Schedule C shows $71,000 of net profit, and that number drives both your income tax and your self-employment tax.

cards.core: Section 179 lets a business deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment in the year it is placed in service instead of depreciating it.
cards.detail: Normally equipment is depreciated for tax over several years using MACRS. A Section 179 election lets a business deduct the whole cost in the first year, up to an annual limit set by law, which lowers taxable income right away. It is a tax rule only; the financial statements still depreciate the asset over its useful life under GAAP, which creates a temporary difference. The asset must be used more than half for business, and records of the purchase must be kept.
cards.example: Maya bought a $12,000 camera used only for her business and elected Section 179, so the full $12,000 is deducted on this year's Schedule C instead of spreading it over several years.
cards.say_it: Electing Section 179 lets you deduct the whole $12,000 camera this year, which lowers both your income tax and your self-employment tax now.
cards.mistakes: Thinking Section 179 changes the book depreciation on the financial statements.

cards.core: Health insurance premiums of a self-employed person are deducted on Form 1040, not as a Schedule C business expense.
cards.detail: A self-employed person who is not eligible for an employer-sponsored plan (for example through a spouse's job) can deduct health insurance premiums for themselves and their family as an adjustment to income on Form 1040. Because it is not on Schedule C, it lowers income tax but does not lower self-employment tax. The deduction cannot be more than the business's net profit. Placing it on the right form is a common tax issue to spot in a role play.
cards.example: Maya paid $4,800 of health insurance premiums. They stay off Schedule C, so net profit is still $71,000 for SE tax, but she may deduct the $4,800 on Form 1040 if she is not eligible for an employer plan.
cards.say_it: Your health insurance is still deductible, just not on Schedule C; it goes on Form 1040, so it lowers your income tax but not your self-employment tax.

cards.core: Self-employed people pay both halves of Social Security and Medicare: 15.3% on 92.35% of net profit.
cards.detail: An employee pays 7.65 percent FICA and the employer matches it. A self-employed person is both, so pays 15.3 percent (12.4 percent Social Security up to an annual wage base, plus 2.9 percent Medicare with no limit) on Schedule SE. The 92.35 percent factor gives the same result as an employer deducting its share first. Half of the self-employment tax is deductible on Form 1040 (it lowers income tax, not the SE tax itself). This tax is owed in addition to regular income tax, which surprises many new freelancers.
cards.formula: SE tax = Net profit x 92.35% x 15.3%; deductible half = SE tax / 2
cards.example: Maya: 71,000 x 92.35% = 65,568.50; x 15.3% = about $10,032, or roughly $10,000. About $5,016 (half) is deductible on Form 1040.
cards.say_it: Because no employer is paying half your Social Security and Medicare, you pay the full 15.3%, about $10,000 on $71,000 of profit, on top of income tax.
cards.mistakes: Applying 15.3% to the full net profit without the 92.35% factor, or forgetting SE tax altogether.

cards.core: A tax professional must be accurate, use due diligence, keep client information confidential and give honest advice.
cards.detail: Treasury Circular 230 governs people who practice before the IRS (CPAs, enrolled agents, attorneys), and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services guide CPAs. Duties include due diligence on the facts, not taking positions without support, telling clients about errors and their consequences, meeting deadlines, and keeping client data confidential. A preparer must not deduct personal items just because the client asks, and must sign returns they prepare. Explaining rules clearly is part of the service.
cards.example: Maya asks to deduct her vacation and everyday clothing. The accountant explains why they are personal, leaves them off, and documents the conversation.
cards.say_it: I'm required to prepare an accurate return, so I'll explain why these personal items don't qualify and find every legitimate deduction instead.

cards.core: Paying too little tax during the year brings a penalty, avoided by paying 90% of this year's tax or 100% of last year's.
cards.detail: The underpayment penalty works like interest on each quarterly amount that was paid late or not at all. An individual avoids it by paying, through withholding and estimated payments, at least 90 percent of the current year's tax or 100 percent of the prior year's tax (110 percent if the prior year's adjusted gross income was over $150,000). Paying everything in April does not avoid the penalty because the earlier quarters were still late. Planning estimated payments is one of the most useful things an accountant does for a new freelancer.
cards.example: If Maya skips her four $4,500 payments and pays $18,000 in April, she owes a penalty on each missed quarter. If last year's total tax was $15,000, paying at least $15,000 during the year (100% of last year) would protect her.
cards.say_it: Paying it all in April still means three quarters were late, so the safe harbor is to pay at least what you owed last year, spread over four payments.

cards.core: A favorable variance increases income compared with the budget; an unfavorable variance decreases it.
cards.detail: For revenue, actual above budget is favorable (F). For costs, actual below budget is favorable. Favorable does not always mean good: a favorable materials price from low-quality inputs can create unfavorable quantity and quality problems, and a favorable cost variance from skipping maintenance can hurt later. Always label each variance F or U and explain its likely cause.
cards.example: Crumb & Co.: sales volume $6,000 F; flour price $500 F but flour quantity $500 U; labor $2,800 U.
cards.say_it: The flour price variance is favorable, but it may be the reason we used 1,000 extra pounds, so favorable isn't automatically good news.

cards.core: The labor rate variance measures paying a different wage than standard; the efficiency variance measures using more or fewer hours than allowed.
cards.detail: Rate variances come from overtime, using higher paid workers or raises. Efficiency variances come from training, scheduling, machine problems or poor materials. Standard hours allowed = actual output x standard hours per unit. The production supervisor usually owns both. Together they explain the total labor variance, which is often the largest cost problem in a case.
cards.formula: Rate variance = (Actual rate minus Standard rate) x Actual hours; Efficiency variance = (Actual hours minus Standard hours allowed) x Standard rate
cards.example: Crumb & Co.: rate ($16 minus $15) x 1,300 hours = $1,300 U; efficiency (1,300 minus 1,200) x $15 = $1,500 U; total labor $2,800 U.
cards.say_it: Labor is our biggest problem: 100 extra hours at a dollar more per hour, so let's look at overtime, new hires and scheduling.

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: Investigate the largest and most controllable variances first instead of every small difference.
cards.detail: Managers have limited time, so they focus on variances that are large in dollars or percentage, keep repeating, or can be controlled. Each variance is assigned to the responsible manager: price variances to purchasing or sales, quantity and labor variances to production. Reports should be prepared regularly (often monthly) by responsibility, followed by action plans. Small, random variances are usually left alone.
cards.example: Crumb & Co.: investigate first the $3,000 U selling price variance (sales manager) and the $2,800 U labor variance (production supervisor), then the flour usage and the $500 U fixed overhead spending.
cards.say_it: I'd start with the two biggest variances, the $3,000 price variance and the $2,800 labor variance, and assign each to the manager who controls it.

pis.text: Discuss the role of standard costing in the preparation and analysis of budgets
Discuss the use of variance analysis in managerial accounting

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: The materials price variance measures paying more or less than standard; the quantity variance measures using more or less than allowed.
cards.detail: The price variance is usually the purchasing manager's responsibility; the quantity variance belongs to production. Standard quantity allowed = actual output x standard quantity per unit. A favorable price can cause an unfavorable quantity (cheap materials that waste more), so the two should be read together. The total materials variance = actual cost minus standard cost allowed.
cards.formula: Price variance = (Actual price minus Standard price) x Actual quantity; Quantity variance = (Actual quantity minus Standard quantity allowed) x Standard price
cards.example: Crumb & Co. flour: price ($0.48 minus $0.50) x 25,000 lbs = $500 F; quantity (25,000 minus 24,000) x $0.50 = $500 U; net $0.
cards.say_it: We saved $500 buying cheaper flour but wasted $500 by using 1,000 extra pounds, so purchasing and production should check whether the cheaper flour caused the waste.
cards.mistakes: Using standard quantity in the price variance or actual price in the quantity variance.
