examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.term: Sales volume variance vs. flexible budget variance
cards.core: The total variance splits into a sales volume variance (selling more or fewer units) and a flexible budget variance (prices and cost control).
cards.detail: Static budget versus actual = total variance. Flexible budget minus static budget = sales volume variance, caused only by the change in units; it equals the change in units times the standard contribution margin per unit. Actual minus flexible budget = flexible budget variance, which breaks into the selling price variance and the cost variances for each line. A favorable volume variance can hide unfavorable cost performance, which is the key insight in these cases.
cards.formula: Sales volume variance = (Actual units minus Budgeted units) x Standard CM per unit; Flexible budget variance = Actual result minus Flexible budget
cards.example: Crumb & Co.: total $600 U (24,000 vs 23,400). Volume variance 2,000 extra loaves x $3.00 = $6,000 F. Flexible budget variance 23,400 minus 30,000 = $6,600 U (price $3,000 U, labor $2,800 U, variable overhead $300 U, fixed overhead $500 U, flour $0).
cards.say_it: The extra 2,000 loaves earned us $6,000, but we gave back $6,600 through lower prices and higher costs, so operations are not fine.

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: The selling price variance measures the effect of selling at a different price than budgeted.
cards.detail: It compares actual revenue with flexible budget revenue at the actual volume, so it reflects price only. A lower average price, from promotions or discounts, gives an unfavorable variance; higher prices give a favorable one. The sales manager is usually responsible. A price cut may be a sound choice if it brings lasting extra volume, so the variance should be weighed against the sales volume variance.
cards.formula: Selling price variance = (Actual price minus Budgeted price) x Actual units sold
cards.example: Crumb & Co. sold 12,000 loaves for $69,000, an average of $5.75: ($5.75 minus $6.00) x 12,000 = $3,000 U.
cards.say_it: The promotion cost us $3,000 in lower prices, so the sales manager should show that those new accounts will stay at full price.

pis.text: Describe the nature of flexible budgets

examples.title: Crumb & Co. Bakery: flexible budget and standard cost variance analysis

cards.core: Variance analysis compares actual results with the budget or standard and finds the causes of the differences.
cards.detail: A variance is the difference between actual and budgeted (or standard) amounts. Managerial accountants break the total difference into pieces: sales volume, selling price, materials price and quantity, labor rate and efficiency, and overhead spending. Each piece points to a different cause and a different responsible manager (sales, purchasing, production). The goal is not blame but learning and correction.
cards.example: Crumb and Co.'s $6,600 unfavorable flexible budget variance breaks into selling price $3,000 U, flour $0, labor $2,800 U, variable overhead $300 U and fixed overhead $500 U.
cards.say_it: Breaking the $6,600 into parts shows that the promotion and labor are the real problems, while flour costs actually balanced out.

cards.core: Accountants work in four main places: public accounting, industry (corporate), government and nonprofit organizations.
cards.detail: Public accounting firms (from the Big Four to small local CPA firms) sell audit, tax and advisory services to many clients. Industry or corporate accountants work inside one business, for example as staff accountant, cost accountant, controller or CFO. Government accountants work for agencies such as the IRS, the GAO, the FBI or state auditor offices. Nonprofit accountants manage donor funds, grants and the Form 990 for charities, hospitals and schools. Many people start in public accounting and later move to industry.
cards.example: A new graduate audits clients at a CPA firm for three years, then becomes a senior accountant at a hospital and later its controller.
cards.say_it: Accounting is not one job: you can serve many clients at a CPA firm, work inside one company, protect taxpayers in government, or help a nonprofit stretch every donated dollar.
cards.mistakes: Saying accounting only means doing taxes; judges want to hear the range of settings.

cards.core: Accountants record transactions accurately, report them under the rules, analyze the numbers and protect the public trust.
cards.detail: Core duties are: record and organize transactions honestly; prepare financial statements and tax returns that follow GAAP and tax law; analyze results to help owners decide; design and test internal controls; keep client information confidential; and act ethically, which includes refusing to misstate numbers and reporting fraud through proper channels. Because banks, investors and governments rely on their work, accountants have a duty to the public, not only to the employer.
cards.example: A controller refuses to record November sales in October even though a manager's bonus depends on it.
cards.say_it: An accountant's first responsibility is accuracy, because lenders, owners and investors make real decisions with these numbers.

cards.core: A CPA explains how a decision affects the business's finances, but the owner or manager makes the final decision.
cards.detail: When a client considers buying equipment, borrowing or expanding, the CPA shows the effect on the income statement, balance sheet, cash flow and taxes, points out risks and may recommend an option. Responsibility for the decision stays with management. This also protects the CPA's objectivity, and for audit clients, independence rules forbid the auditor from making management decisions.
cards.example: The CPA shows the landscaping owner that the $50,000 mower adds $40,000 of net income a year, then lets the owner choose.
cards.say_it: My job is to give you clear numbers and a recommendation; the decision is yours because you know the business best.

cards.core: Bookkeepers record transactions, accountants analyze and report them, and only licensed CPAs may sign audit and review reports.
cards.detail: A bookkeeper (often no degree required) enters transactions, pays bills, runs payroll and reconciles accounts. An accountant usually has a bachelor's degree and prepares statements, analyzes results and gives advice. A CPA is licensed by a state board of accountancy; state law reserves the CPA title and audit and review reports for licensed CPAs and CPA firms. Bookkeepers and tax preparers may still prepare returns for pay with an IRS PTIN.
cards.example: Tanya's bookkeeping firm may offer payroll and tax preparation, but it must refer a nonprofit audit to a licensed CPA firm.
cards.say_it: You can offer bookkeeping, payroll and tax preparation without a license, but advertising audits requires a CPA firm license.
cards.mistakes: Advertising "CPA quality audits" without a license, which misleads clients and can break state law.

cards.core: Inside a company, accountants rise from staff accountant to senior accountant, accounting manager, controller and finally CFO.
cards.detail: Staff accountants record transactions, run accounts payable and receivable, and reconcile accounts. Cost accountants track the cost of making products. Accounting managers supervise the monthly close. The controller heads the accounting department, owns financial reporting and internal controls, and usually reports to the CFO. The chief financial officer (CFO) oversees all of finance: accounting, budgeting, financing, investing and strategy. A treasurer manages cash, banking and borrowing.
cards.example: In the jewelry store case, the presenter moved from accounts payable manager to controller and is aiming for CFO.
cards.say_it: The controller keeps the books accurate and the controls strong, while the CFO uses those numbers to set the company's financial strategy.
cards.mistakes: Mixing up controller and CFO; the controller reports to the CFO.

cards.core: Good first jobs are staff accountant, audit or tax associate, accounts payable or receivable clerk, payroll clerk and bookkeeper.
cards.detail: With a bachelor's degree, graduates usually start as an audit or tax associate at a CPA firm or a staff accountant in a company. Without a degree, students can start as an accounts payable or receivable clerk, payroll clerk or bookkeeper. High school and college students can gain experience through internships, VITA free tax preparation and part-time office jobs. These roles teach the full accounting cycle and lead to senior positions.
cards.example: The jewelry store controller started in accounts payable before moving up to AP manager and controller.
cards.say_it: A great entry level job is staff accountant, because you touch every part of the accounting cycle and learn how the whole business runs.

cards.core: A forensic accountant is a financial detective who investigates fraud and may testify in court.
cards.detail: Forensic accountants trace hidden money, investigate embezzlement, money laundering and insurance claims, measure losses, and gather evidence in a way that holds up in court. They work for CPA firms, law firms, insurers, banks and agencies such as the FBI or IRS Criminal Investigation. Many earn the Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE) credential. The work can involve travel to collect records or appear as an expert witness, and it uses advanced data analysis tools.
cards.example: A restaurant owner suspects a bookkeeper is skimming cash, so a forensic accountant reviews voided sales and bank deposits.
cards.say_it: Forensic accounting is the most exciting path for students who like mysteries, because you follow the money to find out what really happened.

cards.core: Government and nonprofit accountants track public money and donations and report how they were used.
cards.detail: Government accountants work for federal agencies (IRS, GAO, FBI, Defense agencies), state auditor offices, cities and school districts; state and local governments follow GASB standards, and the federal government follows FASAB standards. Nonprofit accountants manage restricted donations and grants, prepare a statement of financial position and statement of activities, and help file IRS Form 990. These jobs offer stability, good benefits and a mission focus. The AGA and its CGFM credential serve government accountants.
cards.example: A nonprofit accountant shows donors how much of each dollar went to programs instead of fundraising.
cards.say_it: If you want your work to serve the community, government and nonprofit accounting let you protect public and donated money.

cards.term: Job outlook and pay in accounting
cards.core: Accounting offers stable demand and solid pay because every business, government and person needs financial and tax help.
cards.detail: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a median pay for accountants and auditors of roughly $80,000 a year, with steady projected growth and many openings from retirements; check the latest Occupational Outlook Handbook for current numbers. Demand stays steady in good and bad economies because taxes, audits and payroll never stop. A CPA or other credential, a graduate degree and leadership roles (controller, CFO, partner) raise pay considerably.
cards.example: When a middle schooler asks whether accounting pays a stable income, the presenter explains that tax returns are due every year no matter what the economy does.
cards.say_it: Accounting is one of the most stable careers because businesses must keep records and file taxes every single year.
cards.mistakes: Quoting an exact salary as a guarantee; pay varies by city, employer and credential.

cards.core: A management accountant works inside a company, building budgets and analyzing costs so managers make better decisions.
cards.detail: Management (managerial or cost) accountants prepare budgets and forecasts, compare actual results to plans, price products, analyze projects and measure performance. Their reports are for internal users, so they do not have to follow GAAP. The usual credential is the CMA from the IMA. This path leads to controller, vice president of finance and CFO, and usually involves little travel.
cards.example: A management accountant shows that a product line loses money after its own fixed costs and recommends a new price.
cards.say_it: Management accountants look forward, using numbers to plan the business, while financial accountants mainly report what already happened.

cards.core: Public accounting firms serve outside clients in three service lines: audit (assurance), tax and advisory (consulting).
cards.detail: Audit or assurance teams examine clients' financial statements and give an opinion; only licensed CPA firms may issue audit reports. Tax teams prepare returns and plan strategies for people and businesses. Advisory teams help with risk, technology, deals and fraud. The largest firms are the Big Four (Deloitte, PwC, EY and KPMG), but most CPA firms are small and local. Public accounting has a busy season (January to April for tax and calendar year audits) and a clear promotion ladder.
cards.example: A staff auditor visits a manufacturer in February to count inventory and test the year end balances.
cards.say_it: Public accounting is a fast way to learn because you see many different businesses in your first few years.
cards.mistakes: Thinking public accounting means working for the government; "public" means serving the public as clients.

cards.core: A tax advisor prepares returns and plans strategies so clients obey tax law while paying no more than they legally owe.
cards.detail: Tax professionals prepare individual, business and nonprofit returns, research tax rules, plan the timing of income and deductions, and represent clients when the IRS asks questions. CPAs, enrolled agents and attorneys can represent any taxpayer before the IRS. Anyone paid to prepare federal returns needs a PTIN from the IRS. The work peaks during tax season (January to April) and again near extended deadlines.
cards.example: A tax advisor helps a freelancer set up quarterly estimated payments and track business deductions.
cards.say_it: Tax work is steady because every person and every business has to file, and tax laws change almost every year.
cards.mistakes: Saying tax advisors help clients avoid taxes illegally; legal tax planning (avoidance) is fine, evasion is a crime.

cards.core: Auditors and forensic accountants often travel to clients, while tax and management accountants travel much less.
cards.detail: External auditors visit client sites to count inventory, review records and meet managers, sometimes across the country or abroad at large firms. Forensic accountants travel to gather evidence or testify in court. Internal auditors at global companies visit plants and branches. Tax advisors, bookkeepers and management accountants mostly work in one office or remotely, and cloud software has made remote work common across the field.
cards.example: A Big Four auditor on a global client may spend a week at a factory in Mexico.
cards.say_it: If you love to travel, audit or forensic work can take you to clients; if you prefer to stay close to home, tax or management accounting fits better.

cards.core: Every type of organization needs accountants: businesses of all sizes, banks, hospitals, schools, governments and nonprofits.
cards.detail: Any organization that earns revenue, pays employees, owes taxes or receives grants must keep records and report. Accountants are hired by retailers, manufacturers, restaurants, tech firms, sports teams and entertainment companies, banks and insurers, hospitals and universities, cities and federal agencies, and charities. Small businesses often hire an outside CPA firm or bookkeeper instead of a full-time staff member.
cards.example: A jewelry store, a professional baseball team and a city water department all employ accountants.
cards.say_it: Accounting lets you work in any industry you love, from sports to fashion, because every organization needs someone to manage its money.

cards.core: Finance careers include banking, corporate finance, investments, financial planning, insurance and real estate.
cards.detail: Banks hire loan officers, credit analysts and branch managers. Companies hire financial analysts and treasurers (corporate finance). Investment firms hire stock analysts, portfolio managers, brokers and investment bankers. Financial planners help families save and invest; insurance firms hire underwriters and actuaries. Accounting knowledge is the base for all of them because every finance job reads financial statements. Common credentials are the CFA (investments) and the CFP (personal planning), and many roles need FINRA licenses.
cards.example: A credit analyst at a bank reads a company's GAAP statements before approving a loan.
cards.say_it: Accounting is the language of business, so it opens doors across banking, investing and planning, not just accounting firms.

cards.core: Accountants can start their own bookkeeping, tax or CPA firm, or serve small businesses as a part-time (fractional) CFO.
cards.detail: Entrepreneurs in this field open bookkeeping and payroll services, tax preparation offices, consulting businesses, or licensed CPA firms (which must register with the state board and usually be majority owned by CPAs). Others build accounting apps or work as freelance or fractional CFOs for start-ups. Benefits are independence and unlimited earnings; risks are irregular income, finding clients and handling all the business tasks. Ownership rules for CPA firms vary by state.
cards.example: Tanya runs her own bookkeeping firm; earning the CPA license would let her firm add audit services.
cards.say_it: Accounting skills are perfect for entrepreneurs, because you already understand cash flow, taxes and pricing before you open your doors.

cards.core: GAAP assumes a separate economic entity, a going concern, a stable monetary unit and reporting in set time periods.
cards.detail: Economic entity: the business's records are kept separate from the owner's personal finances. Going concern: the business is expected to keep operating, so assets are reported at cost rather than liquidation value; suppliers and lenders check this. Monetary unit: transactions are recorded in a stable currency such as dollars. Time period (periodicity): the life of the business is divided into months, quarters and fiscal years so results can be reported regularly.
cards.example: A supplier checks the frozen yogurt shop's statements to confirm it is a going concern before selling on credit.
cards.say_it: Keeping your personal spending out of the business books is the economic entity assumption, and it is the first rule I would fix.

cards.core: GAAP is the common set of U.S. accounting rules, set by the FASB, that makes financial statements consistent, reliable and comparable.
cards.detail: GAAP includes the concepts, principles, standards and procedures for recording and reporting transactions. Since 2009 it is organized in the FASB Accounting Standards Codification (ASC). The SEC requires U.S. public companies to follow GAAP, and most private companies use it because banks, investors and suppliers require GAAP statements. State and local governments follow a separate GAAP set by the GASB. Following GAAP lets an outside reader trust and compare statements from different companies and years.
cards.example: Because the frozen yogurt shop will borrow from a bank, its records must follow GAAP instead of a private system only the owner understands.
cards.say_it: GAAP is the common language of accounting, so anyone reading your statements, from a banker to an investor, understands them the same way.
cards.mistakes: Saying GAAP is a law passed by Congress; it is set by the private FASB and given legal force for public companies by the SEC.

cards.core: Core GAAP principles are historical cost, revenue recognition, matching (expense recognition) and full disclosure.
cards.detail: Historical cost: assets are generally recorded at what was paid. Revenue recognition: record revenue when it is earned, that is when goods or services are delivered to the customer (ASC 606), not necessarily when cash is received. Matching or expense recognition: record expenses in the same period as the revenue they helped earn. Full disclosure: report all information a user needs, in the statements or the notes. Consistency, materiality and conservatism guide how these are applied.
cards.example: A $500 web hosting bill for October is an October expense, even though it is paid on November 15.
cards.say_it: Under GAAP, timing follows the earning and the using, not the cash, so each month shows its true profit.

cards.core: IFRS bans LIFO, allows reversing write-downs and impairments, and allows revaluing property; U.S. GAAP does the opposite.
cards.detail: Inventory: GAAP allows LIFO; IFRS prohibits it. Inventory write-downs: GAAP never reverses them (the lower value is the new cost); IFRS reverses up to original cost if value recovers. Impairment of long-lived assets: GAAP prohibits reversal; IFRS allows it (except goodwill). Property, plant and equipment: GAAP uses historical cost only; IFRS allows a revaluation model at fair value. Development costs: expensed under GAAP, capitalized under IFRS when criteria are met. Contingencies: different probability thresholds and measurement. Revenue recognition is now largely the same (ASC 606 and IFRS 15).
cards.example: Apex Electronics cannot write its tablets back up under GAAP if prices rebound, but an IFRS company could.
cards.say_it: The quickest GAAP versus IFRS test: IFRS bans LIFO and lets you reverse write-downs; GAAP allows LIFO and never reverses them.
cards.mistakes: Saying the two are now identical; convergence aligned revenue and leases but many differences remain.

cards.core: Useful information must be relevant and faithfully represented, and is better when comparable, verifiable, timely and understandable.
cards.detail: The FASB conceptual framework names two fundamental qualities: relevance (it can make a difference in decisions, including materiality) and faithful representation (complete, neutral and free from error). Enhancing qualities are comparability (including consistency over time), verifiability, timeliness and understandability. Standard setters judge new rules by these qualities and by whether benefits exceed costs. They explain why GAAP exists and why IFRS and GAAP sometimes choose different treatments.
cards.example: Investors comparing Novus (IFRS) with a U.S. competitor (GAAP) face a comparability problem until both are put on the same basis.
cards.say_it: Every accounting rule aims to give users information that is relevant to their decision and a faithful picture of what really happened.

cards.term: Who sets the accounting and auditing rules
cards.core: FASB sets U.S. GAAP, GASB sets government GAAP, IASB sets IFRS, the SEC enforces for public companies and the PCAOB oversees their auditors.
cards.detail: Accounting standards: FASB (businesses and nonprofits), GASB (state and local governments), FASAB (the federal government) and IASB (IFRS, international). Legal authority: the SEC for public company reporting. Auditing standards: the PCAOB for public company audits, the AICPA's Auditing Standards Board for private company audits, the GAO's Yellow Book for government audits and the IAASB internationally. Tax rules: Congress and the IRS. Licensing: state boards of accountancy. Knowing who does what is a common judge question.
cards.example: A private nonprofit follows FASB GAAP, its auditor follows AICPA standards, and the state board licenses the CPA firm.
cards.say_it: The FASB writes the rules, the SEC enforces them for public companies, and the PCAOB checks the auditors.
cards.mistakes: Saying the SEC writes GAAP day to day; it has the authority but relies on the FASB.

cards.term: Why a business must use GAAP
cards.core: Businesses use GAAP so outsiders can trust, compare and audit their statements, which lenders, investors and the SEC require.
cards.detail: Reasons: consistency (the same rules every year), comparability (one company against another), reliability (outside users can trust the numbers), auditability (an external auditor can only give an opinion against a recognized framework), and access to money (banks and suppliers usually require GAAP statements before lending or giving credit). Public companies are legally required to use GAAP. Even small private businesses benefit because GAAP accrual statements show true profit for each period.
cards.example: A bank compares a jewelry store's GAAP statements with other retailers before approving its line of credit.
cards.say_it: Using GAAP is what lets a banker who has never met you trust your numbers enough to lend you money.

cards.core: The FASB organizes all U.S. GAAP in the Accounting Standards Codification and changes it by issuing Accounting Standards Updates.
cards.detail: The ASC, effective in 2009, is the single authoritative source of U.S. GAAP for nongovernmental entities, organized by topic numbers, for example ASC 330 Inventory, ASC 450 Contingencies, ASC 606 Revenue from Contracts with Customers and ASC 730 Research and Development. New or changed rules are issued as Accounting Standards Updates (ASUs) after a public due process: research, an exposure draft, public comments and a board vote. Accountants must track ASUs, which is a big reason for continuing education.
cards.example: Novus's U.S. competitor follows ASC 730 and expenses all research and development as incurred.
cards.say_it: GAAP is not frozen; the FASB updates the Codification every year, and accountants must keep up.

cards.core: When in doubt, choose the treatment that does not overstate assets or income.
cards.detail: Conservatism means recognizing probable losses when they are known but waiting to record gains until they are realized. It explains rules such as writing inventory down to the lower of cost or net realizable value, testing long-lived assets for impairment, accruing probable losses, and U.S. GAAP's choice to expense research and development. It does not allow deliberately understating results; information must still be neutral.
cards.example: Tablets that cost $400 but will sell for only $330 net must be written down, even though the CFO wants to keep them at cost.
cards.say_it: GAAP does not let a balance sheet show assets worth more than the cash they are expected to bring in.

cards.core: The FASB is the independent private board that writes and updates U.S. GAAP for businesses and nonprofits.
cards.detail: Created in 1973 and based in Norwalk, Connecticut, the FASB has seven full-time members and is overseen and funded by the Financial Accounting Foundation (FAF). The SEC officially recognizes its standards as authoritative GAAP for public companies. It follows an open due process: research, exposure drafts, public comment and roundtables before voting. It publishes the Accounting Standards Codification and issues Accounting Standards Updates, and its Private Company Council recommends simpler options for private companies.
cards.example: The FASB wrote the current revenue recognition standard (ASC 606) jointly with the IASB.
cards.say_it: The FASB is the rule writer for U.S. GAAP, and it listens to public comments before changing any standard.
cards.mistakes: Calling the FASB a government agency; it is a private, independent organization.

cards.core: Under GAAP a probable, estimable loss is accrued (minimum of a range); IFRS accrues a provision when more likely than not (midpoint of a range).
cards.detail: U.S. GAAP (ASC 450): probable (likely to occur) and reasonably estimable losses are accrued; reasonably possible losses are disclosed in the notes; remote losses are ignored. If no amount in a range is more likely, GAAP accrues the minimum. IFRS (IAS 37) records a provision when an outflow is probable, meaning more likely than not, so it can accrue sooner, and it uses the midpoint of a range when all outcomes are equally likely. Both require note disclosure of significant contingencies.
cards.example: A lawsuit loss estimated between $30,000 and $50,000 with no best estimate is accrued at $30,000 under GAAP and $40,000 under IFRS.
cards.say_it: Accruing a probable loss is not admitting guilt; it simply keeps the statements from misleading lenders and investors.

cards.core: An item is material if leaving it out or misstating it could change the decision of a reasonable user.
cards.detail: Materiality depends on size and nature. Accountants may use simpler treatments for immaterial items (such as expensing a $20 stapler), but material items must follow GAAP and be disclosed. Auditors set a materiality amount, often a percentage of a benchmark such as pre-tax income, total revenue or assets, plus a lower performance materiality to plan testing. Some small items are material by nature, such as fraud by an executive.
cards.formula: Example benchmark: materiality = 5% x pre-tax income; performance materiality = about 50% to 75% of materiality
cards.example: With pre-tax income of $600,000, 5% materiality is $30,000 and 75% performance materiality is $22,500, so $15,000 of errors is not material but should still be corrected.
cards.say_it: An error is material when it is big enough, or serious enough, to change what a banker or investor would decide.
cards.mistakes: Thinking immaterial errors can be ignored; they should still be corrected and tracked.

cards.core: The PCAOB, created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, oversees the auditors of public companies.
cards.detail: Before 2002 the profession regulated itself; after the Enron and WorldCom scandals, SOX created the PCAOB, a nonprofit overseen by the SEC. It registers audit firms that audit public companies, sets auditing, quality control, ethics and independence standards for those audits, inspects firms regularly and disciplines firms and individuals that break the rules. Private company audits are not under the PCAOB; they follow AICPA standards and peer review.
cards.example: A CPA firm that wants to audit a listed company must first register with the PCAOB.
cards.say_it: The PCAOB is the watchdog for the auditors of public companies, so investors can trust the audit opinion.

cards.term: Public vs private company reporting rules
cards.core: Public companies must follow GAAP and file with the SEC; private companies use GAAP mainly because lenders and investors demand it.
cards.detail: Public (SEC registrant) companies must file audited GAAP statements, have their audits done under PCAOB standards and comply with Sarbanes-Oxley. Private companies are not legally required to use GAAP, but banks, investors and buyers usually require it; the FASB's Private Company Council approves some simpler alternatives for them. Very small businesses sometimes use a tax basis or cash basis framework for internal and tax purposes. Private company audits follow AICPA auditing standards.
cards.example: A family brewery planning an IPO must move from reviewed statements to audited GAAP statements and SOX controls.
cards.say_it: Going public changes everything: your statements, audits and controls must meet SEC and Sarbanes-Oxley rules.

cards.term: Research and development costs: GAAP vs IFRS
cards.core: U.S. GAAP expenses all R&D as incurred; IFRS expenses research but capitalizes development once strict criteria are met.
cards.detail: Under U.S. GAAP (ASC 730), research and development is expensed because future benefits are uncertain (software has special rules). Under IFRS (IAS 38), research is expensed, but development costs must be capitalized as an intangible asset when the company can show technical feasibility, intent and ability to complete and use or sell it, probable future benefits, resources to finish and reliable measurement. The asset is amortized once available for use. IFRS therefore shows higher income and assets in the year of spending.
cards.formula: IFRS income advantage this year = capitalized development costs
cards.example: Of $1,000,000 R&D, IFRS expenses $400,000 research and capitalizes $600,000 development; GAAP expenses all $1,000,000, so IFRS income and assets are $600,000 higher.
cards.say_it: Capitalizing is not fake profit; IFRS records proven development as an asset and expenses it later through amortization.

cards.core: The SEC is the federal agency that regulates public companies and securities markets and has legal authority over their financial reporting.
cards.detail: Created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, the SEC protects investors and keeps markets fair. It requires public companies to file audited annual reports (10-K), quarterly reports (10-Q) and current reports (8-K) on its EDGAR system, enforces securities laws, investigates fraud and oversees the PCAOB. It recognizes the FASB's standards as GAAP and lets foreign companies listed in the U.S. file using IFRS as issued by the IASB.
cards.example: Before its IPO, Lakeshore Brewing must register with the SEC and then file audited GAAP statements every year.
cards.say_it: The SEC is the referee for public companies: it does not write most rules itself, but it can enforce them with real penalties.

cards.term: Comparing a GAAP company with an IFRS company
cards.core: Before comparing companies on different frameworks, put both on the same basis and read their accounting policy notes.
cards.detail: Steps: 1) identify the framework each uses (stated in the notes and the auditor's report); 2) read the significant accounting policies note; 3) adjust key items to one basis, such as expensing an IFRS company's capitalized development costs to match GAAP; 4) compare measures that are the same under both, such as cash spent and operating cash flows; 5) then compare ratios. Companies can help investors by disclosing reconciliations or key figures on both bases.
cards.example: An investor subtracts Novus's $600,000 of capitalized development from assets and income before comparing it with its U.S. rival.
cards.say_it: To compare fairly, I would put both companies on the same accounting basis first, then compare the ratios.

cards.core: The FASB and IASB worked together, starting with the 2002 Norwalk Agreement, to reduce differences, but the U.S. never adopted IFRS.
cards.detail: Joint projects produced nearly identical standards for revenue recognition (ASC 606 and IFRS 15, issued in 2014) and similar lease standards. The SEC dropped its reconciliation requirement for foreign IFRS filers in 2007 and studied, but did not adopt, IFRS for U.S. companies. Formal convergence has slowed, and each board now sets its own agenda while keeping in contact. Remaining differences mean accountants still need to know both frameworks.
cards.example: A U.S. and a French company now recognize revenue from customer contracts under almost the same five-step model.
cards.say_it: GAAP and IFRS have moved closer, especially on revenue, but the U.S. still uses its own GAAP.

cards.core: The GASB sets GAAP for U.S. state and local governments such as states, cities, counties and school districts.
cards.detail: Created in 1984 and, like the FASB, overseen by the Financial Accounting Foundation, the GASB writes standards that help citizens, lawmakers and bond investors see how governments raise and spend public money. Government reporting uses funds and government-wide statements, and many governments publish an Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR). The federal government follows a different body, FASAB. Government auditors follow the GAO's Yellow Book.
cards.example: A city school district reports under GASB standards, while a private charter school organized as a nonprofit follows FASB.
cards.say_it: Governments use their own GAAP from the GASB because their goal is accountability for taxpayers, not profit.

cards.core: The IASB is the independent international board in London that issues IFRS.
cards.detail: The IASB, formed in 2001, is overseen by the IFRS Foundation, which also created the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) in 2021 for sustainability disclosures. The IASB has no power to force companies to use IFRS; each country decides by law or regulation. Its standards are named IFRS (newer) and IAS (older ones still in force, such as IAS 38 on intangible assets). It follows a public due process similar to the FASB's and has worked with the FASB on joint projects.
cards.example: Novus, listed in South Korea, follows IFRS issued by the IASB.
cards.say_it: The IASB writes the global rulebook, IFRS, but each country decides whether its companies must use it.

cards.core: IFRS are global accounting standards issued by the IASB and required or permitted in more than 140 jurisdictions.
cards.detail: IFRS is used by listed companies in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, South Korea, Brazil and many others. U.S. domestic public companies must use U.S. GAAP, but since 2007 the SEC has allowed foreign companies listed in the U.S. to file using IFRS as issued by the IASB without reconciling to GAAP. Many U.S. multinationals also prepare IFRS reports for foreign subsidiaries, so U.S. accountants benefit from knowing both.
cards.example: A Korean battery maker reports under IFRS while its U.S. competitor reports under U.S. GAAP.
cards.say_it: Most of the world uses IFRS, while U.S. companies use GAAP, so global investors often have to translate between the two.

cards.term: Rules based GAAP vs principles based IFRS
cards.core: U.S. GAAP is more rules based with detailed guidance, while IFRS is more principles based and relies on judgment.
cards.detail: GAAP gives more specific rules, bright lines and industry guidance, which improves consistency and makes rules easier to audit but can encourage structuring transactions to fit the rule. IFRS states broad principles and expects accountants to use professional judgment to show economic substance, which can better fit unusual situations but leads to more variation between companies. In practice both use principles and rules; the difference is one of degree.
cards.example: IFRS lets Novus judge when development work has become a valuable asset, while GAAP simply says expense all R&D.
cards.say_it: GAAP tends to give you the exact rule, while IFRS gives you the principle and trusts your judgment.

cards.core: An audit is an independent examination that gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance that statements are free of material misstatement.
cards.detail: Auditors plan the audit around risk and materiality, test internal controls, gather evidence (confirmations, observation, inspection of documents, recalculation, analytical procedures, inquiry), and then issue an opinion on whether the statements are fairly presented under the framework, such as GAAP. Because auditors test samples and fraud can be hidden through collusion, an audit cannot guarantee there is no error or fraud. Management, not the auditor, is responsible for the statements.
cards.example: Keystone Components needs an audit because its bank relies on the opinion for a $5 million loan decision. The CEO asks whether a clean opinion means there is no fraud: it means no material misstatement was found with reasonable assurance, not that fraud is impossible.
cards.say_it: An audit gives high but not absolute assurance; it is not a guarantee, and management still owns the numbers.
cards.mistakes: Saying a clean audit opinion guarantees there is no fraud.

cards.term: Audit quality: peer review and PCAOB inspections
cards.core: CPA firms prove audit quality through quality management systems, peer reviews and, for public company auditors, PCAOB inspections.
cards.detail: Firms must have a system of quality management covering ethics, independence, client acceptance, staffing, supervision and monitoring. Firms that audit private companies usually must undergo an AICPA peer review, an outside review by another CPA firm, typically every three years, and many state boards require it for licensing. Firms auditing public companies are inspected by the PCAOB. These checks keep auditing standards meaningful.
cards.example: A small CPA firm that begins offering audits must enroll in peer review before its state license renewal.
cards.say_it: Auditors get audited too, through peer review and PCAOB inspections, which is why their opinions can be trusted.

cards.core: Private company audits follow AICPA generally accepted auditing standards (GAAS); public company audits follow PCAOB standards.
cards.detail: The AICPA's Auditing Standards Board issues Statements on Auditing Standards (SASs), codified as GAAS, for audits of private companies, nonprofits and others that are not SEC registrants. The PCAOB issues Auditing Standards (AS) for audits of public companies and broker-dealers, including the integrated audit of internal control under SOX 404. Both require competence, independence, professional skepticism, planning, sufficient appropriate evidence and a written report. Internationally, the IAASB issues International Standards on Auditing (ISAs).
cards.example: Keystone, a private company borrowing from a bank, is audited under AICPA standards; after an IPO, it would be audited under PCAOB standards.
cards.say_it: Who the client is decides the rulebook: AICPA standards for private companies, PCAOB standards for public ones.

cards.term: Attestation standards (SSAE, SSARS and SOC reports)
cards.core: Attestation standards govern CPA reports on things other than audits of financial statements, such as controls or compliance.
cards.detail: An attestation engagement is when a CPA reports on a subject matter or someone else's assertion, such as a company's controls, forecast or compliance with a contract. The AICPA issues Statements on Standards for Attestation Engagements (SSAEs); well known examples are SOC 1 reports (controls relevant to clients' financial reporting) and SOC 2 reports (security, availability and privacy controls of service organizations like cloud providers). Compilations and reviews of private company statements follow SSARS. The PCAOB has its own attestation standards for public company work.
cards.example: A hardware store moving to cloud accounting asks for the software provider's SOC 2 report to judge its data security.
cards.say_it: Before trusting a cloud provider with your books, ask for its SOC report, which is an independent CPA's attestation on its controls.

cards.core: Audits of governments and of organizations spending federal money follow the GAO's Government Auditing Standards, called the Yellow Book.
cards.detail: The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) issues Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS). They build on AICPA standards and add rules on independence, continuing education and reporting on internal control and compliance. Nonprofits, universities and local governments that spend federal awards above a set threshold (raised to $1,000,000 for fiscal years beginning on or after October 1, 2024) need a Single Audit under federal Uniform Guidance.
cards.example: A nonprofit spending $1.5 million in federal grants needs a Single Audit performed under the Yellow Book.
cards.say_it: When public money is involved, auditors follow the GAO's Yellow Book because taxpayers are the users.

cards.core: Auditors keep a questioning mind and rely on evidence from independent sources rather than management's word.
cards.detail: Professional skepticism means critically assessing evidence and staying alert to error and fraud, without assuming management is dishonest. Evidence is more reliable when it comes from outside the company (bank or customer confirmations), is obtained directly by the auditor (observing an inventory count, recalculating) and is documented. Common procedures: confirmation, observation, inspection, vouching and tracing, recalculation, analytical procedures, inquiry, cutoff testing and the search for unrecorded liabilities.
cards.example: A CFO says confirmations are unnecessary because customers always pay; the auditor still needs outside evidence or alternative procedures.
cards.say_it: Trust is not evidence; that is why auditors confirm balances directly with third parties.

cards.core: In public accounting you move from staff to senior, manager, senior manager and partner; in industry from staff accountant to CFO.
cards.detail: Public accounting ladder: staff or associate, senior (about years 2 to 4), manager, senior manager, then partner (owner), often after 10 or more years. Industry ladder: staff accountant, senior accountant, accounting manager, assistant controller, controller, vice president of finance, CFO. Careers also move sideways: auditors often leave public accounting for industry, internal audit or government roles, and some switch from tax to advisory. Promotion depends on performance, credentials (especially the CPA), leadership and relationships.
cards.example: An auditor becomes a senior in year three, a manager in year six, then leaves to become a controller at a former client.
cards.say_it: Accounting has a clear ladder, and the CPA plus strong communication skills are what move you up each rung.

cards.term: High school steps toward an accounting career
cards.core: In high school, take accounting, math and business classes, learn Excel, join DECA or FBLA and look for job shadowing or part-time work.
cards.detail: Useful steps: take accounting, business, statistics and strong math courses (and dual credit or AP courses if offered); learn spreadsheets; compete in DECA or FBLA to build presentation skills; job shadow or interview an accountant; get a part-time job that handles money; manage a club treasury; and research colleges with strong accounting programs and the CPA requirements in your state. Good grades, curiosity and honesty matter more than knowing every rule now.
cards.example: A student serves as treasurer of the school's DECA chapter, tracking fundraiser money in a spreadsheet.
cards.say_it: My advice for high schoolers is simple: take an accounting class, learn Excel, join DECA and talk to a real accountant about their day.

cards.core: To move up, accountants need technical knowledge plus analysis, communication, leadership, technology and ethical judgment.
cards.detail: Technical skills: GAAP, tax, internal controls and a credential such as the CPA. Analytical and problem-solving skills to interpret numbers and spot issues. Communication and presentation skills to explain results to non-accountants, owners and boards. Leadership and teamwork to manage staff and projects. Technology skills (accounting systems, Excel, data tools). Business and strategic thinking for executive roles like CFO. Integrity, because one ethical failure can end a career.
cards.example: The controller who wants to become CFO works on strategy and board presentation skills, not just debits and credits.
cards.say_it: Technical skills get you hired, but communication and leadership skills get you promoted.

cards.core: Good career information comes from the Occupational Outlook Handbook, O*NET, professional associations, counselors and informational interviews.
cards.detail: The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook gives duties, education, pay and job outlook for hundreds of jobs. O*NET OnLine and CareerOneStop describe skills and interests for each occupation. Professional associations (the AICPA's student site This Way to CPA, IMA, state CPA societies) explain paths and credentials. Other sources are school counselors, college career centers, job postings, company websites, career fairs, job shadowing and informational interviews with people in the field.
cards.example: Before a career day talk, an accountant checks the Occupational Outlook Handbook for current pay and growth figures.
cards.say_it: I would start with the Occupational Outlook Handbook for facts, then talk to real accountants to learn what the job is really like.

cards.core: Students gain experience through internships, part-time jobs, volunteering, job shadowing, co-ops and school leadership roles.
cards.detail: Internships (paid or for credit) give real professional work and often lead to job offers; accounting firms offer winter (busy season) and summer internships. Cooperative education (co-op) alternates school and work. Part-time jobs teach responsibility and handling money. Volunteering, such as VITA tax help or serving as a nonprofit's volunteer treasurer, builds skills and contacts. Job shadowing, school store jobs, DECA chapter treasurer roles and competitions all count on a resume.
cards.example: A high school junior keeps the books for her family's restaurant and volunteers at a VITA site during college.
cards.say_it: Even before college, you can build accounting experience by handling money for a club, a family business or a volunteer group.

cards.core: Build relationships in finance by joining associations, finding mentors, using LinkedIn, attending events and volunteering.
cards.detail: Ways to build a network: join the state CPA society, AICPA, IMA or affinity groups (NABA, ALPFA, Ascend) as a student or associate; find a mentor; keep a professional LinkedIn profile and share useful content; attend chamber of commerce, alumni and association events; volunteer with VITA tax programs or nonprofit boards; and keep in touch with former classmates, professors and coworkers. In finance, relationships bring client referrals, job leads and advice. Trust is built by being reliable, ethical and helpful over time.
cards.example: A bookkeeper who refers audit clients to a CPA firm builds a two-way referral relationship with that firm.
cards.say_it: Finance runs on trust, so I would build relationships by giving help and referrals long before I ever ask for something.

cards.core: Entrepreneurs start and run their own businesses, trading a steady paycheck for independence and higher possible rewards.
cards.detail: Entrepreneurial careers include starting a new business, buying a franchise, buying an existing business, freelancing, or innovating inside a large company (intrapreneurship). Useful traits are initiative, risk tolerance, creativity, persistence and money management. Every new business needs basic accounting, which is why accounting students make strong founders. Help is available from the Small Business Administration (SBA), SCORE mentors and local Small Business Development Centers.
cards.example: A student who does bookkeeping for local shops during college turns it into a small business after graduation.
cards.say_it: Many entrepreneurs fail because of cash flow, so accounting knowledge is a real advantage when starting a business.

cards.core: Non-exempt employees must be paid overtime under the FLSA; exempt employees (salaried professionals and managers) usually are not.
cards.detail: To be exempt, an employee generally must be paid a salary above a minimum level and do executive, administrative or professional duties. Many staff accountants and auditors are exempt, so long busy season hours do not earn overtime pay, although some firms give bonuses or time off. Bookkeepers and clerks are often non-exempt. Classifying a worker wrongly can lead to back pay and penalties for the employer.
cards.example: An audit associate on salary works 55 hours during busy season without overtime, while the hourly AP clerk earns time and a half.
cards.say_it: Before accepting an offer, I would ask whether the role is exempt so I understand how busy season hours are paid.

cards.core: An informational interview is a short meeting where you ask a professional about their career, not for a job.
cards.detail: Request 15 to 30 minutes, prepare questions (What does a typical day look like? What skills matter most? How did you get started? What would you do differently?), dress professionally, arrive on time, take notes and send a thank-you note within a day. Job shadowing means spending a day watching the person work. Both help you test a tentative career interest and grow your network.
cards.example: A student emails a local CPA, asks for a 20-minute chat about tax season and later shadows her during a client meeting.
cards.say_it: Informational interviews let you learn what a career is really like from the people doing it every day.
cards.mistakes: Asking for a job during an informational interview; the goal is learning and relationships.

cards.core: A mentor is an experienced professional who gives advice, feedback and introductions to help you grow.
cards.detail: Mentors can be supervisors, senior colleagues, professors or members of a professional association. They explain unwritten rules, help with career decisions, review your resume, and introduce you to their network. Good mentees come prepared with questions, follow through on advice, respect the mentor's time and say thank you. Many firms assign a formal mentor or "buddy" to new hires, and associations run mentoring programs.
cards.example: Tanya could ask a CPA at the firm that receives her audit referrals to mentor her through the licensing process.
cards.say_it: A mentor who already walked the CPA path can save you years of trial and error.

cards.core: Workers have legal rights to fair pay, a safe workplace, freedom from discrimination, protected leave and the right to organize.
cards.detail: Key federal laws: the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets the federal minimum wage, overtime at 1.5 times pay over 40 hours a week for non-exempt workers, and child labor limits for teens. OSHA requires safe workplaces. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (enforced by the EEOC), the ADA, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act and the Equal Pay Act ban discrimination. FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave. The NLRA protects the right to organize. Many states add higher minimum wages and more protections.
cards.example: A non-exempt payroll clerk who works 46 hours in a busy week must be paid overtime for the extra 6 hours.
cards.say_it: Knowing your rights, like overtime pay and protection from discrimination, helps you recognize a fair employer.
cards.mistakes: Assuming every salaried worker gets overtime; exempt professionals usually do not.

cards.term: Self assessment of interests and skills
cards.core: Career planning starts by honestly listing your interests, skills, values and personality, then matching them to careers.
cards.detail: Tools include interest inventories (such as the O*NET Interest Profiler, based on the Holland RIASEC types), skills checklists, personality and values assessments, and feedback from teachers and employers. Accounting tends to fit people who like organized, detail oriented and analytical work (the Holland "Conventional" type), solving puzzles and helping others make decisions. Success in business also needs communication, teamwork, reliability and ethics, so assess those too.
cards.example: A student who enjoys spreadsheets, solving puzzles and keeping the club budget discovers that accounting matches her interests.
cards.say_it: I chose accounting because my self assessment showed I love solving problems with numbers and helping people make good decisions.

cards.core: A tentative occupational interest is a career you choose to explore now, knowing you may change it as you learn more.
cards.detail: After self assessment and research, you pick one or two careers to test, then try them through classes, job shadowing, informational interviews, part-time jobs and internships. "Tentative" means the choice is flexible: experiences may confirm it or point you elsewhere. Writing down why the career fits and what education it requires turns the interest into a plan. In accounting, a student might start interested in tax and discover a love for forensic work.
cards.example: A student lists "forensic accountant" as a tentative interest and arranges to shadow a fraud examiner for a day.
cards.say_it: Choosing a tentative career goal gives your high school and college choices a direction, while still leaving room to change.

cards.core: VITA is an IRS program where trained volunteers prepare free tax returns for people with lower incomes.
cards.detail: Volunteers complete free IRS training and certification, then prepare basic returns at community sites, often at colleges, libraries and community centers, during tax season. It is a strong resume item for students: real tax experience, client service, community service and contact with CPAs and other professionals. A related program, Tax Counseling for the Elderly (TCE), serves taxpayers 60 and older. Volunteers do not need a PTIN.
cards.example: A college accounting student volunteers 60 hours at a VITA site and talks about it in a Big Four internship interview.
cards.say_it: VITA lets students gain real tax experience while helping families in the community, which looks great to employers.

cards.core: Workers advance by promotion up a ladder, lateral moves to gain skills, moving to a new employer or starting their own business.
cards.detail: Vertical advancement is a promotion to more responsibility and pay. A lateral move changes departments at the same level to build new skills (for example from audit to tax). A career lattice combines both. Changing employers can bring a bigger title faster. Some people advance by becoming specialists (technical experts) rather than managers. Advancement usually requires strong performance reviews, more education or credentials, and visible leadership.
cards.example: A payroll clerk moves sideways into accounts payable to learn more, then is promoted to accounting supervisor.
cards.say_it: Sometimes the smartest career move is sideways, because new skills prepare you for the next promotion.

cards.core: A well-governed company has an independent board, accurate and timely reporting, transparency, and internal and external audit functions.
cards.detail: Key components: a board of directors with independent members and committees (audit, compensation, nominating and governance); regular financial reporting to the board, such as quarterly budget versus actual reports; transparency and full disclosure to owners, members and the public; an internal audit function testing controls; an annual independent external audit; a code of conduct and whistleblower hotline; clear policies such as conflict of interest rules; and timely tax and regulatory filings (for nonprofits, the Form 990).
cards.example: A nonprofit association plans quarterly board reports, an annual audit after its December 31 year end and timely Form 990 filing.
cards.say_it: Quarterly reports to the board, an annual independent audit and on-time filings are the backbone of good governance.

cards.core: Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and oversight by which a company is directed and controlled for its owners.
cards.detail: Governance defines who has power (shareholders, the board, management), how decisions are made and checked, and how the company stays accountable. It exists because owners (shareholders) hire managers to run the company, and managers might act in their own interest (the agency problem). Good governance protects shareholders and other stakeholders, makes financial reporting trustworthy, lowers the cost of borrowing and raising capital, and prevents scandals like Enron. It also limits finance functions: for example, big deals and audits need board approval and oversight.
cards.example: Before an IPO, a family brewery must replace "the founder decides" with board oversight, committees and written controls.
cards.say_it: Good governance means no one person, not even the founder, can make major financial decisions without checks.

cards.core: SOX is a 2002 federal law, passed after Enron and WorldCom, that tightened reporting, internal control and audit rules for public companies.
cards.detail: Key sections: 301 requires independent audit committees that oversee the outside auditor; 302 requires the CEO and CFO to certify each quarterly and annual report; 404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting each year, with auditor attestation for larger companies; 806 protects whistleblowers from retaliation; 906 sets criminal penalties for false certifications; 802 punishes destroying records. SOX also created the PCAOB, limits non-audit services auditors can sell to audit clients and requires lead audit partner rotation.
cards.example: Lakeshore Brewing's CEO and CFO will have to personally certify every 10-K and 10-Q after the IPO.
cards.say_it: Sarbanes-Oxley puts executives' names, and their personal liability, behind every financial report.
cards.mistakes: Saying SOX applies fully to private companies; it mainly targets public companies, though many private firms copy its best practices.

cards.core: The audit committee is a board committee of independent directors that oversees financial reporting, internal control and the outside auditor.
cards.detail: Under Sarbanes-Oxley and exchange rules, public company audit committees must be fully independent, and companies disclose whether at least one member is a financial expert. The committee hires, pays and oversees the external auditor, reviews the financial statements and internal control reports, oversees internal audit and the whistleblower process, resolves disagreements between management and the auditors, and makes sure auditors get full access to records and third parties. It reinforces the tone at the top for honest reporting.
cards.example: When Keystone's CFO blocks receivable confirmations, the auditors report the scope limitation to the audit committee.
cards.say_it: The audit committee is the auditor's real client, so if management blocks the audit, that is where the issue goes.

cards.term: Board of directors and fiduciary duty
cards.core: The board of directors is elected by shareholders to oversee management, and it owes the company fiduciary duties of care and loyalty.
cards.detail: The board hires, evaluates and can fire the CEO, approves strategy, major deals, budgets and dividends, oversees risk and financial reporting, and sets executive pay. Fiduciary duty means acting carefully (duty of care: staying informed, asking questions) and loyally (duty of loyalty: putting the organization ahead of personal interests). Nonprofit boards have the same duties toward the mission. Many governance experts recommend separating the CEO and board chair roles or naming a lead independent director.
cards.example: The Society for Marketers' board reviews quarterly financial reports and the annual audit as part of its fiduciary duty.
cards.say_it: The board's job is not to run the company day to day, but to make sure management runs it honestly and well.

cards.core: A compliance program is a company's system of policies, training, monitoring, reporting channels, discipline and review that keeps it within the rules.
cards.detail: Elements: written policies and a code of conduct; a compliance officer with authority and access to the board; regular training; monitoring and auditing; confidential reporting channels such as a hotline; consistent discipline and incentives; and periodic risk assessment and review to update the program. Compliance costs money (staff, systems, audits, directors' fees), but violations can cost far more in fines, lawsuits and lost trust.
cards.example: Lakeshore's first-year governance and compliance costs total $840,000 (400,000 + 250,000 + 160,000 + 30,000), the price of access to public capital markets.
cards.say_it: A compliance program is like insurance: it costs money every year, but it prevents much larger losses.

cards.core: Stronger governance makes decisions more documented, reviewed and shared with the board: slower, but better checked.
cards.detail: Major decisions (acquisitions, large borrowing, budgets, executive pay, auditor selection) move from the founder alone to the board and its committees. Management prepares more analysis and documentation and reports regularly on results and risks. Approval limits and controls apply to everyone, including executives. Independent directors bring outside views and protect all shareholders. The trade-off is less speed and flexibility in exchange for fewer costly mistakes, better risk management and greater investor confidence.
cards.example: Instead of the CEO signing a new brewery lease alone, the board reviews the financial analysis and votes.
cards.say_it: Governance adds a second set of eyes to big decisions, which costs some speed but saves the company from expensive mistakes.

cards.core: Nonprofit boards oversee finances and the mission through regular financial reports, annual audits, clear policies and public Form 990 filings.
cards.detail: Nonprofits have no owners, so the board acts for donors, members and the public. Good practices: a finance or audit committee, quarterly budget versus actual reports, an annual independent audit (often required by grantors or state law above certain revenue levels, which vary by state), conflict of interest and whistleblower policies, document retention rules, and timely filing of Form 990, which asks about these governance policies. Weak governance can cost a nonprofit its donors or its tax-exempt status.
cards.example: The Society for Marketers moves to a calendar fiscal year and schedules its audit and Form 990 around the new year end.
cards.say_it: Donors give more to nonprofits that show strong governance, because they can see how every dollar is used.

cards.core: Tone at the top is the ethical climate set by leaders' words and actions, and it shapes how every employee behaves.
cards.detail: When the board and executives model honesty, follow the same controls as everyone else and respond seriously to concerns, employees follow. When leaders override controls, pressure staff to hit numbers at any cost or ignore misconduct, fraud becomes more likely. Tone at the top is part of the COSO control environment. It is reinforced by a code of conduct, training, fair incentives, consistent discipline and visible support for whistleblowers. Middle managers carry it forward as the "tone in the middle".
cards.example: A vice president who asks to leave a known lawsuit out of the notes to protect a bonus sends a dangerous tone to staff.
cards.say_it: If leaders bend the rules, employees will too, so ethics has to start at the top.

cards.core: Transparency means openly sharing accurate, complete and timely information with owners, lenders, members and regulators.
cards.detail: Transparent organizations publish audited financial statements and full notes, disclose risks, related-party transactions, executive pay and governance practices, and report bad news promptly instead of hiding it. Public companies meet this through SEC filings; nonprofits through annual reports and the public Form 990. Transparency builds trust, while hiding liabilities or losses is misleading and can be fraudulent financial reporting.
cards.example: A company discloses a reasonably possible $100,000 patent claim in its notes even though no liability is recorded.
cards.say_it: Sharing the bad news clearly is what makes people believe your good news.

cards.core: A whistleblower hotline is a confidential, often anonymous channel for employees to report suspected wrongdoing.
cards.detail: Sarbanes-Oxley requires public company audit committees to set up procedures for confidential, anonymous employee complaints about accounting and auditing matters, and section 806 protects whistleblowers from retaliation. Dodd-Frank (2010) also lets the SEC reward people whose tips lead to successful enforcement. Hotlines are among the most common ways fraud is detected, according to the ACFE, so they are a key governance tool for companies of every size.
cards.example: An employee who suspects a fake vendor reports it through the hotline instead of confronting the manager.
cards.say_it: A hotline gives employees a safe way to speak up, and tips are one of the top ways fraud is caught.

cards.core: Strong governance builds investor trust, lowers the cost of capital, prevents fraud and keeps the company within the law.
cards.detail: Investors and lenders pay more for, and lend more cheaply to, companies with independent boards, audited statements and strong controls. Governance reduces fraud and errors by separating duties and adding oversight, protects the company's reputation, ensures compliance with SEC, SOX and stock exchange rules, and improves long-term decisions by bringing outside views. Weak governance has led to collapses such as Enron and WorldCom, which harmed employees, investors and auditors.
cards.example: A bank considering a $5 million loan relies on the audit and the audit committee's oversight of financial reporting.
cards.say_it: Governance is not just paperwork; it is what lets investors trust you with their money at a fair price.

cards.core: Besides the audit committee, boards use a compensation committee for executive pay and a nominating committee to choose directors.
cards.detail: The compensation committee sets CEO and executive pay and designs incentives that reward long-term performance, not short-term number manipulation. The nominating and governance committee finds and evaluates director candidates, plans leadership succession and reviews governance policies. Public company exchanges generally require these committees to be made up of independent directors. Some boards add risk, finance or technology committees.
cards.example: Before its IPO, Lakeshore forms audit, compensation and nominating committees made of independent directors.
cards.say_it: Independent committees stop executives from setting their own pay or choosing their own bosses.

cards.core: The board oversees risk by setting the risk appetite and reviewing how management identifies and handles major risks.
cards.detail: Enterprise risk management (ERM) is an organization-wide process for identifying, scoring (likelihood times impact) and responding to risks, linked to strategy. Management owns each risk and reports regularly; the board or a risk committee approves the risk appetite, challenges assumptions and checks that high impact risks have plans. Regulated industries such as banking add compliance requirements, like anti-money-laundering programs.
cards.example: A community bank's board reviews a heat map of interest rate, cyber and compliance risks before approving a merger.
cards.say_it: The board does not manage every risk, but it must know the biggest ones and make sure someone owns each of them.

cards.term: Employee's role in achieving governance objectives
cards.core: Every employee supports governance by following the code and controls, keeping accurate records, completing training and reporting concerns.
cards.detail: Governance is not only the board's job. Employees follow the code of conduct and internal controls in daily work, keep complete and accurate records, never override or work around a control, complete compliance and ethics training, protect confidential information, and report concerns through supervisors or the hotline without fear of retaliation. Managers model ethical behavior and enforce policies fairly. Accountants have a special role because they prepare the numbers the board and investors rely on.
cards.example: A payroll clerk refuses to add a new employee without the required HR approval form, even when the manager is in a hurry.
cards.say_it: Governance works only if every employee follows the controls, even when it is inconvenient.

cards.core: Governance is shaped by ownership and size, laws and listing rules, industry regulation, investor expectations, risk profile and culture.
cards.detail: Ownership and size: a family business answers to a few owners; a public company answers to thousands of shareholders. Legal form and regulation: SEC rules, Sarbanes-Oxley, stock exchange listing standards, state corporate law and industry regulators (banking, alcohol, health care). Stage of life: start-up, growth, IPO. Investor and lender demands, such as institutional investors' voting policies. Risk profile and complexity, such as global operations. Culture and leadership, the tone at the top. Nonprofits are also shaped by donors and IRS rules.
cards.example: A brewery faces SEC rules, exchange listing standards and federal and state alcohol licensing rules when it goes public.
cards.say_it: A company's governance should fit who owns it, what laws apply and how much risk it carries.

cards.core: An independent director has no employment, family or significant business ties to the company, so he or she can judge management objectively.
cards.detail: Insiders such as the CEO, CFO and their family members are not independent. Paid advisers whose firms earn significant fees from the company, like a long-time family attorney, are also not independent, no matter how loyal. U.S. stock exchanges generally require a majority of independent directors and fully independent audit, compensation and nominating committees, with phase-in periods for newly listed companies. Independent directors protect all shareholders, not just the founders.
cards.example: Lakeshore Brewing has only 1 independent director of 5; its attorney's firm earns $80,000 a year from the company, so he does not count.
cards.say_it: Independence is about relationships, not character: a loyal adviser paid by the company cannot judge it objectively.
cards.mistakes: Counting a trusted outside adviser or a relative as independent.

cards.core: 302: CEO and CFO certify reports; 404: management assesses internal control yearly; 806: whistleblowers are protected from retaliation.
cards.detail: Section 302 makes the CEO and CFO personally certify that each 10-Q and 10-K is accurate and that they are responsible for disclosure controls. Section 404 requires management to assess internal control over financial reporting every year, and larger public companies (accelerated filers) also need the outside auditor's attestation; smaller and emerging growth companies may be exempt from the auditor part for a time. Section 806 protects employees of public companies who report fraud from firing or other retaliation. Section 906 adds criminal penalties for knowingly false certifications.
cards.example: After its IPO, Lakeshore must assess its controls annually, and its CFO can no longer approve his own expenses.
cards.say_it: With 302 and 404, executives cannot claim they did not know; they sign that the numbers and controls are sound.

cards.core: The CPA is a state license that is the top accounting credential and the only one that lets you sign audit reports.
cards.detail: Each state board of accountancy grants the license after the candidate meets the "three Es": education, exam and experience, and in many states an ethics exam. The Uniform CPA Examination is written by the AICPA and given nationwide. CPAs may perform audits and reviews, represent taxpayers before the IRS and use the protected CPA title. They must follow the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct and state rules and complete continuing professional education to renew.
cards.example: A nonprofit that receives large federal grants must hire a licensed CPA firm for its audit.
cards.say_it: The CPA is the gold standard: it is a legal license from the state, and it is the only credential that lets you sign an audit opinion.
cards.mistakes: Saying the AICPA grants the license; state boards license CPAs, the AICPA writes the exam.

cards.core: Licensed and certified accountants must complete CPE hours every year to keep their credential and stay current.
cards.detail: CPE is measured in credit hours earned through courses, webinars, conferences, college classes and self-study. For CPAs the state board sets the rules; a common pattern is 120 hours every three years with at least 20 each year (about 40 a year on average), plus ethics hours, but it varies by state. Other credentials have their own rules: the CMA needs 30 hours a year, the EA 72 hours every three years, and the CIA and CFE have yearly requirements. Failing to complete CPE can lead to losing the license or credential.
cards.example: A CPA takes an online course on a new FASB standard and a two-hour ethics course before her license renewal.
cards.say_it: Earning the CPA is not the finish line; we keep learning every year through CPE because the rules and tools keep changing.
cards.mistakes: Giving one national CPE number for CPAs; the requirement is set by each state.

cards.core: A professional designation proves expertise through education, a tough exam and work experience, and it raises pay and opportunities.
cards.detail: Most accounting credentials follow the same pattern: meet education requirements, pass an exam, gain verified experience, follow a code of ethics and complete continuing education to keep the credential. The CPA is a state license (required by law to audit); most others (CMA, CIA, CFE) are voluntary certifications granted by professional organizations. The EA is granted by the IRS. Credentials signal competence to employers and clients and often lead to promotions.
cards.example: Two staff accountants apply for a controller job; the one with a CMA stands out.
cards.say_it: A designation tells employers you have proven your skills to an outside organization and promised to follow its code of ethics.
cards.mistakes: Calling every credential a license; only the CPA is a state license (the EA is a federal authorization).

cards.core: Professional organizations offer credentials, continuing education, ethics codes, publications, networking, job boards and advocacy.
cards.detail: Accounting associations help members grow by awarding certifications (CPA exam, CMA, CIA, CFE), offering CPE courses and conferences, publishing journals and technical guidance, writing codes of ethics, running job boards and mentoring programs, giving scholarships and student memberships, and lobbying lawmakers on issues such as tax law and licensing. Membership signals professionalism and keeps members current on changes in standards and technology.
cards.example: A staff accountant uses her state CPA society's webinars for CPE and meets her next employer at its networking night.
cards.say_it: Joining a professional organization keeps you current, gives you a network and shows employers you are serious about the profession.

cards.core: Most states have required 150 college semester hours for the CPA license, about 30 more than a bachelor's degree.
cards.detail: A bachelor's degree is usually 120 semester hours, so candidates add 30 hours through a master's in accounting, extra undergraduate courses or a combined five-year program. Because of a shortage of new CPAs, many states changed their laws starting in 2024 to also accept a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience (instead of 150 hours plus one year). States also set a minimum number of accounting and business credits. Check the specific state board, since requirements differ.
cards.example: A student graduates with 120 hours, then either completes a one-year master's program or, in a state with the new pathway, works two years before licensure.
cards.say_it: The traditional rule is 150 credit hours, but many states now let you substitute an extra year of experience for the extra 30 hours of school.
