cards.core: The AICPA is the national association of CPAs; it writes the CPA Exam, the Code of Professional Conduct and private company auditing standards.
cards.detail: Founded in 1887, the AICPA represents CPAs in public practice, business, government and education. It develops the Uniform CPA Examination, sets the Code of Professional Conduct (integrity, objectivity, independence, confidentiality), issues auditing, review and attestation standards for private companies through its senior committees, runs the peer review program for CPA firms, publishes the Journal of Accountancy, offers CPE and resources for students such as This Way to CPA, and advocates for the profession. Since 2017 it has partnered with CIMA in the Association of International Certified Professional Accountants, which offers the CGMA.
cards.example: A CPA unsure whether accepting a gift from an audit client is allowed checks the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct.
cards.say_it: The AICPA is the voice of the CPA profession: it writes the exam, sets our ethics rules and keeps us learning.
cards.mistakes: Saying the AICPA sets GAAP; the FASB sets GAAP. Saying the AICPA grants licenses; state boards do.

cards.core: The CFE, granted by the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE), certifies skill in preventing, detecting and investigating fraud.
cards.detail: The CFE exam covers four areas: financial transactions and fraud schemes, law, investigation, and fraud prevention and deterrence. Eligibility uses a points system that combines education (usually a bachelor's degree) and professional experience, with at least two years of experience related to detecting or deterring fraud. CFEs must complete yearly continuing education (20 hours, including fraud related and ethics hours) and follow the ACFE Code of Ethics. It fits forensic accountants, investigators and auditors.
cards.example: A bank investigator earns the CFE before leading an embezzlement investigation.
cards.say_it: The CFE is the credential for financial detectives: it shows you know how fraud is committed, how to prove it and how to prevent it.

cards.core: The CIA, granted by the Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA), is the global credential for internal auditors.
cards.detail: Candidates pass a three-part exam (Essentials of Internal Auditing, Practice of Internal Auditing, Business Knowledge for Internal Auditing) and meet the IIA's mix of education and internal audit or related experience; more education means fewer required years, so check the IIA's current rules. CIAs follow the IIA's Global Internal Audit Standards (effective January 2025) and complete continuing education each year (40 hours for practicing CIAs, including ethics). It fits careers testing controls, risk and operations inside organizations.
cards.example: An internal auditor at a retail chain earns the CIA before leading audits of store cash controls.
cards.say_it: The CIA shows you can evaluate a company's risks and controls from the inside and report independently to the audit committee.

cards.core: The CMA, granted by the IMA, certifies expertise in management accounting: budgeting, cost analysis, performance and strategy.
cards.detail: Requirements: IMA membership, a bachelor's degree (or an approved professional certification), passing a two-part exam (Part 1: Financial Planning, Performance and Analytics; Part 2: Strategic Financial Management, each with multiple choice and essays), and two continuous years of professional experience in management accounting or financial management. CMAs complete 30 CPE hours a year, including 2 in ethics, and follow the IMA Statement of Ethical Professional Practice. It suits accountants who work inside companies and aim for controller or CFO.
cards.example: A cost accountant at a manufacturer earns the CMA to qualify for a plant controller job.
cards.say_it: The CMA is for accountants who want to help run the business from the inside, through budgets, cost analysis and strategy.
cards.mistakes: Saying the CMA lets you audit; only CPAs can sign audit reports.

cards.core: Groups such as NABA, ALPFA, Ascend, AFWA and Beta Alpha Psi build networks, mentoring and scholarships for future accountants.
cards.detail: NABA (National Association of Black Accountants), ALPFA (Association of Latino Professionals For America), Ascend (Pan-Asian business professionals) and the Accounting and Financial Women's Alliance (AFWA) offer conferences, mentoring, scholarships and recruiting events. Beta Alpha Psi is the honor and service organization for college accounting, finance and information systems students. In high school, DECA and FBLA build business and presentation skills. The AGA serves government accountants.
cards.example: A college freshman meets a Big Four recruiter at a NABA conference and lands a summer leadership program.
cards.say_it: Groups like NABA, ALPFA, Ascend and AFWA help students find mentors who look like them and open doors to internships.

cards.core: An Enrolled Agent is a tax expert authorized by the IRS to represent any taxpayer before the IRS.
cards.detail: The EA is the highest credential the IRS awards. Candidates get a PTIN, pass the three-part Special Enrollment Examination (individuals; businesses; representation, practices and procedures) and pass a tax compliance check; no college degree is required, and some former IRS employees qualify through experience. EAs have unlimited practice rights before the IRS, like CPAs and attorneys, and must complete 72 hours of continuing education every three years (at least 16 per year, including 2 in ethics). It is a fast route into a tax career.
cards.example: A bookkeeper who prepares returns becomes an EA so she can represent a client in an IRS audit.
cards.say_it: The EA is a great option for tax lovers because it is a federal credential focused only on tax and does not require a degree.
cards.mistakes: Saying the EA is a state license; it comes from the IRS and is valid in every state.

cards.core: The IIA serves internal auditors and grants the CIA; the ACFE serves fraud examiners and grants the CFE.
cards.detail: The Institute of Internal Auditors (IIA), founded in 1941, sets the Global Internal Audit Standards, publishes Internal Auditor magazine, grants the CIA and offers training and local chapters. The Association of Certified Fraud Examiners (ACFE), founded in 1988, grants the CFE, publishes Fraud Magazine and the Occupational Fraud report (Report to the Nations), which estimates organizations lose about 5% of revenue to fraud each year, and offers anti-fraud training.
cards.example: A forensic accountant cites the ACFE report to show a restaurant owner why fraud controls are worth the cost.
cards.say_it: If you want to protect companies from the inside, the IIA is your home; if you want to fight fraud, it is the ACFE.

cards.core: The IMA is the professional organization for management accountants and awards the CMA.
cards.detail: The IMA supports accountants and finance professionals working inside organizations. It awards the CMA, publishes Strategic Finance magazine and research, offers CPE and leadership training, runs local chapters and student chapters for networking, and sets the IMA Statement of Ethical Professional Practice (principles of honesty, fairness, objectivity and responsibility; standards of competence, confidentiality, integrity and credibility).
cards.example: A college student joins an IMA student chapter, enters its case competition and meets corporate recruiters.
cards.say_it: For students who want to work inside a company, the IMA and its CMA credential are the best resources.

cards.term: Matching a designation to a career
cards.core: Choose the credential that fits the job: CPA for public accounting, CMA for corporate, CIA for internal audit, CFE for fraud, EA for tax.
cards.detail: Ask what work you want to do and who grants the credential. Public accounting and audit: CPA (state board). Corporate finance and cost management: CMA (IMA). Internal audit: CIA (IIA). Fraud investigation: CFE (ACFE). Tax practice: EA (IRS) or CPA. Many professionals hold two, such as CPA and CFE. In a role play, naming the credential, the organization that grants it and one requirement shows real mastery.
cards.example: A middle schooler who loves detective shows hears that a forensic accountant often holds both the CPA and the CFE.
cards.say_it: Each designation tells employers your specialty: the CPA for audit and tax, the CMA for management, the CIA for internal audit and the CFE for fraud.

cards.term: Other finance credentials (CFA, CFP, CGMA, CISA, CGFM)
cards.core: Beyond accounting credentials, the CFA covers investments, the CFP personal financial planning, and others cover IT audit and government.
cards.detail: CFA (Chartered Financial Analyst, CFA Institute): three levels of investment analysis exams plus about 4,000 hours of relevant experience. CFP (Certified Financial Planner, CFP Board): a bachelor's degree, planning coursework, an exam and 6,000 hours of experience (or 4,000 in an apprenticeship). CGMA (Chartered Global Management Accountant): offered by the AICPA and CIMA through their joint association. CISA (ISACA) certifies information systems auditors. CGFM (AGA) certifies government financial managers. Pick the credential that matches the career path.
cards.example: A CPA who moves into investment research adds the CFA; one who advises families on retirement adds the CFP.
cards.say_it: I would match the credential to the career: CPA for audit and tax, CMA for corporate finance, CFA for investing and CFP for helping families plan.

cards.core: Become a CPA by completing the education, passing the Uniform CPA Exam, gaining supervised experience and applying to your state board.
cards.detail: Step 1: earn a bachelor's degree with the required accounting and business courses. Step 2: meet the state's education rule; most states have required 150 semester hours, and a growing number now also allow a bachelor's degree (120 hours) with two years of experience instead of one. Step 3: pass all four exam sections within the state's credit window. Step 4: complete relevant experience, usually verified by a licensed CPA. Step 5: pass an ethics exam if your state requires one, apply for the license, then complete CPE to renew. Rules vary by state, so always check the state board.
cards.example: Tanya has 24 accounting credits; she should compare them with her state board's accounting hour requirement before applying for the exam.
cards.say_it: The CPA path is education, exam and experience, and because the details vary by state, the first step is to check your own state board of accountancy.
cards.mistakes: Stating the 150-hour rule as universal; many states now offer a 120-hour plus experience pathway.

cards.core: Anyone who prepares federal tax returns for pay must get a PTIN from the IRS and renew it every year.
cards.detail: The PTIN identifies the paid preparer on each return. It does not make someone a CPA or EA and does not by itself give full rights to represent clients before the IRS. CPAs, EAs and attorneys can represent any client; other preparers have limited rights. Some states add their own registration rules for tax preparers. VITA volunteers who prepare free returns do not need a PTIN.
cards.example: Tanya's PTIN lets her prepare client returns for a fee, but it does not let her perform audits.
cards.say_it: A PTIN lets you prepare returns for pay, but it is a registration number, not a professional license.

cards.core: Key professional development resources are trade journals, professional associations, classes and seminars, trade shows and mentors.
cards.detail: Trade journals and periodicals report new standards, laws and best practices. Professional and trade associations (AICPA, IMA, IIA, state societies) offer CPE, certifications and networking. Classes and seminars, in person or online, teach new skills. Trade shows and conferences show new software and let you meet vendors and peers. Mentors give personal advice, feedback and introductions. Good professionals combine several of these each year.
cards.example: A staff accountant reads the Journal of Accountancy monthly, attends the state society's fall conference and meets a mentor quarterly.
cards.say_it: I use trade journals to stay informed, associations to stay connected and a mentor to stay on track.

cards.core: Each state's board of accountancy licenses CPAs and CPA firms, sets requirements and disciplines rule breakers.
cards.detail: There are 55 boards (the 50 states, D.C. and U.S. territories). A board sets education, exam, experience and ethics requirements, approves exam candidates, issues and renews licenses, sets CPE rules, registers CPA firms (and often requires peer review), investigates complaints and can fine, suspend or revoke licenses. State accountancy laws reserve the CPA title and audit and review reports for licensees. NASBA is the association of these boards, and mobility rules let CPAs serve clients across state lines.
cards.example: A board fines a bookkeeper who advertised "CPA quality audits" without a license.
cards.say_it: The state board protects the public by making sure only qualified, ethical people can call themselves CPAs and sign audit reports.
cards.mistakes: Saying the AICPA or federal government licenses CPAs.

cards.core: State CPA societies are local member groups for CPAs and students; NASBA is the association of state boards that regulate CPAs.
cards.detail: State CPA societies (for example a state society of CPAs) are voluntary associations offering CPE, conferences, networking events, mentoring, scholarships, high school and college outreach, and advocacy with state lawmakers. They are not the regulator. NASBA (National Association of State Boards of Accountancy) supports the state boards: it helps process CPA Exam applications and scores, keeps the CPAverify license lookup and runs a registry of approved CPE sponsors. Students can often join a state society free.
cards.example: Tanya joins her state CPA society as a student member to find a mentor and learn the licensing steps.
cards.say_it: The state society helps CPAs grow, while the state board, supported by NASBA, protects the public by regulating them.

cards.core: The CPA Exam has three required Core sections (AUD, FAR, REG) plus one Discipline section the candidate chooses (BAR, ISC or TCP).
cards.detail: Since January 2024 the exam follows the CPA Evolution model. Core: Auditing and Attestation (AUD), Financial Accounting and Reporting (FAR) and Taxation and Regulation (REG). Discipline, pick one: Business Analysis and Reporting (BAR), Information Systems and Controls (ISC) or Tax Compliance and Planning (TCP). Each section takes four hours and needs a score of 75 to pass. The AICPA writes the exam, NASBA and the state boards handle applications and scores, and testing happens at Prometric centers. Passed sections must all be completed within a credit window, now 30 months in most states (it used to be 18).
cards.example: A student who loves tax takes AUD, FAR, REG and then TCP as the discipline.
cards.say_it: The new CPA Exam tests the core everyone needs and then lets you specialize in analysis, technology or tax.
cards.mistakes: Listing BEC (Business Environment and Concepts) as a current section; it was retired at the end of 2023.

cards.core: Accountants keep learning because standards, tax laws, technology and business risks change constantly.
cards.detail: The FASB issues new Accounting Standards Updates every year, Congress and the IRS change tax rules, the SEC and PCAOB update reporting and audit rules, and technology (cloud systems, data analytics, AI, cybersecurity) changes how work is done. An accountant who stops learning gives wrong advice and can harm clients. Ongoing education is also required to keep a license, and it opens promotions: graduate degrees, new credentials and leadership training move people up the ladder.
cards.example: A tax advisor who missed a new tax law change would file returns that cost clients money or penalties.
cards.say_it: In accounting, what you learned five years ago may already be out of date, so lifelong learning is part of the job.

cards.core: Improper accounting misleads lenders, investors and customers and can lead to fines, lawsuits, prison and business failure.
cards.detail: Wrong or manipulated numbers cause bad decisions: banks lend to weak borrowers, investors overpay, suppliers extend credit that is never repaid, and customers may face higher prices or lose products and services when the company fails. Intentional misstatement is fraud and can bring SEC penalties, criminal charges (Sarbanes-Oxley raised penalties for false certifications), lawsuits and loss of licenses. Famous cases such as Enron and WorldCom led directly to the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
cards.example: If the frozen yogurt shop hid debts, a supplier might extend credit and never be paid when the shop closes.
cards.say_it: Improper accounting is not just a paperwork problem; it hurts real customers, lenders and employees.

cards.core: The AICPA Code requires CPAs to act with integrity, objectivity, independence, due care and confidentiality in the public interest.
cards.detail: Its principles are: Responsibilities, The Public Interest, Integrity, Objectivity and Independence, Due Care, and Scope and Nature of Services. Key rules include independence for audit and review clients, not misrepresenting facts, complying with GAAP and professional standards, protecting confidential client information, and limits on contingent fees, commissions and misleading advertising. State boards adopt similar rules, and violations can cost a CPA the license.
cards.example: A CPA declines to audit a company in which she owns stock because it would impair her independence.
cards.say_it: CPAs serve the public interest, so integrity and objectivity matter even when a client or boss pushes back.

cards.term: IMA Statement of Ethical Professional Practice
cards.core: IMA members follow four principles (honesty, fairness, objectivity, responsibility) and four standards (competence, confidentiality, integrity, credibility).
cards.detail: Competence means keeping skills current and following rules. Confidentiality means not disclosing or misusing information. Integrity means avoiding conflicts of interest and actions that discredit the profession. Credibility means communicating information fairly and objectively and disclosing everything users need. For an ethical conflict, the IMA advises following company policy, discussing it with a supervisor (or the next level if the supervisor is involved), getting confidential advice and consulting an attorney if needed.
cards.example: A management accountant pressured to delay recording expenses to hit a bonus target raises it with the controller.
cards.say_it: Credibility means reporting the bad news as clearly as the good news.

cards.core: Handle an ethical dilemma by getting the facts, checking rules and codes, weighing who is affected, choosing the honest option and acting tactfully.
cards.detail: Steps: 1) identify the facts and the ethical issue; 2) check the law, professional standards and company code; 3) identify stakeholders and how each option affects them; 4) consider alternatives, using tests such as "would I be comfortable if this were public?"; 5) choose the option that is honest and legal; 6) act and communicate it respectfully, offering a practical solution; 7) escalate through proper channels if needed. Delivering the message with tact keeps relationships intact.
cards.example: Tanya is told kindly but clearly to drop "CPA-quality audits" from her ads and refer the audit to a CPA firm.
cards.say_it: The right answer here is clear, so my job is to explain it respectfully and offer a solution that still works for you.

cards.core: Internal users work for the company and make managerial decisions; external users are outsiders who make lending, investing or credit decisions.
cards.detail: Internal users (owner, managers, internal auditor, marketing manager, employees in their jobs) see detailed reports such as quantities sold, salaries and budgets. External users (banks, suppliers, investors, external auditors, government agencies, customers) usually see only the GAAP financial statements. Because external users cannot ask for internal reports, GAAP and audits exist to protect them. An external auditor is an external user even though it reviews internal records, because it is independent.
cards.example: Owner, internal auditor and marketing manager are internal; bank, suppliers and external auditor are external.
cards.say_it: Insiders use the numbers to run the business; outsiders use the GAAP statements to decide whether to trust it with their money.
cards.mistakes: Classifying the external auditor as internal because it works inside the company's records.

cards.core: Annual reports cover a full fiscal year and are usually audited; interim reports cover shorter periods like quarters for timely information.
cards.detail: Interim reports (monthly or quarterly) give owners, boards and investors timely updates; public companies' quarterly statements are reviewed by the auditor rather than audited. Internal monthly reports often compare budget to actual. The fiscal year does not have to match the calendar year; organizations choose a year end that fits their business cycle, and changing it can create a short transition year that needs its own reporting and tax return.
cards.example: A board receives quarterly budget versus actual reports and an audited report after the December 31 year end.
cards.say_it: Quarterly reports keep the board informed in real time, and the annual audit confirms the full year's picture.

cards.term: Full set of external financial statements
cards.core: External GAAP reports include the income statement, balance sheet, statement of cash flows, statement of equity and the notes.
cards.detail: The income statement shows revenues, expenses and net income for a period. The balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. The statement of cash flows shows cash from operating, investing and financing activities. The statement of owner's or stockholders' equity explains changes in equity. The notes explain accounting policies, estimates, contingencies, debt terms and other details, and are part of the statements. Audited reports add the auditor's report.
cards.example: A bank asks the frozen yogurt shop for all four statements plus notes before approving a loan.
cards.say_it: The notes are not extra reading; they are part of the statements and often where the most important information is.

cards.term: Levels of CPA service: compilation, review, audit
cards.core: A compilation gives no assurance, a review gives limited assurance and an audit gives reasonable assurance with an opinion.
cards.detail: Compilation: the CPA puts management's information into financial statement form without testing it (no assurance). Review: the CPA performs inquiry and analytical procedures and states whether any material changes seem needed (limited, negative assurance); cheaper than an audit and often enough for small bank loans. Audit: the CPA gathers evidence, tests controls and balances, and issues an opinion (reasonable, high but not absolute assurance); required for public companies and many lenders, grants and nonprofits. Compilations and reviews follow AICPA SSARS; only licensed CPA firms may issue audit and review reports.
cards.example: Lakeshore Brewing's reviewed statements are not enough for an IPO; it needs audited statements.
cards.say_it: Think of it as a ladder: a compilation organizes, a review checks for anything that looks wrong, and an audit tests the evidence and gives an opinion.
cards.mistakes: Saying a review is a "small audit"; it gives a different and lower level of assurance.

cards.core: Public company filings are posted on the SEC's EDGAR system and tagged in XBRL so computers can read the data.
cards.detail: EDGAR (Electronic Data Gathering, Analysis and Retrieval) is the SEC's free online database of filings such as 10-Ks, 10-Qs and 8-Ks. XBRL (eXtensible Business Reporting Language) tags each number in the statements, for example "Revenue" or "Cash", so analysts and software can compare companies automatically. Public companies must file using Inline XBRL, which is readable by both people and machines.
cards.example: An investor downloads tagged revenue data for ten retailers from EDGAR into a spreadsheet in seconds.
cards.say_it: Thanks to XBRL, anyone can compare public companies' numbers instantly using free SEC data.

cards.core: MD&A is management's plain language explanation of results, trends, cash and risks, found in the 10-K and annual report.
cards.detail: In the MD&A, management explains why revenue and expenses changed, discusses liquidity and capital resources (cash, borrowing, major spending plans), describes known trends and uncertainties, and identifies critical accounting estimates. It is not audited like the financial statements, but it must not be misleading. Investors read it to understand the story behind the numbers.
cards.example: A company explains in its MD&A that new drone regulations caused an impairment loss and will reduce future depreciation.
cards.say_it: The financial statements show what happened; the MD&A explains why it happened and what management expects next.

cards.core: Public companies file an audited annual 10-K, quarterly 10-Qs, 8-Ks for major events and a proxy statement before shareholder meetings.
cards.detail: Form 10-K: annual report with audited statements, notes, management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), risk factors and the internal control report; due 60, 75 or 90 days after year end depending on company size. Form 10-Q: quarterly report with financial statements that are reviewed, not audited; due 40 or 45 days after quarter end. Form 8-K: reports major events (such as a merger, an executive leaving or a change in auditor), generally within four business days. Proxy statement: information for shareholder votes, including director elections and executive pay. All are filed on EDGAR.
cards.example: After its IPO, Lakeshore Brewing must file three 10-Qs and one 10-K each year.
cards.say_it: The 10-K is audited and annual, the 10-Q is reviewed and quarterly, and the 8-K tells investors about big news fast.

cards.core: Sustainability reporting shares environmental, social and governance data, such as emissions and energy use, alongside financial results.
cards.detail: Investors and customers increasingly ask about climate risk, energy use, waste, worker safety and governance. The ISSB (under the IFRS Foundation) issued its first standards, IFRS S1 and S2, in 2023, and some jurisdictions such as the European Union and California have their own disclosure rules; U.S. federal requirements have been unsettled, so check the current rules. Claims must be supported by data; false or exaggerated claims are greenwashing and can bring legal and reputation damage.
cards.example: A packaging company reports its energy savings with measured data instead of copying a competitor's "carbon neutral" claim.
cards.say_it: Any environmental claim should be as well supported as the numbers in the financial statements.

cards.core: Job letters and emails use a clear, professional format: proper greeting, short focused paragraphs, polite closing and full contact information.
cards.detail: A business letter includes your contact information, the date, the recipient's name and address, a greeting ("Dear Ms. Lopez:"), body paragraphs, a closing ("Sincerely,") and your name. Professional emails need a clear subject line ("Thank you: Staff Accountant interview"), a proper greeting, short paragraphs and a signature with phone and email. Use a professional email address, correct spelling and a respectful tone; proofread before sending.
cards.example: A thank-you email with the subject "Thank you for the tax internship interview" is sent the same evening as the interview.
cards.say_it: Every letter or email I send to an employer is a work sample, so I keep it short, polite and error free.

cards.term: Common interview questions and questions to ask
cards.core: Prepare answers to common questions and bring two or three thoughtful questions of your own for the interviewer.
cards.detail: Common questions: "Tell me about yourself", "Why do you want this job?", "What are your strengths and weaknesses?", "Tell me about a time you worked on a team or made a mistake" and "Where do you see yourself in five years?". Good questions to ask: "What does a typical day look like?", "How do you train new staff?", "What do your most successful employees do differently?" and "What are the next steps?". Avoid asking first about pay or time off; save those for the offer stage.
cards.example: Asked about a weakness, a candidate says she used to avoid public speaking and joined DECA role plays to improve.
cards.say_it: I prepare my questions in advance, because good questions show I researched the company and care about the role.

pis.text: Interview for a job

cards.core: Fill out every job application completely, honestly, neatly and exactly as instructed.
cards.detail: Read all directions first. Have ready your contact information, work history with dates and supervisor contacts, education, references (asked for permission in advance), availability and any certifications. Answer every question (write "N/A" if it does not apply), use correct spelling, avoid "see resume" when the form asks for details, and never exaggerate; false information can be grounds for firing later. Proofread before submitting and keep a copy.
cards.example: An applicant lists three references, a teacher, a former manager and a DECA advisor, after asking each of them first.
cards.say_it: An application is the employer's first test of whether I follow directions and pay attention to detail.

cards.core: A cover letter is a one-page business letter that introduces you, explains why you fit the job and asks for an interview.
cards.detail: Address a specific person if possible. Opening: name the position and how you found it (mention a referral). Middle: connect two or three of your strongest experiences or skills to the employer's needs, with examples. Closing: thank the reader, restate interest and request an interview, with contact information. Keep it short, tailored to each employer and error free; do not simply repeat the resume.
cards.example: A student writes that running VITA returns taught her accuracy under deadline, which matches the firm's tax internship.
cards.say_it: A cover letter tells the story behind the resume and shows I researched the company.

cards.core: An elevator pitch is a 30-second introduction of who you are, your strengths and what you want next.
cards.detail: Structure: your name and current role or school; one or two strengths or experiences with proof; the opportunity you are seeking; and a question or call to action. Practice until it sounds natural, not memorized, and adjust it for the listener. Use it at career fairs, networking events, interviews ("tell me about yourself") and even role play introductions.
cards.example: "Hi, I'm Jordan, a high school senior who manages our DECA chapter's budget. I plan to study accounting and I'd love to hear how you started in forensic work."
cards.say_it: A strong elevator pitch makes it easy for someone to remember you and want to help.

cards.core: Send a short thank-you message to each interviewer within 24 hours, restating your interest and one key strength.
cards.detail: Email is standard; a handwritten note can add a personal touch. Thank the interviewer by name for their time, mention something specific from the conversation, restate why you fit the role, add anything you forgot to say, and close politely. Keep it brief and error free. If you have not heard back by the date given, a polite follow-up email checking on the status is appropriate.
cards.example: A candidate thanks the audit manager and mentions how much she enjoyed hearing about the firm's data analytics tools.
cards.say_it: A quick thank-you note shows professionalism and keeps me in the interviewer's mind.

cards.core: Prepare for an interview by researching the company, practicing answers, dressing professionally, arriving early and asking good questions.
cards.detail: Before: research the employer, review the job description, prepare stories that prove your skills and plan questions to ask. During: arrive 10 to 15 minutes early, greet with a firm handshake and eye contact, listen carefully, answer with specific examples, stay positive about past employers, and show enthusiasm. Ask about the role, training and team. After: send a thank-you note within 24 hours. Interviews may be in person, by phone or by video; test the technology ahead of time.
cards.example: Asked about a mistake, a candidate explains how she found and fixed an error in a club budget and what she changed afterward.
cards.say_it: I prepare for interviews the same way I prepare for a role play: research, practice and a clear plan for what I want them to remember.

cards.core: References are people, such as teachers or past supervisors, who can confirm your skills and character to an employer.
cards.detail: Choose two to four people who know your work well (supervisors, teachers, advisors, coaches), not relatives. Ask permission first, tell them about the job and send your resume so they can speak to relevant strengths. List each reference's name, title, organization, phone and email on a separate page or the application. Thank them afterward and let them know the result.
cards.example: A student lists her DECA advisor, her manager at a part-time job and her accounting teacher as references.
cards.say_it: I always ask my references first, so they are ready to speak about the skills this job needs.

cards.core: Search for jobs through networking, campus recruiting and career fairs, online job boards, company websites and internships.
cards.detail: Steps: define the job you want; prepare a tailored resume and LinkedIn profile; use several channels (networking and referrals, career fairs, college career centers and platforms like Handshake, job boards, company career pages, professional association job boards, staffing agencies); track every application; follow up politely. In accounting, firms recruit early: many hire interns a year or more ahead and turn successful interns into full-time hires, so start in the first years of college.
cards.example: A sophomore attends a Big Four leadership program, which leads to a junior year internship and then a full-time offer.
cards.say_it: Most accounting jobs come through internships and relationships, so I would start networking long before I need the job.
cards.mistakes: Only applying online; referrals and internships produce most accounting hires.

cards.core: Keep a professional LinkedIn profile and clean social media, because employers search online before they hire.
cards.detail: A strong LinkedIn profile has a professional photo, a clear headline (for example "Accounting student | DECA | VITA volunteer"), a short summary, experience, skills, certifications and recommendations. Connect with people you meet, with a personal note, and follow firms and professional associations. Review public social media posts and remove anything unprofessional. Many recruiters find candidates through LinkedIn and check social media as part of screening.
cards.example: After a career fair, a student connects with three recruiters on LinkedIn with a note recalling their conversation.
cards.say_it: My online presence is part of my resume, so I keep it professional and up to date.

cards.core: Networking means building relationships that lead to advice and job leads, using an elevator pitch, events, LinkedIn and follow-up.
cards.detail: Prepare a 30-second elevator pitch (who you are, what you are studying, what you are looking for). Attend career fairs, association meetings and alumni events; ask open questions and listen. Exchange contact information, connect on LinkedIn with a personal note, and follow up within a day or two. Give before you ask: share articles, congratulate people and offer help. Keep a simple list of contacts and stay in touch over time.
cards.example: At a state CPA society student night, a student introduces herself, asks a tax manager about busy season and follows up with a thank-you message.
cards.say_it: Good networking is not collecting business cards; it is building relationships where both people help each other.

cards.core: A resume is a one-page summary of your education, experience, skills and achievements, tailored to each job.
cards.detail: Sections: contact information, an optional summary, education (school, expected graduation, GPA if strong, relevant courses), experience (newest first, with action verbs and numbers, such as "reconciled 200 transactions a month"), activities and leadership (DECA, treasurer roles), skills (Excel, QuickBooks, languages) and certifications or awards. Keep it to one page for students, use a clean format, proofread carefully and save it as a PDF. Tailor keywords to the job posting because many employers use applicant tracking systems.
cards.example: A student writes "Managed $3,000 DECA fundraising budget and tracked deposits in Excel" instead of "Was treasurer".
cards.say_it: For an accounting job, a resume with even one typo is a red flag, because the job itself is about accuracy.
cards.mistakes: Listing duties instead of results; numbers make achievements believable.

pis.text: Prepare a resume

cards.core: Answer behavioral questions with STAR: Situation, Task, Action and Result.
cards.detail: Behavioral questions start with "Tell me about a time when...". Describe the Situation briefly, the Task or goal you faced, the Action you personally took (most of the answer), and the Result, ideally with a number, plus what you learned. STAR keeps answers focused, specific and about two minutes long. Prepare four or five STAR stories that show teamwork, leadership, problem solving, handling a mistake and meeting a deadline.
cards.example: S: our fundraiser money did not match the sales log. T: find the gap. A: I reconciled receipts line by line. R: found a $40 recording error and set up a daily count.
cards.say_it: Using STAR, I can prove a skill with a real story instead of just claiming it.

cards.term: Tailoring a resume to the job
cards.core: Tailor each resume to the posting by matching its keywords and putting your most relevant experience first.
cards.detail: Many employers screen resumes with an applicant tracking system (ATS) that looks for keywords from the job posting, such as "account reconciliation", "Excel" or "accounts payable". Read the posting, mirror its exact terms where they truthfully describe you, use a simple format without tables or graphics that confuse the software, and move the most relevant experience and skills near the top. Never add skills you do not have.
cards.example: For a tax internship, a student moves her VITA volunteer work to the top and adds "tax software" to her skills.
cards.say_it: I tailor every resume, because the first reader is often software looking for the posting's exact keywords.

cards.core: Fit your words, examples and length to the audience, using plain language and relatable stories for non-accountants.
cards.detail: Identify who is listening (middle schoolers, a business owner, a board, a college class), what they already know and what they need. Avoid jargon or define it simply, use analogies and real examples, organize with a clear opening, three or four main points and a summary, and invite questions. For young students, keep energy high and connect careers to their interests (sports, detectives, travel). For owners, connect every point to their business.
cards.example: For 12 to 14 year olds, a forensic accountant is described as "a financial detective who follows the money".
cards.say_it: I will keep this simple and use examples from your own business, so the rules make sense for you.

cards.core: Solve problems by identifying the real problem, finding its cause, generating solutions, choosing and applying one, then checking it worked.
cards.detail: Good problem solvers separate symptoms from causes. Steps: describe the problem precisely; collect data; find the root cause (ask "why" several times); brainstorm options; pick and implement the best one; confirm the fix and prevent the problem from recurring, for example with a new control or training. In accounting, problems often show up as numbers that do not match, such as a bank reconciliation or trial balance that does not balance.
cards.example: An intern's bank reconciliation is off by $10; the accountant traces it to a $5 interest item placed on the wrong side and fixes the process.
cards.say_it: I did not just fix the number; I found the cause and explained how to prevent it next month.

cards.core: Set goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound (SMART).
cards.detail: Personal goals give direction and motivation. A SMART goal states exactly what you will do, how you will measure it, that it is realistic, how it connects to your bigger plans, and the deadline. Break long-term goals (become a CPA) into short-term goals (pass FAR by June) and action steps (study 10 hours a week). Write goals down, review progress regularly and adjust when needed.
cards.formula: SMART = Specific + Measurable + Achievable + Relevant + Time-bound
cards.example: "Pass the FAR section of the CPA Exam by June 30 by studying 10 hours per week" instead of "Study for the CPA."
cards.say_it: I turn big dreams like becoming a CPA into SMART goals with deadlines I can track every week.
cards.mistakes: Writing vague goals like "do better at accounting" that cannot be measured.

cards.core: Appropriate creativity means finding new ideas and better ways of working while staying within rules, ethics and standards.
cards.detail: Creativity in accounting means improving processes (automating a report, redesigning a dashboard), explaining numbers in fresh, clear ways for non-accountants, and finding legal solutions to client problems. It never means "creative accounting", that is bending GAAP or hiding facts to make results look better. Brainstorming, asking "what if", looking at problems from the user's view and borrowing ideas from other fields all build creativity.
cards.example: An accountant uses a simple pie chart and a pizza analogy to explain an income statement to middle schoolers.
cards.say_it: I am creative in how I present and improve the work, but never creative with the rules themselves.
cards.mistakes: Confusing creativity with "creative accounting", which is a warning sign of fraud.

cards.core: Company policies are written rules on how work is done, and following them protects the company, its customers and you.
cards.detail: Common policies cover attendance, dress code, technology and data security, confidentiality, expense reimbursement, purchasing approvals, record retention, conflicts of interest and harassment. In accounting, protocols also include approval limits, segregation of duties, month-end close procedures and document retention rules (for example keeping tax records at least three years). Employees usually sign that they received the handbook, and breaking policies can lead to discipline or termination.
cards.example: A clerk refuses to pay an invoice that lacks a purchase order, as the purchasing policy requires.
cards.say_it: Policies are not red tape; in accounting they are the controls that keep money and information safe.

cards.core: Organizational goals are the results a company aims for, flowing from its mission into long-term and short-term targets.
cards.detail: The mission states why the organization exists and the vision where it wants to go. Goals can be financial (profit, revenue growth, cost control, return on investment, cash flow) or nonfinancial (customer satisfaction, quality, market share, employee retention, sustainability, community impact). Strategic goals are long term and set by top management; tactical and operational goals break them into department and individual targets. Nonprofits set mission goals, such as people served, instead of profit.
cards.example: A non-profit association sets a goal of quarterly budget reports to the board and an annual audit to show good stewardship.
cards.say_it: Every number in a budget should connect back to the organization's goals and mission.

cards.core: A career plan links a long-term goal to short-term goals and action steps with deadlines.
cards.detail: Long-term goals take years (become a CPA and a controller). Short-term goals take weeks or months (pass an accounting class with an A, earn an internship). Steps: set the long-term goal, list the education, experience and credentials it requires, break them into short-term SMART goals, schedule action steps, track progress and adjust when circumstances change. Sharing goals with a mentor adds accountability.
cards.example: Long term: CFO by 40. Short term: accounting degree, CPA within two years of graduation, then promotions to senior accountant and controller.
cards.say_it: My long-term goal guides my short-term choices, like which classes I take and which internships I pursue.

cards.core: Soft skills like communication, teamwork, adaptability and professionalism decide how well you work with people.
cards.detail: Hard skills are teachable technical abilities (journal entries, Excel). Soft skills include listening, explaining clearly, cooperating, handling conflict, adapting to change, managing time, taking initiative and staying positive under pressure. Accountants use them every day with clients, managers and teams, especially when delivering bad news such as an audit adjustment. Employers rank soft skills among the top reasons they hire and promote.
cards.example: Telling a client tactfully that her advertising breaks state rules while keeping the referral relationship strong.
cards.say_it: In accounting, how you explain a number matters as much as getting the number right.

cards.core: Modern accountants need Excel, accounting software, data analytics and an understanding of automation, AI and cybersecurity.
cards.detail: Daily tools include spreadsheets (formulas, pivot tables), accounting systems (QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, SAP), tax software and data visualization tools. Automation and AI now handle routine entry, so accountants spend more time analyzing, checking controls and advising. Data analytics helps auditors test whole populations and forensic accountants spot unusual patterns. The CPA exam now includes a technology focused discipline (Information Systems and Controls), showing how central these skills are.
cards.example: An auditor uses data analytics to scan all 40,000 sales invoices for duplicates instead of sampling 60.
cards.say_it: Technology does not replace accountants; it removes typing so we can spend our time on analysis and advice.
cards.mistakes: Saying AI will eliminate accounting jobs; it shifts the work toward judgment and analysis.

cards.core: If a difference divides evenly by 2, look for an amount on the wrong side; if it divides by 9, look for a transposition.
cards.detail: When records do not agree, first find the exact difference. If half of it equals an actual amount, that item was probably added instead of subtracted (or debited instead of credited). If the difference is evenly divisible by 9, two digits were probably swapped (transposition, such as 54 written as 45) or the decimal slid (slide error). Otherwise look for an omitted item equal to the difference. These quick tests turn a frustrating search into a targeted check.
cards.formula: Difference / 2 = amount entered on the wrong side; Difference divisible by 9 = transposition or slide error
cards.example: The book side is $10 too high; $10 / 2 = $5, the exact interest amount the intern subtracted instead of added.
cards.say_it: Because the difference was exactly twice the $5 interest, I knew right away the item was on the wrong side.

cards.core: Balance work and personal life by setting priorities and boundaries, planning ahead for busy periods and protecting your health.
cards.detail: Strategies include planning around known busy seasons (tax season, year end audits), communicating availability, using flexible or remote options, taking breaks and vacation, keeping exercise, sleep and family time, and saying no to nonessential commitments. Burnout lowers accuracy and judgment, so balance protects work quality. Many firms now offer flexible schedules, summer Fridays and wellness benefits to retain staff.
cards.example: An auditor schedules family time and a vacation in May, right after busy season ends.
cards.say_it: Accounting has busy seasons, so I plan ahead to give full effort at peak times and recharge when the season ends.

pis.text: Balance personal and professional responsibilities
Use time-management skills

cards.core: Generate creative ideas by brainstorming many options without judging them, then evaluating the best ones.
cards.detail: Techniques: free brainstorming (quantity first, no criticism), mind mapping (branching ideas from a central problem), asking "what if" and "how might we" questions, looking at the problem from a customer's or user's point of view, and borrowing ideas from other industries. After generating ideas, judge them by cost, benefit, risk, ethics and fit with company rules. Creativity is "appropriate" when it solves the real problem within professional standards.
cards.example: A team brainstorms 15 ways to speed up the month-end close and picks bank feeds and a shared checklist.
cards.say_it: I came up with several options first and then chose the one that is practical, affordable and fully within the rules.

pis.text: Demonstrate appropriate creativity
Explain the need for innovation skills
Demonstrate problem-solving skills

cards.core: The chain of command is the line of authority in an organization; you bring issues to your direct supervisor first.
cards.detail: Following the chain of command means taking questions, requests and complaints to your immediate supervisor before going higher, and passing instructions down through the proper levels. It keeps communication clear and respects managers' responsibility. The exception is wrongdoing: if your supervisor is involved in fraud or ignores it, you can go higher, to the audit committee, an ethics hotline or legal channels; whistleblower laws protect people who report in good faith.
cards.example: A staff accountant who spots an error reports it to the accounting manager, but she would use the hotline if the manager had caused it on purpose.
cards.say_it: I would follow the chain of command, and if the problem involved my manager, I would use the ethics hotline or go to the audit committee.

pis.text: Follow chain of command

examples.title: Lakeshore Brewing: governance and compliance before an IPO

cards.core: A code of conduct is a written statement of the ethical behavior expected of every employee and director.
cards.detail: Typical topics: honesty and accurate records, conflicts of interest, gifts, confidentiality, fair treatment, harassment, use of company assets, legal compliance and how to report concerns. Public companies must disclose whether they have a code of ethics for senior financial officers (a Sarbanes-Oxley requirement), and stock exchanges require codes of conduct. Employees typically certify each year that they follow it, and violations lead to discipline. Professional codes (AICPA, IMA, IIA) add rules for accountants.
cards.example: Before its IPO, Lakeshore Brewing adopts a code of conduct and an ethics hotline because it had neither.
cards.say_it: A code of conduct turns values into clear rules, so every employee knows what is expected and how to speak up.

pis.text: Follow rules of conduct
Ascertain employee's role in achieving governance objectives

examples.title: Lakeshore Brewing: governance and compliance before an IPO

cards.core: Make decisions by defining the problem, gathering facts, listing options, weighing pros and cons, choosing, acting and reviewing results.
cards.detail: Steps: 1) define the decision clearly; 2) gather relevant information; 3) identify alternatives; 4) evaluate each by costs, benefits, risks and ethics; 5) choose the best option; 6) implement it; 7) evaluate the results and learn. In accounting, relevant numbers (costs and revenues that differ between options) and qualitative factors (quality, reputation, employee morale, legal rules) both count.
cards.example: Deciding whether a small firm should buy cloud accounting software by comparing cost, security, time saved and staff training.
cards.say_it: I compared every option on both the numbers and the risks before making my recommendation.

pis.text: Make decisions

cards.term: Employee's role in meeting organizational goals
cards.core: Employees reach organizational goals by aligning their own goals and daily work with the company's targets.
cards.detail: Company goals are broken into department goals and then individual goals and key performance indicators (KPIs). Each employee contributes by understanding the goals, doing quality work efficiently, meeting deadlines, suggesting improvements, cooperating with other departments and tracking results. Performance reviews and incentives often tie personal goals to company goals. In accounting, accurate and timely reports help managers make the decisions that reach those goals.
cards.example: A company wants to cut costs 5%, so the AP clerk takes every early payment discount (such as 2/10, n/30).
cards.say_it: Even a single accounting clerk helps meet company goals by delivering accurate numbers on time.

pis.text: Ascertain employee's role in meeting organizational goals
Determine the nature of organizational goals

cards.core: Employers expect reliability, honesty, a strong work ethic, teamwork, a positive attitude, good communication and willingness to learn.
cards.detail: Beyond technical skills, employers expect employees to show up on time, meet deadlines, follow policies, keep information confidential, accept feedback, take initiative, dress and act professionally, and work well with others. In accounting, accuracy, integrity and confidentiality are especially important because mistakes and leaks hurt clients. Employees in turn can expect fair pay, a safe workplace and respect for their legal rights.
cards.example: A new staff accountant double checks every reconciliation and asks questions early instead of guessing.
cards.say_it: Employers can teach software, but they hire for reliability, honesty and attitude.

pis.text: Analyze employer expectations in the business environment
Adhere to company protocols and policies

cards.core: First impressions form in seconds, so combine professional appearance with good posture, eye contact, a smile and a firm handshake.
cards.detail: Nonverbal signals include posture, eye contact, facial expression, gestures, handshake, voice tone and personal space. Stand or sit up straight, face the listener, make natural eye contact, avoid fidgeting and crossed arms, and speak clearly at a steady pace. Arrive prepared and on time. In a DECA role play, the judge forms an impression during the greeting, so open with a confident handshake, introduce yourself and thank the judge.
cards.example: A student walks in, shakes the judge's hand, introduces herself as the firm's accountant and sets her notes neatly on the table.
cards.say_it: Thank you for meeting with me today; I am excited to walk you through my recommendations.

pis.text: Maintain appropriate personal appearance
Analyze employer expectations in the business environment

cards.core: Handle peak workloads by planning ahead, breaking work into steps, asking for help early and protecting sleep, exercise and breaks.
cards.detail: Accounting has predictable crunch times: month-end close, year end, tax deadlines and audits. Healthy strategies: plan workloads before the season, set daily priorities, communicate early if a deadline is at risk, take short breaks, keep regular sleep and exercise, and use employer wellness resources. Stress management protects accuracy, because tired people make more errors and poorer ethical choices.
cards.example: During tax season, a preparer sets a fixed stopping time most nights and tells her manager early when a client is late with documents.
cards.say_it: Busy season is a sprint, so I plan for it and protect my health to keep my work accurate.

pis.text: Balance personal and professional responsibilities
Use time-management skills

cards.core: Innovation skills help workers and companies adapt to change, improve processes and stay competitive.
cards.detail: Innovation is turning new ideas into useful products, services or processes. Businesses need it because technology, customers and competitors keep changing; firms that do not adapt fall behind. Innovation skills include curiosity, creativity, collaboration, experimenting, learning from failure and adopting new technology. In accounting, innovation has brought cloud systems, automation, data analytics and AI tools that free time for advisory work.
cards.example: A small CPA firm moves clients to cloud accounting with bank feeds, cutting manual data entry and adding advisory services.
cards.say_it: Innovation lets accountants shift from typing numbers to giving advice that helps a business grow.

pis.text: Explain the need for innovation skills

examples.title: Riverside Hardware: moving the books to the cloud, preserving records and XBRL

cards.core: Dress and groom for the setting: business attire for interviews, client meetings and role plays, following the employer's dress code.
cards.detail: Appearance is part of a first impression. Choose clean, well-fitting clothes suited to the workplace: business professional (suit or blazer) for interviews, client meetings, presentations and DECA competition; business casual for many offices. Good grooming, minimal distractions and good posture matter as much as the clothes. Accountants represent their firm to clients, so dressing one level above the client is a common rule. Follow company dress code policies.
cards.example: An auditor visiting a bank client wears a blazer even though her own office allows jeans on Fridays.
cards.say_it: Clients trust us with their money, so looking professional is part of earning that trust.

pis.text: Maintain appropriate personal appearance

cards.core: Systematic behavior means working in an organized, step by step way using checklists, routines and clear files.
cards.detail: Systematic workers plan their tasks, follow procedures in order, keep files and email organized, document their work and check results before moving on. In accounting this shows up as month-end close checklists, consistent file naming, reconciliations performed on a set schedule and workpapers that let a reviewer follow every step. It reduces errors, saves time and makes work easy to hand off.
cards.example: A staff accountant uses a close checklist so bank reconciliations, accruals and depreciation are done in the same order every month.
cards.say_it: I follow a checklist for repeating work, because a systematic process catches errors before a client or auditor does.

pis.text: Demonstrate systematic behavior
Use time-management skills

cards.core: Manage time by listing tasks, prioritizing by urgency and importance, scheduling deadlines and avoiding distractions.
cards.detail: Techniques: keep a to-do list or calendar; rank tasks with the urgent versus important matrix (do, schedule, delegate, delete); work backward from deadlines; block focused time; batch small tasks; and limit interruptions like phone notifications. Accounting is deadline driven (month-end close, payroll dates, April 15 tax filing, SEC filing dates), so planning ahead prevents last-minute errors. In a role play, budget your prep time across all tasks.
cards.example: During tax season, a preparer schedules the most complex returns early and leaves simple ones for short time slots.
cards.say_it: In accounting the deadlines do not move, so I plan backward from the due date and tackle the most important work first.

pis.text: Use time-management skills
Demonstrate systematic behavior
